text:
🏈 2026 NFL TRADE DEADLINE: WINNERS & LOSERS 📈📉

Some teams went all-in. Others cashed out. A few front offices apparently have no idea what year it is.

From championship gambles to fantasy football gold mines and one of the most questionable QB management sagas in recent memory, this deadline had everything.

And the biggest winners weren’t necessarily the guys who got traded.

Let’s break it down. 👇

🏆 THE WINNERS

🐆 JACKSONVILLE JAGUARS — ALL GAS, NO BRAKES
Jacksonville didn’t just participate in the deadline. They attacked it.
✅ Jessie Bates III
✅ Jordan Davis
✅ Davon Godchaux
Three defensive additions addressing immediate weaknesses for a 6–2 team with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations.
Bates brings elite playmaking to the secondary. Davis gives them a massive interior presence. Godchaux provides experienced defensive line depth.
The Jaguars gave up serious draft capital, including a first and multiple seconds, but they’re operating like a team that recognizes its championship window.
Nobody improved their defense more aggressively than Jacksonville.

🎯 JUSTIN JEFFERSON — FREEDOM AT LAST
After surviving Minnesota’s quarterback carousel, Jefferson finally gets his old running mate back.
Kirk Cousins is returning to Minnesota.
The last few seasons have been a frustrating reminder that even generational receivers need competent quarterback play.
Cousins already knows Kevin O’Connell’s system, has established chemistry with Jefferson, and understands how to feed his best playmaker.
For Jefferson and his fantasy owners, this might be the biggest development of the entire deadline.
Somewhere, a fantasy manager just went from questioning his first-round pick to planning a championship parade.

🎰 FERNANDO MENDOZA & THE RAIDERS — THE FUTURE STARTS NOW
This is how you handle a rebuilding season.
Las Vegas signed Cousins as a veteran bridge, got respectable production, and flipped him to Minnesota for a third-round pick.
Now Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick, gets his opportunity.
The Raiders aren’t winning the Super Bowl this year. Why not use the remaining games to evaluate the player who’s supposed to lead your franchise for the next decade?
Mendoza gets experience. The Raiders get draft capital. Fans finally get to see their future.
A rebuilding team actually behaving like a rebuilding team. Revolutionary concept.

🚀 JOSH DOWNS & FANTASY OWNERS — MAHOMES EFFECT
From Indianapolis to Kansas City.
From a struggling Colts offense to catching passes from Patrick Mahomes.
Josh Downs might have landed in the best possible situation for his skill set.
His ability to separate, work underneath and create after the catch fits naturally into Andy Reid’s offense.
There’s still competition for targets, and chemistry takes time, but the PPR upside is significant.
If you held Downs through the first half of the fantasy season, congratulations. Your patience might finally pay off.

🐻 CHICAGO BEARS — SUPER BOWL OR BUST?
Two first-round picks for Jeffery Simmons.
That’s an enormous investment, but it’s also a statement.
Chicago has a young quarterback, an ascending offense and legitimate playoff aspirations. Simmons gives Dennis Allen the interior defensive presence the Bears desperately needed.
This is the type of move championship contenders make.
But there’s a catch.
If Chicago wins the NFC, Ryan Poles looks like a genius. If the Bears flame out early, everyone will remember those two first-round picks.
High risk. High reward. Exactly what makes this deadline fascinating.

💰 TENNESSEE TITANS — KNOW WHEN TO FOLD ’EM
While contenders were spending draft capital, Tennessee was collecting it.
The Titans moved Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker for a substantial package of future picks.
Losing established defensive talent hurts, but pretending you’re one offseason away from contention can hurt even more.
Tennessee recognized its situation, accepted reality and committed to rebuilding.
There’s something refreshing about a front office understanding the difference between being competitive and being a contender.

🔁 KIRK COUSINS — BACK WHERE HE BELONGS?
At 38 years old, Cousins goes from mentoring a rookie in Las Vegas to potentially quarterbacking a 6–2 Vikings team with one of football’s best defenses.
He gets Kevin O’Connell, Justin Jefferson and a realistic opportunity to compete in January.
Minnesota gets a quarterback who already understands the offense.
And Cousins gets the chance to remind everyone why the Vikings paid him in the first place.
Not a bad Tuesday afternoon.

📉 THE LOSERS

🚨 MINNESOTA VIKINGS FRONT OFFICE — FULL CIRCLE, ZERO POINTS FOR STYLE
Let’s review Minnesota’s quarterback masterclass.
❌ Let Kirk Cousins walk
❌ Draft J.J. McCarthy
❌ Revive Sam Darnold’s career, then let him leave
❌ Trade McCarthy for a fifth-round pick
❌ Try Kyler Murray
❌ Turn to Carson Wentz
✅ Trade a THIRD-ROUND PICK to bring Cousins back
You couldn’t script this any better.
Meanwhile, Minnesota has Justin Jefferson and one of the NFL’s most dominant defenses.
The Cousins reunion might save the season. It doesn’t excuse the years of questionable decisions that made the reunion necessary.
They spent years trying to upgrade from Cousins, only to spend more draft capital getting Cousins back.
That’s not a quarterback strategy. That’s a very expensive game of musical chairs.

⚡ LOS ANGELES CHARGERS — WHAT EXACTLY IS THE PLAN?
You’re winless.
Your season is over.
You have veterans with potential trade value, including Khalil Mack.
And your biggest move is sending Daiyan Henley to a division rival?
Maybe there wasn’t a worthwhile offer for Mack. But if Los Angeles had an opportunity to turn aging talent into meaningful future assets, this was the time.
Instead, the Chargers largely stood pat while other struggling organizations embraced their rebuilds.
Loyalty is admirable. Failing to maximize assets during a lost season isn’t.
The worst thing an NFL team can be isn’t bad. It’s bad without a plan.

💔 INDIANAPOLIS COLTS — FIRE SALE WITHOUT THE FIREWORKS
Quenton Nelson. DeForest Buckner. Josh Downs. Keenan Allen.
Gone.
The Colts were right to sell, but was the return really enough?
Nelson and Buckner went for middle-round draft capital, while Downs landed in Kansas City for a fourth and fifth.
Indianapolis acquired picks, but it’s fair to question whether the front office maximized the value of its departures.
And Jonathan Taylor? He’s still there, watching his offensive supporting cast disappear.
Rebuilding is one thing. Getting full value for your assets is another.

🦅 PHILADELPHIA EAGLES — THE PRICE OF STARTING OVER
Philadelphia moved Jordan Davis and Cam Jurgens, two foundational players in the trenches, in exchange for valuable future draft capital.
From a long-term perspective, there’s a legitimate argument that the Eagles did excellent business.
But for the remaining veterans hoping to compete in 2026?
This is a tough pill to swallow.
Philadelphia is essentially acknowledging that its championship window needs to be rebuilt rather than repaired.
Good long-term business doesn’t always feel like winning in November.

🏅 THE GAMBLER’S GAZETTE DEADLINE AWARDS

🏆 Biggest Team Winner: Jacksonville Jaguars
🔥 Boldest Championship Gamble: Chicago Bears
📈 Biggest Fantasy Winner: Josh Downs
🎯 Biggest Individual Winner: Justin Jefferson
🌟 Biggest Opportunity: Fernando Mendoza
💰 Best Rebuilding Strategy: Las Vegas Raiders / Tennessee Titans
🚨 Worst Front Office Management: Minnesota Vikings
💀 Biggest Missed Opportunity: Los Angeles Chargers
🤔 Biggest Question Mark: Seattle Seahawks

Seattle paid a reasonable price for Quenton Nelson, but he’s already dealing with a knee injury requiring a procedure. Great player, unfortunate timing. Hard to celebrate the acquisition until he’s healthy and contributing.

🧠 FINAL THOUGHTS

The 2026 deadline highlighted something that separates the NFL’s best organizations from the rest.
You have to know what you’re building toward.
Jacksonville and Chicago believe they can win a Super Bowl right now.
Tennessee and Las Vegas understand their futures matter more than meaningless wins in November.
Kansas City found another weapon for Mahomes.
And Minnesota somehow spent three years and a collection of draft picks to arrive at the exact same quarterback it started with.
Some teams are playing chess.
Some are playing checkers.
And the Vikings are playing quarterback roulette with Justin Jefferson’s prime. 🎰

Who’s your biggest winner and loser? Which front office made the smartest move, and which trade will age the worst? 👀

text:
$NBIS $META $MSFT

A lot of people are talking about Vineland tonight. Fair, it's the biggest near-term risk. But the 2027 guide, the number that actually moves this stock, rests on sites most people can't name.

Vineland, New Jersey
• ~300 MW campus behind the $17.4B Microsoft contract, up to $19.4B. The 20-F says it delivers in nine tranches across 2025 and 2026

• The local planning board approved Phase 2 on Aug 17, so the site is still expanding. DataOne has proposed taking it as high as ~350 MW

• Aterio's satellite work says ~140 MW could slip into 2027. The developer was fined $1.07M for unpermitted gas engines and given 45 days to apply for permits or shut them off. Microsoft's CFO said some third-party GPU contracts moved to its fiscal second half, which starts in January, without naming providers

• Scale check: ~300 MW is ~6% of the 5 GW Nebius targets contracting this year (my math). A slip hurts the end-2026 ARR line and pushes that revenue into 2027

Where 2027 actually comes from
1. Meta: $12B of dedicated capacity on Vera Rubin, delivered starting early 2027 across multiple, unnamed locations. On top of that, Meta committed to buy up to $15B over five years of capacity in certain upcoming clusters that Nebius doesn't sell to other customers first. That's a backstop for the build. Meta's first deal with Nebius, $3B, came in November 2025

2. Independence, Missouri: up to 1.2 GW on ~400 acres. Approved in March, broke ground May 12, and Nebius said in May it expects the site to be operational in 2027. Power comes through the city utility, with the retired Blue Valley plant next door being rebuilt, first ~250 MW phase targeted for 2027 and 1,100+ MW by 2029. Neighbors sued in August and asked for a construction halt in October. I haven't seen an order stopping work

3. Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania: 1.2 GW at full build. Nebius's own schedule is 260 MW by October 2027, 660 MW by January 2029 and 1 GW+ by November 2029. Land was bought in April for $187.5M, the state stormwater permit came in June and the township zoning vote passed 2-1 on Aug 31. Power runs through a dedicated agreement with PPL

4. Lappeenranta, Finland: up to 310 MW, with first capacity available to customers in 2027

Owned sites were more than 75% of contracted power at Q1. At the $20-25M of annual revenue per MW Q2 deals were priced at, Pennsylvania's first 260 MW alone would be ~$5.2-6.5B of ARR (my math).

What I want on the call
• First-phase MW and dates for Missouri and Finland

• Whether Pennsylvania's 260 MW by October 2027 still holds

• Which sites carry Meta's Vera Rubin capacity, and when the first racks go live

• How much of the 1 GW+ for 2027 is already contracted

• A hard number on any Vineland slip

Caveat: outside Pennsylvania, Nebius hasn't published site-level MW for 2027. The power timelines come from utility and city filings, and lawsuits and permits can slow any of these.

Vineland mostly decides how 2026 ends. The 2027 guide rests on Meta, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Finland.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL FREE PICKS — TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 2026

Ranked from strongest to weakest confidence based on independent projections, historical betting systems, matchup advantages, Luck Factor, worldwide opening-line movement and trusted sharp intelligence.

These selections are more aggressive than our premium standards, but each still requires a defensible handicapping argument and a playable sportsbook price.

WESTERN MICHIGAN–AKRON UNDER 48.5 — 7:00 PM ET

Good to: Under 48.5 at -120 or better. Preferred: Under 49.5 if available.

This is our strongest free selection tonight, with the best combination of trusted sharp support, offensive tendencies, situational factors and a favorable adjustment from the worldwide opening total of 47 to the current 48.5.

Western Michigan enters 6-3 and is still competing for the MAC championship, but the Broncos aren't built around a high-tempo, pass-heavy offense. They run the football approximately 62% of the time and average only about 60 offensive snaps per game. Their preference for establishing the ground game, sustaining possessions and controlling field position is conducive to keeping the clock moving.

Akron is averaging only 19.1 points per game, while Western Michigan is allowing 19.2. The Zips have struggled to finish drives and protect the quarterback, surrendering 25 sacks against a Western Michigan defense that has generated 23. Akron has also committed 18 turnovers, creating another obstacle to consistent offensive production.

The strongest argument against the Under is Akron's defense, which allows 32.2 points per game and 5.8 yards per rushing attempt. Western Michigan could produce explosive gains against that vulnerable front. Nevertheless, the Broncos' run-heavy approach provides a reasonable basis for expecting longer possessions and fewer total scoring opportunities.

The contrarian evidence is particularly interesting. One sportsbook-specific betting report shows approximately 75% of tickets on the Over but 88% of the money on the Under. Those figures are not representative of every sportsbook, but they suggest that larger wagers may be concentrated on the lower-scoring outcome.

An additional outside handicapper independently projects Western Michigan winning 27-14, producing only 41 combined points. That assessment also emphasizes Akron's red-zone difficulties and Western Michigan's defensive strengths.

Trusted sharp agreement provides the final supporting factor. Although our independent projections remain closer to 49, the combination of outside support, pace and betting-market divergence is sufficient for a free selection.

Projected score: Western Michigan 27, Akron 17.

OHIO BOBCATS -1.5 AT MIAMI (OH) — 8:00 PM ET

Good to: Ohio -2 at -110 or better. Preferred: Ohio -1.5. Moneyline -120 or better is an alternative.

Ohio presents the strongest statistical case among tonight's three sides. The Bobcats enter 7-2 overall and 5-0 in MAC play, with advantages in quarterback efficiency, third-down execution, red-zone finishing and defensive production.

Ohio converts 47.3% of third downs compared with Miami's 35.9%. The Bobcats have converted approximately 77% of their red-zone opportunities into touchdowns, while Miami has converted approximately 59%. Those differences are particularly important in a rivalry matchup with a spread of fewer than three points.

Quarterback Nick Poulos provides a dual-threat dimension that Miami may struggle to contain. The RedHawks have been much better against the run than the pass, allowing approximately 98 rushing yards but nearly 280 passing yards per game. If Miami concentrates on stopping Ohio's conventional ground attack, Poulos has opportunities to extend plays and exploit coverage downfield.

Miami has also experienced substantial quarterback disruption this season, losing its original top two options. Caleb Heavner has provided some mobility, but the offense has lacked consistent passing efficiency and has struggled to sustain drives.

Independent projections favor Ohio by approximately three to seven points, with the primary benchmark making the Bobcats 3.2-point favorites. At the current -1.5, that leaves a modest potential advantage.

The worldwide opener was Miami -1.5, so the market has reversed by three points. We generally prefer investigating opportunities against substantial movement, but the statistical support for Ohio is sufficient to justify an exception at the less restrictive free-pick standard.

The principal concern is Ohio's favorable Luck Factor of +1.1 compared with Miami's +0.2. The Bobcats have also played a relatively soft conference schedule, while Miami's recent overtime loss to Buffalo was more competitive than the final result suggests.

Still, Ohio's offensive efficiency and red-zone advantages provide a credible path to victory. Independent outside analysis also supports Ohio based on quarterback mobility and Miami's defensive vulnerabilities.

Projected score: Ohio 27, Miami (OH) 23.

KENT STATE +5.5 AT BOWLING GREEN — 7:00 PM ET

Good to: Kent State +5.5 at -110 or better. Preferred: +6 if available.

This is our most aggressive free selection, primarily because Bowling Green's offensive limitations make it difficult to justify laying nearly six points against another struggling MAC program.

Bowling Green enters 2-7 and averages only 17.8 points per game. Kent State is 3-6 and averages 14.3. Neither offense has demonstrated consistent scoring efficiency, increasing the importance of individual possessions, field position and turnovers.

Bowling Green has a legitimate defensive advantage through its pass rush, especially Myles Bradley, who has nine sacks. However, the Falcons also allow approximately 212 rushing yards per game. Kent State's rushing offense has struggled, but any improvement in early-down efficiency could substantially reduce the pressure on quarterback Dru DeShields.

Kent State's most recent 31-10 loss to Sacramento State was influenced by an unusually demanding cross-country trip on a short week. The Golden Flashes are now returning to a more conventional conference travel assignment, making that disappointing performance a potentially misleading indicator of their current ability.

The Luck Factor also provides a modest argument for the underdog. Kent State rates +0.4 compared with Bowling Green's -0.8. That differential warrants investigation, although it isn't sufficient by itself to establish betting value.

The worldwide opener was Bowling Green -5.5, and the current line remains essentially unchanged. There is no significant spread movement to fade, but the absence of movement also means Kent State bettors haven't lost value relative to the opening number.

The primary independent projection makes Bowling Green only a 5.3-point favorite, effectively matching the current line. A second model favors Bowling Green by eight, so this is not a strong computer-model selection. The free-pick case rests instead on Bowling Green's difficulty creating separation, Kent State's deceptive recent result and the potential for a competitive, low-possession game.

An independent Action Network handicapper also supports Kent State, although the preferred outside price is +6 rather than +5.5.

Projected score: Bowling Green 23, Kent State 20.

NFL Play Of The Day🏆

James Cook Over 82.5 Rush Yards

Averaging 101 yards per game this season🚀

❤️Like and follow if you are tailing!

Cook has been one of the most productive running backs in the NFL this season, rushing for 707 yards and seven touchdowns through seven games. He's averaging an impressive 101 rushing yards per game, nearly 19 yards above the number we're targeting. Cook has cleared 82.5 rushing yards in four of his seven games this season (57.1%), and he's rushed for at least 95 yards in each of those four performances. With Buffalo continuing to lean on its ground game, I like Cook's chances of reaching the 83 yards we need.

The biggest reason I like this play is Cook's combination of workload and efficiency. He's averaging 19.7 rushing attempts per game and 5.1 yards per carry this season. At that efficiency, Cook would need approximately 17 carries to clear tonight's line. What's particularly encouraging is that he's received at least 21 carries in five of his seven games, and he's rushed for at least 95 yards in all five games where he's received 20 or more carries except his most recent outing. When Buffalo commits to getting Cook the football, he's consistently shown the ability to produce significant yardage.

Another reason I'm backing Cook is his recent production. Over his last five games, he's recorded 154 → 75 → 111 → 95 → 80 rushing yards, averaging 103 yards per game during that stretch. Against the Chargers, Cook exploded for 154 yards on 24 carries. He followed that up with 111 yards and two touchdowns against the Rams and 95 yards against the Raiders. Even in last week's 36-10 victory over Baltimore, Cook finished with 80 rushing yards on 21 carries, falling just 2.5 yards short of tonight's number. His workload remained strong despite Buffalo controlling the game, which is encouraging heading into another important matchup.

The matchup against Minnesota gives me another reason to like this over. The Vikings are allowing approximately 116.7 rushing yards per game this season, including 103 rushing yards per game to opposing running backs. That's a manageable matchup for a player averaging more than 100 rushing yards per contest. Both teams enter Monday night with identical 6-1 records, making this a potentially competitive game where Buffalo will need to establish offensive balance. With Josh Allen commanding so much defensive attention, Cook should have opportunities to find running lanes and remain heavily involved throughout the game.

My earlier analysis (the spreadsheet and summary) found consistent directional patterns: Republican trifectas associated with higher net in-migration, lower unemployment, lower gas prices, and lower tax burden; Democratic trifectas associated with the opposite. Violent crime showed little difference at the pure state-trifecta level, but higher rates in large cities led by Democratic mayors.

Applying those observed patterns to the new political map produces these directional expectations for the next two years (roughly 2027–2028). These are forecasts based on the historical correlations I documented, not proven causation. National factors (interest rates, oil markets, broader economic conditions) will still dominate in many cases.

State Migration
Expect the existing pattern to continue or strengthen. Remaining strong Republican trifecta states (Florida, South Carolina, Tennessee, Idaho, and similar) should keep attracting net domestic migrants. Newly formed or strengthened Democratic trifectas (especially Texas if its shift holds, plus Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Minnesota) are more likely to see reduced in-migration or net outflows relative to the recent past. The long-running flow from high-tax/high-cost Democratic states toward lower-tax Republican ones has been persistent; the 2026 results expand the number of states under the policy mix previously linked to net losses.

Unemployment
Relative unemployment should track the pattern: remaining Republican trifectas more likely to stay at or near the lower end of the range; new Democratic trifectas more likely to see higher rates or slower improvement. The median gap in my data was meaningful (roughly 15 vs. 32 in the summary table). Two years is short for large structural shifts, so differences may appear more in relative performance than absolute levels.

Tax Burden
This is one of the clearer policy channels. New Democratic trifectas have greater ability to raise taxes or expand spending programs without internal vetoes. Expect upward pressure on state and local tax burdens in those states (especially if they pursue housing, education, or climate agendas). Remaining Republican trifectas are more likely to hold the line or continue restraint. My data already showed a large median difference on this metric.

Violent Crime
At the pure state-trifecta level, my analysis found little difference, so do not expect a clean statewide partisan split. At the city level, the mayoral-party pattern I noted remains relevant: large cities under long-term Democratic mayors (and progressive prosecutors) continue to account for a disproportionate share of violent crime, particularly homicides. Any expansion of soft-on-crime policies in newly Democratic-controlled states could reinforce that concentration. Cities that elect or retain more enforcement-oriented leadership would be the main counterexamples.

Gas Prices
Energy policy is a direct lever. Democratic trifectas have historically been more likely to impose additional regulations, fees, or restrictions on production and refining. Expect relatively higher gas prices in new or expanded Democratic trifectas and relatively lower prices in remaining Republican ones (holding national oil markets constant). The median gap in my summary was substantial.

Bottom line: The 2026 results expand the number of states under the Democratic-trifecta policy mix previously associated with higher taxes, higher unemployment, higher gas prices, and lower net migration. Remaining Republican trifectas should continue the opposite pattern. City-level crime remains more tightly linked to mayoral and prosecutorial control than to statewide trifectas. The correlations are observational and can be overridden by national economic conditions, but the directional signals from the data are consistent enough to serve as a baseline forecast.

text:
Do you really not understand why the original Big 12 split after 2009 and Texas’ role in it?

Nebraska learned of a plot where Texas, A&M, Tech, Colorado, OU and Oklahoma State were planning to join the PAC-10 to form the first 16-team super conference. Fearing stability issues and being left behind, they called the Big Ten.

The main reason realignment was even on the table was Texas wasn’t satisfied. The PAC-16 super conference nearly happened, but ESPN stepped in and offered Texas a pile of money for the Longhorn Network to keep them from leaving the Big 12. ESPN couldn’t lose Texas to what would have been a Fox aligned super conference.

Colorado ended up leaving for the PAC-12 anyways given how unstable the Big 12 had become with Texas being dissatisfied and then accepting the Longhorn Network deal at the expense of having a Big 12 network deal. A&M got super pissed about the LHN and left for the SEC. Missouri got left since the SEC had to take two schools.

All of this was a plan by ESPN to destroy the Big 12 and shove the biggest brands into the SEC, which ESPN has an interest in.

The Big 12 was a strong conference from 1996-2009. It appeared in as many national championship games as the SEC and many more than the Big Ten, ACC, and PAC-10.  The Big 12 was a threat to the SEC and Big Ten.  ESPN was working Texas for years to blow up the conference.

So the rub from me with Texas is we could have had so much more balance in college football had they exercised steady leadership to keep the original Big 12 together.

It’s like they joined the conference in 1996 but didn’t seem really committed? Or just biding their time? If so, that made them shitty partners then.

text:
$CWEN Q3 2026 earnings: Clearway Energy adds power projects, but debt costs eat cash

Clearway Energy, an owner of wind, solar and natural gas power plants, grew operating profit while debt payments ate most of the extra cash. Third-quarter operating profit excluding one-offs rose 13%, but cash available for dividends gained only 4% because cash interest and debt repayments climbed. Chief executive Craig Cornelius held the 2026 cash outlook steady, opened the 2027 cash plan at $520–590 million, and set a new 2031 cash target of $3.20–3.40 per share.

• Operating profit, excluding one-offs (Adjusted EBITDA): $𝟒𝟑𝟓𝐌 (+13% from a year ago)
• Cash available for distribution (CAFD): $𝟏𝟕𝟑𝐌 (+4.2% from a year ago)
• Initial 2027 CAFD outlook: $𝟓𝟐𝟎–𝟓𝟗𝟎𝐌 (middle of the range: +23% vs 2026 plan)
• New 2031 CAFD per share target: $𝟑.𝟐𝟎–𝟑.𝟒𝟎 (7–8% yearly growth from 2025 base)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because a growing project pipeline still collides with rising debt costs and pending share dilution. On the positive side, stronger third-quarter wind and solar output left just $40 million of cash needed in the fourth quarter to meet the 2026 midpoint by our math, and two new solar and battery deals locked in future growth. The caution: by our math the middle of the new 2027 cash plan equals $2.70 per share only on today's share count, leaving no room for planned stock sales unless results beat the midpoint.

The question now is whether buying more power plants turns into higher cash per share or gets absorbed by new debt and share sales. If new plants beat their target returns, cash per share will climb toward the $3.20–3.40 goal; if interest and share issuance eat the gains, per-share growth will stall. Full-year 2027 cash delivery and the pace of stock sales over the next चार quarters will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐓𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟏
Clearway Energy buys operating wind, solar and battery projects from its controlling sponsor, Clearway Group, to grow its cash available for distribution (CAFD, the cash left for dividends after project debt payments). Chief executive Craig Cornelius announced an "initial 2031 financial target range of $3.20 to $3.40 of CAFD per share, representing a compound annual growth rate of 7–8% from our 2025 baseline".

The clean power producer backed that target with three sponsor deals. It signed agreements to buy Honeycomb Phase 2, a Utah battery portfolio, and Swan Solar in Missouri, while receiving an offer for Heartland Solar Plus Storage in California.

• Honeycomb Phase 2 (210 megawatts): $119 million price for $12 million of annual CAFD starting in 2028
• Swan Solar (650 megawatts): $230 million price for $24 million of annual CAFD starting in 2029
• Heartland Solar Plus Storage (439 megawatts): about $130 million potential commitment, targeting late 2028 operations
• Sponsor pipeline: about 16 gigawatts total, with over 6 gigawatts identified for Clearway Energy through 2030

These deals matter because the two signed purchases generate a 10.3% cash return by our math, matching the 2030 plan. Having 6 gigawatts of projects lined up gives Clearway visibility to grow through 2031 without buying from outside sellers.

What to watch: the final price and cash return on Heartland Solar Plus Storage when the board committee approves it. A return above 10% would confirm that sponsor deals still clear the company's hurdle rate.

🟢 𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐖𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐥𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐔𝐩𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐈𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞
Alongside buying new plants, the power producer upgrades its existing wind farms (repowering) and signs new contracts for its California natural gas plants (Flexible Generation). On November 4, Clearway contracted between 200 and 500 megawatts of capacity at its Walnut Creek gas plant from 2027 through 2034 "at terms consistent with the budgetary assumptions for the Company’s long-term financial targets".

Across the gas fleet, the company has now signed or won 774 megawatts of contracts lasting eight to ten years, while advancing over 600 megawatts of wind upgrades. Gas segment operating profit excluding one-offs rose 17% to $70 million as plant availability reached 93.8%. Locking in multi-year gas revenue removes price risk while wind upgrades build toward 2027 completion.

What to watch: on-time completion of the Mount Storm and Goat Mountain wind upgrades in 2027. Keeping those schedules is necessary to deliver the cash step-up built into the 2028 and 2030 targets.

🟢 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐅𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬
Last quarter, weak wind conditions forced management to cut its 2026 cash outlook by $40 million, raising concern that poor weather would persist through the second half. In the third quarter, renewable power generation rose 12% from a year ago to 5.84 million megawatt-hours, with solar output up 16.2% and wind output up 6.5%.

That output lifted third-quarter CAFD by 4.2% to $173 million, near the top of the $145–175 million range implied by the full-year outlook by our math. With $410 million of cash generated in the first nine months, Clearway needs only $40 million in the fourth quarter to reach the $450 million full-year middle of the range, fading the near-term weather concern.

What to watch: fourth-quarter CAFD against the $40 million needed for the full-year midpoint. A result above $40 million would put full-year cash in the top half of the revised range.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐄𝐚𝐭 𝐌𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
Clearway's central pitch is that buying power plants grows cash per share, and Cornelius said "our initial 2027 guidance range aligned with our prior commitments". Those commitments called for $2.70 or more of CAFD per share in 2027.

The numbers show a wide gap between project profit and distributable cash. In the third quarter, operating profit excluding one-offs (Adjusted EBITDA) grew by $50 million, or 13.0%, but CAFD grew by only $7 million, or 4.2%, because debt service took almost all the gain.

• Q3 Adjusted EBITDA: $435 million, up $50 million from a year ago
• Q3 cash interest paid: $137 million, up $35 million (+34.3%)
• Q3 principal debt payments: $114 million, up $18 million (+18.8%)
• 2027 CAFD outlook: $520–590 million ($555 million middle of the range)

For 2027, the $555 million midpoint equals $2.703 per share on today's 205.3 million shares by our math. Because Clearway plans to sell new shares to fund its 2026–2029 investments, the middle of the 2027 dollar range falls below $2.70 per share once share count rises.

What to watch: whether 2027 CAFD tracks toward the $590 million top of the range as new projects open. Without results above the midpoint, stock sales will dilute 2027 cash per share below $2.70.

🔴 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭
Clearway plans to fund over $500 million of its 2026–2029 investments using leftover cash after dividends, targeting a long-term payout ratio below 70% of CAFD. On November 9, the board raised the quarterly Class C dividend to $0.4824 per share, up 6.5% from a year ago. In the third quarter, common dividends and distributions to Clearway Group totaled $98 million.

By our math, $98 million per quarter equals $392 million a year, or 87.1% of the $450 million full-year 2026 CAFD midpoint. Even against the 2027 CAFD midpoint of $555 million, today's payout rate starts at 70.6% before counting another year of dividend increases, leaving less retained cash for investments.

What to watch: the 2027 dividend growth target on the conference call. A dividend increase above 6% in 2027 would keep the payout ratio above 70% unless CAFD beats the midpoint.

🔴 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐀𝐰𝐚𝐲
Management highlights power complexes built next to data centers (co-located digital infrastructure) as a driver that could push growth above its long-term targets. Cornelius said those projects could lift results "as our first complex targets completion over 2029-2030". The third-quarter release included no new data center power contracts, no dollar investment figures, and no projected cash return for Clearway Energy.

This matters because the sponsor, Clearway Group, develops and owns these data center projects today. Clearway Energy will only buy them around 2029 or 2030, and management has not said whether they will add to or merely replace standard solar and storage purchases.

What to watch: announcement of a signed data center power contract before year-end, as management previously targeted. Silence through the fourth quarter would show that data center deals are moving slower than planned.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing risks around funding, accounting and supply chains received no resolution in the third-quarter release.

• Stock sales for growth: Clearway raised $0 from common stock in the third quarter and $50 million year-to-date, leaving $450–950 million still to raise through 2029; the 10-Q and Q4 release will track new issuance.
• Tax-equity accounting swings: GAAP net income attributable to Clearway fell 78% to $51 million because $72 million of profit went to non-controlling partners, versus a $172 million loss allocation a year ago; CAFD remains the only usable cash measure.
• Tariff and supply-chain rules: the release gave no update on domestic solar equipment sourcing for 2029–2030 projects; conference call Q&A is the next test.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟗𝐌 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔): $𝟗𝟑𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Operating cash flow jumped 83.8% in the first nine months from $511 million a year ago, and rose 44.0% in the third quarter to $324 million. The nine-month surge came from $282 million of proceeds from selling transferable tax credits, which the power producer mainly used to pay off project bridge loans rather than for dividends.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟗,𝟒𝟑𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Total debt (short-term plus long-term debt) rose 9.6% by our math from $8,606 million at the end of 2025, and increased from $9,061 million last quarter. Clearway issued $1,245 million of long-term debt in the first nine months, including $600 million of corporate notes due 2034, lifting total liquidity to $1,102 million.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟒𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Customer bills waiting to be collected rose 50.6% by our math from $162 million at the end of 2025, compared with nine-month operating revenue growth of 21.3%. Part of the increase reflects higher summer electricity generation between May and September, when power prices and solar output peak.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐂𝐀𝐅𝐃): $𝟒𝟑𝟎–𝟒𝟕𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $430–470 million
Unchanged. The full-year plan still calls for $450 million at the middle of the range, up 4.7% from 2025 after last quarter's $40 million weather-related cut. By our math, that leaves $40 million for Q4, up 14.3% from $35 million a year ago. In the past two years, Clearway beat its initial full-year cash midpoint by an average of 5.0%.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐂𝐀𝐅𝐃): $𝟓𝟐𝟎–𝟓𝟗𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from $2.70+ per share

Source: Goldman Sachs

Equity Research

achs 6 November 2026 | 4:00AM EST

AMERICAS TECHNOLOGY

US Data Center Capacity update: Framing risks to our data center forecasts

Following several gubernatorial election flips (from Republican to Democratic), and campaigns in many states which featured stricter data center regulation including Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Georgia, and Michigan (D-incumbent), we analyze data center capacity at the state level to help frame risks to the data center buildout.

Looking only at under construction data centers, which we view as lower-risk, we see US data center net additions of 22/24/5 GW-IT for 2027/28/29 (assuming a 1.5 PUE, using Aterio data) compares to our US data center net addition forecasts of 20/24/23 GW-IT and gives us confidence in our forecasts. We believe our forecasts have been appropriately conservative and recognize that they have likely been below consensus expectations.

Based only on under construction data centers, Texas represents 20% of 2027E net additions and 27% of 2028E net additions. We focus on Texas as a market given that the Governor elect has called for an immediate moratorium on data centers. We note that moratoriums are not bans or cancellations, and believe the key risks to data center operators are related to delays to ready-for-service and higher costs.

Goldman Sachs does and seeks to do business with companies covered in its research reports. As a result, investors should be aware that the firm may have a conflict of interest that could affect the objectivity of this report. Investors should consider this report as only a single factor in making their investment decision. For Reg AC certification and other important disclosures, see the Disclosure Appendix, or go to https://t.co/ssQiDtCZy9. Analysts employed by non-US affiliates are not registered/qualified as research analysts with FINRA in the U.S.

Goldman Sachs

6 November 2026

Americas Technology

The US currently has 57 GW-gross of active data center capacity today with an additional 9GW-gross under construction for 65 GW-gross by the end of 2026. Beyond 2026, there are 78GW-gross of under construction data centers with net additions of 33/37/8/0 GW-gross for 2027/28/29/30 (Exhibit 1). We view these as low-risk data center capacity net additions. Assuming a 1.5 PUE (average global PUE, with newer data centers at lower PUE, per Uptime Institute Global Data center Survey 2026), that would imply US data center net additions of 22/24/5 GW-IT for 2027/28/29 (per Aterio) and compares to our US data center net addition forecasts of 20/24/23 GW-IT and gives us confidence in our recently revised forecasts. We believe our forecasts have been appropriately conservative.

A common area of investor pushback to our data center capacity forecasts has been that upstream measures of compute (e.g., CoWoS capacity or chip methodologies) would suggest that more data center capacity is needed to support IT-equipment forecast to ship. This is also supported by announced data center capacity that is not yet under construction. Aterio sees an additional 137GW-gross of “high-likelihood” data center capacity being added from 2027-30 (Exhibit 2), which is defined as “high-likelihood” based on a combination of factors including permitting, financing, and power secured. In our view, we view data center capacity that is announced, but not under construction as having a higher-risk of execution (at least as it relates to timing), particularly given heightened uncertainty due to potential moratoriums and believe it’s prudent to evaluate these data centers on a project-by-project basis.

**Report: Analysis of the @LFATVUS Video Claiming Abdul El-Sayed Cannot Legally Enter the U.S. Senate Due to Muslim Brotherhood Ties**

### Video and Post Overview
The X post from Live From America TV (@LFATVUS), published November 9, 2026, features a roughly 2.3-minute video of host Jeremy Herrell (wearing a “Herrell 2028” cap) speaking directly to camera. On-screen text states: “PROOF THAT ABDUL EL SAYED CAN’T LEGALLY BE ALLOWED TO SWEAR IN AND/OR HAVE CLASSIFIED INFO!” The accompanying text urges viewers to share the information widely and asserts that “Abdul cannot be allowed to enter the US Senate as part of the Muslim Brotherhood.” Replies in the thread amplify calls for action, including tagging Trump-related accounts and alleging treason-level concerns.

The video presents the host’s argument that documented associations disqualify El-Sayed from the constitutional oath and access to classified information that senators receive by virtue of office.

### Background on Abdul El-Sayed
Abdul El-Sayed is a Michigan-born physician and epidemiologist who previously served as Detroit’s health director and Wayne County health director. He won the Democratic nomination for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat and then the general election in early November 2026 against Republican Mike Rogers, becoming the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. He is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, 2027, succeeding retiring Sen. Gary Peters. His campaign emphasized universal healthcare, reducing corporate influence in politics, and affordability issues, while criticizing certain U.S. foreign policy positions (including regarding Israel and Gaza).[](<https://t.co/jd8FqdZgG3>)

### Alleged Evidence of Muslim Brotherhood Ties Cited by Critics
Conservative outlets, opponents (including Rogers and Trump), and the video’s framing rely on several lines of association rather than proof of formal membership:

- **Family statements**: El-Sayed’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, posted on social media in 2012 that the family had “long been MB” (Muslim Brotherhood) and described an “amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.” El-Sayed’s parents divorced when he was about three; he was raised primarily by his father and stepmother and has said he never discussed these matters with his mother.
- **Mother’s employment**: Reports indicate his mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA), which the U.S. Treasury designated in 2004 over links to terrorist financing involving Hamas and other groups.
- **2012 open letter**: El-Sayed (then a medical student) signed a letter with other Egyptian-Americans supporting then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi (backed by the Muslim Brotherhood) and calling for a purge of media and police institutions of holdovers from the prior regime. Fact-checkers note the letter does not mention the Muslim Brotherhood by name.
- **College leadership**: He held leadership roles (including vice president and outreach positions) in the University of Michigan chapter of the Muslim Students Association (MSA). Some historical Brotherhood documents and a 2007 FBI assessment have described the MSA as having early links to Brotherhood networks in the U.S.
- **Later associations**: He spoke at and/or fundraised for events involving the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA), Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), and related groups. These organizations appear in historical Brotherhood lists or were named unindicted co-conspirators in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing case (involving Hamas); they were not convicted. A six-part Investigative Project on Terrorism (IPT) report (October 2026) maps these organizational appearances and writings over two decades but explicitly does not claim El-Sayed was a formal Brotherhood member.
- **Broader context**: Certain branches of the Muslim Brotherhood have been designated by the U.S. for material support to Hamas. Critics also reference other family or in-law connections to Islamic charities or organizations that faced scrutiny.

These points form the core of the “proof” presented in conservative commentary, including the video’s framing around eligibility for the Senate oath and classified access.[](<https://t.co/KkrGqReEPK>)

### El-Sayed’s Responses and Denials
El-Sayed has repeatedly stated he has no personal ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, that he was not raised by his mother, and that assumptions of family involvement are “insane.” At a October 2026 town hall, when asked if he would disavow the group, he replied “Sure, yeah, absolutely,” then challenged the premise as implying dual loyalty due to his faith. He has compared the scrutiny to questions faced by John F. Kennedy about Catholicism and has emphasized that he will swear an oath solely to the U.S. Constitution. He has also condemned Hamas’s actions while criticizing Israeli government policies.[](<https://t.co/bzKaefZohH>)

### Independent Assessments
Multiple fact-checks (Bridge Michigan, PolitiFact, The Guardian, Media Bias/Fact Check, and others) conclude there is no verified evidence that El-Sayed is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, pledged support to it, or has personal operational ties. They describe the claims as overstating family social media posts, a letter that does not name the Brotherhood, and historical organizational associations common in some Muslim American activist circles. Critics of the fact-checks argue the associations and family statements are relevant for a role involving national security oversight.[](<https://t.co/Xl162IYOqs>)

### Legal and Practical Context on the Oath and Classified Access
The U.S. Constitution (Article VI) prohibits religious tests for office and requires senators to take an oath to support the Constitution. There is no established legal mechanism that bars an elected member from being sworn in based on family associations or organizational appearances of the type documented here.

Members of Congress receive access to classified information by virtue of their constitutional office and Senate rules; they are not required to obtain a formal executive-branch security clearance (unlike most staffers or executive officials), according to the Congressional Research Service. Access is still subject to need-to-know principles and chamber procedures. Opinion pieces (e.g., Wall Street Journal) and some national-security commentators have argued that El-Sayed’s associations would likely raise flags in a standard clearance process if one were required, but election itself confers the role. Recent viral claims that he “failed a background check” for Senate briefings have been fact-checked as false or satirical; no such requirement or failure exists.[](<https://t.co/KbNF61tGeU>)

### Summary Assessment
The video reflects post-election conservative advocacy that treats documented family statements, a 2012 political letter, MSA leadership, and appearances with certain Islamic organizations as sufficient grounds for disqualification from the Senate oath and classified access. El-Sayed’s denials, disavowal, and the absence of evidence of personal membership are the counter-position, supported by multiple independent reviews that find the strongest claims unsubstantiated. Legally, election determines eligibility to take the oath; associations do not create an automatic bar under current constitutional and congressional practice. The episode illustrates ongoing debates over how personal, family, and organizational histories should be weighed for elected officials who handle sensitive national security matters.

Current Status of Earth's Polar Vortex (November 2026)  Record-Early Reversal. 

Normally, the polar vortex spins counterclockwise (west-to-east) at roughly 25 m/s during November. 

As of November 10–11, 2026, those winds reversed to easterly speeds around -0.1 to -2.0 m/s. 

The previous earliest November SSW in modern records occurred on November 28 (in 1958, 1968, and 2025).  

Atmospheric Drivers. 

Meteorologists at NOAA, the UK Met Office, and Météo-France point to large planetary waves (Rossby waves) pushing upward from the lower atmosphere and destabilizing the vortex. 

These waves are being amplified by an exceptionally strong El Niño in the Pacific and a persistent high-pressure ridge over Scandinavia and northwestern Russia.  

Short-Term Outlook. 

Forecast models from The Weather Network and Severe Weather Europe  indicate this specific wind reversal will be brief, with stratospheric winds expected to bounce back to normal westerly speeds by the third week of November. 

However, the ripple effects of this disruption can still buckle the jet stream and increase the risk of cold snaps across North America, Europe, or Asia in late November and December.

Earth's magnetic field does weaken slightly over decades and undergoes geomagnetic excursions (like the Laschamp event ~41,000 years ago), but it is not collapsing or causing stratospheric wind shifts.

Furthermore, Venus's famous "double-eyed" polar vortices are permanent, super-rotating atmospheric features driven by intense solar heating of its ultra-dense carbon dioxide atmosphere and its slow 243-day rotation, completely unrelated to Earth's seasonal stratospheric vortex."

text:
Welcome back to The State of AI, a new collaboration between the Financial Times and MIT Technology Review. Every Monday, writers from both publications debate one aspect of the generative AI revolution reshaping global power.

In this week’s conversation MIT Technology Review’s senior reporter for features and investigations, Eileen Guo, and FT tech correspondent Melissa Heikkilä discuss the privacy implications of our new reliance on chatbots.

Eileen Guo writes:

Even if you don’t have an AI friend yourself, you probably know someone who does. A recent study found that one of the top uses of generative AI is companionship: On platforms like https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, Replika, or Meta AI, people can create personalized chatbots to pose as the ideal friend, romantic partner, parent, therapist, or any other persona they can dream up. 

It’s wild how easily people say these relationships can develop. And multiple studies have found that the more conversational and human-like an AI chatbot is, the more likely it is that we’ll trust it and be influenced by it. This can be dangerous, and the chatbots have been accused of pushing some people toward harmful behaviors—including, in a few extreme examples, suicide. 

Some state governments are taking notice and starting to regulate companion AI. New York requires AI companion companies to create safeguards and report expressions of suicidal ideation, and last month California passed a more detailed bill requiring AI companion companies to protect children and other vulnerable groups. 

But tellingly, one area the laws fail to address is user privacy.

This is despite the fact that AI companions, even more so than other types of generative AI, depend on people to share deeply personal information—from their day-to-day-routines, innermost thoughts, and questions they might not feel comfortable asking real people.

After all, the more users tell their AI companions, the better the bots become at keeping them engaged. This is what MIT researchers Robert Mahari and Pat Pataranutaporn called “addictive intelligence” in an op-ed we published last year, warning that the developers of AI companions make “deliberate design choices … to maximize user engagement.” 

Ultimately, this provides AI companies with something incredibly powerful, not to mention lucrative: a treasure trove of conversational data that can be used to further improve their LLMs. Consider how the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz explained it in 2023: 

“Apps such as https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, which both control their models and own the end customer relationship, have a tremendous opportunity to  generate market value in the emerging AI value stack. In a world where data is limited, companies that can create a magical data feedback loop by connecting user engagement back into their underlying model to continuously improve their product will be among the biggest winners that emerge from this ecosystem.”

This personal information is also incredibly valuable to marketers and data brokers. Meta recently announced that it will deliver ads through its AI chatbots. And research conducted this year by the security company Surf Shark found that four out of the five AI companion apps it looked at in the Apple App Store were collecting data such as user or device IDs, which can be combined with third-party data to create profiles for targeted ads. (The only one that said it did not collect data for tracking services was Nomi, which told me earlier this year that it would not “censor” chatbots from giving explicit suicide instructions.) 

All of this means that the privacy risks posed by these AI companions are, in a sense, required: They are a feature, not a bug. And we haven’t even talked about the additional security risks presented by the way AI chatbots collect and store so much personal information in one place. 

So, is it possible to have prosocial and privacy-protecting AI companions? That’s an open question. 

What do you think, Melissa, and what is top of mind for you when it comes to privacy risks from AI companions? And do things look any different in Europe? 

Location

A location I care about is

Generating your personalized response…

Melissa Heikkilä replies:

Thanks, Eileen. I agree with you. If social media was a privacy nightmare, then AI chatbots put the problem on steroids. 

In many ways, an AI chatbot creates what feels like a much more intimate interaction than a Facebook page. The conversations we have are only with our computers, so there is little risk of your uncle or your crush ever seeing what you write. The AI companies building the models, on the other hand, see everything. 

Companies are optimizing their AI models for engagement by designing them to be as human-like as possible. But AI developers have several other ways to keep us hooked. The first is sycophancy, or the tendency for chatbots to be overly agreeable. 

This feature stems from the way the language model behind the chatbots is trained using reinforcement learning. Human data labelers rate the answers generated by the model as either acceptable or not. This teaches the model how to behave. 

Because people generally like answers that are agreeable, such responses are weighted more heavily in training. 

AI companies say they use this technique because it helps models become more helpful. But it creates a perverse incentive. 

After encouraging us to pour our hearts out to chatbots, companies from Meta to OpenAI are now looking to monetize these conversations. OpenAI recently told us it was looking at a number of ways to meet $1 trillion spending pledges, which included advertising and shopping features. 

AI models are already incredibly persuasive. Researchers at the UK’s AI Security Institute have shown that they are far more skilled than humans at persuading people to change their minds on politics, conspiracy theories, and vaccine skepticism. They do this by generating large amounts of relevant evidence and communicating it in an effective and understandable way. 

This feature, paired with their sycophancy and a wealth of personal data, could be a powerful tool for advertisers—one that is more manipulative than anything we have seen before. 

By default, chatbot users are opted in to data collection. Opt-out policies place the onus on users to understand the implications of sharing their information. It’s also unlikely that data already used in training will be removed. 

We are all part of this phenomenon whether we want to be or not. Social media platforms from Instagram to LinkedIn now use our personal data to train generative AI models. 

Companies are sitting on treasure troves that consist of our most intimate thoughts and preferences, and language models are very good at picking up on subtle hints in language that could help advertisers profile us better by inferring our age, location, gender, and income level.

We are being sold the idea of an omniscient AI digital assistant, a superintelligent confidante. In return, however, there is a very real risk that our information is about to be sent to the highest bidder once again.

Eileen responds:

I think the comparison between AI companions and social media is both apt and concerning. 

As Melissa highlighted, the privacy risks presented by AI chatbots aren’t new—they just “put the [privacy] problem on steroids.” AI companions are more intimate and even better optimized for engagement than social media, making it more likely that people will offer up more personal information.

Here in the US, we are far from solving the privacy issues already presented by social networks and the internet’s ad economy, even without the added risks of AI.

And without regulation, the companies themselves are not following privacy best practices either. One recent study found that the major AI models train their LLMs on user chat data by default unless users opt out, while several don’t offer opt-out mechanisms at all.

In an ideal world, the greater risks of companion AI would give more impetus to the privacy fight—but I don’t see any evidence this is happening. 

Further reading 

FT reporters peer under the hood of OpenAI’s five-year business plan as it tries to meet its vast $1 trillion spending pledges. 

Is it really such a problem if AI chatbots tell people what they want to hear? This FT feature asks what’s wrong with sycophancy 

In a recent print issue of MIT Technology Review, Rhiannon Williams spoke to a number of people about the types of relationships they are having with AI chatbots.

text:
[미 민주당 또 시작함 ㅋㅋㅋ 의회 먹자마자 트럼프 청문회 지옥 + 이란전 총력전 오픈 준비 (feat. 3C 프레임)]

미 민주당 얘네 진짜 레퍼토리 안 바뀌고 한결같네 ㅋㅋㅋ

2026년 중간선거에서 상·하원 다수당 먹자마자 뭘 준비하는지 아냐?

민생 경제 살리기? 인플레 잡기? 서민 생활 안정?

뭐 겉으로는 당연히 그런 거 하겠다고 입 털고 있지.

근데 정작 민주당 지도부가 각 잡고 준비하는 메인 프로젝트는 따로 있음.

바로 이란 전쟁 멈추겠다고 총력전 선포하면서, 트럼프 행정부 탈탈 털어버릴 대규모 의회 조사랑 청문회 러시 때리는 거임.

11월 6일 액시오스(Axios) 보도에 따르면, 
민주당이 벌써 상·하원 여러 위원회 엮어서 트럼프 행정부 상대로 장기 조사랑 정치 메시지 때려 박을 판을 짜고 있다고 함.

심지어 거창하게 이름까지 붙였음. 이른바 '3C 전략'.

Cost — 비용 (이란 전쟁 여파에 물가까지 겹쳐서 니들 지갑 털리는 경제적 부담)

Chaos — 혼란 (나라 꼴이랑 중동 판 돌아가는 꼬라지)

Corruption — 부패 (비리 덩어리)

야, 이거 어디서 많이 본 빌드업 아니냐?

아직 제대로 된 조사 결과도 안 나왔는데, 대중들 머릿속에 박아 넣을 핵심 키워드부터 세팅해 놓은 거임.

물론 의회가 행정부 견제하고 감시하는 건 당연한 권한임. 

민주당 측에서는 의회 승인 없이 밀어붙인 이란 전쟁을 끝내고, 행정부의 정책 실패나 권한 남용 의혹을 철저히 검증해 책임을 묻는 게 의회의 본분이라는 입장이겠지.

잘못한 게 있으면 털어야 하는 게 맞긴 함.

근데 정상적인 조사라면 증거부터 모으고, 팩트 체크하고, 그 결과로 결론을 내리는 게 순서잖아?

조사도 시작하기 전에 정치적 프레임부터 짜놓고 시작하면 어떻게 되겠음?

모든 청문회가 진실 규명이 아니라, 미리 정해둔 결론을 뒷받침할 '그림'만 뽑아내는 쇼로 변질될 위험이 크다는 거임.

1. 공화당 RINO까지 가세한 피트 헤그세스 탄핵 빌드업? (J6 시즌2 각)

심지어 이번엔 민주당만 숟가락 얹는 게 아님. 

이미 공화당 내부 반트럼프 성향(일명 RINO)으로 꼽히는 토마스 매시(Thomas Massie) 하원의원이 이란 전쟁 무단 개시 등을 문제 삼아 피트 헤그세스(Pete Hegseth) 국방장관 탄핵소추안까지 발의해서 판을 깔아놨음.

비록 11월 10일 표결에서 공화당 지도부가 법사위로 넘겨버리면서 당장 본회의 통과는 막았지만, 민주당 지도부는 내년 1월 새 의회 열리자마자 다수당 힘으로 다시 불 지필 각을 재고 있음. (반면 헤그세스 장관이나 트럼프 측은 이란 핵 위협을 막기 위한 역사적 성과인데 정치 쇼로 발목 잡는다고 맞받아치는 중임.)

트럼프 1기 때 기억나지? 

러시아 스캔들, 탄핵 정국, 1월 6일 의사당 난입 사태 조사까지 임기 내내 청문회랑 조사로 미국 언론 도배됐던 거.

특히 J6 특위 때는 증언이랑 영상 기가 막히게 편집해서 대중한테 각인시키는 방식으로 엄청난 화제를 모았음. 
요즘 미국 정치판에서 청문회는 그냥 의원들이 묻고 증인이 답하는 자리가 아님. 카메라 앞에서 자극적인 짤 생성하는 거대한 미디어 이벤트에 가까움.

의원이 책상 치면서 호통침 → 증인이 당황해서 말 더듬음 → 관련 문건 화면에 띄움 → 그중 제일 자극적인 15초만 잘라서 CNN이랑 MSNBC에 송출함 → SNS에서 조회수 수백만 찍음.

나중에 전체 맥락 까보니까 앞뒤 사정이 달랐다고? 

이미 늦었지. 

대중 머릿속엔 그 15초짜리 짤만 남아 있으니까.

결국 실제로 위법 행위가 입증됐느냐보다, 유권자들이 뭘 사실로 믿게 만드느냐의 싸움으로 변질될 가능성이 높다는 거임.

2. 진짜 무서운 건 미국인들의 경제적 피로감임
이번 민주당 전략에서 제일 영리하면서도 쎄한 부분이 바로 'Cost(비용)'를 맨 앞에 세운 거임.

왜 하필 경제 문제를 1번으로 꽂았겠음? 

지금 미국 유권자들이 제일 예민하게 반응하는 역린이 바로 먹고사는 문제니까.

실제로 2026년 중간선거에서 CBS가 인용한 여론조사 보면 유권자의 89%가 생활비 문제를 중요하거나 결정적인 투표 요인으로 꼽았음. 

장바구니 물가 미쳤지, 이란 전쟁 때문에 유가랑 인플레 압박까지 겹쳤지, 집세랑 보험료에 허리 휘지, 미국 서민들 경제적 피로감이 한계치까지 쌓인 상태임.

이런 사람들한테 민주당이 어떤 메시지를 던지겠음?

"니들이 지금 이렇게 뼈 빠지게 일하고도 힘든 이유는 다 트럼프 행정부가 벌인 무리한 전쟁과 혼란, 부패 때문이다."

이보다 직관적이고 쏙쏙 박히는 정치적 선동이 또 있겠냐?

문제는 현실 경제가 그렇게 단순하지 않다는 거임. 물가랑 생활비는 통화정책, 글로벌 공급망, 에너지 가격, 노동시장, 기업 가격 정책 등 온갖 변수가 복잡하게 얽혀 있음.

근데 이 복잡한 원인을 특정 정권의 무능과 부패라는 단 하나의 서사로 퉁쳐버리면? 

당장 숨넘어가는 유권자들 귀에는 그럴싸하게 들릴 수밖에 없음. 사람이 경제적으로 쪼들릴수록 복잡한 분석보다는 당장 욕할 수 있는 명확한 타겟을 원하게 되거든.

앞으로 민주당이 이란 전쟁 청문회부터 시작해서 월가 금융권, 제약회사, 빅테크 줄소환하고 그 장면을 전부 트럼프 행정부 책임론이랑 엮어버린다면?개별 의혹의 진위 여부를 떠나서, 끊임없이 반복되는 프레임만으로도 여론이 쏠릴 수 있음. 

아직 검증 안 된 의혹도 계속 때리다 보면 기정사실처럼 굳어지는 게 프레임 정치의 무서운 점임. 지금 미국의 팍팍한 경제 상황이 딱 그 판이 먹혀들기 좋은 환경이라는 게 씁쓸할 따름임.

From Thomas Massie's Hegseth impeachment bid to the "3C" playbook: Is the incoming Democratic Congress gearing up for genuine war-powers oversight or a viral soundbite factory?

According to a November 6 report from Axios, Democratic leadership is preparing a coordinated wave of congressional investigations and hearings targeting the Trump administration once the new Congress convenes in January 2027 following their 2026 midterm victories. Alongside a pledged all-out push to halt the ongoing war in Iran, multiple House and Senate committees plan to align their oversight around a unified messaging framework dubbed the "3Cs":

Cost – Everyday financial strain, compounded by inflation and the economic fallout of Middle East conflict

Chaos – Perceived instability in domestic governance and unauthorized overseas military campaigns
Corruption – Allegations of executive misconduct, abuse of power, and corporate favoritism
This week, that dynamic escalated dramatically when outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY)—who lost his GOP primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger—introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. 
Massie’s 34-page resolution accuses Hegseth of waging unauthorized war against Iran in violation of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, alongside charges stemming from U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, maritime strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels, and retaliation against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly.

While House Republicans voted on Tuesday, November 10 to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee—effectively blocking an immediate floor vote—Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has already endorsed the impeachment push, stating that Hegseth "must stand trial before the Senate". 

Meanwhile, Hegseth dismissed the effort as a "political spectacle" and "sabotage" during a Pentagon briefing, and President Donald Trump defended his Pentagon chief on social media, calling the House vote an exoneration of "a Great American Patriot".

Constitutional scholars and supporters of congressional oversight argue that reasserting legislative war powers and investigating executive actions in Iran, Venezuela, and Yemen is a vital constitutional duty. Yet from a political communication standpoint, rolling out a pre-branded "3C" campaign before the new Congress even takes office raises serious questions about how these hearings will actually operate.

1. Pre-packaging the narrative before the hearings begin (J6 Hearings 2.0?)

In a traditional congressional inquiry, lawmakers gather evidence, establish facts, and then draw conclusions. When party leadership locks in the core takeaways—Cost, Chaos, and Corruption—upfront, every subsequent committee hearing risks becoming a stage set designed to manufacture viral moments that reinforce a pre-existing storyline.

We saw how this plays out during Trump’s first term—from the Russia probe and impeachment trials to the January 6th Committee hearings. Regardless of the underlying legal merits, modern congressional hearings double as made-for-TV media events. A lawmaker delivers a sharp rebuke, a witness hesitates, a document flashes on screen, and the most dramatic 15-second clip dominates cable news and social media feeds. Even when fuller context emerges later, that initial 15-second clip is what cements itself in the public consciousness. With Massie’s impeachment articles already handed to Democrats on a silver platter, the temptation to turn war-powers oversight into a continuous impeachment spectacle ahead of 2028 will be immense.

2. Merging war fatigue with economic anxiety

The most calculated—and potentially polarizing—element of the Democrats' playbook is placing Cost at the top of the list.

According to exit polling cited by CBS News during the 2026 midterms, 89% of voters identified the cost of living as an important or deciding factor in their vote. Americans are worn down by high grocery prices, steep housing and insurance bills, and anxiety over how prolonged conflict with Iran could further shock global energy markets.

In that environment, linking household financial pain directly to foreign intervention and executive dysfunction—essentially telling voters, "Your life is expensive because of this administration's unauthorized wars, chaos, and corruption"—is an extraordinarily potent political message.

The catch is that macroeconomic reality is rarely that straightforward. Inflation and living costs are driven by a complex web of monetary policy, supply chains, labor markets, energy dynamics, and corporate pricing decisions. However, when voters are financially exhausted, simple narratives that offer a clear villain are far more persuasive than nuanced economic breakdowns. If Democrats pair high-profile hearings on the Iran war and Pentagon leadership with subpoenas for Wall Street banks, pharmaceutical companies, and Big Tech executives, repetition alone could reshape public perception regardless of what is legally proven.

TL;DR: 
Following Rep. Thomas Massie’s blocked impeachment bid against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, Democrats are preparing to take control of Congress in January with an all-out push to halt the conflict and launch "3C" (Cost, Chaos, Corruption) oversight hearings. While defenders see this as a necessary reassertion of congressional war powers, critics warn that pre-branding the narrative turns oversight into a 15-second soundbite factory and oversimplifies complex economic pressures for partisan leverage.

What’s your take? 
Does pairing war-powers oversight with a "Cost, Chaos, and Corruption" message effectively hold the administration accountable, or does pre-scripting the narrative undermine the credibility of Congress's investigations before they even start?

text:
BELONGING: SONIA GANDHI'S ACCOUNT OF INDIA'S IDEOLOGICAL DIVIDE, NEHRU AND THE POLITICS OF POWER

When history becomes a political battleground, the real question is not who controls the narrative, but whether citizens have access to facts, competing perspectives and independent evidence.

SOURCE: Sanket Upadhyay, DoubleCheck by Awadh Punch [Watch the full discussion on YouTube]
https://t.co/CoLSm7XyLn

WHAT SONIA GANDHI'S MEMOIR REVEALS

In Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi offers her assessment of Narendra Modi, the RSS-BJP ideological project, Jawaharlal Nehru's legacy and India's changing political and economic landscape.

One central distinction runs through her account: the disagreement is not merely between political parties but between competing ideas of India.

She describes her vision as rooted in pluralism, secularism, liberty and equality, while arguing that the RSS-influenced political vision places greater emphasis on religious and cultural hierarchy.

Her criticism of the repeated targeting of Nehru is particularly significant. She argues that Nehru's commitment to parliamentary democracy and secularism represents precisely the constitutional foundations that the Sangh Parivar challenges.

These are Sonia Gandhi's political assessments, but they raise questions that deserve examination through historical records and constitutional principles.

NEHRU: WHY DOES HIS LEGACY REMAIN A POLITICAL BATTLEGROUND?

Nehru's historical significance cannot be reduced to the shortcomings of his governments. His contribution must also be assessed through the institutions and principles established during India's formative democratic years.

Parliamentary democracy, scientific temper, secular constitutionalism, independent institutions and a plural national identity were central to the vision of the republic.

Criticism of Nehru is legitimate. Historical mistakes should be examined honestly. But criticism becomes distortion when selective facts, misinformation and personal abuse replace serious historical inquiry.

The real test is whether political criticism strengthens historical understanding or merely delegitimises an entire constitutional inheritance.

THE ECONOMIC QUESTION: WHO OWNS INDIA'S WEALTH?

One of the most consequential claims discussed in the video concerns wealth concentration.

The World Inequality Report 2026 provides independent estimates:

Share of India's total wealth held by the richest 1%  : 40.1%

Richest 10% : 65%

Bottom 50% : 6.4%

World Inequality Report 2026, estimates for 2024.

WID - World Inequality Database +1

These figures substantiate the seriousness of wealth inequality. However, they do not independently establish that the entire problem originated after 2014. Inequality has deep historical roots, and its changing trajectory requires careful examination across governments.

The relevant questions concern employment, wages, taxation, public investment, access to education and healthcare, and the concentration of economic power.

THE BJP'S COUNTERARGUMENT ALSO DESERVES HISTORICAL SCRUTINY

The BJP has accused Sonia Gandhi of overlooking or softening Congress-era historical wrongs, particularly the 1975 Emergency and the 1984 anti-Sikh violence. Sonia's memoir addresses these episodes, but the extent of responsibility and the adequacy of her account remain contested. Reuters +1

No political party should receive immunity from historical accountability.

The Emergency was an assault on democratic freedoms. The victims of the 1984 anti-Sikh violence deserve justice and remembrance. Equally, present-day governments must answer for their own record.

Historical accountability cannot operate selectively.

THE LARGER DEMOCRATIC QUESTION

India belongs equally to people of every religion, language, caste and cultural background. Neither a political party nor an ideological organisation owns the nation.

Nehru's legacy deserves scrutiny, as does the RSS's ideological influence, the Congress's governing record and the Modi government's performance.

The standard must remain consistent: constitutional democracy, secular citizenship, equality before law, institutional independence and economic justice.

A nation cannot build its future by selectively rewriting its past. History must be examined, power must be questioned, and every generation must remain free to debate what kind of India it wants.

text:
**JD Vance opened Veterans Small Business Week by tying veteran-owned firms directly to both net U.S. job growth and the industrial supply chain that arms the troops.**

### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A standard administration event celebrating veterans and small business, with the usual photo-op praise for service and entrepreneurship.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** The vice president used the kickoff to spotlight two concrete administration claims—$1.3 billion already deployed to veteran-backed firms and a post-COVID fraud crackdown at the SBA—while linking those firms to national-security production and reminding the room that small businesses, not big ones, drive net job creation.

### 2. Observations
- Vance explicitly credited SBA Administrator Kelly with the $1.3 billion figure and positioned her as the administration’s lead on fraud prevention, stating that “money that should have been going to small businesses… was actually going to fraudsters” after the COVID era (ASR).
- He drew a straight line from veteran small businesses to weapons supply chains: “Whether it’s a Patriot missile or whether it’s the 1,200 small businesses that support the people who are developing the sidearms for our troops” (ASR). This is the administration’s steelman for why these firms merit targeted support beyond generic small-business policy.
- Vance contrasted big-business churn with small-business net job growth and noted his own pre-politics experience investing in veteran-owned tech and industrial-supply-chain companies in Cincinnati—personal credentialing rather than abstract talking points.
- The Ohio State football aside (backup QB Luke Fehey, “any Ohio people here?”) was deliberate audience calibration; it humanized the speaker without derailing the policy message.
- The closing ask—“talk to us and tell us what we can do better”—is the standard feedback loop the administration wants from this constituency, not a vague platitude.
- No new dollar amounts or legislative commitments were announced; the speech recycled and reinforced existing SBA numbers and the fraud narrative already in circulation.

### 3. Snapshot
On November 9, 2026, Vice President JD Vance delivered opening remarks at the National Veterans Small Business Week kickoff in Washington, DC (YouTube: https://t.co/n1yGE0GNvI). The event honored veteran-owned, American-made businesses; Vance highlighted SBA funding, fraud reduction, national-security supply-chain contributions, and small businesses as the net job engine. Primary source is the administration’s own video and ASR transcript.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **2026-11-09**: Vance delivers remarks at National Veterans Small Business Week kickoff (video published same day). (LT)
- **Recent years (post-COVID era referenced)**: Administration claims massive fraud in SBA programs; current effort focused on eligibility verification. (IT per Vance ASR)
- **Under current SBA leadership**: $1.3 billion directed to veteran-backed small businesses. (IT per Vance ASR)
- **Pre-2024**: Vance’s private-sector experience as tech investor in veteran-owned and defense-supply-chain firms in Ohio. (LT per Vance ASR)

### 5. Sides
**Trump administration / Vance (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: Veteran small businesses deliver measurable job growth, reduce fraud leakage, and directly support the defense industrial base; targeted federal support plus tighter eligibility rules is the efficient mechanism.  
Critique: LT on the $1.3 billion and fraud problem statement; IT on the scale of impact and the assumption that additional hundreds of millions/billions will translate cleanly into the claimed outcomes.

**Veteran small-business owners / attendees**  
Steelman: They bring discipline, resilience, and instinctive understanding of national security needs; they want capital access without excessive regulatory friction.  
Critique: Their incentive is straightforward—more reliable funding and fewer fraudsters competing for the same dollars.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns**: Small businesses are the net job creators in the U.S. economy; veteran-owned firms participate in defense supply chains; post-COVID SBA fraud was real and large.
- **Known Unknowns**: Exact verification rate improvements from the new eligibility checks; precise ROI on the $1.3 billion already deployed.
- **Unknown Knowns**: Internal SBA data on which specific veteran firms received the $1.3 billion and their subsequent hiring or production metrics.
- **Unknown Unknowns**: Whether broader economic conditions or other policy changes will swamp the marginal effect of the additional hundreds of millions/billions pledged.

### 7. Incentives map
- Administration: Demonstrates delivery on veteran and small-business constituencies while reinforcing the “fraud was rampant, we fixed it” narrative that plays well with both populist and fiscal audiences.
- SBA leadership (Kelly): Status and budget protection by being named the fraud fighter and fund deployer.
- Veteran small-business owners: Direct access to capital and political attention.
- Media/engagement stack: Veteran + small business + national security + fraud = high-engagement topic; the speech supplies clean clips on all four.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Track the actual disbursement data and fraud-recovery numbers the administration releases next; veteran small businesses are a high-signal constituency—support that produces measurable hiring and supply-chain output is worth continuing; support that mostly buys political goodwill is not.

**Evil AI Advice:** Milk the veteran brand for maximum political capital, announce big future numbers without tight metrics, and make sure the fraud crackdown story stays louder than any stories about legitimate applicants still getting delayed.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch for the next SBA quarterly report on veteran-backed loan volume and any published fraud-recovery figures.
- Treat the “hundreds of millions this year, billions over the next couple of years” line as a directional commitment, not a locked appropriation.
- Note which congressional attendees respond to Vance’s request for feedback and what specific regulatory or funding changes they propose.
- Compare future claims against the $1.3 billion baseline already cited.
- Primary source remains the administration video itself—read the ASR or watch the clip before secondary summaries.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- SBA data showing the $1.3 billion produced negligible net new hiring or supply-chain output.
- Evidence that the fraud crackdown is primarily slowing legitimate veteran applicants rather than catching fraudsters.
- Announcement of the pledged additional funding being redirected or significantly scaled back.
- Internal metrics (if released) showing big-business job churn actually outpacing small-business net growth in the relevant sectors.
