Bloomberg reports OpenAI’s downsized fundraising deal, combined with rival Anthropic PBC’s decision to pursue an IPO at a lower-than-expected valuation, has sent shockwaves throughout the venture landscape. Suddenly, an industry already rattled by a weeks-long public market AI selloff is worrying more about whether private companies are on the cusp of a correction. (BBG)

Following the election results, both Meta and OpenAI executives said that they believe it will be more difficult to build data centers in the future, according to public comments and remarks OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made at a company Q&A. (WSJ)

Congressional Democrats are planning an initial push for bipartisan healthcare, tariff and Iran-war legislation next year, with reconciliation expected to move up the agenda if Republicans block their bills. (Burgess Everett, Laura Weiss)

Sovereign wealth fund assets are set to surge nearly 50% to $22.4 trillion by 2030 as state-backed investors deepen their involvement in artificial intelligence and infrastructure, according to a PwC report released on Thursday. (RTRS)

Japan’s producer inflation accelerated to 7.1% y/y in October from 6.8%, defying expectations for a slowdown. Prices rose 0.7% m/m, the fastest increase since May, reinforcing the case for another BOJ hike. (BBG)

BOJ’s Toichiro Asada urged caution on further tightening, seeking evidence that higher wages are generating demand-driven inflation. He said he was neither advocating a cut nor categorically opposed to hikes. (WSJ, BBG)

Japan’s FX chief Atsushi Mimura warned recent currency moves were “too fast” and said it was too early to forget this summer’s intervention. Government spokesperson Minoru Kihara later called yen undervaluation a problem and pledged continued coordination with the US Treasury. (BBG)

State Street’s Masahiko Loo warned that a yen move into the mid-160s per dollar could trigger a stronger policy response than investors anticipate. (WSJ)

New Zealand’s April 2037 bond auction drew bids for 7.46 times the amount offered, the strongest demand for any tenor since February 2013. The benchmark 10-year yield extended its decline, falling 4bp to 4.64%. (BBG)

UK GDP grew 0.7% q/q and 1.9% y/y in Q3, with quarterly growth matching forecasts and accelerating from 0.5% in Q2. Services and manufacturing each grew 0.9%, while construction fell 0.7%; September output rose 0.2% m/m versus flat expected, and August was revised to flat from 0.1%. (ONS, BBG)

Britain's economy grew at the fastest rate in two-and-a-half years in the third quarter of 2026, helped by investment in artificial intelligence, extending a strong first half and defying predictions of a slowdown made after the Iran war began. (RTRS)

UK estate agents’ expectations for sales and house prices fell to three-year lows in October. Rics’ year-ahead sales balance dropped to -17 from +1, while price expectations fell to -17 from zero. (FT)

France has signaled it may support Spain's nominee Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as European Central Bank president next year, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing sources. (FT)

Sentiment among European companies has picked up across industry and services since June, but there are growing concerns about rising inflation and sovereign debt, according to a survey published by BusinessEurope on Thursday. (RTRS)

The EU and UK are set to postpone the 10% tariff due to hit most electric vehicles traded between them from January. Brussels is consulting on a one-year delay or a two-year arrangement allowing manufacturers to offset non-compliant exports against compliant domestic sales, people familiar said. (FT)

Jefferies’ Mohit Kumar said the bank would be inclined to short French debt against Germany if the ten-year spread fell below 140bp. The spread was 147bp in early European trading. (WSJ)

Chatter on the online discussion site Reddit can tell policymakers how retail investors are feeling sooner than traditional surveys, particularly when markets are under stress, two European Central Bank economists concluded. (RTRS)

Norwegian oil and gas companies have cut their projected investments for 2026 while raising the outlook for 2027 compared with estimates made three months ago, an industry survey by the statistics office (SSB) showed on Thursday. (RTRS)

Bank Indonesia confirmed intervention in spot, offshore and domestic forwards, alongside secondary-market government-bond purchases, after the rupiah hit a record low. The currency weakened as much as 0.5% to 18,241/$, while the 10-year yield rose 4bp to 7.66%. (BBG)

Vietnam put its planned international bond sale on hold because borrowing costs were too high, Finance Minister Ngo Van Tuan told parliament. Officials will continue engaging investors so they can proceed when conditions improve; Bloomberg previously reported a potential deal of up to $1 billion. (BBG)

Mexico wants to buy more US steel as it seeks better tariff treatment from Washington, Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez told Bloomberg. Imports from mainly Asian countries without Mexican free-trade agreements fell more than 27% in January–September following higher tariffs and anti-dumping measures. (BBG)

China and Turkey have signed a preliminary agreement for China to invest some $15 billion to build solar and wind power plants with a total capacity of 7,000 MW in Turkey, the Turkish energy minister said on Thursday. (RTRS)

Turkey's central bank raised its end-2027 inflation forecast to 21% and its end-2028 forecast to 13.5% on Thursday, with Governor Fatih Karahan saying the bank would maintain a tight policy stance until prices stabilise. (BBG)

IRAN:

USS George H.W. Bush families were told the carrier would not return before the holidays and to prepare for a worst-case 12-month deployment, according to audio obtained by MS NOW. Navy leaders said Iranian drones continue to threaten ships enforcing the blockade. (MS NOW)

US and allied military officials told WSJ that the ballistic-missile threat requires a rethink of America’s military posture as interceptor shortages persist. No changes have been announced; a senior Western defense official said countries with their own missile defenses could become preferred US base locations. (WSJ)

India’s crude imports through Hormuz rose to 2.1 million b/d so far in November, overtaking Russian supplies of 1.8 million b/d for the first time since the Iran war began, according to Kpler. Shuttle tankers and ship-to-ship transfers are helping restore Gulf flows. (BBG)

GEOPOLITICAL:

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow for talks with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, following two days of trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi. They planned to travel onward to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (BBG)

EQUITIES:

CoreWeave plans to raise at least $4 billion through an investment-grade loan, potentially launching as soon as next week, according to people familiar. Morgan Stanley and MUFG are leading the proposed financing, which is expected to use chips and customer contracts as collateral. (BBG)

Alphabet began marketing its first Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bonds. Initial guidance ranged from roughly 4.6% for two-year HKD notes to 5.5% for 10-year paper, and from 2.75% for two-year SGD notes to 4% for 30-year debt. (BBG)

Google suffered a setback on Thursday as an adviser to Europe's top court faulted a lower tribunal's decision to scrap a €1.49 billion ($1.7 billion) fine levied against the US tech giant seven years ago for anti-competitive practices related to online advertising. (RTRS)

Blackstone is expected to announce an Andhra Pradesh data-centre investment of roughly 1 trillion rupees, or $10.7 billion, in coming days, Naidu told Bloomberg. AirTrunk did not immediately respond to a request for comment. (BBG)

Pfizer secured up to $1.5bn from Blackstone Life Sciences to fund development of obesity drug berobenatide. Blackstone can earn milestone payments, while Pfizer retains operational control and ownership of the drug. (WSJ)

Strategy will leave MSCI’s global benchmarks at the November 30 close under its non-operating-company rules. The confirmed deletion could prompt selling by index-tracking funds. (WSJ)

ExxonMobil is seeking an interim order suspending EU requirements to build CO₂ storage infrastructure, the FT revealed from a confidential Commission memo. The previously filed arbitration invokes an investment treaty and challenges deadlines Exxon says are impossible to meet. (FT)

Eli Lilly on Thursday became the first drugmaker to have a GLP-1 weight-loss pill approved in China, giving it an edge over Danish rival Novo Nordisk in the world's second-largest pharmaceutical market. (RTRS)

Tencent founder Pony Ma told staff he was willing to deploy half the workforce toward AI-native businesses, according to people familiar with a private anniversary speech. The sources characterised it as a strategic push to embrace AI rather than an announced wholesale restructuring. (BBG)

Shares of Chinese chipmakers Hosin Electronics and Amicro Technology rose in their Hong Kong debut on Thursday after the companies raised a combined HK$1.78 billion ($227 million) in initial public offerings. (RTRS)

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are reallocating some enterprise SSD supply from Chinese customers to US buyers, ZDNet Korea reports. Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent have reduced planned orders as AI-chip restrictions constrain their buildouts; US demand is expected to absorb the released volumes. (ZDNet Korea)

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Thursday that Samsung Electronics' 6 trillion won ($4.48 billion) investment in a high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chip packaging plant in Asan, South Korea, would be followed by about 40 trillion won in investment in advanced equipment. (RTRS)

Samsung Electronics brought the Asan HBM packaging line’s opening forward one year to June 2028. President Lee outlined KRW6tn of construction and about KRW40tn of equipment spending under the wider programme announced in July. (RTRS)

SK Hynix’s HBM4 yield has exceeded 70%, according to industry sources cited by Chosun Biz. The company has not officially disclosed a numerical yield, and differing measurement methods limit comparisons with competitors. (Chosun Biz)

Naver reported Q3 net profit down 45% to KRW402.5bn versus KRW476.19bn expected, with revenue up 11% to KRW3.472tn. Operating profit fell 21% as AI costs rose; its CFO expects AI-expense growth to moderate in 2027 after peaking this year. Naver secured approximately KRW2tn ($1.5bn) of computing-service contracts with a US AI inference company for its initial 2027 capacity. (WSJ)

Naver is negotiating what it describes as Asia’s largest Nvidia server procurement, seeking early access to Vera Rubin systems and better costs. This remains a negotiation; management also said it is discussing additional short- and longer-term supply contracts with global AI firms. (EBN)

Japan's biggest oil and gas explorer Inpex on Thursday lifted its 2026 net profit forecast by 7.8% to a record 550 billion yen ($3.4 billion) on higher oil and gas prices and robust output at its Australian Ichthys liquefied natural gas project. (RTRS)

Foxconn reported Q3 net profit of T$77.5bn, up 34%, versus T$69.6bn expected. It forecast high double-digit sequential AI-rack shipment growth in Q4 and high double-digit growth in 2027, while warning that chips, memory and other components remain tight. (RTRS, WSJ)

Metro Bank put itself up for sale and appointed Morgan Stanley as lead adviser following its restructuring. The lender said it is currently in no active discussions with potential buyers. (FT)

Burberry’s Q2 comparable sales rose 4%, slightly ahead of consensus, led by 11% growth in the Americas. China grew 5%, below the 7% expected; the company retained its full-year revenue and margin-growth outlook. (BBG)

Rolls-Royce announced a £1.5bn interim buyback running to February, within its existing programme of up to £9bn through 2028. Power-systems orders rose 62% in the first nine months, taking the backlog to £8.6bn, with defence and civil-aerospace demand remaining strong. (WSJ)

BAE Systems raised its 2026 free-cash-flow forecast to about £3bn from more than £2bn, partly reflecting customer advances. Orders reached £33bn year to date, versus more than £27bn a year earlier; sales and earnings growth guidance was maintained. (WSJ)

Wizz Air’s first-half net income fell 67% to €108.1 million from €323.5 million as higher jet-fuel costs hit earnings. Fuel remains a major headwind heading into winter. (BBG)

HSBC has discussed giving its Singapore business greater independence to diversify its reliance on Greater China, according to people familiar with “Project Sirena.” HSBC confirmed plans to combine its Singapore units but said it had no plans to change the ownership or management of its Asia-Pacific banking entities. (BBG)

Siemens’ Q4 orders jumped 58% to a record €34.77bn and net profit rose to €2.16bn from €1.62bn. It raised its medium-term growth ceiling to 11% from 9%; FY2027 targets are 9–11% comparable growth and €10.20–10.80 EPS, with a proposed €5.50 dividend versus €5.35. (WSJ, BBG)

Merck KGaA raised annual sales guidance to €21.5–21.9bn from €21.0–21.8bn and adjusted EBITDA to €6.2–6.4bn from €5.9–6.3bn, its third upgrade this year. Q3 sales of €5.63bn beat €5.46bn expected; adjusted EBITDA of €1.68bn exceeded €1.61bn. (WSJ)

Hapag-Lloyd reported Q3 revenue of €5.97bn versus €6.13bn expected and EBITDA of €1.49bn versus €1.63bn expected. CEO Rolf Habben Jansen said unit costs remained under pressure from geopolitical tensions and operational disruption. (WSJ)

Munich Re’s Q3 major reinsurance losses were €646mn, or 14.9% of net reinsurance revenue versus 18% anticipated. Insurance revenue rose 14% to €16.63bn; its profit-guidance increase was announced last month. (WSJ)

Telefonica cut its revenue-growth forecast to 1%–1.5% from 1.5%–2.5%, citing weaker handset sales. It nevertheless raised its adjusted EBITDA-growth outlook to slightly above 2.5%, after Q3 adjusted EBITDA increased 6.2% to €3.08 billion. (BBG)

Zurich Insurance’s natural-catastrophe loss ratio rose to 3.2% over the first nine months from 1.4% a year earlier, following European storms and a Colombian earthquake. Property-and-casualty gross written premiums increased 7% on a like-for-like basis to $42.1 billion as pricing moderated. (BBG)

text:
Former NFL quarterback Philip Rivers is set to become NC State's new head football coach, with the school's board of trustees expected to finalize his contract on Friday, sources told ESPN.

Rivers, 44, has never coached in college but is one of the Wolfpack's most revered former players. He played quarterback at NC State from 2000 to 2003, breaking nearly every school and ACC record with 13,484 passing yards and 95 touchdowns, and led the program to four straight bowl games under the late Chuck Amato.

He is in his sixth season as coach at St. Michael Catholic High School in Fairhope, Alabama, where he built the program from the ground up and reached the state semifinals in 2024 and 2025. He would replace Dave Doeren, who was fired on Oct. 24. His son Gunner, a quarterback, committed to NC State in February.

Rivers played 17 NFL seasons, all but one with the Chargers, and came out of retirement last year to start three games for the Colts. In January, he interviewed for the Bills' head coaching job before withdrawing from the search.

Can Rivers make the jump from high school to the ACC?

text:
Obviously my usual in game day posts and commentary was missing today. I didn’t watch the game today.

That’s because I was in St Croix USVI.

40th Anniversary trip for the Fall 1986 line of The Xi Zeta Chapter of Phi Beta Sigma from NC State University. Also joined by the brothers from Spring 1987.

Our Dean of Pledges, who pledged Spring 83 was the last Sigma on campus at NCSU (Raleigh NC). He refused to let the chapter die. So he went hard recruiting and 9 bros crossed Nov 6th 1986. Four more bros crossed Spring 87. So many successful brothers from this group. 

We’re here in St Croix because our of fraternity brother and St Croix native Sam Positive Nelson crossed the same semester at St Augustine’s college, also in Raleigh NC. He’s been back in St Croix for many years now working to make it a better place.

I love all these bros.

It’s a blessing to have known all these guys for FORTY YEARS. It puts life in perspective. Especially for me because they all live in NC (plus one in VA and one in St Croix) and I don’t see them regularly. So when we get together it’s a reminder of how many years have past and that we have more behind us than ahead of us.

There are two who have passed on to glory and a couple who couldn’t make the trip. But I’m thankful for this time with these men.

He’s jumping straight from Alabama high school football into an ACC head-coaching job.

A massive gamble? Absolutely.

The deal has not yet been officially announced.

text:
Philip Rivers is set to become NC State's next head coach, according to multiple reports. He has never coached a college game.

What he has done is coach high school football. Since 2021, Rivers has been the head coach at St. Michael Catholic, a small school in Fairhope, Alabama. Through last season, his teams went 43-15 and reached the state semifinals the last two years.

Then, last December, weeks after one of those semifinal games, the 44-year-old came out of retirement and played three games for the Indianapolis Colts. His high school players packed a local restaurant to watch their coach throw an NFL touchdown pass.

Now he's going home. Rivers started a then-NCAA record 51 straight games at NC State from 2000 to 2003, and led the Wolfpack to a school-record 11-3 season in 2002. His number is retired there. He'll become just the fourth former NC State player to lead the program, and the last one was his own college coach, Chuck Amato, who died last month at 80.

And his first quarterback might be at his own dinner table. Rivers' son Gunner, a four-star senior quarterback, is already committed to NC State. He's one of Rivers' 10 kids.

NC State fired Dave Doeren in October after a 3-4 start. Rivers reportedly wants to finish his high school season first.

From https://t.co/iODbrq8Yli - Space Exploration - Launches & Spacecraft - What time will SpaceX launch Starship Flight 15, its 1st double landing test, on Nov. 13? (Full mission timeline)  NewsBy Tariq Malik  Edited by Mike Wall
     SpaceX will make history with the world's first full recovery of an orbital rocket on Starship Flight 15. Here's when to watch.
     What time is the launch?
     How to watch the launch
     How long is the flight?
     What if Starship doesn't launch?
     SpaceX is days away from what might be its most ambitious test flight yet of the company's massive Starship megarocket, the largest launch vehicle ever built.
     On Friday (Nov. 13), SpaceX will launch its next Starship test flight on a mission that, if successful, will return both its Super Heavy first-stage booster and Ship upper stage to Earth for back-to-back landings at their launch pad. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. And if you want to watch it live, you'll need to know what time and where to tune in.
     In our guide below, we'll explain exactly when and how to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission. It is the 15th test flight of the giant stainless-steel reusable rocket, which SpaceX wants to use for everything from Starlink internet satellite launches to landing NASA Artemis astronauts on the moon in 2028, and even for a crewed flight to Mars. But first, SpaceX has to successfully recover and refly both stages, something it's never done before — and that's where Flight 15 comes in. It's the first time the company will try to land an entire Starship rocket. Here's when to tune in.
     What time is SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch (and landing)?
    The Starship Flight 15 test mission is currently scheduled to launch no earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. But there is a chance of a later liftoff time.
     SpaceX has said it has a 75-minute window in which to launch Starship Flight 15 to add some flexibility into its preflight countdown. That means the launch could take place anytime between 5:45 p.m. and 7 p.m. EST (2245-0000 Nov. 14). The local time for the launch window will be 4:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. CST.
     What time will SpaceX launch its 1st orbital Starship test on Flight 14 today? (Full mission timeline)
     SpaceX has not formally announced if it has backup days for the launch, but if the company does have those options, liftoff would likely occur at the same time, based on past Starship missions that saw delays.
     One thing that separates Starship Flight 15 from past Starship test flights is its length. The mission, if it runs its full duration, will last just over 22.5 hours until Ship lands back at Starbase. That landing would occur on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT). If SpaceX launches at the end of its window on Friday, at 7 p.m. EST, the Ship landing would occur on Saturday at 5:32 p.m. EST (2232 GMT).
     Meanwhile, the Super Heavy, known as Booster 22, will land about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.
     Can I watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch?
Watch OnWatch live! SpaceX launches Starship Flight 15 with potential double catch attempts - YouTube.
     Yes, you'll be able to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch online, and you have many ways to do so.
     https://t.co/iODbrq8Yli will host a livestream simulcast of Starship Flight 15 on this page, as well as on our homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. That webcast will begin about 30 minutes before liftoff, at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT).
     SpaceX, of course, will offer its own Starship Flight 15 livestream on its Flight 15 mission page, as well as on its X account. That livestream will also begin 30 minutes before launch, at 5:15 p.m. EST (it's the same one as on https://t.co/iODbrq8Yli).
     A prelaunch show Watch OnWaiting for Flight 15 Full Stack | Countdown To Launch - YouTube.
     If you need your Starship launch preparations fix before the Nov. 13 launch, good news: You can see SpaceX's prep work live online.
     NASASpaceflight's YouTube channel offers live views of SpaceX's Starship pads at Starbase 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
     On Wednesday (Nov. 11), the channel will stream live views of the Starship Flight 15 rocket stacking, starting at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT).
     The NASASpaceflight Flight 15 launch webcast will begin on Nov. 13 at 11:45 a.m. EDT (1645 GMT), about six hours before launch. NASASpaceflight typically offers live commentary and constantly changing views of the Starship launch pad via remote cameras positioned around Starbase.  Watch OnSPACEX LAUNCHES STARSHIP FLIGHT 15 - Launch & Booster Catch - YouTube.
     In-person launch options
     If there was ever a SpaceX Starship test flight to see in person, this just might be it.
     In addition to watching the world's largest rocket launch into space, Starship Flight 15 offers the chance to see both parts of that megarocket return to Earth and be caught in mid-air, 22 hours apart.
     If you've read our past Starship launch viewing guides, you'll know that SpaceX doesn't have an official viewing site for Starship launches. But you can see the spectacle from several public beaches (as well as private campgrounds).
     Cameron County Amphitheater at Isla Blanca Park on South Padre Island is always my first recommendation (I watched the first Starship launch from there in April 2023). The park offers a clear view of the Starship launch site across the bay and includes views of boats on the water. There are also bathrooms close by for your convenience. It's 5 miles (8 kilometers) from the launch site as the crow flies. But plan to head out early as traffic can be heavy, especially if you have to cross the bridge from Port Isabel.
     Speaking of Port Isabel, there are stretches along Highway 48 between Port Isabel and Brownsville, Texas where you can pull over to the shoulder to watch the launch from 6 to 8 miles (10 to 13 km) away. But it's just the side of a highway, so don't expect bathrooms there. 
     The website https://t.co/NPgvinQKQ3 does report that there are "open pull-offs" to park, from which you can get "wide wetland views." And, of course, it's free. 
     I've driven along Highway 48 during two Starbase visits but have not pulled over to the shoulder to test this site.
     If you're on the Mexico side of the border, you may be able to watch Starship Flight 15 from Playa Bagdad, a public beach with a "head-on view of the launch tower and a festive vibe," according to https://t.co/NPgvinQKQ3.
     Finally, there is the Rocket Ranch campground, where you can get a closer view of Starship launches — but you have to pay $200 a ticket (kids under age 17 are $40). The ranch is 3.8 miles (6.1 km) from the Starbase launch site, and your ticket allows you to camp there for one day and one night. Longer four-day stay packages are available.
     The Rocket Ranch has two primary viewing locations: The "Outpost" offers the closest view and "unmatched media service," so you can stay connected. The second location is a bit farther away on the campground itself. 
     Please note: Tickets include bus transportation from the ranch campground to a viewing site and back, but it is for one launch attempt only. Be sure to read the full Rocket Ranch FAQ for details on the site.
     How long is SpaceX's Starship Flight 15?
     If everything goes to plan, SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 orbital launch and landing test could last up to 22.5 hours and orbit the Earth 14 times.
     "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in a mission overview.
     But the test flight could end early. That's what happened on SpaceX's first orbital Starship test mission, Flight 14 on Sept. 28, which was expected to last nearly 10 hours and orbit Earth six times. Instead, SpaceX ended the mission after three hours and two orbits of Earth as a safety precaution.
     "Starship’s initial return to launch site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of ~275 km and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight," SpaceX wrote in the mission description. "Similar to Starship’s first orbital mission, the flight profile has been designed with the opportunity to insert into a passively safe suborbital trajectory or safely deorbit at multiple pre-determined areas over the ocean after raising to an orbital altitude."
     SpaceX Starship Flight 15 Launch Timeline
     TIME (Hr:Min:Sec)EVENT
     T-0:50:00 Flight director polls for fueling
     T-0:35:33 Super Heavy liquid oxygen loading begins
     T-0:35:30 Super Heavy liquid methane loading begins

     Starship Flight 15 Mission Timeline

     T+00:00:00 Liftoff!
     T+00:00:58 Ship/Super Heavy reach "Max Q"
     T+00:02:19 Super Heavy main engine cutoff

     T+00:02:26 Super Heavy boostback burn startup
     T+00:03:02 Super Heavy boostback burn engine shutdown
     T+00:06:10 Super Heavy landing burn startup
     T+00:06:35 Super Heavy landing burn shutdown (followed by 'chopsticks" catch)
     T+00:08:09 Starship engine cutoff
     T+00:26:10 Starship orbital insertion engine burn begins
     T+00:26:30 Starship orbital engine burn shutdown
     T+00:35:01 Payload deploy starts
     T+01:17:40 Payload deploy complete
     T+01:27:46 Early Hawaii return check
     T+07:15:35 Mid-Chile return check

     T+21:35:57 Deorbit burn start
     T+21:36:07 Deorbit burn shutdown
     T+22:10:46 Ship reentry

     T+22:30:13 Ship subsonic
     T+22:32:16 Landing burn start
     T+22:32:18 Landing flip.
     T+22:32:26 Landing burn three to two engines
     T+22:32:33 Landing burn two to one engines
     T+22:32:34 "An exciting landing!" SpaceX says.
     If SpaceX has to end the Starship Flight 15 test flight early, it has three primary splashdown zones to land the Ship upper stage in the ocean.
     The company could drop the Ship vehicle in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Hawaii in early and late stages of the mission, according to a reentry overview. A mid-mission splashdown window off the coast of Chile is available if needed at that time. A late-mission splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico is also available.
     The Gulf is also a wave-off splashdown zone for SpaceX's Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 in case it is unable to land shortly after liftoff.
     As with Starship Flight 14, SpaceX is loading Flight 15 with 26 operational Starlink V3 internet satellites. They will be deployed in orbit within the first 90 minutes of the flight.
     "The Starship upper stage’s primary objectives include the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites and the first return to launch site and catch at Starbase," SpaceX wrote in its overview. "Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy."
     What if Starship Flight 15 can't launch on Nov. 13?
     While SpaceX is hoping to launch Starship Flight 15 on time, there is a chance that a technical issue or bad weather could prevent liftoff on Nov. 13.
     SpaceX has not announced any official backup days for the Starship Flight 15 launch, but it is likely that the company has at least one if not two additional opportunities to try again, based on past Starship launches. Any backup launch attempts will depend greatly on the nature of a launch delay.
     A good website to watch is the official Starbase page for Boca Chica Beach and Highway 4 closure alerts here. Those beach closures can be a good indicator of SpaceX's available flight windows.

text:
A Father in Gaza. A Genocide Inquiry. NVIDIA’s AI Chips. Who Answers?

A chief executive admits infidelity, and his private life becomes a public reckoning. His company’s processors appear in military systems, including a munition designed to kill, and the reckoning becomes harder to find. What an absurd moral arrangement: we can organize an inquiry into whom a man slept with while struggling to establish who profits from the machinery of mass killing. A UN commission has found genocide in Gaza. What did Jensen Huang know about the military uses of NVIDIA’s chips, what did his company earn, and what did he do when evidence of abuse became public? Those questions deserve an investigation at least as persistent as the scrutiny of his sex life.

By Alan Clements · November 12, 2026

Muhib was nineteen. His brother Elyas was seventeen. On February 12, 2024, in the Al-Shaboura refugee camp in Rafah, their father, Osama Abu Jama, heard gunfire outside the family tent. He stepped out to see what was happening. People were running. The sound woke his sons. Within a minute, he told the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, a quadcopter overhead opened fire on the tent. Osama was wounded. Both boys were killed. His testimony preserves a detail I have been unable to get past. Among the last things he could tell us about his sons was something a parent sees a thousand times and scarcely thinks to remember. They woke up.

Half a world away, five people who worked at NVIDIA helped The New York Times report on an alleged affair between Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive, and an executive who reported to him. Five sources for one relationship. Think of the calls that went unanswered before someone agreed to speak. Think of the patience it takes to earn the confidence of a person whose livelihood may depend upon your discretion. That is a capacity I want the American press to keep—and bring, with equal appetite, to the business of killing. A newspaper can reconstruct the intimacies of a billionaire. What could that persistence discover about the machinery above a family’s tent?

I have no evidence that the aircraft over his tent contained an NVIDIA chip. An Israeli arms manufacturer does, however, identify an NVIDIA processor in a drone it designed to kill. The distance between those two sentences is where a reporter’s work begins. It is also where a great deal of public interest seems to end.

Huang acknowledged to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He did not name his partner in that admission. The New York Times reported that American intelligence had identified a Chinese businesswoman with whom he had a close relationship as an intelligence asset. Beijing dismissed the allegation. NVIDIA’s board opened an investigation. In a separate story, the Times reported an affair with an NVIDIA executive who reported to him. Those are distinct accounts involving different women. The public knows less about the private circumstances of either relationship than a week of headlines might lead one to believe.

As for the bare fact that a married man had sex outside his marriage, my response as a citizen is simple. So, fucking what? His wife has standing to answer that question very differently. An employee whose career depends upon the judgment of the man she reports to has interests a board must take seriously. A foreign intelligence service obtaining privileged access to a chief executive would be a substantial public matter. Journalism earns its keep by making these distinctions. The sheer fact of intercourse, however, confers no public entitlement to the sheets.

Yet the sheets offer something the contracts do not: immediate moral fluency. Everybody knows how to have an opinion about adultery. Put a processor inside a weapon, move it through a reseller and a defense contractor, and suddenly the same public must acquire a graduate education in procurement before it is allowed to be appalled. Sex gives us a scandal we can understand over coffee. Mass killing comes with an explanation of why responsibility is complicated.

The absurdity lies in what happens next. A sexual relationship becomes a question of judgment, access, power and accountability. The sale of technology used by military institutions becomes a question of distribution channels. We recognize the obligations of a man who has power over someone across a desk. Put a purchasing ministry and six thousand miles between his company and a person exposed to its products, and we begin to lose our vocabulary. At what point along that route does the obligation expire? And who had the authority to decide?

The relationship disclosed in the accounts

In its fiscal year ending in January 2026, NVIDIA recorded $19.677 billion in sales to direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong. In the following six months it recorded another $12.430 billion. More than $32 billion across those eighteen months. You can find the numbers in the company’s financial filings. They tell you where the customer was headquartered. They do not tell you where every processor went, which government could ultimately draw upon its computing power, or what proportion served the People’s Liberation Army.

Here is the peculiarity of Washington’s alarm. A woman may have obtained access to a man whose company openly does tens of billions of dollars of business with customers headquartered in her country. Espionage is a serious allegation. Ordinary commerce offers no defense to it. Yet ordinary commerce presents questions of its own, and the Times turned up a remarkable one. Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company associated with the businesswoman, reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion in NVIDIA chips over two years. Who took delivery? Which customers bought access to the machines? One can ask both questions without learning another thing about anybody’s marriage.

On November 11, Reuters supplied an example of what that journalism looks like. A Chinese university with deep military ties bought two NVIDIA H200 chips for 874,700 yuan through a domestic supplier. The purchasing department was the management school. Its cybersecurity school rented computing capacity under separate agreements. Good reporting leaves the management school in the sentence. It resists promoting a university purchase to a missile program for the sake of a better headline. It also makes it considerably harder for the company to say the destination of its products is beyond the reach of human curiosity. Reporters found the paperwork.

Apply that curiosity at home. On May 1, the Pentagon publicly named NVIDIA among the companies with which it had reached agreements to deploy artificial intelligence on its classified networks. The public announcement gave no dollar figure for NVIDIA. At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, a single American supercomputer called Sierra contained more than 17,000 NVIDIA processors. Its work included assessing the nuclear weapons stockpile. Seventeen thousand in one machine. You need no speculative theory of Silicon Valley’s proximity to military power. You can count the processors.

Can I tell you the Pentagon puts billions of dollars a year into NVIDIA’s pocket? I cannot. Consider a modest purchase that illustrates why. The Air Force Research Laboratory bought two NVIDIA computing systems for $485,455. Look up the award by recipient and you will find Sterling Computers. A search for NVIDIA alone can miss it. Assign the entire sum to NVIDIA and you have made a different mistake. Multiply that problem across contractors, foreign resellers and computing time bought by the hour. A citizen can be taxed to pay for the machine and still be unable to discover how much the company whose name it bears earned from the sale.

Here, apparently, is where our appetite for disclosure becomes exhausted. We can pursue the identity of a sexual partner through frightened sources and private denials. Following public money into military computing is harder, so the unanswered questions remain unanswered. Difficulty is a reason to fund the reporting. It is a grotesque reason to accept the silence.

What a father can know

Elbit Systems, an Israeli arms manufacturer, identifies the onboard computer in its LANIUS loitering munition as the NVIDIA Jetson TX2. Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor reported the use of small drones in Gaza, including aircraft it classified as LANIUS, in the same investigation that recorded Osama Abu Jama’s testimony. His account identifies a quadcopter. There is no serial number in that testimony, no recovered processor identifying the aircraft that killed his sons. I return to that missing piece because it is precisely where an honest indictment of our priorities begins. Why should a wounded father carry the burden of tracing an international supply chain before anyone asks its beneficiaries to account for it?

In September 2025, the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel rejects that finding. South Africa’s case against Israel remains before the International Court of Justice. I use the word genocide here deliberately, and I name the body that made the finding. The word war alone leaves too much unsaid about what that commission examined and concluded.

Read those matters beside each other. A chief executive has acknowledged infidelity. A UN commission has found genocide. An arms manufacturer names his company’s processor inside a killing machine. These facts do not establish his responsibility for that genocide. They establish the urgency of finding out what his company supplied, what it knew and what it could have done. The evidentiary gap calls for investigation. It does not make the bedroom the more consequential place to look.

But put the letters AI in front of genocide and something curious happens to the grammar. The machine seems to acquire a will. The human being who authorized its use can slip out of the sentence altogether. Investigators have documented Israel’s use of intelligence systems called Lavender and The Gospel. The Israeli military says analysts independently assess intelligence before designating a military objective. I have found no public record identifying the processors on which those systems ran. What I want to know is who decided their output was reliable enough to act on, who could call a halt, and what happened when a family said the machine, or the people relying on it, had got it wrong.

Journalism has already shown what such questions can accomplish. The Associated Press documented a three-year, $133 million Microsoft contract with Israel’s defense ministry. In September 2025, after reporting on the surveillance of Palestinians, Microsoft disabled specified cloud storage and AI services to one ministry unit. Its review found evidence supporting elements of the reporting. The company could examine its business records. It could identify subscriptions. It could withdraw a service. These are useful verbs for the next annual meeting of any technology company whose directors profess uncertainty about what, in practice, they can do.

A chip possesses no special faculty for concealing its use. People make choices about what to record, what to disclose, whom to supply and what to do when credible evidence of abuse arrives. Hardware sold years ago can change hands beyond the maker’s knowledge. A current contract with a named customer presents a different degree of visibility and a different opportunity to act. A company can reasonably be asked to account for the information it had at the moment it still had a choice.

That is a recognizable inquiry into human conduct. What did you know? Whom did you expose to harm? When could you have stopped? We ask versions of those questions about sexual betrayal without finding them impossibly abstract. A company’s commercial relationships deserve the same insistence, especially when the potential harm is measured in human lives.

The countries inside the question

Russia offers two pieces of evidence that belong beside each other. Bloomberg traced $300 million in Dell servers imported by two Russian trading companies in five months of 2024. Specifications identified NVIDIA H100 chips in 998 of the 1,111 servers. Separately, Ukrainian investigators identified NVIDIA hardware in a Russian Lancet loitering munition and reported finding it in an S-71 cruise missile. NVIDIA says it stopped direct sales to Russia in March 2022. Nothing in the server investigation establishes that those shipments supplied those weapons. Together the accounts establish an uncomfortable fact about the reach of an American commercial decision. Direct sales can end on a certain date. The life of the product continues on somebody else’s calendar.

Iran comes into view through an Iranian-manufactured Shahed recovered in Ukraine, in which Ukrainian investigators identified an NVIDIA module. In France, reporting describes a classified defense supercomputer with more than a thousand GPUs, most of them NVIDIA’s. In Spain, an €18 million initial drone tender selected Skydio aircraft that carry NVIDIA hardware. Different countries, different purposes, different degrees of responsibility. The question travels because the technology does. Its answer has to be earned in each place.

Burma is where that discipline costs me something personally. I have known people there for whom the sound of an aircraft overhead carries the whole history of what the state is capable of doing to a village. Mizzima reported a delivery of fifteen drones to Min Aung Hlaing’s military in April 2024. I have found no evidence identifying an NVIDIA processor in that delivery. I will leave the sentence there. After years of asking the world to believe Burmese witnesses, the last thing I would do is spend their credibility on a detail I cannot establish. What they deserve is somebody willing to go looking.

An inquiry into mass killing must be exact because the accusation is grave. It must distinguish a manufacturer from a reseller, knowledge from ignorance, a preventable sale from hardware already beyond a company’s control. Such distinctions make an investigation credible. They should never become the paperwork behind which everyone disappears.

I could call Huang the butcher of Silicon Valley. How convenient that would be for the official who authorized procurement, the minister who could release the records, the commander who selected the target, the director who approved the terms. All of them could read to the end of the piece secure in the knowledge that the butcher was somebody else. I would prefer to see Huang at a hearing with the contracts in front of him. Which military customers have you investigated? What did you learn? Has your company ever walked away from a sale it could legally have made because of what the evidence told you would happen to other human beings?

And I would like the people asking those questions to arrive as thoroughly prepared as the reporters investigating his affairs. Bring the correspondence. Establish the dates. Identify who knew. Examine the power relationship. Follow the money. The skills already exist. What remains in question is the scale of suffering required to command their sustained attention.

I have spent enough of my life in the company of Buddhist teachings to distrust the pleasure of catching another human being in disgrace. There is a small relief in discovering that a billionaire has made an ordinary mess of his life. For a moment we understand the whole story. We know whom to judge. We can even enjoy our own good judgment on the way to breakfast.

There is something almost unbearable about that breakfast. We sit with a device in our hands, reading about a man’s sexual conduct, while elsewhere a father is trying to explain how his children died. The affair supplies the recognizable drama: desire, secrecy, betrayal. The father supplies names, ages and a tent. Somehow, it is the father whose story requires the more elaborate justification for our attention.

Sex can wound. Coercion, exploitation and betrayal deserve serious scrutiny. But what a civilization reveals about itself when the possibility of mass murder has to compete with the revelation that a powerful man has been having sex. What an obscene disproportion between the intimacy we demand from his private life and the opacity we tolerate in the commercial arrangements that may expose strangers to death.

Osama Abu Jama offers us no such satisfaction. He could give investigators the place, the gunfire, the order in which things happened. He could give them his sons’ names. Imagine asking him for more. Imagine explaining that before a board of directors can reasonably be troubled, he must identify the aircraft, establish who supplied its electronics and produce a chain of invoices reaching back from Rafah to the country of manufacture. Then imagine turning to the people who keep those invoices and asking, with the same persistence we bring to the private life of one married man, to see them.

A married man’s admission of infidelity tells us nothing about his responsibility for a military supply chain. The records might. Open them. Establish what was sold, who received it, what warnings arrived and who decided to continue. If there is evidence of knowing assistance in unlawful killing, pursue it to the people responsible, however wealthy, celebrated or far from the bodies they may be.

Muhib was nineteen. Elyas was seventeen. They woke up. Their father has given his account. We have heard the admission about sex. Now let us hear from the people with the records about the business of death.

About the Author

Alan Clements is an American author, human rights journalist, spoken-word artist, and former Buddhist monk. Ordained in Rangoon in 1979, he studied with Mahāsi Sayadaw and Sayadaw U Pandita. He later returned to Burma as a writer. In 1995, soon after Aung San Suu Kyi’s release from house arrest, he began the conversations that became The Voice of Hope. His reporting on Burma and its borderlands has followed the lives of people who have risked imprisonment, exile and death to bear witness to military rule.

Clements founded World Dharma Publications and is the author of Politics of the Heart: Nonviolence in an Age of Atrocity — Psychedelic Activism to End War, a work of spoken-word theatre that brings his experience as a meditator and war correspondent onto the same stage. His forthcoming three-volume collection, Patriarchy, Authoritarianism and the Role of the Divine Feminine in Contemporary Society: Conversations with Visionary Women, grew out of three years of conversations with fifty-five women. Readers can find his books, essays, and performances at https://t.co/SE9uLs89dH.

text:
[NVIDIA's Board Must Not Fire Jensen Huang. Congress Should Stop Its Excessive Pursuit. My Theory: An Emotional Campaign to Punish Jensen Huang Could Cost Humanity Opportunities We Can Never Recover]

Imagine America losing the very person who helped build its technological advantage, all in the name of protecting that advantage.
I believe we are dangerously close to confusing the means with the goal.

===================================
[The AI Revolution Was Never Inevitable]

Today, we talk about the AI revolution as though it was bound to happen.

But that is hindsight.

Before the breakthroughs, nobody knew how far deep learning would go.

Researchers were exploring possibilities, not following a guaranteed road to success.

And long before ChatGPT appeared, NVIDIA was making enormous bets on the computing power that would eventually make it possible.

That is what I find extraordinary.

-----------------+-----------------
[The Investment Came Before the Breakthrough]

In 2012, AlexNet showed that deep neural networks could achieve remarkable results in image recognition.

It was an important turning point.

But nobody could look at AlexNet and confidently predict the language AI revolution we see today.

The Transformer architecture appeared in 2017.

GPT-2 followed in 2019.

GPT-3 arrived in 2020.

By then, NVIDIA had already introduced the Volta V100 GPU with Tensor Core technology in 2017.

Tensor Cores are specialized circuits designed to perform the matrix calculations that neural networks rely on.

They did not appear overnight.

A chip released in 2017 reflects engineering and investment decisions made years earlier.

NVIDIA reported that Volta involved thousands of engineers working for more than three years.

Think about what that meant.

NVIDIA was a publicly traded company.

It had shareholders to satisfy, competitors to fight, and products to sell.

Yet it committed major resources to hardware whose future market was still uncertain.

A graphics company was betting heavily on a future beyond graphics.

And Jensen Huang was the CEO responsible for that direction.

Of course, engineers and other executives shaped those decisions.

We cannot simply attribute every successful invention to one person.

But the final responsibility for a strategic gamble of that size rests at the top.

If the gamble had failed, there would have been no applause.

Just wasted investment, weaker products, and angry shareholders.

-----------------+-----------------
[Hardware Made the Discoveries Economically Possible]

The Transformer did not succeed because it required Tensor Cores.

The original Transformer research used NVIDIA P100 GPUs, which did not have them.

But the architecture was well suited to the massive parallel calculations that GPUs could perform.

That mattered enormously.

A brilliant algorithm is not enough if training it takes an impossible amount of time or money.

GPUs turned many previously impractical experiments into affordable ones.

Then faster hardware made larger experiments possible.

Those experiments revealed new capabilities.

Researchers invested more effort.

Companies invested more money.

Hardware improved again.

This feedback loop helped drive the AI revolution.

The scaling laws did not come from NVIDIA.

But without sustained improvements in computing performance and cost, exploiting those laws at today's scale would have been much harder.

[The mathematics mattered. The hardware made it usable.]

===================================
[NVIDIA Was Willing to Abandon Its Own Assumptions]

NVIDIA did not reach this position by protecting everything it had already built.

In the 1990s, it backed an unusual graphics architecture with the NV1.

That approach did not become the industry standard.

NVIDIA changed direction and embraced the triangle-based graphics pipeline.

The RIVA 128 helped put the company on a much stronger footing.

Later, NVIDIA moved toward programmable graphics processors and unified shader architectures.

These were not minor product adjustments.

They required changes in how the company designed hardware and how developers used it.

David Kirk, NVIDIA's former chief scientist, was among the important technical leaders behind that evolution.

The lesson is simple.

A company that becomes too attached to its existing technology can miss the next wave.

NVIDIA repeatedly chose to rebuild parts of its own foundation.

-----------------+-----------------
[The Engineers Deserve Their Share of the Credit]

It would be ridiculous to tell NVIDIA's history as though Jensen Huang personally invented everything.

Ian Buck worked on the Brook programming system at Stanford and joined NVIDIA in 2004.

He became an important figure in the development of CUDA.

CUDA allows developers to use NVIDIA GPUs for general computing rather than graphics alone.

John Nickolls was another key architect of CUDA.

Bill Dally joined NVIDIA as chief scientist in 2009 and brought deep expertise in parallel computing and computer architecture.

Bryan Catanzaro played an important role in deep learning software and the development of cuDNN.

cuDNN is a library of highly optimized operations used to train neural networks.

These contributions mattered just as much as the physical chips.

A fast GPU is not particularly useful to AI researchers if exploiting its speed requires writing everything from scratch.

-----------------+-----------------
[The Talent Had to Change, Too]

NVIDIA originally grew around computer graphics, games, and C++ programming.

Deep learning required a different mix of expertise.

AI researchers increasingly worked in Python.

High-performance computing specialists understood how to make thousands of processors work efficiently together.

Compiler engineers knew how to turn high-level instructions into fast machine operations.

NVIDIA needed people who understood all these worlds.

And those worlds did not always speak the same language.

Python is convenient for research, but executing numerical calculations directly in Python can be slow.

The solution is not to make the GPU execute Python instructions one by one.

It is to let Python control highly optimized operations implemented in C++, CUDA, and specialized GPU hardware.

Libraries such as cuDNN helped make that approach practical.

The result was an ecosystem in which researchers could experiment quickly while the heavy calculations ran efficiently.

I suspect NVIDIA's willingness to bring together such different kinds of talent was one of its greatest organizational achievements.

-----------------+-----------------
[Supporting Developers Also Helped Design Better GPUs]

NVIDIA's software investments were not merely a way to sell existing hardware.

They also helped the company understand what its future hardware should do.

CUDA developers revealed which operations were slow.

AI researchers exposed bottlenecks that graphics applications might never encounter.

Engineers could then use that feedback when designing the next generation of GPUs.

Stephen Jones, a CUDA architect at NVIDIA, has described the close collaboration between software teams and hardware designers.

This creates another feedback loop.

Better software attracts more developers.

More developers reveal more problems.

Those problems guide better hardware.

Then the better hardware attracts still more developers.

That is difficult for competitors to reproduce quickly.

The advantage is not simply a chip.

It is an entire system of people, tools, hardware, and accumulated experience.

===================================
[Running a Chip Company Without Owning the Factories]

NVIDIA does not manufacture its advanced chips in its own semiconductor factories.

That does not make the manufacturing challenge disappear.

It makes coordination even more important.

NVIDIA must persuade other companies to invest billions of dollars in capacity for products whose demand may change dramatically.

The supply chain is a chain of enormous financial commitments.

One weak link can delay the entire product.

-----------------+-----------------
[HBM and CoWoS Are Strategic Decisions]

Modern AI accelerators need more than fast computing circuits.

They need enormous memory bandwidth.

HBM, or High Bandwidth Memory, places multiple memory layers together to move data rapidly.

SK-Hynix is one of the major suppliers of this technology.

But producing memory chips is only part of the problem.

The GPU and its memory must also be assembled into an advanced package.

TSMC's CoWoS technology helps connect these components at the required scale.

CoWoS is an advanced packaging method that allows powerful chips and high-bandwidth memory to work closely together.

As AI demand surged, both HBM and advanced packaging capacity became critical constraints.

NVIDIA could not simply order unlimited supplies.

Suppliers had to build facilities, purchase equipment, recruit engineers, and accept huge financial risks.

That requires credible demand forecasts, long-term commitments, and difficult negotiations.

If NVIDIA overestimates demand, the financial damage can be enormous.

If it underestimates demand, customers may wait months for hardware.

And if one supplier expands while another cannot, the extra capacity may be difficult to use.

This is not the kind of problem that can be solved by designing a faster circuit alone.

It requires leadership across an entire industrial network.

-----------------+-----------------
[The Foundry Relationship Was Built Over Decades]

NVIDIA's relationship with TSMC goes back to the 1990s.

The decision to rely on external semiconductor manufacturing helped NVIDIA focus resources on chip design and software.

Other companies, including Qualcomm and Broadcom, also helped establish the fabless semiconductor business model.

Apple later became another major customer of advanced contract manufacturing.

This division of labor transformed the industry.

But it also created deep interdependence.

NVIDIA's success now depends partly on investments made by TSMC, SK-Hynix, equipment manufacturers, and many less visible suppliers.

[Jensen Huang's job is not just to predict the future of AI.]

He must help convince an industrial ecosystem to invest in that future before the demand is certain.

And NVIDIA must keep making money while doing it.

That is a much harder task than the phrase "AI boom" suggests.

===================================
[When a Founder Leaves, the Company May Change]

This brings me to a difficult question.

How much does an exceptional founder still matter after a company becomes enormous?

A company is not just a collection of engineers and factories.

Its leaders influence which risks are tolerated, which projects survive, and which opportunities are ignored.

The effects can take years to become visible.

-----------------+-----------------
[Apple After Steve Jobs]

Steve Jobs was not Apple's only source of innovation.

And Apple did not stop innovating after his death.

Apple Watch, AirPods, and Apple Silicon were major achievements.

Apple Silicon, in particular, demonstrated extraordinary engineering capabilities.

But Apple has not yet established another consumer platform with the historical impact of the iPhone.

That does not prove Steve Jobs was irreplaceable.

It does raise an interesting question.

Can a company remain financially and technically excellent while becoming less willing to pursue a genuinely disruptive future?

A company can become exceptionally good at improving what already exists.

That is valuable.

But inventing the next category is a different skill.

-----------------+-----------------
[Microsoft Shows the Opposite Is Also Possible]

Bill Gates helped build Microsoft and recognized the importance of the internet during the 1990s.

But a founder is not always necessary for a company's next transformation.

Satya Nadella was not Microsoft's founder.

Under his leadership, Microsoft strengthened its cloud business and made an unusually early commitment to modern AI.

Microsoft announced a $1 billion investment in OpenAI in 2019, years before ChatGPT became a global phenomenon.

This is an important counterexample.

Removing or replacing a founder does not automatically destroy innovation.

What matters is whether the successor can recognize a new technological direction and commit resources before success becomes obvious.

Still, identifying such a successor is extremely difficult.

-----------------+-----------------
[Google Had the Research but Missed the First Consumer Breakthrough]

Google researchers introduced the Transformer architecture in 2017.

It became one of the foundations of modern language AI.

Google also had world-class AI researchers, enormous computing resources, and an established global business.

Yet OpenAI reached the public first with ChatGPT's explosive consumer breakthrough.

Google later reorganized its AI research efforts, bringing Google Brain and DeepMind together in 2023.

Demis Hassabis, one of DeepMind's founders, became the leader of Google DeepMind.

Google has since demonstrated major AI capabilities of its own.

So it would be simplistic to blame everything on Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepping back from day-to-day management.

But the case still illustrates a crucial point.

[Having the technology is not the same as having the organization that knows when to bet on it.]

-----------------+-----------------
[Meta Shows Why Founder-Led Bets Can Be Dangerous, Too]

Mark Zuckerberg committed enormous resources to virtual and augmented reality.

That strategy has been controversial, and its long-term return remains uncertain.

A founder with strong control can take risks that professional managers might avoid.

Sometimes that produces the next great platform.

Sometimes it burns through extraordinary amounts of money.

Meta has also pursued aggressive AI investment, including recruiting Alexandr Wang, the co-founder of Scale AI, into a senior leadership role.

Its AI products, including Muse, reflect that commitment.

But technical progress does not automatically establish that every strategic investment was financially wise.

Founder-led management has real dangers.

My argument is not that founders should be immune from accountability.

It is that their willingness to make unusual long-term bets can have immense value.

And that value must be included when judging whether to remove them.

===================================
[The Cost of an Innovation That Never Happens]

Corporate boards are often very good at identifying visible risks.

A failed investment shows up in financial statements.

A delayed product can be measured.

A scandal becomes a headline.

A stock-price decline is visible immediately.

But what about an investment that a cautious successor never approves?

What about a research program that gets canceled before it produces anything?

What about a talented engineer who leaves because the company no longer tolerates unusual ideas?

Those losses do not appear neatly in quarterly earnings.

Nobody can count the discoveries that were never made.

Nobody can interview the researchers who never got funding.

That is precisely why I worry about excessive caution.

[The most expensive corporate mistake may be the technology that is never born.]

And in a field moving as rapidly as AI, those lost opportunities could affect much more than one company's shareholders.

===================================
[Huawei Shows How Export Restrictions Can Backfire]

During the first Trump administration, the United States tightened restrictions on Huawei in 2019.

In 2020, those restrictions expanded to certain semiconductors manufactured overseas using American technology.

Then, in 2022, the Biden administration introduced broader restrictions on advanced AI chips destined for China.

The goal was to limit China's access to strategically important computing technology.

But there is a serious paradox.

When Chinese companies cannot buy NVIDIA GPUs, they must find alternatives.

One alternative is Huawei's Ascend family of AI processors.

Huawei had already announced Ascend in 2018, so the restrictions did not create the project from nothing.

But restrictions gave China an even stronger reason to accelerate domestic development.

Companies that might otherwise have bought NVIDIA products began exploring Chinese hardware.

Developers adapted software to run on those processors.

Engineering problems generated practical experience.

More customers created more reasons to improve the ecosystem.

Suppliers expanded.

Government investment followed.

Even if the domestic chips initially lagged behind NVIDIA, real-world adoption could help them improve.

Semiconductor competitiveness does not come from manufacturing chips alone.

It also depends on customers, developers, software, and years of practical experience.

[By restricting NVIDIA's sales, America may be handing China's AI chip industry the customers and development opportunities it needs to grow.]

That is quite a paradox.

A policy designed to protect American technological superiority may also strengthen the incentives for China to become technologically independent.

I believe this unintended effect deserves far more serious attention.

===================================
[Compliance Is a Means, Not the Ultimate Goal]

I am not arguing that the United States should abandon national security controls.

Advanced AI chips have legitimate military and intelligence applications.

Restrictions may be necessary to prevent sensitive technology from strengthening hostile military capabilities, weapons development, or mass surveillance.

The law must be followed.

And violations must be investigated.

But I worry about a different problem.

What happens when enforcing restrictions becomes more important than understanding why those restrictions exist?

The original goal is to protect national security.

Not to maximize the number of prohibited transactions.

Not to punish technology companies for the sake of punishment.

And certainly not to weaken American innovation without considering the consequences.

A government can enforce a policy so aggressively that it undermines the very advantage the policy was meant to protect.

[That is what happens when the means replace the goal.]

-----------------+-----------------
[An Alleged Workplace Affair Should Not Automatically End a Career]

There have also been reports concerning an alleged inappropriate personal relationship involving Jensen Huang and another NVIDIA executive.

Personal misconduct by a CEO cannot simply be dismissed as irrelevant.

A relationship involving unequal authority can raise serious questions about consent, favoritism, conflicts of interest, and workplace fairness.

Those issues deserve independent examination.

But the punishment should be proportionate to what is actually established.

An affair, by itself, should not automatically justify removing someone who has played such an important role in a company's technological development.

If an investigation establishes coercion, abuse of authority, retaliation, or serious violations of corporate obligations, that changes the assessment.

The point is not to excuse misconduct.

It is to distinguish the seriousness of the conduct from the intensity of public outrage.

Destroying a career should not be the default response to every personal scandal.

-----------------+-----------------
[Investigation and a Campaign for Dismissal Are Different Things]

American lawmakers have legitimate reasons to question how advanced AI chips are exported.

The controversy should not be reduced to a dispute between Democrats and Republicans.

On November 9, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Republican Representative Jim Banks issued a joint statement concerning advanced chip exports and the reported foreign intelligence operation.

Their statement raised questions about export controls.

It should not be presented as a direct demand to fire Jensen Huang.

NVIDIA's independent directors also have a responsibility to investigate serious allegations and protect the company.

That is corporate governance.

But an investigation should establish facts before deciding outcomes.

If weaknesses are found in export compliance, the company should correct them.

If governance needs strengthening, the board should strengthen it.

If conflicts of interest exist, they should be addressed.

There are many possible responses between doing nothing and removing the CEO.

I do not believe a dismissal should be treated as the inevitable proof that an investigation was taken seriously.

===================================
[What We Might Lose Has Not Been Invented Yet]

NVIDIA is far from perfect.

Jensen Huang is not beyond criticism.

A founder does not own a public company.

And no executive should be placed above the law.

But there is another side to the balance sheet.

Jensen Huang helped lead NVIDIA through multiple technological transitions.

He supported long-term investments that were far from guaranteed to succeed.

He helped build an organization combining graphics engineers, AI researchers, software developers, semiconductor architects, and manufacturing partners.

That organization became one of the foundations of the modern AI revolution.

This does not mean he is irreplaceable.

It means replacing him could carry consequences that are extraordinarily difficult to measure in advance.

The next generation of AI hardware has not been fully designed.

The next architectural breakthrough has not been discovered.

The next unexpected application of AI may not even have a name.

Those are the possibilities at stake.

I understand the need for export controls, corporate accountability, and independent investigations.

But I am deeply uncomfortable with the idea of treating the removal of Jensen Huang as an end in itself.

[What we need to protect is not just the GPUs that exist today.]

It is also the possibility of technologies that do not exist yet.

And if NVIDIA's board ever seriously considers removing him, I hope it weighs not only the risks of keeping him but also the enormous, invisible cost of what humanity might lose.

text:
@seanhannity: Now, soon-to-be House Minority Leader Jim Jordan, thank you for joining us. I know it's your first interview. I know you've been very busy. Let me start with this. You had a meeting with John Thune, who is the Minority Leader now going forward in the Senate. And Rick Scott had a resolution that the Senate stays in session. Now, there's a lot of work that can be done. Can a reconciliation bill be done? Can we fund the Department of War, for example? What do you think could be done?

@Jim_Jordan: As much as possible. We've got to use the majority while we have a chance, before the Democrats spend all the next Congress going after Republicans. So it was mostly a social meeting with Leader Thune. Congratulated him on getting re-elected as the leader of the Senate Republicans. And then we did talk a little bit about the lame duck. But of course, Speaker Johnson and Leader Scalise and our whole team will be working to try to get things done. We've got to fund the government. We've got to make sure that the debt ceiling gets dealt with. We've got this permitting bill. There's a FISA bill out there. So there's a lot of things we have to deal with. So we talked about a number of those things, but we'll be following the leadership of Speaker Johnson and trying to get as much done as we can while we still have the majority. And then next year, it's going to be about telling the American people how Republicans will be fighting for American families, fighting for the principles and values that I think really make our country special.

Sean Hannity: All right. Let's talk a little bit more about, specifically, the agenda items that you think you might be able to accomplish. Do you anticipate in any way that some members that are leaving may not be inclined to show up? Because if they're not willing to show up, that would really piss me off, and a lot of the American people off.

Jim Jordan: Well, first of all, Sean, I think we've got a strong leadership team now and going into the future. Strong leadership team. Whip Emmer is staying. Tom Emmer is going to stay as our whip. I think he's going to work on getting those guys here. We're all going to work on doing that so we can get things done. Lisa McClain is going to be our conference chair, continuing that role. And we've got a new guy in Brian Jack, young, sharp, talented guy, who will be heading the political operation for House Republicans as we go into the future. So we've got a good team. I think we're going to work on making sure everyone is here. Unlike the Democrats last night, we beat them on that vote because we had people here. We're going to be doing that, because we've got important things we need to try to get done in this lame duck session while we still have the majority.

Sean Hannity: All right. Let me ask you about this, on the issue of lawfare, which we do anticipate. What are your thoughts going into that battle and those fights?

Jim Jordan: It'll be every committee. There'll be a third impeachment. They can't help themselves. They're going to go after everyone in the cabinet. We've already seen that with Secretary of War Hegseth. They're going to go after people in the private sector, which I think is ridiculous. They've already sent hundreds of letters out to people in the government, outside the government. And then, of course, I think what they're probably going to also do, I think they're going to go after whoever they think our nominee is going to be. Will they go after Vice President Vance? Will they go after Secretary Rubio, Governor DeSantis, Governor Youngkin, Senator whoever they think might be our nominee? I think you'll see them target them, because for the Democrats, it's all about politics and going after their political opponents. So I think you're going to see all that. Every single committee, we'll have to work every day in committee, pushing back, going for the facts, because the letter that came from the Justice Department highlighted what they're up to. We had first Garcia on election night saying, lawyer up. And then the Justice Department sent out the letter and said, you can't just go after people for political harassment. There has to be a legislative purpose. And right now they can't cite one. They're just attacking their political opposition. But it'll be across the board in every single committee. And we are committed, as House Republicans, pushing back and giving the facts and the truth to the American people.

Sean Hannity: How do you reconcile secure borders and open borders? How do you reconcile higher taxes and lower taxes? How do you reconcile energy dominance versus no energy at all? I don't see how you thread the needle. I don't see the middle ground that people think might exist there.

Jim Jordan: No. You do what you just did, Sean. You do what Ronald Reagan talked about. You paint with big, bold colors and you show the difference. They're for big government and higher taxes. We're for lower taxes and more freedom. They're for an open border, sanctuary jurisdiction, and more violence. We're for a secure border and less crime. They're for a weak military. We're for a strong military. You highlight the differences. Dick Armey used to talk — former leader Dick Armey used to say, he says, when we act like us, we win. When we act like them, we lose. We need to act like Republicans and go to the American people every single day and tell them the truth. Here's what we're trying to do to help you and your family. Think about this, Sean. Right now, the average age of a first-time home buyer is 39 years old. We'd like to lower that. And how do you do that? There's things in the tax code that can incentivize people, and housing stock increases, and all those things you can do that are going to help that young family. And here's the other thing I'm excited about. Although it was a tough night for us a week and a half ago, we got 35 new Republicans coming in. Amazing people. This newer, younger generation of Republicans that I think are going to help us re-energize our party. People like Austin Rogers from Florida. Michael Alfonso, 26-year-old from northern Wisconsin. Sydney Gruters from Tampa, Florida. We got all these young people. Jessica Steinman, a lawyer from Texas. All these new young people coming into our party who are going to help us show the American people why we're fighting for them. Even though Democrats say it, they're going to do all this crazy lawfare stuff and these crazy investigations. We're going to be fighting for American families.

Sean Hannity: And as you said, when Democrats offer more government, we will offer more freedom. And there's one thing that I don't think any of them are thinking about. Donald J. Trump is still president. That is a massive check and balance on any agenda item they may have. Don't you think?

Jim Jordan: No, it sure is. And I'm sure we have to set the House position and argue when they bring it up. We've got to fight in committee and on the House floor and tell the truth and the facts about what they're trying to do. Medicare for All, take away private health insurance. We got to do all that. And then you have the president with the ability to veto the crazy things that they pass.

Sean Hannity: All right. Jim Jordan, congratulations. We hopefully will talk to you often.

Jim Jordan: Thank you.
