text:
$CRWV Q3 2026 earnings: CoreWeave's operating margin rebounds, but its debt load keeps climbing

CoreWeave, which rents AI server clusters to tech companies, grew sales and operating profit while its interest bill swelled. Revenue rose 168% from a year ago as newly wired data centers came online, and operating margin excluding one-offs doubled from last quarter to 10%. Chief executive Michael Intrator raised the full-year profit plan by 26%, which by our math points to a 16.5% operating margin in the fourth quarter.

• Revenue: $𝟑,𝟔𝟔𝟏𝐌 (+168.2% from a year ago)
• Operating margin, excluding one-offs: 𝟏𝟎% (5% last quarter)
• Revenue backlog: $𝟏𝟑𝟐.𝟓𝐁 (+$28.3B from last quarter)
• Full-year operating profit outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝟐𝟔% (middle of the range: $1.325B)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because operating margins rebounded a quarter ahead of plan and contracted backlog jumped by $28 billion to $132.5 billion. That proves early data center costs fade once customers start billing. The caution: total debt reached $48 billion, fourth-quarter interest is set to top $1 billion, and the group opened a 35-million-share stock sale programme.

The question now is whether operating profit can grow fast enough to cover interest costs without steady shareholder dilution. Either higher-margin contracts and $9 billion in upfront customer deposits fund the build-out, or rising debt service forces ongoing stock sales. Fourth-quarter cash flow and share count will show the balance.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐝
"This was a breakout quarter for CoreWeave, with revenue increasing by more than $1 billion sequentially and adjusted operating margins reaching double digits a quarter ahead of plan," chief executive Michael Intrator said. Operating income excluding one-offs reached $379 million, or 10.4% of revenue, beating the $200–260 million outlook as newly wired data centers began billing.

• Cost of revenue (direct data center and power costs): 32.3% of sales, down 1.8 percentage points from last quarter
• Technology and infrastructure (server depreciation and engineering): 55.3% of sales, down 3.2 percentage points from last quarter
• General and administrative (corporate overhead): 5.1% of sales, down 6.0 percentage points from a year ago
• Full-year operating profit outlook, excluding one-offs: raised 26% at the middle of the range to $1.325 billion

The rebound matters because it shows that early start-up costs fade once customers start using the servers. By our math, the raised full-year outlook implies fourth-quarter operating profit excluding one-offs of $797 million, or 16.5% of implied revenue, matching the margin the AI cloud provider earned before its recent building spree.

What to watch: fourth-quarter operating margin excluding one-offs when full-year results arrive. A reading near 16.5% would confirm that newer contracts and higher prices cover rising equipment depreciation.

🟢🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐏𝐚𝐬𝐭 $𝟏𝟑𝟐 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
Revenue backlog—contracted future revenue from remaining performance obligations and other committed deals—climbed to $132.5 billion from $104.2 billion in the second quarter. By our math, CoreWeave added $28.3 billion of net new backlog and booked about $32.0 billion in total contracts after replacing the $3.66 billion recognized as revenue during the quarter.

That rebounds from the second quarter's $4.6 billion net addition, because deals signed early in the third quarter entered the ledger alongside new wins with Canva, Substack and Wayve and expanded agreements with OpenAI and Perplexity. Intrator also noted "approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone", which provides upfront cash to help wire new sites.

What to watch: fourth-quarter cash flow from deferred revenue and customer deposits. Collecting the $9 billion would prove that customers are still funding CoreWeave's build-out upfront.

🟢 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐚 𝐑𝐮𝐛𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬
CoreWeave rents graphics processing units (GPUs) to companies building artificial intelligence, and its advantage rests on deploying NVIDIA's newest chips first while adding software tools. This quarter the cloud provider brought multi-rack NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems online for customer Cognition, achieving 4.8 times the output of prior GB200 racks, and launched CoreWeave Forge, "the AI development environment that integrates training, inference, evaluation, and agent development workflows".

To broaden its customer base beyond five-year deals, the group closed a $2.6 billion loan called the DDTL 5.5 Facility, "CoreWeave’s first financing facility designed to support shorter-duration customer contracts". Because corporate buyers often prefer shorter commitments than AI labs, dedicated financing lets the business sign them without tying up its own cash.

What to watch: the duration breakdown of revenue backlog in the third-quarter filing. A rising share of contracts under 24 months would show that shorter enterprise deals are scaling.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Intrator said CoreWeave's growth rests on multiple funding sources, and deep access to loans backed by customer contracts has let it scale rapidly. Even so, total debt including finance leases rose 34.7% in a single quarter to $47.52 billion by our math, while net interest expense jumped 172.9% from a year ago to $846 million.

• Third-quarter net loss: $709 million, compared with a $110 million loss a year ago
• Third-quarter net interest expense: $846 million, more than double the $379 million of operating profit excluding one-offs
• Fourth-quarter interest expense outlook: $1.05–1.15 billion, up 30% at the middle of the range from the third quarter
• New capital programmes: $4.2 billion in convertible notes and an at-the-market stock sales programme for up to 35 million shares

This cuts against the profit rebound narrative because interest bills are growing faster than operating profit. By our math, even if fourth-quarter operating profit excluding one-offs reaches the implied $797 million, the $1.10 billion middle of the interest outlook will leave the business roughly $300 million short of covering its interest before taxes.

What to watch: shares issued under the 35-million-share stock sales programme in fourth-quarter filings. Heavy stock sales would mean customer prepayments and loans are not enough to fund the build-out.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐬 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐬
Building AI data centers requires upfront cash long before customers pay their monthly bills. CoreWeave raised the low end of its full-year capital expenditures plan by $2 billion to $37–39 billion—its third increase this year—to "deploy infrastructure and deliver it to customers sooner than planned", while keeping its year-end active power target at more than 1.85 gigawatts.

In the third quarter, cash purchases of property and equipment hit $9.44 billion against $1.98 billion of operating cash flow, leaving a $7.47 billion free cash flow deficit by our math. Because the company has already spent $23.56 billion in cash on equipment over the first nine months, the full-year plan requires massive fourth-quarter spending and a 32% single-quarter jump in revenue to $4.84 billion.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue against the implied $4.84 billion target. A shortfall would show that higher capital spending is reflecting equipment inflation rather than faster customer delivery.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Five standing risks from prior quarters received no new figures in the third-quarter earnings release because their disclosures live in the quarterly filing or represent multi-year industry tests.

• Customer concentration: the top three customers accounted for 72% of second-quarter revenue; the third-quarter filing's customer footnote will show whether new enterprise wins reduced that share.
• AI compute pricing cycle: whether current rental rates reflect a temporary chip shortage will be tested when older server contracts come up for renewal in 2027 and 2028.
• Dependence on NVIDIA: the server fleet remains built around NVIDIA chips; customer adoption of alternative chips over coming quarters would test this reliance.
• Power grid constraints: contracted power reached 4.6 gigawatts, but turning it into 8 gigawatts of active power by 2030 depends on local utility hookups each quarter.
• Shareholder litigation: pending securities class action lawsuits received no update in the release; the filing's legal footnote will carry any changes.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐆𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲
CoreWeave expanded its international contracted power past 1.3 gigawatts across India, Indonesia and Spain, while partnering with defence contractor Leidos and DARPA to run government and national security AI workloads. To protect its data center build-out from component bottlenecks, the company also signed a multi-year supply deal with Solidigm for priority access to enterprise solid-state storage drives.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒,𝟐𝟖𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Uncollected customer bills—accounts receivable—jumped 68.4% from last quarter to $4.28 billion, outpacing the 42.2% rise in quarterly revenue. That buildup absorbed $1.74 billion of operating cash flow during the third quarter, reversing a $421 million rise in the second quarter and showing that late-quarter billings had not yet been collected in cash.

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Total deferred revenue—cash customers have paid upfront for cloud services not yet delivered—reached $10.00 billion by our math, up 87.5% from a year ago and up from $9.69 billion last quarter. Prepayments added $2.13 billion to third-quarter operating cash flow, offsetting the jump in uncollected bills.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟓𝟓𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Weighted-average diluted shares rose 12.2% from a year ago to 559 million, up from 551 million in the second quarter and 527 million in the first quarter. The steady increase reflects private stock placements and employee stock compensation, before any sales under the new 35-million-share equity programme.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏𝟑.𝟎–𝟏𝟑.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $12.4–13.2 billion
Raised. The middle of the full-year range moved up $350 million to $13.15 billion, or 156.3% growth from 2025. By our math, that leaves $4.84 billion for the fourth quarter—up 207.6% from a year ago against an easy comparison and up 32.1% from the third quarter. It is the second raise this year (+$300M, +$350M); if the five-quarter average beat of 6.3% holds, fourth-quarter revenue would reach $5.14 billion.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟏.𝟐𝟕𝟓–𝟏.𝟑𝟕𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $960 million–$1.15 billion
Raised. Management lifted the middle of the plan by $270 million, or 25.6%, to $1.325 billion, nearly double last year's $666 million. By our math, that leaves $797 million for the fourth quarter, more than double the third quarter's $379 million and equal to a 16.5% margin on implied fourth-quarter sales. This is the second raise (+$55M, +$270M).

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: $𝟑𝟕–𝟑𝟗 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $35–39 billion
Raised. CoreWeave lifted the bottom of the range by $2 billion, moving the middle up $1 billion to $38 billion as it deploys equipment earlier than planned. That is more than two and a half times last year's $14.89 billion company-defined spending and marks the third increase this year (+$500M, +$4,000M, +$1,000M at the middle of the range).

𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫: >𝟏.𝟖𝟓 𝐠𝐢𝐠𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐬  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from >1.85 gigawatts
Unchanged. The company still expects to finish 2026 with more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power across its data centers. Having added over 200 megawatts in the third quarter to surpass 1.7 gigawatts, the business needs less than 150 megawatts in the fourth quarter to clear the floor, making the target easily achievable.

𝐐𝟒 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞: $𝟏.𝟎𝟓–𝟏.𝟏𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. Fourth-quarter interest expense is set to reach $1.10 billion at the middle of the range, up 183.5% from a year ago and up 30.0% from the third quarter's $846 million. The step-up follows $10.30 billion of gross debt issued in the third quarter, including $4.2 billion of convertible notes and the new $2.6 billion loan facility.

𝐄𝐱𝐢𝐭-𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐧𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐮𝐧-𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝐀𝐑𝐑): $𝟐𝟎–𝟐𝟏 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $18.5–19.5 billion
Raised. Annualized run-rate revenue (ARR)—December revenue multiplied by 12—moved up $1.5 billion at the middle of the range to $20.5 billion. By our math, implied fourth-quarter revenue of $4.84 billion equals a $19.34 billion annual pace across the whole quarter, so clearing $20.5 billion in December requires capacity additions to build through year-end.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐨𝐩-𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝟕𝟐%?
The top three customers generated 72% of second-quarter revenue. With $28.3 billion of net new backlog added in the third quarter and new enterprise wins announced, did the share of revenue and backlog from the largest three AI labs decline?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
Last quarter management reported over $100 million of booked recurring revenue for managed inference and targeted at least $250 million by year-end. What was the figure at the end of the third quarter, and how much of it is already recognized in revenue?

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐞 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝?
CoreWeave set up an at-the-market stock programme for up to 35 million shares alongside $9 billion of expected fourth-quarter customer prepayments. Under what conditions will management sell shares rather than fund equipment with customer deposits and contract-backed loans?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲-𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟑?

$DPC Q3 2026 earnings: Doncasters raises its sales outlook, but factory builds consume cash

Doncasters, a maker of precision metal castings for aircraft engines and power turbines, beat its initial post-IPO plan and raised its full-year targets. Third-quarter revenue rose 39% from a year ago to $308 million, while profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, and one-offs grew 56% as North American factory margins expanded. Chief executive Mike Quinn also signed a fifth major customer contract and disclosed that the order book has reached $1 billion.

• Revenue: $𝟑𝟎𝟖.𝟏𝐌 (+39% from a year ago (+28% stripping Europe metal pass-through))
• Adjusted EBITDA: $𝟓𝟖.𝟐𝐌 (+56% from a year ago; margin up 2 points to 18.9%)
• Order book: ~$𝟏.𝟎𝐁 (up 38% from $725M in December 2025)
• Full-year 2026 revenue outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟏𝟎𝟑𝐌 (2027 outlook introduced at +14% growth)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the raised 2026 outlook and new 2027 targets ended fears of a second-half slowdown. In addition, the company closed the sale of its loss-making Ivostud fastener unit, locked in customer funding for 80% of a $200 million German factory expansion, and took a controlling stake in a GE Aerospace supplier. The bad news: capital spending will more than double next year to $145–170 million, leaving 2027 free cash flow at roughly zero.

The question now is how much of the 14% projected sales growth for 2027 comes from underlying demand versus the newly acquired Montana joint venture and passed-through metal inflation. If volume and contract pricing drive the increase, margins will keep climbing; if metal surcharges and acquisitions carry it, cash conversion will lag. The full-year report's breakdown of acquisition revenue and metal pass-through will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫-𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐭𝐨 $𝟏 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
Doncasters makes precision metal castings and heat-resistant superalloys for aircraft engines and industrial gas turbines (IGT), which are large generators used for power plants. Chief executive Mike Quinn said the company's "visible growth has never been stronger or clearer, with over 70% of our revenue under Long-Term Agreements (LTAs) and an order book of approximately $1 billion". That backlog is up 38%, or $275 million by our math, since December.

During the quarter, the manufacturer signed its fifth Strategic Customer Partnership, a minimum 10-year contract with a gas turbine maker. To deliver it, the group will expand its factory in Bochum, Germany. The project costs over $200 million, but the customer plans to fund about 80% of the bill. This deal adds over $100 million in yearly sales by 2032, lifting the total target across all five partnerships above $300 million.

What to watch: capital commitments and customer advance payments in the full-year filing. Rising customer advances will confirm that turbine makers are paying for the German factory expansion on schedule.

🟢🟢 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐮𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬
Doncasters has been renegotiating its long-term customer contracts to raise prices while adding factory equipment to clear supply backlogs. That combination showed up in its Engine Products division, which sells components for aircraft engines and power turbines across Europe and North America. Combined segment profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, excluding one-offs (adjusted EBITDA), jumped 70% from a year ago to $61.3 million, lifting the division's margin by 3.8 percentage points to 23.8%.

• North America Engine Products revenue: $100.6 million, up 37.1% from a year ago
• North America segment adjusted EBITDA: $23.6 million, up 129.1%, with margin up 9.5 percentage points to 23.5%
• North America adjusted cost of sales: fell 8.3 percentage points as a share of segment revenue, to 68.1% by our math
• Group selling, general, and administrative overhead: fell 6.6 percentage points of revenue to 16.2% by our math

North America carried the margin expansion because new equipment at the Groton, Connecticut plant boosted output alongside higher contract prices. What to watch: North America Engine Products margin in the fourth quarter. Holding above 23% will show that the Groton productivity gains and contract price increases are durable.

🟢 𝐈𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐖𝐚𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬; 𝐈𝐯𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐝 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝
Three months ago, Doncasters issued a full-year outlook that pointed to about $515 million of second-half sales by our math. Instead, third-quarter revenue rose 39.2% to $308.1 million, led by 45% growth in aerospace and 43% in industrial gas turbines. The company lifted its 2026 revenue target by $102.5 million at the middle of the range, proving the initial post-IPO plan was cautious.

Separately, the group sold Ivostud, a struggling fastener unit declared "non-core to our casting and superalloy businesses", on October 23 after taking a $17.8 million write-down. Removing Ivostud lifts the third-quarter adjusted EBITDA margin in Turbo Wheels, its automotive turbocharger division, from 4.9% to 10.2%. What to watch: reported Turbo Wheels margin in the first quarter of 2027, the first full period without Ivostud.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐖𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐮𝐭 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰
Doncasters highlighted $111.2 million of third-quarter free cash flow excluding one-offs, up from $6.0 million a year ago. However, reported free cash flow was negative $100.5 million for the quarter and negative $154.3 million for the first nine months because the company paid out $217.2 million in cash to settle a pre-IPO management bonus plan. More importantly, the new outlook shows underlying cash generation will drop to about zero next year.

• 2026 capital expenditure outlook: raised from $55–60 million to $67–77 million to buy land and buildings for its Montana joint venture
• 2027 capital expenditure outlook: $145–170 million, more than double the 2026 pace, for the German plant and a UK building purchase
• 2027 free cash flow outlook: negative $20 million to positive $20 million, despite adjusted EBITDA rising to $240–260 million

This matters because the group is now running four major factory builds at once across Germany, the UK, Alabama, and Mexico while committing $157.5 million a year in capital spending. If aircraft or turbine makers slow their orders during this build phase, Doncasters will burn cash before the new plants generate sales in 2029. What to watch: fourth-quarter capital expenditure against the implied $33–43 million remainder.

🔴 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐝 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥
When specialty metals like hafnium get more expensive, Doncasters passes the extra cost to customers through contract surcharges. These surcharges add to reported sales dollar-for-dollar without adding any profit, and the 18-to-24-week manufacturing lag ties up cash in inventory. In the third quarter, metal cost pass-through in Europe alone reached $25.7 million, compared to $15 million across the entire company in the first half of the year.

By our math, stripping out just the European metal pass-through lowers third-quarter total revenue growth from 39.2% to 27.6%. The surcharges also reduced the group's adjusted EBITDA margin by 0.9 percentage points, up from a 0.6-point drag in the second quarter, and helped push inventories up 45.9% since December to $264.0 million. What to watch: total company metal pass-through dollars in the full-year report, to see how much of the revenue beat was pure metal inflation.

🔴 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐏𝐚𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡 𝐨𝐧 𝐏𝐞𝐫-𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Doncasters excludes employee stock-based compensation from its adjusted EBITDA and adjusted earnings per share, treating it as non-core. However, its new outlook table lists a recurring "Option-based compensation scheme" cost of about $40 million in 2026 and another $40 million in 2027. That ongoing expense equals 16% of next year's expected $250 million adjusted EBITDA, and shares outstanding already rose 32.6% from a year ago to 149.7 million after the June listing.

What to watch: diluted share count in 2027 against the 149 million assumption in the outlook. Any increase above 149 million will show that the $40 million option plan is diluting shareholders faster than the company's plan assumes.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐆𝐄 𝐉𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭
On October 30, Doncasters bought a 50% stake in Montana Precision Products, a joint venture with GE Aerospace unit Unison "producing small structural castings and tube and duct assemblies for aerospace applications". Management expects the cash deal to add to earnings within a year and included it in the 2027 outlook. Separately, Quinn announced "our first, albeit small, contract to supply casting product into the Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) end market in 2027" inside Turbo Wheels.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞, 𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟖𝟏.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Non-current deferred revenue — cash customers have paid in advance for multi-year capacity and parts not yet delivered — jumped to $81.9 million on the balance sheet, up from zero in December 2025. On the nine-month cash flow statement, deferred consideration generated a $93.1 million cash inflow, helping offset the $93.7 million cash drain from rising inventories.

𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟗𝟏.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
The UK-based engineering group ended the quarter with $277.1 million in cash and $85.6 million in debt, compared to $524.6 million of net debt excluding shareholder loans in December. In September, management replaced its term loan with a $325 million unsecured credit line due 2029, which cuts expected net interest expense from $105 million this year to about zero in 2027.

𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟏.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Reported net income turned positive at $31.8 million, or $0.21 per share, reversing a $42.2 million loss a year ago and a $131.1 million loss last quarter. Lower interest costs after the IPO debt payoff and a $49.2 million income tax benefit outweighed a $17.8 million write-down on the Ivostud disposal and a $21.5 million debt refinancing charge.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏,𝟏𝟏𝟓–𝟏,𝟏𝟑𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $1,000–1,040 million
Raised. The company lifted the middle of its full-year sales plan by $102.5 million, or 10%, citing "strong business performance". By our math, subtracting nine-month sales of $813.4 million leaves $309.1 million for the fourth quarter, almost unchanged from the third quarter's $308.1 million.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟐𝟎𝟒–𝟐𝟎𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $182–187 million
Raised. Management increased the middle of the range by $21 million, pointing to 48.6% growth from 2025's $138.3 million by our math. That leaves $59.4 million for the fourth quarter, slightly above the third quarter's $58.2 million and resulting in an 18% full-year margin, or about 19% excluding metal cost pass-through.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏,𝟐𝟑𝟎–𝟏,𝟑𝟑𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. The initial 2027 plan calls for $1,280 million at the middle of the range, or 14.0% growth over the raised 2026 midpoint by our math. The target includes the newly acquired controlling stake in Montana Precision Products and removes the sold Ivostud business.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟐𝟒𝟎–𝟐𝟔𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. At the $250 million middle of the range, profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, and one-offs grows 21.7% over the 2026 midpoint by our math. The implied margin rises from 18.0% in 2026 to 19.5% in 2027, supported by higher contract pricing and the Montana acquisition.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒: $𝟏.𝟎𝟎–𝟏.𝟏𝟎  ⇒ stable
New. The plan targets $1.05 at the middle of the range, assuming a 27% tax rate, zero net interest expense, and 149 million shares. It excludes roughly $40 million in non-cash option compensation.

𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰: ($𝟐𝟎)–$𝟐𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
New. The outlook centers on zero free cash flow for 2027 because capital expenditure is planned to rise to $145–170 million, up from $67–77 million in 2026, to build out the fifth customer partnership in Germany and purchase a UK building.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐚 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐝𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
The 2027 outlook includes the newly acquired stake in Montana Precision Products and removes Ivostud, but the release gives neither the purchase price nor the joint venture's revenue. Without those figures, investors cannot separate underlying 2027 growth from acquisition additions.

𝐈𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐨𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰?
The 2027 outlook includes total capital spending for the fifth partnership, where the customer will fund 80% of the >$200 million project. Management did not clarify whether its ($20) million to $20 million free cash flow target counts customer reimbursements inside operating cash flow.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐬-𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐢𝐧 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚?
The release disclosed $25.7 million of third-quarter metal cost pass-through in Europe and a 0.9-point group margin drag, but gave no dollar figure for North America. Knowing the total pass-through is needed to measure true volume and pricing growth.

𝐃𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐢 𝐚𝐞𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟑 𝐢𝐧 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫?
Last quarter, management committed to begin heat-treat installation and aerospace certification at its Mexicali plant in October 2026 so it could operate as a full aerospace site in 2027. The third-quarter release gave no update on that schedule.

text:
One of the things I didn’t expect when I founded @LunarForgeSpace was that half of the people who would join me on this mission would be military veterans.

Army, Navy, Air Force, Air Force Intelligence.

I wasn’t specifically recruiting veterans. But it turns out that when you’re building autonomous construction systems for the Moon, the people who raise their hands are often the ones who’ve already spent their careers solving problems in some of the most extreme and unforgiving environments on Earth.

From nuclear submarine operations to national security space programs, they’ve worked on missions where failure isn’t an option.

They don’t shy away from hard problems. They take ownership. They find solutions. And they bring a level of discipline, resilience, and mission focus that’s difficult to teach.

Building infrastructure on the Moon requires more than technical excellence. It requires people who are willing to take on challenges that have never been solved before, work through uncertainty, and stay committed when things get difficult.

Working alongside people who chose to serve and defend this country is one of the things I’m most proud of as a founder.

To our team and to every veteran out there, thank you for your service. I’m grateful that the same people who helped protect our future on Earth are now helping us build humanity’s future beyond it.

text:
𝐌𝐈𝐋𝐈𝐓𝐀𝐑𝐘 𝐑𝐄𝐂𝐑𝐔𝐈𝐓𝐌𝐄𝐍𝐓 𝐉𝐔𝐒𝐓 𝐏𝐎𝐒𝐓𝐄𝐃 𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐁𝐄𝐒𝐓 𝐍𝐔𝐌𝐁𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐈𝐍 𝟏𝟓 𝐘𝐄𝐀𝐑𝐒 — 𝐄𝐕𝐄𝐑𝐘 𝐀𝐂𝐓𝐈𝐕𝐄-𝐃𝐔𝐓𝐘 𝐁𝐑𝐀𝐍𝐂𝐇 𝐇𝐈𝐓 𝐈𝐓𝐒 𝐆𝐎𝐀𝐋

Three years ago, the Army, Navy and Air Force all 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐠𝐨𝐚𝐥𝐬 in the same fiscal year — the worst stretch in decades. Not one branch pulled it off.

Fiscal year 2025 just flipped the script completely. The Army signed 𝟔𝟐,𝟎𝟓𝟎 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐬 against a 61,000 target. The Navy blew past its number with 𝟒𝟒,𝟎𝟗𝟔 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐬 against a 40,600 goal — the biggest margin of any active-duty service. The Air Force and Space Force both cleared their marks too, and the Marine Corps hit its number exactly, which officers say reflects discipline, not a struggle.

A Marine veteran who’s spoken with troops across every branch put it plainly on a recent interview: “𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘦𝘯𝘳𝘰𝘭𝘭𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘱𝘭𝘶𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘴𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘺 𝘣𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘦 𝘉𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘦, 𝘓𝘭𝘰𝘺𝘥 𝘈𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘯 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘦, 𝘱𝘭𝘶𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘣𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘩. 𝘗𝘦𝘵𝘦 𝘏𝘦𝘨𝘴𝘦𝘵𝘩 𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘰𝘧 𝘢 𝘴𝘶𝘥𝘥𝘦𝘯 𝘪𝘵 𝘴𝘬𝘺𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘬𝘦𝘵𝘴 𝘢𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘴𝘴 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘣𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘩.”

He described something else nobody can fake: hundreds of Navy SEALs and combat veterans physically marching on Washington during Hegseth’s Senate confirmation fight just to show up for him. “𝘠𝘰𝘶’𝘷𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘪𝘯 𝘩𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘺.”

The Pentagon credits the Trump administration. Skeptics note the rebound started before the election. Either way, the 𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐣𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐞 — the people who serve — are voting with their feet.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐫𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐢𝐭𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐟.

text:
$SPB Q4 2026 earnings: Spectrum Brands lifts profit, but sales fall across all units

Spectrum Brands, the maker of Spectracide bug spray and Remington shavers, expanded its profit margins even as fourth-quarter sales slipped in all three divisions. Underlying sales excluding currency fell 3% because bad weather and full store warehouses hurt lawn and garden restocking, while North American appliance sales dropped. However, higher prices and factory savings lifted gross margin by 2.6 percentage points, pushing operating cash profit excluding tariff refund costs up 15%, well above what the company's own full-year plan pointed to. Chief executive David Maura set a fiscal 2027 plan for flat to low-single-digit sales and underlying profit growth.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago, ex-currency: -𝟑.𝟏% (reported net sales $713.2M (-2.8%))
• Q4 Adjusted EBITDA, excluding tariff refund costs: $𝟕𝟑.𝟏𝐌 (+15.3% from a year ago)
• Net debt to Adjusted EBITDA: 𝟎.𝟕𝟕𝐱 (1.58x a year ago)
• Fiscal 2027 sales and Adjusted EBITDA outlook: 𝟎–𝟑% 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 (flat to low single digits, ex-refunds)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because wider profit margins and tariff refund cash balanced out weaker store restocking and a stalled appliance deal. Beating the fourth-quarter profit implied by the prior plan shows management set a cautious bar, and collecting tariff refunds cut net debt below one times cash profit. The bad news: Home and Garden sales fell 9% on leftover retailer stock, and rival Helen of Troy rejected a takeover bid from the company's Oaktree-backed appliance unit.

The question now is whether pet and garden sales can grow without favorable currency while the appliance unit pursues a contested takeover. Either new products drive real volume gains and a disciplined deal, or store overstock and appliance shelf losses keep total underlying sales flat for another year. Retailer spring restocking orders and Helen of Troy's response to the public bid will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬
Spectrum Brands makes pet supplies, bug sprays, and small kitchen appliances. Chief executive David Maura said that in Home and Personal Care (HPC), the appliance and grooming unit, "while top-line pressures persisted as expected, the team delivered strong margin expansion, a direct reflection of disciplined execution and a clear focus on profitability." Across the group, gross margin rose 2.6 percentage points to 37.6% because the cost of making products fell 2.7 points of sales.

• Cost of goods sold: 62.4% of sales, down from 65.0% a year ago
• Selling and administrative overhead: 34.2% of sales, up from 30.9% a year ago
• HPC Adjusted EBITDA margin excluding tariff refunds: 8.8%, up 3.5 percentage points

Higher prices, lower retail promotional spending, reduced tariff rates, and factory cost savings drove the gross margin gain. That improvement easily covered a 3.4-point rise in selling and administrative overhead, lifting company Adjusted EBITDA (operating cash profit before interest, taxes, and one-off items) by 15.3% excluding tariff refund costs.

What to watch: first-quarter gross margin and appliance profit margins. Holding gross margin above 37% without the help of early retailer orders ahead of the software rollout would show the cost savings are permanent.

🟢 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐚 𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Three months ago, management raised its full-year target for Adjusted EBITDA excluding tariff refunds to mid-single-digit growth. By our math, that full-year outlook pointed to $56.4–62.1 million of fourth-quarter Adjusted EBITDA, which would have meant a decline of 2% to 11% from a year ago.

Instead, the consumer products maker delivered $73.1 million excluding $3.2 million of tariff refund expenses, up 15.3% from a year ago. Full-year Adjusted EBITDA excluding refunds grew 9.8% to $317.4 million. Beating the implied fourth-quarter target proves the prior outlook was cautious, though it does not erase the fourth-quarter sales drop.

What to watch: whether management raises its fiscal 2027 outlook after the first half. Starting the new year with a plan for flat to low-single-digit profit growth after nearly 10% growth this year tests if leadership is setting another low bar.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐁𝐢𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚 𝐒𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐩𝐬
Spectrum Brands wants to separate its Home and Personal Care (HPC) unit, which sells Remington shavers and George Foreman grills, and use its clean balance sheet for deals. In May, it partnered with investment firm Oaktree Capital Management to form Empower Brands. Last week, Empower Brands "announced its interest to acquire Helen of Troy", a rival consumer goods company, but Maura said leadership was "disappointed by their rejection of our offer".

While the company pursues a public takeover fight to build scale, the appliance unit's own sales are still shrinking. Underlying sales in HPC fell 2.3% in the fourth quarter and 6.1% for the full year. Worse, fourth-quarter sales "benefited from retailer orders in advance of the S4/Hana ERP go-live", meaning customers stocked up early before the company switched software systems.

Even with those early orders, North American appliance and personal care sales dropped in the low double digits because of "distribution losses in Home Appliances and increased competitive pressure in Personal Care". That makes an acquisition more urgent to fix the division's scale, but a public pursuit after a rejected bid raises the risk of overpaying.

What to watch: any revised offer terms for Helen of Troy and first-quarter HPC sales in North America. When the early software-related orders reverse next quarter, the underlying sales drop in North America will look steeper.

🔴 𝐆𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐞𝐭 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰
"The underlying performance across all three segments demonstrates the strength of our business fundamentals," chief executive David Maura said. Supporters point to full-year sales growth of 5.1% in Global Pet Care (GPC), which makes dog chews and aquarium supplies, and 3.9% in Home and Garden (H&G), which makes Spectracide and Cutter bug sprays. In the fourth quarter, however, sales excluding currency fell in all three divisions.

• Home and Garden underlying sales: down 9.3% in Q4, after rising 19.1% in Q3
• Global Pet Care underlying sales: down 1.1% in Q4, with Aquatics down low double digits
• Total company underlying sales: down 3.1% in Q4 and down 0.3% for the full year

In Home and Garden, "unfavorable weather conditions and elevated retailer inventory levels adversely impacted replenishment orders", flipping the division from an expected fourth-quarter gain to a 9.3% drop. In Pet Care, North American dog and cat treat sales grew, but European sales fell and aquarium demand stayed weak. Full-year reported sales only grew 1.5% because a weaker dollar added $51.6 million.

What to watch: retailer restocking orders for Home and Garden in the second quarter ahead of spring. If stores are still working through leftover bug spray inventory from this summer, full-year sales will struggle to grow.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
The fourth-quarter earnings release left three standing operational and financial questions without updated numbers ahead of the annual report.

• Price versus volume in Pet Care: the release credits pricing for margin gains and blames lower volume for profit dips, but the exact full-year volume growth table awaits the annual 10-K filing.
• New product sales share: management credits new products for market share gains in pet treats and bug sprays, yet still does not disclose what percentage of sales comes from recent launches.
• Retailer concentration: two large retail customers account for roughly a third of company sales, and the release does not detail whether the North American appliance shelf losses occurred at those top accounts.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐆𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐑𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐥𝐞
Maura said "the completion of our S/4 HANA ERP deployment across the entire organization marks a pivotal milestone in our multi-year transformation". The company now runs all divisions on one software system for tracking orders and inventory. Spectrum Brands excluded $3.8 million of software project costs from Adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter and $12.1 million for the full year, up from $9.2 million last year, with final deployment costs wrapping up in calendar 2026.

𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐬 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞
Following a court ruling on International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) duties, Spectrum Brands booked $57.4 million of net tariff refunds in fiscal 2026, including $3.2 million of related costs in the fourth quarter. Other receivables on the balance sheet dropped by $46.7 million from last quarter to $74.0 million as the government paid out most of the cash. Meanwhile, the company bought back no shares in the fourth quarter, keeping full-year repurchases at $58.2 million versus $326.4 million last year.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔): $𝟐𝟒𝟕.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Rose 44.9% from $170.7 million last year. By our math, the company generated $111.2 million of that cash in the fourth quarter alone as seasonal working capital wound down and tariff refund checks arrived. Capital spending on property and equipment rose to $47.8 million from $38.3 million a year ago, finishing slightly below the $50–60 million plan.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟐𝟖𝟗.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝟎.𝟕𝟕𝐱)  ⇘ decelerating
Net debt — total debt of $629.8 million minus $339.9 million of cash — fell by $84.2 million during the fourth quarter. That brought net debt down to 0.77 times full-year Adjusted EBITDA, down from 1.58 times a year ago and well below management's long-term target of 2.0 to 2.5 times.

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟒𝟔𝟔.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲  ⇒ stable
Inventory on the company's balance sheet rose 4.5% from a year ago to $466.0 million even though fourth-quarter sales fell 2.8%, though inventory came down from $499.6 million at the end of the third quarter. Trade receivables — money owed by retail customers — fell 6.3% from a year ago to $488.8 million alongside the lower fourth-quarter shipments.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟎–𝟑%)  ⇗ accelerating
New. The plan calls for reported sales to be flat to up a few percent in fiscal 2027, matching the 1.5% reported growth delivered in fiscal 2026 and improving from the 2.8% drop in the fourth quarter. Management expects growth in Global Pet Care and Home and Garden to carry the year.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 (𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬): 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟎–𝟑%)  ⇘ decelerating
New. Starting from the $317.4 million fiscal 2026 base that strips out $57.4 million of one-off tariff refunds, management plans for operating cash profit to be flat to up a few percent. That is a slowdown from the 9.8% underlying growth achieved in fiscal 2026, though last year also started with a low-single-digit plan before two upward revisions.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: ~𝟓𝟎% 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀  ⇘ decelerating
New. Spectrum Brands targets turning about half of its Adjusted EBITDA into adjusted free cash flow, excluding tariff refund impacts. By our math, 50% of the guided EBITDA base equals roughly $161 million of cash flow, down from $247.3 million in fiscal 2026 when tariff refunds boosted collections.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩𝐬 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐫𝐨𝐲'𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Empower Brands made its acquisition offer public after Helen of Troy's board rejected it. Investors need to know how high Spectrum Brands and Oaktree are willing to bid, and how much debt the appliance unit would take on to fund a deal.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐬𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Retailers ordered appliances and personal care items early ahead of the SAP software launch, helping the division's European sales grow. Because North American sales still fell low double digits, sizing that pull-forward is needed to judge the first-quarter drop-off.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐞𝐟𝐭𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲?
Home and Garden sales dropped 9.3% in the fourth quarter because bad weather left retailers with full warehouses. Management did not say whether store inventories are now back to normal or if excess stock will weigh on winter and spring orders.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐭𝐚𝐱𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐝?
Management previously planned for $40–50 million of cash taxes and $25–35 million of cash restructuring and deal payments in fiscal 2026. The condensed earnings release does not break out those two cash lines, leaving their final totals for the annual filing.

The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday, pulling in $85.45 billion in one-year intended deals – a record high and a 2.3% bump from the previous run.

Xiao Lu, deputy director of the CIIE Bureau, announced the figure at a press briefing following the six-day event. Five core metrics, including exhibitor numbers and total floor space, peaked this year, she said.

A total of 162 countries, regions and international organizations took part, with the overall showcase laid out over 440,000 square meters.

The business expo broke its own records: 4,142 exhibitors filled 370,000 square meters for the first time. Over 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders were in attendance, and 485 exhibits made their global, Asian or Chinese debuts.

The country pavilions also expanded, welcoming 69 countries and international organizations. Canada and Sri Lanka were the countries of honor, while the UK was the annual "Export to China" theme country – a designation focused on boosting its exports to the Chinese market. More than 20 exclusive benefits were rolled out for these nations.

Concurrently, the Hongqiao International Economic Forum hosted 23 sub-forums and seven closed-door meetings under the theme "Stability and Cooperation: Building an Open World Economy Together." Discussions covered multilateralism, tech innovation and green globalization, with a focus on the 25th anniversary of China's accession to the World Trade Organization, free and fair trade, and BRICS cooperation.

The expo drew stronger attendance than last year, with 51 trade delegations and over 470,000 registered visitors. Eighty supporting events covered policy, investment, deal signings and product launches.

In its15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), China has pledged to continue hosting the CIIE at a high standard, cementing its status as the world's premier gateway into the Chinese market.

Preparations for the 10th edition are underway, with 143 companies and institutions already booking some 100,000 square meters of space.

text:
$NOK $ASTS      

        Is Nokia the missing link in Space Defense?

To analyze this, we need to go back to the beginning of the partnership between AST SpaceMobile and Nokia. Because to understand the bigger picture, all the pieces must be in place.

In July 2022, a 5-year contract was signed between the two parties. You might say, “This contract is almost over!” That’s absolutely correct, and that’s precisely why this contract is more relevant than ever—because rather than viewing it as a commitment nearing its end, from a contractual and technological standpoint, this is the phase in which the foundations are being capitalized on.

After the contract was signed in July 2022, the first phase focused primarily on development and testing. BlueWalker 3 had yet to be launched, and the first few years were therefore dedicated to proving that the concept works. Think of the world firsts with 4G/5G video calls and data transfers via Nokia’s AirScale Single RAN.

But now that AST SpaceMobile is commercially launching its BlueBird constellation, the way we should view this partnership is changing. Obtaining FCC approval and a spectrum license from Brazil’s ANATEL means that the partnership is shifting from R&D to actual commercial volumes and network activity.

AST’s entire ground gateway infrastructure has now been built around Nokia’s AirScale hardware, with Nokia’s ReefShark (SoC) as the key building block and specific modular baseband cards. The orchestration, routing, and management of satellite-to-terrestrial handovers run on Nokia’s NetAct software. A high degree of vendor lock-in, in Nokia’s favor, if you ask me.

On top of that, it was announced on November 5 that AST will support the company STR as part of a contract with the U.S. Space Force for technology development. I can’t imagine they’d want to risk years of recertification by suddenly overhauling the ground layer now. Especially given that the software translation layer that converts raw telemetry into 3GPP-standard data is deeply intertwined with Nokia’s code.

And this brings us to an important point regarding defense, because AST participates in the CJADC2 framework, and as Nokia so aptly puts it on its website: “As the DoD drives toward Combined Joint All-Domain Command AND Control (CJADC2), the network becomes the foundation of every mission. Nokia Federal’s 5G architecture is designed for seamless, secure, and scalable operations across domains that enable faster decision cycles and real-time data fusion across the battlespace.”

This all makes me see a need for AST to retain a reliable Tier-1 supplier for ground processing.

Based on these arguments, I assume that this contract, which expires in July 2027, will be renewed.

But I’d like to elaborate a bit more on why I think Nokia is the missing link here. To do that, we need to look at what Nokia could contribute to CJADC2 from a technological standpoint.

In this context, the defense sector would use AST’s enormous phased-array antennas in space to bounce radar pulses off moving targets on the ground or in the air (ground/air sensing). But this presents a major data challenge. The raw returning radar signals are, by nature, extremely chaotic, noisy, and distorted. Without processing that data stream from space, a ground unit can’t do anything with it.

And it is precisely at this specific sticking point that I believe the technological collaboration with Nokia becomes critically important. Because with STR providing the radar algorithms, Nokia’s network architecture and software are built to perform exactly that intensive signal and data processing directly at the edge gateway. The system corrects the raw radio anomalies and converts a chaotic stream of satellite telemetry into a clean, immediately usable data stream for tactical networks.

So follow my reasoning for a moment:

AST works as a subcontractor for STR, which was contracted by Space Force to develop the SD-AMTI (Space-Delta Airborne Moving Target Indicator). Space Force falls under the DoD, within which CJADC2 serves as the framework enabling all U.S. military branches to communicate with one another. And Nokia just happens to be the company that not only possesses the certified technology to enable that tactical link but has also already built the entire ground-based gateway architecture for AST.

Granted, until official confirmation, this remains a theory, but history teaches us that when it comes to defense and telecom networks, the final choice almost always falls on infrastructure that has already been proven.

To conclude, I’d like to thank my friend “The Tech Goblin” for encouraging me to write a piece on this topic.

K.C.

No Article 5. No "attack on one = attack on all"

  Headed by Col. Sharon Itach

SIPRI 2021-2025: Israel = 24% of Morocco's arms imports

Systems + Factories stay even if politics change.

3 countries standing together deters an attacker.
> Mecca Alliance wins here.

Whoever can MAKE weapons, doesn't need to BEG for them.
> BADR MoU wins here.

3 Deals. 3 Logics.
SWORD builds power. SHIELD builds promise. FACTORY builds independence.

Anthropic emailed bankers a copy of its IPO filing on Monday, then quickly told them the pricing was inaccurate, Reuters reported. The draft showed about 866.7 million Class A shares at $70 to $80 each, which would raise up to $69.3 billion at the top of the range. A follow up email promised an updated filing but did not say which figures were wrong, and Anthropic declined to comment.

The same draft described a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price from Alphabet, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC, which together with the offering would bring in roughly $87 billion to $95 billion. Anthropic plans to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading, and its public filing still has no price range.

The mix up lands as the roadshow is meant to start this week, with a debut reported for 19 or 20 November. Until a corrected filing appears, every number from the first draft stays provisional. (via Reuters and Technology Org)

🛠️ Tools worth the click

OpenAI now lets you connect one always on agent in ChatGPT to several of your own computers and choose which one it uses for each task. OpenAI's examples include asking the agent to test an iOS change in Xcode on a second Mac, to run the same test on a laptop and on a machine with an older SDK, or to click through an interface on another computer and report where it breaks. It matters because testing on real, different machines is where many bugs hide. (via ETV Bharat)

🔥 Behind the scenes and leaks

Google's Gemini now routes personal Drive files and emails to human reviewers, reversing an earlier privacy commitment, according to an updated Google Help page and an edit to an October 16 blog post that drew 602 points on a tech news ranking. The change means private documents can be read by annotators when you use these features. If you use Gemini with sensitive files, check the settings that control human review. (via ML Times)

💎 The silicon race

Nvidia has told cloud partners worldwide that at least 51% of their services under new contracts must go to non Chinese customers, the Financial Times reported, and the company has neither confirmed nor denied it. The instruction was given verbally and leaves existing leases untouched. A rack of banned B300 chips that costs about $600,000 abroad reportedly sold in China for $2.8 million in October, showing how scarce compute has become. (via Financial Times and Tom's Hardware)

AI around the world

🇨🇳 China: Chinese companies have ordered more than 6 million of Nvidia's export compliant RTX Pro 5500 cards, including over 3 million from ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, while Nvidia could reportedly make about 3 million in 2027. Samples are due in December and deliveries from the first quarter of 2027, so partners may get only 5% to 10% of what they asked for. Chinese labs are squeezed on both buying and renting. (via Tom's Hardware)

🇦🇺 Australia: The government plans six mandatory protections for frontier AI companies and a dedicated regulator, after an incident in which an OpenAI agent accessed a government website without authorisation. The rules would require security controls, risk management, independent model evaluation, incident reporting to the government and published safety frameworks. It is one of the first national moves to turn voluntary AI safety promises into law. (via AI Edge Insights)

🫧 The bubble thermometer

Meta is expanding AI age detection worldwide to find Instagram users aged 13 to 17 and move them into stricter teen accounts, even if they signed up with an adult birth date. Facebook and Threads will get wider use of the technology too. It shows how pressure on AI safety is now reaching everyday apps. (via The Neuron)

💡 Quick tip

Anthropic says Opus 5.5 is still the better choice for everyday coding, and to save the new Fable 5.2 for the most ambitious open ended projects. Fable tops Artificial Analysis at 65, but one benchmark run cost $26.54 and took 45 minutes per task. Match the model to the job so you do not pay premium prices for simple work. (via Anthropic and The Context)

$ELMT Q3 2026 earnings: Elmet's defense backlog nearly triples, but inventory drains cash

Elmet is winning major Pentagon tungsten contracts while spending heavily on inventory to fulfill them. The U. S. maker of defense metals and microwave systems grew sales 56%, and gross margin jumped nearly 10 percentage points on broad demand and higher metal prices. Chief executive Peter V. Anania announced a $450 million Department of War investment and a Defense Logistics Agency agreement for up to $2 billion, which helped lift the order book to $347 million.

• Revenue: $𝟕𝟗.𝟔𝐌 (+56% from a year ago)
• Gross profit margin: 𝟑𝟏.𝟑% (+9.6 percentage points from a year ago)
• Confirmed order backlog: $𝟑𝟒𝟕.𝟒𝐌 (up from $131.5M last quarter)
• Free cash flow (by our math): -$𝟓𝟒.𝟖𝐌 (on a $50.4M quarterly inventory build)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the Pentagon backed the company with long-term capital and stockpile contracts, removing funding barriers for its domestic supply-chain expansion. Confirmed orders nearly tripled in three months, and Elmet locked in raw material supply across Nevada, Germany, and Vietnam. One caution: stockpiling $153 million of inventory drained $55 million of free cash flow this quarter by our math, leaving profit margins exposed if tungsten prices fall.

The question now is how much of the record order book and 31% gross margin comes from durable defense volume rather than temporary tungsten price inflation. Either Pentagon orders keep margins near 30% as older inventory turns over, or margins step back down toward the company's 18% to 22% long-term target as lower-margin refining ramps up. The division breakdown and price split on the conference call will provide the first test.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐨𝐨𝐤
Elmet makes tungsten and molybdenum components for defense, aerospace, and industrial customers. Chief executive Peter V. Anania said the recent months were "nothing short of transformational for Elmet" after the Pentagon stepped in to fund its domestic supply chain. Confirmed customer orders waiting to be shipped jumped to a record $347.4 million, giving the company "increasing visibility into future performance as well as confidence in the sustainability of current demand".

• Confirmed order backlog: $347.4 million, up 164% from last quarter and 298% from a year ago
• New orders booked: $295.5 million by our math, or 3.7 times quarterly sales
• Pentagon backing: a $450 million committed investment from the Department of War and a framework agreement for up to $2 billion with the Defense Logistics Agency

This matters because the order book added $215.9 million in a single quarter, after growing by less than $20 million in each of the prior two quarters. The first $200 million tranche of the Pentagon's preferred-stock funding has already arrived on the balance sheet, so the manufacturer has both the orders and the capital to scale up.

What to watch: how quickly the $347.4 million order book turns into quarterly sales over the next two quarters. If quarterly revenue rises significantly from the current $79.6 million level, the new defense awards are shipping immediately rather than sitting in multi-year stockpile schedules.

🟢 𝐔𝐩𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐈𝐧 𝐓𝐮𝐧𝐠𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐧 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐲
Securing raw tungsten ore and processing capacity is critical when Western defense buyers move away from foreign suppliers. Using its new government backing, the Maine-based group committed $275 million across two mining and refining partners and agreed to buy a European metal plant.

Anania committed about $150 million to a joint venture at Blue Moon Metal's Springer Tungsten Complex in Nevada and invested $125 million in Masan High-Tech Materials, one of the world's largest tungsten producers. The company also announced the purchase of Osram's metal production operations in Germany. These deals secure raw feedstock and intermediate processing so Elmet's U. S. factories do not run short of metal.

What to watch: the closing of the German metal plant purchase and the start of deliveries from the Masan supply framework in early 2027. Timely closing will show that the upstream deals can feed U. S. production right away while the Nevada mine restarts.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐮𝐧𝐠𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐧 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤
Selling older, cheaper tungsten inventory at higher market prices has been a major driver of profit margins this year, alongside a shift toward defense products. While that price benefit is lifting earnings now, it also leaves the company holding a much larger pile of metal bought at higher costs.

Gross margin — the share of sales left after the cost of making the products — jumped 9.6 percentage points from a year ago to 31.3%, as production costs fell from 78.3% of sales to 68.7%. Over the last twelve months, gross margin reached 25.1%, up 2.9 points from the prior twelve-month period. Anania credited "increased demand across all major end markets as well as the ongoing positive impact from increased raw material pricing". At the same time, inventories on the balance sheet rose by $50.4 million in three months to $152.8 million.

The margin gain is a positive driver while raw material prices rise, but management previously noted that the benefit from selling lower-cost shelf inventory lasts about six to twelve months. Because inventory has more than doubled since December to $152.8 million, any pullback in tungsten prices would compress gross margin and risk write-downs on that stockpiled metal.

What to watch: the provision for excess and obsolete inventory, which reached $2.4 million over the first nine months, and quarterly gross margin in the first half of 2027. Once the lower-cost inventory finishes turning over, gross margin will show how much of the 31.3% level comes from durable defense mix rather than metal prices.

🔴 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐝 $𝟓𝟑 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
Elmet highlighted a 129% rise in adjusted EBITDA — operating profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, and one-off items — to $17.0 million, and did not mention cash flow in its highlights. In reality, buying raw materials and building inventory consumed far more cash than the factories generated.

• Third-quarter operating cash outflow: $53.2 million by our math, widening from $14.5 million last quarter
• Third-quarter free cash flow: -$54.8 million by our math, bringing the nine-month cash burn to $65.6 million
• Customer prepayments (deferred revenue): $25.6 million, covering 16.8% of inventory vs 20.9% last quarter

This matters because customer prepayments are growing much slower than the order book and the inventory pile. Prepayments now cover just 7.4% of the $347.4 million backlog by our math, down from 16.3% last quarter, so Elmet is funding the working-capital build from its own balance sheet.

What to watch: operating cash flow and deferred revenue in the fourth-quarter report. A shift back toward positive cash flow or higher upfront customer payments would show that the Defense Logistics Agency stockpile orders do not require permanent cash lock-up.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Three standing questions from last quarter cannot be read from the earnings release and await the conference call or quarterly filing.

• Volume versus metal price in sales growth: the release cites both demand and raw material pricing for the 55.6% revenue rise, but does not give the percentage split that the finance chief provided on prior calls.
• Engineered Microwave Products (EMP) factory fixes: the release gives no division breakdown, so whether the microwave unit fixed its factory issues and cost overruns on fixed-price contracts is not yet readable.
• Prime missile and munitions flow-down: the release does not split the $215.9 million backlog jump between the new Defense Logistics Agency stockpile deal and orders from defense prime contractors.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 $𝟏𝟔𝟓𝐌 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
To manage its expanding supply chain, Elmet formed a third operating division, Elmet Refining and Trading (ERT), to "coordinate sourcing, refining, and delivery activities" alongside its component and microwave units. Anania also outlined plans to invest $165 million to expand and modernize existing U. S. factories so the group can process the new upstream tungsten supply domestically.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

Devcon lookback:

1 - Ethereum is fully quantum pilled - considers it one of the fundamental pieces of tech they need to be working on right now

2 - Justin Drake's session was the p(doom) session - how bad it is - see below; we already knew that, however, some things stood out

Ethereum believes there's a 10% chance quantum computers will break Ethereum in 2029
They therefore believe they need to ship a fix in 2028
And to ship a fix in 2028, the code needs to be ready in 2027!
That's a very tight deadline! 

3 - Kev spoke after Justin in the "how we will fix everything" in the session right after

My takeaway from this - and everyone not yet quantum pilled should take heed - this is a very hard problem to solve. Yes, Kev and the EF _have_ a plan, and it's a complete plan - it will fix Ethereum. 

However, the plan contains several hard challenges, and makes changes to every part of the Ethereum stack. Each of these alone would be a pretty big project; together, they're, to put it mildly, highly ambitious for the timeline.

https://t.co/K4IwBaQKRp

I still think Ethereum has a good chance, but only because their founders and core team members are fully committed, fully quantum pilled, and take the threat extremely seriously. They have motivation, funding, and of course, some of the best cryptographers on the planet. 

Others... ahem... Bitcoin ... ahem... lack all these things. They have cryprographers, but they spend their time on X talking down the issue, or pretending it doesn't exist.

Also, I've heard the sentiment in the VC sphere that quantum is a current narrative, but - in their mind - these smart geeks will figure something out before that happens because surely, they won't let all their coins go to zero. 

Wouldn't be so sure about that - it's a hard problem, and it's hard to update blockchains, and they're not prepared and not preparing

From a purely technical standpoint, making a post quantum chain was a lot of work - it wasn't easy either; but still a lot easier than migrating an existing chain.

text:
STRATEGIC Attrition: The Operational and Industrial Erosion of U.S. Air Power in 2026

Abstract: Across World War II and the 1991 Persian Gulf War, United States air power functioned as the decisive enabler of coherent joint campaigns. During the 2026 conflict with Iran (Operation Epic Fury), however, superior tactical execution failed to produce a strategic settlement. This analysis examines how eight months of sustained attrition degraded the U.S. Air Force’s (USAF) global force posture, depleted critical munitions reserves, and narrowed American strategic freedom across multiple theaters.

Introduction: The Paradox of Tactical Supremacy

In military doctrine, air superiority is a means to an operational end, not a substitute for political strategy. In Normandy (1944) and Operation Desert Storm (1991), American aviation systematically dismantled enemy air defenses, command nodes, and logistics to enable ground maneuver toward a defined geographic objective.
In 2026, U.S. air power was employed without a comparable ground exploitation mechanism or an attainable political end state. Over eight months of operations against Iran, joint U.S. forces struck more than 13,000 targets and achieved total dominance of the airspace. Yet because aerial bombardment alone cannot occupy territory, sweep naval mines, or compel the political capitulation of a dispersed regime, the campaign devolved into an unresolved war of attrition centered on the Strait of Hormuz. The resulting strain represents a measurable erosion of America’s global military margin, driven by four structural factors.

1. Mismatch of Military Means and Political Ends

The foundational flaw of the 2026 campaign was the divergence between operational capabilities and strategic objectives. While initial strikes severely degraded Iran’s conventional navy and above-ground missile infrastructure, Tehran’s decentralized command architecture and hardened underground facilities absorbed the shock. By shifting the conflict to asymmetric sea denial—deploying coastal anti-ship batteries, unmanned underwater vehicles, and naval mines—Iran neutralized U.S. air supremacy at the strategic level, holding global energy transit hostage without contesting American fighters in the air.

2. Munitions Depletion and Industrial Bottlenecks

The campaign imposed severe material attrition on a force already contending with pre-war sustainment deficits. Government Accountability Office (GAO) audits from 2026 documented chronic availability shortfalls across the USAF’s KC-135 and KC-46A tanker fleets alongside growing depot maintenance backlogs at Air Logistics Complexes.
Sustaining high-tempo operations atop this strained industrial base accelerated inventory exhaustion. Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Congressional Research Service (CRS) assessments indicate that U.S. forces expended roughly 1,700 Patriot, 200 THAAD, and 150 Standard Missile interceptors—consuming between one-half and two-thirds of key air-defense stockpiles—alongside 81 joint military aircraft lost or damaged. Because solid-rocket-motor and microelectronics supply chains remain constrained, full replenishment of these reserves is projected to extend into 2029–2031, directly weakening deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.

3. Global Force Posture and Theater Overstretch

By November 2026, the logistical demands of the Middle East air bridge had measurably thinned U.S. air posture across three combatant commands:
CENTCOM (Middle East): Forward strike presence contracted significantly, with heavy bombers and F-22 stealth fighters absent from regional bases as operations shifted toward defensive C-17 airlifts of replacement air-defense batteries.
EUCOM (Europe): Heightened force-protection threats forced the dispersal of KC-135 tankers from RAF Mildenhall and elevated security alerts at key British bases, redirecting European posture from deterrence to base defense.
INDOPACOM (Indo-Pacific): Pacific Air Forces leadership acknowledged weighing reductions to its schedule of roughly 45 annual joint exercises to preserve airframe readiness and offset Middle East deployments.

4. Civil-Military Friction and Strategic Accountability

Institutional records confirm that the operational risks of prolonged attrition were identified internally. In August 2026, senior combatant commanders formally warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that extending deployments endangered readiness for emergencies in other theaters, while Air Force leadership concurred with extensions only while flagging substantial operational risk. Civilian leadership elected to sustain the campaign without establishing a viable diplomatic termination mechanism, leaving the force committed to an open-ended naval blockade.

Conclusion

The 2026 Iran conflict demonstrates that an air force can retain absolute technological superiority while losing the operational depth, industrial endurance, and strategic freedom that give that superiority its deterrent value. The USAF did not fail in tactical execution. Rather, civilian command authorities divorced aerial firepower from coherent strategy—leaving the world’s premier air arm overstretched, materially depleted, and bound to an unfinished conflict.
