text:
SkyCeptor and NATO Missile Defence: European–Israeli Industrial Cooperation – Russian Threat Perceptions and Hybrid Warfare 
Principal judgment — Moderate confidence: European air and missile defence is undergoing a strategic industrial transformation, but the gap between announced cooperation and operational manufacturing capacity remains substantial.

Romania’s SkyCeptor initiative illustrates this divide. The 2022 cooperation framework involving Raytheon, ROMARM and Electromecanica Ploiești established an ambition to produce a Stunner-derived interceptor in Romania. The verified manufacturer record does not, however, demonstrate that serial production has commenced or that a Romanian-produced SkyCeptor has achieved operational qualification.

Other European–Israeli programmes have advanced materially further. Germany received its first operational Arrow 3 system in December 2025; Slovakia received BARAK MX equipment in April 2026; Czechia had received two of four SPYDER batteries by September 2026; and Greece signed an approximately €3 billion multilayer air-defence agreement in August 2026.

NATO has also committed to increasing defence investment to 5% of GDP annually by 2035, while a separate $5.5 billion procurement contract supports the expansion of Patriot missile manufacturing in Europe.

The Russian threat is an established driver of these decisions. NATO has formally attributed hybrid activities to Russia, including sabotage, cyber interference and other hostile operations.

ENISA additionally confirmed cyber incidents affecting commercial refrigeration systems across several EU member states during October–November 2026. These incidents demonstrate vulnerabilities in connected civilian infrastructure but have not been officially established as a unified Russian reconnaissance campaign.

Strategic conclusion: NATO’s long-term resilience will depend on converting industrial agreements into sustainable production, maintaining diverse interceptor supplies, protecting critical support infrastructure and distinguishing verified adversary operations from analytically plausible but unproven intelligence-gathering activity.

Europe’s Missile Defence Paradox: Billions in Contracts, Fragile Industrial Sovereignty and Russia’s Hybrid Pressure
From Romania’s stalled SkyCeptor programme to Germany’s Arrow 3 and NATO’s expanding interceptor commitments, Europe is discovering that purchasing missile defence is not the same as controlling its production.

Europe is committing billions to missile defence while the industrial capacity needed to sustain it remains uneven, externally dependent and exposed to disruption. Romania’s proposed SkyCeptor production illustrates the contradiction: cooperation with American and Israeli technology providers has been documented since 2022, yet operational Romanian manufacturing remains unverified. Germany, Finland, Slovakia, Czechia and Greece have advanced through different stages of procurement and implementation, but none of these arrangements automatically confers technological sovereignty. Meanwhile, NATO’s expanding defence commitments confront a second vulnerability: cyberattacks and hybrid operations capable of disrupting the civilian infrastructure on which industrial continuity depends. The governing question is no longer simply how many interceptors Europe can purchase, but whether it can manufacture, replenish and sustain them under prolonged strategic pressure without transferring critical dependencies to foreign suppliers.

1. Romania’s SkyCeptor Programme Exposes the Gap Between Agreements and Production
Romania’s proposed SkyCeptor manufacturing programme has become a revealing test of Europe’s defence-industrial ambitions. In May 2022, Raytheon Missiles & Defense concluded a cooperation memorandum with Romanian industrial partners, subsequently announced in November that year. The initiative involved ROMARM and Electromecanica Ploiești, with the objective of developing Romanian production of a Stunner-derived interceptor compatible with the Patriot air-defence ecosystem. Rafael provided the underlying Israeli technological heritage, while Raytheon represented the American industrial and integration relationship. The proposed benefit was not merely another missile acquisition but the establishment of a domestic manufacturing capability with potential access to the wider European Patriot market.

On 2 August 2023, Electromecanica Ploiești and Raytheon signed a further letter of intent, presented by Romania’s Ministry of Economy as a continuation of the earlier industrial framework. Yet the distinction between a memorandum, a manufacturing contract and qualified production remains decisive. No verified public record establishes Romanian SkyCeptor serial production, completed Patriot qualification, accepted deliveries or a binding production timetable. Renewed industrial discussions cannot be treated as evidence that those requirements have been satisfied. Raytheon’s Romanian SkyCeptor cooperation announcement, November 2022.

SkyCeptor’s technical proposition is commercially significant. Derived from the Stunner technology developed for David’s Sling, it is intended to provide kinetic interception against selected missile threats at a lower cost than some existing alternatives. Raytheon has promoted affordability as a defining advantage. However, the public record does not establish a comparable contracted unit price against Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3 MSE, nor does it demonstrate operational equivalence across their respective engagement requirements. The economic argument remains conditional on actual manufacturing costs, integration, certification and the availability of a sufficiently large customer base.

2. Europe’s Contracts Are Growing Faster Than Its Verified Manufacturing Independence
The scale of European missile-defence investment is already substantial. Germany received its first operational Arrow 3 system in December 2025, establishing a high-altitude ballistic missile defence capability developed through Israeli–American cooperation. In January 2026, Israel Aerospace Industries announced an approximately $3.1 billion expansion contract, describing the broader German Arrow 3 programme as exceeding $6.5 billion. The handover confirms material implementation; the contract expansion confirms additional industrial commitments. Neither establishes complete nationwide coverage or German ownership of the interceptor’s underlying technology. Israeli Ministry of Defence, December 2025; Israel Aerospace Industries, January 2026.

Finland adopted a different model. Its April 2023 acquisition of David’s Sling involved an initial commitment of approximately €316 million excluding VAT, consisting of a €213 million main contract and €103 million in immediately exercised options, with additional options requiring subsequent decisions. Finnish industry was assigned integration and command-and-control responsibilities, while a governmental security-of-supply arrangement addressed access to critical components. The structure provides industrial participation and supply assurances without establishing independent Finnish manufacture of complete Stunner interceptors. Finnish Ministry of Defence, April 2023.

Further east, Slovakia’s approximately €560 million BARAK MX agreement, signed in 2024, produced equipment deliveries announced in April 2026. Czechia had received two of four SPYDER batteries by September 2026, with production of all four reported complete. Greece subsequently signed an approximately €3 billion Achilles Shield agreement in August 2026, combining David’s Sling, BARAK MX, SPYDER, surveillance radars and command-and-control elements. The Greek arrangement represents an integrated acquisition rather than a completed domestic production architecture. Israeli Ministry of Defence, Slovakia, April 2026; Czechia, September 2026; Greece, August 2026.

These contracts illustrate Europe’s divergent approaches: Germany prioritises strategic acquisition, Finland combines procurement with integration and supply guarantees, Slovakia and Czechia demonstrate physical deliveries, Greece is investing in an integrated defensive architecture, and Romania is seeking domestic interceptor manufacture. Their contract values cannot be converted into equivalent production capacity, interceptor inventories or technological independence.

3. NATO’s 5% Commitment Cannot Manufacture Missiles by Decree
NATO’s June 2025 Hague Summit established a commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually by 2035, including at least 3.5% for core defence requirements and up to 1.5% for broader security, infrastructure and resilience. The commitment reflects a structural shift in Allied priorities, but spending authorisations do not automatically create industrial throughput. Manufacturing requires qualified suppliers, specialised materials, technical licences, personnel, testing and sustained procurement demand. NATO’s February 2025 Updated Defence Production Action Plan explicitly addresses these constraints through demand aggregation, multinational procurement, industrial-capacity assessments and attention to 12 defence-critical raw materials. NATO Hague Summit Declaration, June 2025; NATO Updated Defence Production Action Plan, February 2025.

The industrial mechanism is visible in NATO’s January 2024 announcement of a $5.5 billion contract for up to 1,000 Patriot missiles, involving Germany, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain, with production expansion supported through COMLOG, the Raytheon–MBDA joint venture in Germany. This creates a documented European replenishment pathway, but the maximum procurement quantity does not represent missiles already delivered. It also places Romania’s SkyCeptor proposal under commercial pressure: any additional interceptor programme must demonstrate a credible advantage over existing production commitments rather than rely solely on the political appeal of local manufacturing. NATO Patriot procurement announcement, January 2024.

Europe’s financing architecture adds another constraint. The European Commission’s Readiness 2030 framework envisages approximately €800 billion in potential additional defence-related financial capacity, including up to €150 billion in SAFE loans and broader national fiscal flexibility. These are financing mechanisms and potential spending capacity, not completed expenditure or manufactured equipment. The industrial question is whether governments can translate longer-term fiscal commitments into sufficiently predictable orders to justify production investment, while respecting national procurement requirements and the technological rights retained by foreign manufacturers. European Commission, Future of European Defence and Readiness 2030.

4. Industrial Sovereignty Ends Where Foreign Technology Rights Begin
The Stunner–SkyCeptor relationship illustrates why domestic assembly cannot automatically be described as technological sovereignty. A national manufacturer may receive authorisation to produce selected components, assemble imported subsystems or conduct maintenance without obtaining the right to modify the complete design, control sensitive software or export independently. Finland’s David’s Sling acquisition explicitly required United States approval because the technology emerged from joint US–Israeli development. The Romanian programme faces the same fundamental category of legal and industrial questions: what manufacturing rights are granted, which components remain foreign-controlled, and who authorises subsequent configuration changes and exports? The published SkyCeptor framework does not answer these questions comprehensively.

This distinction creates different calculations for European governments. France and Italy maintain established industrial participation in the European Aster and SAMP/T ecosystem, giving them an interest in preserving technological authority alongside procurement efficiency. Germany has opted for major Israeli–American strategic capability while remaining engaged in European Patriot production arrangements. The United Kingdom’s Strategic Defence Review 2025 emphasises integrated air and missile defence, including resilient command-and-control, rather than portraying any individual interceptor as sufficient for national protection. These choices reflect different balances between delivery speed, domestic manufacturing, foreign technology access and long-term military sustainment. Italian Ministry of Defence, 2024–2026 Defence Planning Document; UK Strategic Defence Review, June 2025.

The decisive industrial distinction is therefore between possessing equipment, manufacturing under licence and retaining control over the technology required to sustain it. European factories can diversify supply while remaining dependent on imported components, governmental authorisations and proprietary engineering. Conversely, secure contractual access to foreign technology can deliver practical resilience without complete national ownership. Industrial sovereignty is measured by enforceable capabilities and continuity of supply, not the location of the factory gate.

5. Russia’s Hybrid Pressure Exposes the Civilian Systems Behind Military Readiness
European defence-industrial expansion is occurring alongside officially documented Russian hybrid activity. On 2 May 2024, the North Atlantic Council identified hostile operations affecting multiple Allies, including sabotage, cyber interference, violence and disinformation. The European Union’s 18 July 2025 declaration subsequently condemned systematic Russian malicious activity, including operations attributed to the GRU. These statements establish a state-sponsored threat environment, but do not attribute every contemporary infrastructure incident to Russia. North Atlantic Council, May 2024; Council of the European Union, July 2025.

On 4 November 2026, ENISA and the European Commission confirmed cyber incidents affecting commercial refrigeration systems across several EU member states since 11 October, including a further wave on 1–2 November. ENISA, Europol, national cybersecurity response teams and EU-CyCLONe coordinated information-sharing and mitigation. The incidents exposed the consequences of digitally connected civilian equipment, but the official statement did not identify a common perpetrator or establish a military intelligence objective. ENISA–European Commission joint statement, November 2026.

The 3 June 2024 Synnovis ransomware attack provides a different demonstration of systemic dependence. Disruption to NHS pathology services affected blood grouping, antibody screening and crossmatching, while UK government records documented 10,152 disrupted acute outpatient appointments and 1,710 postponed elective procedures at the two most affected trusts during the relevant reporting interval. The attack demonstrated how the compromise of a specialised service provider could disrupt institutions outside the initially affected network. It did not establish a Russian military reconnaissance operation. UK Home Office, Supply-Chain Resilience Against Ransomware, October 2025.

Aviation incidents expose a different dimension. On 18 October 2026, Austrian Airlines flight OS82, carrying 51 passengers and six crew members, diverted to Sofia after a bomb threat, with a Bulgarian Air Force fighter escorting the aircraft. The responsible actor and motive were not established in the official announcement. By contrast, a September 2026 UK statement to the OSCE reported Germany’s attribution to Russia of an 4 August explosive-drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, a strategically significant logistics facility. The latter provides stronger evidence of state-directed hostile activity; neither incident establishes that the October refrigeration disruptions belonged to the same campaign. Bulgarian Ministry of Transport, October 2026; UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, September 2026.

The hypothesis that some disruptions are intended to measure European response capacity is credible but unproven. An incident may generate observable emergency decisions without having been designed to collect intelligence. The distinction matters because inaccurate attribution can distort procurement priorities and military planning just as severely as underestimating a documented hostile campaign.

6. The Next 24 Months Will Separate Industrial Commitments from Defensive Capacity
Germany’s military planning identifies 2029 as a potential horizon for a more substantial Russian conventional threat to NATO, explicitly distinguishing possible military capability from an inevitable attack. Against that timetable, the 12–24 months following November 2026 will be an important period for measuring whether European procurement commitments translate into industrial results. The decisive evidence will be binding production contracts, qualified manufacturing processes, completed integration, accepted deliveries and sustained replenishment arrangements—not additional political declarations. Bundeswehr, Strategic Military Orientation, 2026.

For Romania, continued SkyCeptor uncertainty would mean postponing the industrial diversification promised in 2022, while existing Patriot procurement channels would remain separate from the unverified domestic manufacturing project. For Germany, Finland, Slovakia, Czechia and Greece, the relevant test will be whether contracted systems can be supported through reliable maintenance, integration and supply arrangements. For France and Italy, the cost of fragmented procurement would fall on national industrial programmes whose competitiveness depends on sustained production and technological control. For NATO, the cost would appear in replenishment uncertainty and the difficulty of converting national acquisitions into collectively sustainable defensive capacity.

The economic burden of inaction would be distributed unevenly. Taxpayers would finance procurement commitments without obtaining equivalent industrial independence; defence manufacturers would face uncertain production demand; armed forces would remain exposed to replenishment constraints; and civilian operators would bear the costs of infrastructure disruption. The refrigeration incidents of October–November 2026 and the Synnovis experience demonstrate that these burdens extend beyond military budgets into logistics, healthcare and commercial continuity.

Europe has already made the financial and political decision to expand missile defence. The unresolved decision is how much of that expansion will become qualified European production, how much will remain dependent on foreign-controlled technology, and whether the infrastructure supporting both can withstand sustained disruption. Over the next 24 months, that distinction will determine whether the defence commitments translate into greater operational resilience or simply a larger portfolio of contracts whose full strategic value remains unrealised.

I hear it, understand &agree on the whole.

That being said-whilst I think there is a an unhinged section of this fan base that would want XA out even if we were top

…I do also believe the majority of this fan base are actually in a state of wanting &willing to persist with a manager (even through pain) for the greater good.

I think the issue right now from those that are very noisy is the fear of persisting with the wrong guy/approach.

For me, from a performance perspective, XA needs to work on giving the fan base something to hold onto, however small

…something that will turn the huge uniformed optimism into informed optimism 

Not easy with the context though-I get it.

I say uninformed optimism because Im not sure many saw the entire journey at Leverkusen (I sure didnt)

…more so, most saw the end outcome without understanding the process=unbeaten title winning season on his CV with beautiful football full of structure, patterns, possession, control etc

So because of that, they have assumed on the likely strategy XA would take &i think whats surprised ppl ‘out of the know’ is his chosen strategy from day 1

I think the majority were likely expecting early glimpses of patterns, possession, structure, control etc

…hence the majority of criticism not necessarily being about results but performances (namely the early lack of the above)

I think the main issue right now is XA is clearly experimenting subsequently weve seen very minimal continuity in systems, tactics &line ups.

This can understandably create feelings of uncertainty in the fan base when the majority are seeking certainty after a tumultuous period in recent yrs.

For me, XA is getting to grips with whats in front of him (league & squad) & clearly likes to build his teams around certain philosophical foundations that are more like poch than Maresca (duels, running, mentality, commitment, passion & individual quality) 

Which is fine, but the disgruntlement is caused by ppl who were expecting the opposite from someone they have ‘blindly’ put a lot of hope &trust in.

Hopefully he continues to learn the lessons hes seeking, fail forward &land somewhere with continuity. Leading to stable &progressive performances &results that better with time 

…once this happens, the noise will quieten - common sense

If he doesnt, the noise will get louder. Also normal

I also think hes trying his best to get to know the squad/league& ‘win now’ with the seasons objectives in mind 

…whilst keeping his eyes on the/his bigger long term vision focusing on mentality, profiles, attitude etc

Obviously hes going to need time&a few transfer windows imo.

So I get it tbh(from all perspectives) 

I can logically understand XA& I also understand why there is the early noise from larger sections of the fan base than expected.

Deserved? Depends on ppl’s early expectations imo

From a behaviour standpoint, consider that; 

 ‘Anger is the emotion created from unmet expectations’

As stated, right now large sections of ppl are moving from ‘uniformed optimism’ to ‘informed pessimism’ in something called the ‘emotional cycle of change’

…fundamentally ppl are afraid.

I personally naively had different ‘day 1 stategy’ expectations of XA tbh so I’m having to use a shit ton of logic to navigate what we’re seeing at times

…so I get it

XA isnt stupid, hes played for the biggest clubs in world football. He understands fan culture at expectant clubs 

…& Im pretty confident (given his external demeanor) that he even agrees with certain aspects of the noise -we need to get better &understands the fan reaction if we don’t

Right now, his team are a reflection of him &he is a proud man =he wont like aspects of what’s he’s seeing as much as us

Disgruntled &fearful? 
I get it

#Xabiout?
Way way way too early imo.
You may not understand (Or agree) with his chosen path/strategy

…but for me, consider allowing him time to actually execute  (even if its painful) &lets see where he takes us

text:
Bloomberg: Rich Country, Poor Citizens: China’s $20 Trillion Paradox. For the Communist Party, a few thousand tycoons are easier to manage than a broad middle class. China’s leadership will soon claim a milestone it has chased since Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 landmark economic reforms: membership in the rich world. The nation’s per capita income is nearing the World Bank’s threshold for high-income countries and should cross it within a year or two of the 25th anniversary of its accession to the World Trade Organization. That 2001 deal turned a $1.3 trillion economy into one approaching $20 trillion, and exports have since multiplied roughly 13-fold, earning China the title of “factory for the world.”

In 2021, President Xi Jinping triumphantly declared that the rising tide had lifted all boats — the Communist Party had won “complete victory” over absolute poverty — and pledged to pursue “common prosperity”1 for all. China does deserve credit: Since 1978 it has lifted close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty, three-quarters of the global total, according to the World Bank. But to claim that victory, Beijing used a poverty line of about $2.30 a day, which critics contend is too low.

Against the World Bank’s $8.30-a-day poverty line for households in upper-middle-income countries — China’s current group — more than one-fifth of its population remained poor as of 2022. Against the $30 a day that marks poverty in the rich-country cohort China will be joining, the average citizen falls well short. China, in other words, is becoming a high-income country whose people, by any rich-world measure, remain exceedingly poor.

Both sets of facts flow from the same political economy, and the tension between them will define China’s next quarter-century — turning less on whether the country grows rich, which by conventional measures it largely has, than on what it does about the millions left behind and the middle class it never allowed to form.

For the US and other Western powers that supported the country’s entry into the WTO, the bet was that prosperity would beget a middle class that would demand a say. But Beijing has spent two decades ensuring that constituency never takes shape, since time and time again history has shown that a secure, propertied population is where pressure for a political voice collects.

The evidence on social activism is instructive. In November 2022 a deadly apartment fire in remote Urumqi set off street protests against zero-Covid lockdowns that swelled into the “white paper revolution,” named after the blank sheets of paper demonstrators held up in wordless dissent. But these protests erupted not on China’s poor periphery but in its bourgeois core — along Urumqi Road in Shanghai, the country’s wealthiest city, and across elite campuses like Beijing’s Tsinghua University. The demonstrations confirmed the Party’s operating assumption: It is not hardship that is politically dangerous, but a comfortable middle class.

On the institutions that underpin a secure middle class — most importantly a social safety net — China diverges sharply from its peers. Social spending sits near 10% of gross domestic product, roughly half the average for countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Xi often warns that welfare programs breed idleness, a surprising stance for an avowed Marxist. The underlying motivation is more likely that households forced to self-insure stay precarious and pliable.

A grinding property crisis has only heightened the sense of vulnerability. Chinese households hold about 47% of their assets in real estate, and prices have fallen roughly a fifth from their 2021 peak, erasing trillions of yuan in wealth. Because a family’s home is often their only form of insurance, the loss of value has made people cling to cash all the more.

The exits for that cash, meanwhile, are being systematically sealed. In 2025, Hong Kong overtook Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth center, with about $2.95 trillion in offshore financial assets booked there, much of it mainland money seeking escape. Beijing responded by tightening controls on outbound capital. A State Council regulation in force since July now governs overseas investment end to end, from first approval to final exit. For the first time the rules apply to individuals as well as to firms, and regulators have separately squeezed the brokerage channels that let mainlanders buy foreign stocks. Money that can be neither invested at home nor sent abroad pools in accounts at state-owned banks instead — a reservoir of funds that can support the government’s industrial and infrastructure priorities.

Beijing has promised for years to rebalance the economy toward household consumption, so as to reduce the country’s reliance on the twin growth engines of exports and investment. Yet after two decades of jawboning and half measures, consumption is stuck at about 40% of GDP, compared with 55% to 70% across the rich world. Households save at extraordinary rates — deposits have roughly doubled since 2019, to some 165 trillion yuan ($24.7 trillion) — not from thrift but because the state offers thin retirement pensions, patchy healthcare coverage and unemployment insurance that reaches barely a third of the workforce. Jobless benefits are pegged to the local minimum wage — not to what a worker earned — and is capped at 90% of that: roughly 2,000 yuan a month. This year the minimum rural pension has increased by just 20 yuan, to 163 yuan a month. A people who cannot count on the government to care for them when they are ill, jobless or old will not spend.

Youth unemployment tells the same story. The rate for 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in school now stands at 18% — an indicator so politically sensitive that Beijing suspended its publication in 2023, and then revised the methodology. A generation that coined the term neijuan, “involution,” shorthand for running ever faster to stay in place, is not the confident spending cohort a middle class is built on.

The artificial intelligence boom deepens the divide between the government’s industrial ambitions and household welfare. Beijing is pouring trillions of yuan into the development of more advanced chips and data centers to support AI, and that spending is, for now, what is powering growth. But it funds those technology investments by starving the basics: hospitals, schools and other elements of the already meager safety net in rural areas, while the rewards accrue to the coastal, educated sliver.

The resulting inequality would look familiar to any American. With the poor and middle held down, one group has been allowed to grow: the rich. China’s richest 10% of the population hold about 68% of its national wealth, close to the US figure of 70%. In 2025 the 1,434 individuals worth at least 5 billion yuan saw their combined wealth soar 42% thanks to a powerful stock market rally, according to an annual list compiled by the Hurun Research Institute, a Shanghai-based firm that has tracked China’s rich since 1999.

The Party has shown that a few thousand tycoons are easier to manage than a broad middle class. In 2020, when Alibaba founder Jack Ma criticized China’s state-owned banks for having a “pawnshop mentality,” financial regulators canceled the initial public offering for his digital payments platform. He subsequently disappeared from public view for several months — a reminder of how those who have accumulated vast private fortunes are disciplined when they stray.

The longer trajectory, measured by earnings rather than wealth, is even starker. In 1978 the top 10% of earners and the bottom half of the population each took home about a quarter of national income. Since then, the top decile’s share has climbed to over 40%, while the bottom half’s has slid to under 14% — two lines that began together, now forked into what the West calls a “K-shaped” chasm. Deng’s founding promise for the reform era that some people would get rich first and the rest would follow increasingly looks like a plan that only ever had a first stage.

Follow these threads forward another quarter-century and the China that comes into view is not the one the WTO’s architects imagined.

With savings high and consumption weak, Beijing keeps doubling down on the supply side — what it calls the “new productive forces.” But a throttled home market cannot absorb what its state-of-the art factories produce, so the surplus will continue to go abroad: China now churns out more than 70% of the world’s electric vehicles, some 80% of its batteries and roughly 80% of its solar panels.

Unlike in the early WTO years, however, the world is putting up walls with tariffs and trade blocs. And what China exports today is no longer toys and textiles but EVs, industrial robots and wind turbines — goods that compete with the crown jewels of advanced economies like Germany and Denmark, whose workers are among the best-paid and most organized anywhere. The higher China climbs up the value chain, the more directly it will encroach on industries that such countries most want to protect, so these tensions will only increase.

Common prosperity, Xi’s supposed sequel to Deng’s “let some get rich first,” is turning out to mean shared restraint, not shared wealth: billionaires disciplined when convenient, the middle class asset-trapped, the poor pacified in 20-yuan increments. Everyone, in the end, is held equally in check.

The Party’s central challenge in the coming decades is demographic. With an expected 400 million retirees by 2035, the state will be forced to spend far more on pensions and care. Economists Michael Pettis and David Daokui Li argue from different directions that Beijing will sooner or later have no choice but to put real money in households’ pockets — Pettis because the investment-led growth model is exhausted, Li because the state owes a debt to the farmers who shouldered much of the burden for China’s industrialization and can afford to repay it. Li reckons that giving China’s 130 million rural elderly a pension that they could actually live on would cost about 1.25 trillion yuan a year, just 4% of government spending, less than a fifth of what the US spends on Social Security.

But a quarter-century of precedent suggests the Party will judge those costs as too high and too risky. Xi has applied this logic more rigidly than any of his reform-era predecessors. During 14 years in power, he’s chosen control over household welfare at every turn, and for the fourth presidential term he’s expected to claim in 2027, there’s no reason to expect a change of course. So the likeliest path is welfare that grows but stays minimal and conditional: enough to keep the peace, and calibrated to sustain dependence rather than end it.

The West wagered in 2001 that trade would make China rich and wealth would make it liberal. It got the first half. Whether a great power can hold the rest together while keeping most of its citizens poor is, at best, a formula for grinding stagnation — at worst, a slow-burning fuse.

GALADIMA: A LEADER WITH A HEART FOR THE PEOPLE AND A VISION FOR A GREATER ADAMAWA

As Adamawa looks towards 2027, Ahmed Tijjani Galadima Aminu presents a vision built around continuity, inclusiveness, human development and purposeful leadership.

Leadership is not measured only by political positions held or influence acquired, but by the lives touched, opportunities created and positive impact made on society.

These are qualities increasingly associated with Ahmed Tijjani Galadima Aminu, the APC gubernatorial candidate in Adamawa State for 2027.

Beyond politics, Galadima’s leadership philosophy reflects a commitment to human development, compassion, inclusiveness and sustainable progress.

A PHILANTHROPIST WITH A PASSION FOR EDUCATION

One outstanding aspect of Galadima’s public service journey is his commitment to education and human capital development.

During his tenure as Executive Secretary of the Petroleum Technology Development Fund (PTDF), he facilitated educational opportunities and sponsored numerous Nigerian students to pursue studies abroad, including beneficiaries from vulnerable backgrounds.

His interventions reflect a belief that education should not be limited by financial circumstances and that investing in people remains one of the most effective ways to secure a better future.

This is a legacy of opportunity creation that deserves recognition.

SIMPLICITY AND ACCESSIBILITY

Another quality associated with Galadima is his simplicity and accessibility. His interactions with political stakeholders, party members, community leaders and ordinary citizens reflect the importance of maintaining a close relationship with the people.

He represents a leadership disposition that values consultation, respect and listening to different opinions.

For a state as diverse as Adamawa, these qualities are essential in building trust and fostering unity.

A BELIEVER IN FINTIRI’S LEGACY AND CONTINUITY

At virtually every stakeholders’ engagement and party activity, Galadima consistently acknowledges the developmental achievements of Governor Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri.

His message is clear: Adamawa must sustain the progress already recorded and build upon the foundations established by the present administration.

From infrastructure to education, healthcare and urban development, he believes the Fintiri development vision should not be abandoned but strengthened and expanded.

For Galadima, continuity is not about maintaining the status quo; it is about consolidating achievements, addressing existing challenges and taking development to the next level.

A LEADER FOR EVERYONE

Adamawa’s strength lies in its diversity. Its future requires leadership that transcends tribal, religious and ethnic differences.

Observations from people familiar with Galadima describe him as someone who relates with people across different backgrounds without discrimination.

The governorship is an office for every citizen, regardless of religion, ethnicity or political affiliation.

His vision for Adamawa therefore presents an opportunity for inclusive governance in which every community matters, every citizen counts and development reaches all parts of the state.

ADAMAWA RISING AGENDA: A VISION FOR THE FUTURE

Galadima’s Adamawa Rising Agenda provides an insight into his development priorities and ambition for the state.

With emphasis on agriculture, mining, education, healthcare, youth empowerment, enterprise development, investment and innovation, the agenda seeks to unlock Adamawa’s economic potential.

Its focus on improving internally generated revenue without placing unnecessary financial burdens on citizens also reflects the need for responsible economic management.

These priorities demonstrate an ambition to build an economically stronger, more productive and prosperous Adamawa.

MATURITY AND PURPOSEFUL LEADERSHIP

Beyond policies and political calculations, leadership requires maturity, patience, wisdom and the ability to manage

Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif Addressing High-Level Session on “Clean Energy Transition by 2035: Powering the Future” on the sidelines of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), Antalya

Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif set an ambitious clean energy vision, calling for $138 billion investment to transform Pakistan’s energy sector.

Prime Minister Shehbaz informed that before travelling to Antalya, he had inaugurated a key section of Pakistan’s seventh nuclear power plant, a state-of-the-art project that would add 1,200 megawatts of clean electricity to the national grid. Outlining his vision for a cleaner transport sector, the Prime Minister said the recently launched auto policy envisaged making 30 per cent of new vehicles electric by 2030, supported by incentives, including lower tariffs. He added that all future government buses and motorcycles would be electric, noting that, for the first time, more than one in every 10 motorcycles sold in Pakistan this year was electric.

The Prime Minister said that 35 by 35 will be achieved only if finance flows at the speed of ambition through concessional capital and the transfer of affordable technology. He urged the international community to pursue a development model that balanced economic growth with environmental protection, emphasising that countries must be able to power their economies and meet people's energy needs without undermining the planet. Prime Minister reiterated that let us resolve to power our economies without impoverishing our people and light up our homes without darkening our planet, he said, stressing that the promise of clean energy transition must be delivered through collective commitment and action.

Speaking at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, Iraqi President Nizar Amedi said Iraq is preparing to establish a National Afforestation Fund to combat desertification. The fund would provide long-term financing for green belts and soil stabilisation. He said Iraq has planted more than 10 million trees over the past several decades and incorporated environmental topics into school curricula.
Amedi reaffirmed Iraq’s commitment to the Paris Agreement and said the country had updated its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), extending its planning horizon to 2035.
On energy, Amedi said Iraq had reduced the volume of associated gas flared by 75% and was working towards zero routine flaring by 2030. He also said 1,430 MW of renewable power capacity had entered service, with a target of 14,000 MW by 2030.
Iraq has also signed a contract for a seawater treatment project designed to supply 5 million barrels of treated water per day for drilling and injection at oilfields, reducing reliance on groundwater and river water. Amedi said Iraq had established a state-owned carbon economics company and signed memoranda of understanding with Iraqi and international companies to develop emissions reduction projects, carbon bonds and environmental technologies.
He called for easier access to green finance for fragile states and urged partners to remove bureaucratic barriers.

text:
OLUEBUBE AS NEW STAR OF ANAMBRA’S  SPORTING GLORY 

By Christian ABURIME 

(Nov.11th, 2026)

For Anambra State, for Nigeria, and indeed for the whole of Africa, another moment of sporting greatness to be proud of unraveled under the floodlights of Rabat, Morocco, on the evening of November 7, 2026. It was the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. At the heart of it all stood a young girl from Uga Community in Aguata local government area, Anambra State, with the ball at her feet and destiny in her stride. Her name is Oluebube Umejiaku. And the world now knows it.

When Nigeria’s Flamingos defeated Japan 2-1 in the final of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, they did more than lift a trophy. They shattered a ceiling that had stood for decades. For the first time ever, an African women’s national team, at any age level, in any competition, claimed a FIFA World Cup title. It was a rewriting of what the world believes is possible for the African girl child.

And in that golden hour, it was Anambra’s daughter who carried the flame.
Umejiaku did not simply play in the final; she defined it. Scoring the decisive second goal that sealed Nigeria’s triumph, she earned both the Player of the Match award in the final and, more gloriously, the FIFA Golden Ball as the best player of the entire tournament. Step after step, pass after pass, match after match in Morocco, the midfielder from Anambra performed with a maturity and brilliance that made the world take notice. 

They now call her Anambra’s star girl, and rightly so. From the dusty pitches of her childhood to the emerald turf of a World Cup final, hers is a story of talent nurtured under an enabling Anambra environment, of dreams watered with discipline, and of a young woman who looked at the horizon and refused to blink. To other aspiring girls across Anambra and the South-East, Oluebube Umejiaku is proof that their dreams are not too big, that the road from Anambra to the summit of world football is not only walkable, but winnable.

It is most fitting, then, that her homecoming has been marked with the honour she deserves. On November 9, the Chairman of the Anambra State Football Association, Mr Chikelue Iloenyosi, arrived in Abuja to welcome and celebrate the young champion on behalf of the Anambra State Government. 

Speaking at the occasion,  Iloenyosi poured profound appreciation on Professor Chukwuma Charles Soludo, the Governor of Anambra State, for his vibrant commitment to sports development and his keen recognition of sporting talent across the state.

Herein lies the deeper lesson of this triumphant moment. Champions are not born in a vacuum; they are discovered, encouraged, and grown where vision meets investment.
Governor Soludo’s sustained push to make sports a pillar of opportunity in Anambra, building structures that identify and elevate talent from the grassroots, is yielding fruit that all can now see.

The Golden Ball now held by Oluebube Umejiaku is not only hers; in a real sense, it belongs to a state that believes in its children enough to invest in them. Her success is a vindication, and a challenge to do even more.

So, Anambra has a star. Africa has a champion. The world has a new name to remember: Oluebube Umejiaku, the Flamingos’ fire, Africa’s pioneer queen of the U-17 World Cup. As she has made us proud, may her light continue to shine, and may many more rise behind her from Anambra’s light of excellence.

text:
OpenAI has finally released its first open-weight large language models since 2019’s GPT-2. These new “gpt-oss” models are available in two different sizes and score similarly to the company’s o3-mini and o4-mini models on several benchmarks. Unlike the models available through OpenAI’s web interface, these new open models can be freely downloaded, run, and even modified on laptops and other local devices.

In the company’s many years without an open LLM release, some users have taken to referring to it with the pejorative “ClosedAI.” That sense of frustration had escalated in the past few months as these long-awaited models were delayed twice—first in June and then in July. With their release, however, OpenAI is reestablishing itself as a presence for users of open models.

That’s particularly notable at a time when Meta, which had previously dominated the American open-model landscape with its Llama models, may be reorienting toward closed releases—and when Chinese open models, such as DeepSeek’s offerings, Kimi K2, and Alibaba’s Qwen series, are becoming more popular than their American competitors.

“The vast majority of our [enterprise and startup] customers are already using a lot of open models,” said Casey Dvorak, a research program manager at OpenAI, in a media briefing about the model release. “Because there is no [competitive] open model from OpenAI, we wanted to plug that gap and actually allow them to use our technology across the board.”

The new models come in two different sizes, the smaller of which can theoretically run on 16 GB of RAM—the minimum amount that Apple currently offers on its computers. The larger model requires a high-end laptop or specialized hardware.

Open models have a few key use cases. Some organizations may want to customize models for their own purposes or save money by running models on their own equipment, though that equipment comes at a substantial upfront cost. Others—such hospitals, law firms, and governments—might need models that they can run locally for data security reasons. 

OpenAI has facilitated such activity by releasing its open models under a permissive Apache 2.0 license, which allows the models to be used for commercial purposes. Nathan Lambert, post-training lead at the Allen Institute for AI, says that this choice is commendable: Such licenses are typical for Chinese open-model releases, but Meta released its Llama models under a bespoke, more restrictive license. “It’s a very good thing for the open community,” he says.

Researchers who study how LLMs work also need open models, so that they can examine and manipulate those models in detail. “In part, this is about reasserting OpenAI’s dominance in the research ecosystem,” says Peter Henderson, an assistant professor at Princeton University who has worked extensively with open models. If researchers do adopt gpt-oss as new workhorses, OpenAI could see some concrete benefits, Henderson says—it might adopt innovations discovered by other researchers into its own model ecosystem.

More broadly, Lambert says, releasing an open model now could help OpenAI reestablish its status in an increasingly crowded AI environment. “It kind of goes back to years ago, where they were seen as the AI company,” he says. Users who want to use open models will now have the option to meet all their needs with OpenAI products, rather than turning to Meta’s Llama or Alibaba’s Qwen when they need to run something locally.

The rise of Chinese open models like Qwen over the past year may have been a particularly salient factor in OpenAI’s calculus. An employee from OpenAI emphasized at the media briefing that the company doesn’t see these open models as a response to actions taken by any other AI company, but OpenAI is clearly attuned to the geopolitical implications of China’s open-model dominance. “Broad access to these capable open-weights models created in the US helps expand democratic AI rails,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the models’ release. 

Since DeepSeek exploded onto the AI scene at the start of 2025, observers have noted that Chinese models often refuse to speak about topics that the Chinese Communist Party has deemed verboten, such as Tiananmen Square. Such observations—as well as longer-term risks, like the possibility that agentic models could purposefully write vulnerable code—have made some AI experts concerned about the growing adoption of Chinese models. “Open models are a form of soft power,” Henderson says.

Lambert released a report on Monday documenting how Chinese models are overtaking American offerings like Llama and advocating for a renewed commitment to domestic open models. Several prominent AI researchers and entrepreneurs, such as HuggingFace CEO Clement Delangue, Stanford’s Percy Liang, and former OpenAI researcher Miles Brundage, have signed on.

The Trump administration, too, has emphasized development of open models in its AI Action Plan. With both this model release and previous statements, OpenAI is aligning itself with that stance. “In their filings about the action plan, [OpenAI] pretty clearly indicated that they see US–China as a key issue and want to position themselves as very important to the US system,” says Rishi Bommasani, a senior research scholar at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. 

And OpenAI may see concrete political advantages from aligning with the administration’s AI priorities, Lambert says. As the company continues to build out its extensive computational infrastructure, it will need political support and approvals, and sympathetic leadership could go a long way.

text:
Ok I'm calling it now. I have said this before and I am doubling down on this. 

Bookmark this.

Apple partners with SpaceX for the Siri AI rollout, and Grok becomes the brain.

Sounds crazy. But it’s actually the most obvious match in tech. Here's why:

Apple reportedly wants Siri to become an agent. Not answering questions, taking actions and finishing tasks for you. On 2.5B+ active devices. That's the biggest agent launch in history, and Apple has to pick the brain.

The options: OpenAI, Meta, Google Gemini, Anthropic, Grok. Most people will compare benchmarks. Wrong game. Benchmarks change every month, strategy doesn't. Here's how I'd play it if I were the Apple Ceo.

1. Don't arm your rival
Never make a future competitor stronger with your own distribution.
OpenAI paid $6.5B for Jony Ive's io. The man who designed the iPhone is building OpenAI's own device, first one no earlier than end of February 2027 per a court filing. Apple is already suing OpenAI and io over hardware trade secrets.
Meta sells $799 Ray-Ban Display glasses, and in September showed Muse Charm: own OS, built-in 5G, ships in December, made to reach Meta's AI without your phone. Reuters said Zuckerberg took repeated digs at Apple on stage.
Google makes Android and the Pixel. Apple's direct competitor for 17 years.
3 of 5 options are building the thing that replaces the iPhone. Give them Siri and you pay to train the AI that ends up in their hardware. That's a hold-up problem: your supplier is your competitor, and the day it doesn't need you, it squeezes you.

2. Commoditize your complement
Apple's best move has always been to make everything around the iPhone cheap and swappable, and keep the iPhone scarce. A model maker with no device wants to be inside the best device. A model maker with its own device wants your phone to become a dumb pipe to its AI. You don't hand your shelf to someone whose dream is that your shelf disappears.

3. Leverage against Google
Google pays Apple about $20B a year for Safari search. Gemini now powers the new Siri, and Apple pays Google for it. That's a lot of Apple running through one rival. The judge in the search case killed exclusive deals, forced yearly contracts and said Apple is free to push rival AI, Siri included. That's your BATNA, your best alternative if a deal falls through. Every bit of Siri Grok gets weakens Google's hand. Even if Gemini stays, a real second brain makes every renewal cheaper.

4. Anthropic, the honest competitor
No phone, no glasses, no OS. It doesn't threaten the iPhone either. But its own S-1 lists about $121B committed to Google, $110B to Amazon, about $45B to Microsoft and up to $120.5B to SpaceX. Pick Anthropic and your Siri agent runs on compute rented from Google and Amazon, both selling phones, speakers or assistants against you. The rival left through the front door and walked back in through the data center lol

5. The compute game
An agent isn't one question. It's task after task in the background, all day. On 2.5B devices that's the biggest compute bill ever. The question isn't who has the best model this month, it's who can serve 2.5B devices in two years without asking a competitor for chips. SpaceX had about 2.2 GW of its own compute running in October, aiming for 2.5 to 3 GW by year end. Even Anthropic rents from it.

6. Grok checks every box
No phone. Elon: "We are not developing a phone." When the WSJ reported a SpaceX handset prototype in July he called it "Utterly false." Honest part: he also said a phone is "not out of the question at some point." My read: with rockets, satellites, an AI lab and a chip fab to scale, a phone fight with Apple is the last thing SpaceX needs.
Own compute: Colossus. Own satellite layer that already talks to phones: Starlink. Own distribution: X has been #1 in News on the US App Store every day since 23 Sept.
Grok doesn't need Apple to survive, but wants the iPhone shelf more than anyone. Hungry, not desperate, and not building a rival phone. The best kind of partner.

7. The repeated game
Deals like this run year after year, so trust beats price. For years Cook and Elon couldn't do business: App Store fights, iPhone ban threats, a lawsuit. Then Ternus became CEO on 1 Sept, Elon replied "Congrats!", and 13 days later the lawsuit was dropped for good. The filing says "resolved." Terms sealed. That's a fresh start. Both sides proved they'd rather cooperate than fight, and that's worth more than any benchmark.

8. The kingmaker move
Apple doesn't need the strongest AI company. Apple IS the kingmaker. 2.5B devices pick the winner. So crown the one that needs your shelf most, can't threaten your phone and brings its own compute. That's one name on the list.

My guess: Grok lands behind Siri next to Gemini first, and the agent layer goes to whoever can pay the compute bill. I've been early on Apple x SpaceX before, I'll own that. But the board has never set up better than today.

Cook needed a phone to sell. Ternus needs an agent that works. Pick the one that won't become your next competitor.

Russian President Vladimir Putin Bestows Order of Friendship on Patriarch Theophilos III of Jerusalem

MOSCOW / KREMLIN — Russian President Vladimir Putin presented His Beatitude Theophilos III, Patriarch of the Holy City of Jerusalem and All Palestine, with the Order of Friendship during an official meeting at the Kremlin on Thursday, November 5, 2026. The high-level conferral highlights Moscow's ongoing engagement with the historic Patriarchates of the Middle East during a period of complex shifts within the global Orthodox communion.

During the ceremony, President Putin commended Patriarch Theophilos III for his dedicated efforts to strengthen long-standing spiritual and cultural ties between the Patriarchate of Jerusalem and the Russian Orthodox Church, as well as his commitment to preserving the Christian presence and safeguarding sacred sites throughout the Holy Land.  
"It is a great honor for me to present you with this order," President Putin stated during the presentation, acknowledging the Patriarch’s international standing and his initiatives promoting inter-religious stability.  

The conferral followed extensive bilateral discussions held earlier in Moscow between Patriarch Theophilos III and Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia. The primates addressed ecclesiastical developments, the security challenges confronting indigenous Christian communities in the Middle East, and constructive paths toward resolving broader inter-Orthodox divisions. Furthermore, discussions encompassed preliminary regional planning for the upcoming 2030 commemorations marking the anniversary of the Baptism of Jesus Christ in Jordan.  

Patriarch Theophilos III also emphasized the importance of facilitating dialogue and de-escalation in international conflicts, building upon themes of peace and reconciliation previously discussed during high-level diplomatic exchanges, including his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump.
About the Order of Friendship:
The Order of Friendship (Орден Дружбы) is a state decoration of the Russian Federation established to recognize foreign nationals and Russian citizens whose efforts significantly improve international relations, foster mutual understanding, and preserve cultural and spiritual heritage.

text:
AUDI'S $7 BILLION AMERICAN BET: Trump's tariffs are bringing German luxury cars to Georgia | Lauren Fix, Blaze Media

German luxury automaker Audi is preparing to build cars in America for the first time, and its investment could reach $7 billion.

Last month, Audi announced plans for a $4 billion manufacturing plant in Georgia that would employ approximately 4,500 workers and produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually. Now, documents obtained by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reveal that the company is considering a second phase worth another $3 billion, potentially adding 3,000 jobs.

If Audi can sell a luxury SUV for $90,000, moving production to Georgia doesn't mean it will suddenly offer that vehicle for $80,000.

That would bring Audi's total investment to $7 billion and its workforce to 7,500, although the expansion remains a possibility, not a commitment. Even the original plant still awaits final corporate approval.

For an automaker that has spent decades selling German luxury cars to Americans without building a single one here, it's a major change. And President Donald Trump's tariffs are helping drive it.

The cost of importing cars

Until now, every Audi sold in the United States has been imported from factories in Europe or Mexico. But that business model has become considerably more expensive. According to Reuters, Trump's tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminum, and parts cost Audi approximately $1.4 billion in 2025.

That's a substantial expense for a company competing against BMW and Mercedes-Benz, both of which already manufacture vehicles in the United States.

Building cars domestically would allow Audi to avoid tariffs on imported finished vehicles produced at its new factory. It would also give the company greater control over production costs and reduce its exposure to future trade disputes.

Audi isn't simply accepting the current tariffs while it builds a factory, however. The company is also negotiating with Washington for relief. Reuters reported October 29 that Audi wants the Trump administration to reduce the 15% tariff on European Union vehicle imports to 7.5%. Administration officials were reportedly considering a reduction to approximately 10% for automakers making substantial investments in American manufacturing.

In other words, Audi wants to make cars here while also paying less to import the ones it will continue building overseas.

The negotiations illustrate how tariffs are reshaping manufacturers' decisions. Imported cars have become more expensive, while companies willing to invest in American factories may qualify for favorable treatment.

Audi's investment is a particularly striking example.

Why Georgia?

The new factory will occupy the Middle Georgia Mega Site in Peach County, near Macon. Audi plans to begin site work in 2027, with full production projected for 2031.

The plant is expected to manufacture premium SUVs designed for the American market. Audi has not announced specific models, but the emphasis on SUVs makes sense. American buyers continue to favor larger vehicles, particularly in the luxury market, and Audi has been looking to strengthen its position against BMW and Mercedes-Benz.

Georgia also has something Audi needs: an established automotive manufacturing industry.

BMW builds SUVs in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes-Benz has manufactured vehicles in Alabama for decades. Closer to Audi's proposed factory, Kia operates a plant in West Point, Georgia, while Hyundai has invested billions in its own Georgia manufacturing operations.

Those companies have helped create a network of suppliers, skilled workers, and transportation infrastructure that Audi can now draw upon.

Georgia is also offering substantial financial incentives.

According to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, state and local officials proposed at least $958 million in tax breaks, grants, and other support for the first phase. That includes approximately $459 million in property tax savings over 20 years, along with investments in roads, utilities, site preparation, and workforce training.

Those incentives are a significant public expense. Georgia is betting that thousands of jobs, new suppliers, and decades of economic activity will justify the investment.

Will American buyers pay less?

For consumers, the most immediate question is whether building Audis in America will make them more affordable.

The answer depends on what Audi does with the savings.

When an automaker imports a vehicle, tariffs increase the cost of bringing it into the country. The manufacturer can absorb that expense, raise the sticker price, reduce discounts and incentives, or combine those approaches. The customer can end up paying more even when the manufacturer's suggested retail price doesn't change.

Building vehicles in the United States removes the tariff on the imported finished car. That gives Audi more room to compete on price, but it doesn't require the company to pass those savings along to buyers.

And even an American-built Audi won't necessarily be free of tariff-related costs. Imported engines, electronics, transmissions, and other components may still be subject to duties.

There's another consideration. Automakers don't necessarily price vehicles according to what they cost to manufacture. They price them according to what customers are willing to pay and what competing brands charge. If Audi can sell a luxury SUV for $90,000, moving production to Georgia doesn't mean it will suddenly offer that vehicle for $80,000.

What domestic production could do is help Audi hold prices steady, offer more competitive financing or incentives, and protect its margins without making customers absorb every increase in import costs. The company would also have more flexibility to build vehicles specifically for American buyers.

For someone shopping for a new Audi today, however, none of this will change the price at the dealership tomorrow. The first American-built vehicles are still years away.

A long-term American commitment

Audi's announcement came during an October 24 campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, where Trump appeared alongside company CEO Gernot Döllner.

Trump celebrated the project as evidence that his trade policies were bringing manufacturing investment to the United States.

Audi has been more cautious about the politics. In an October 26 statement, the company acknowledged concerns about its appearance with Trump but emphasized the economic reasons for building in America.

Audi also made an important admission: Its U.S. business is currently unprofitable. That puts the Georgia investment in perspective. Tariffs are an important factor, but Audi also needs to improve its American operations. Building vehicles closer to customers could help accomplish both goals.

text:
Impeachment stalled. A CFR fellow says the Pentagon's deeper wound is its officer corps

The House vote on Tuesday to send Representative Thomas Massie's impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee settled one question: impeachment will not end his tenure for now. Linda Robinson, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, argues in a piece published that night that the bigger problem will outlast him.

Robinson writes that the munitions shortages left by the Iran war are short-term problems compared with the lasting damage to the people who make up the force. She points to the dismissal or forced retirement of an unprecedented number of generals and admirals, including a disproportionate number of women and Black officers, and to reports that Hegseth intervened to remove officers from one- and two-star promotion lists in the Army and Navy. It takes decades to grow a four-star leader, she notes, so the gaps will show for a generation.

The morale numbers are striking. A poll by the veterans' group Common Defense Civic Engagement, reported by Military. com, found that 53 percent of active-duty respondents are considering leaving early because they believe the military is becoming politicized. Sixty-seven percent said decisions are being made for political gain.

Women are where Robinson sees the sharpest damage. There are no four-star female officers today, and only eight of 201 nominees for promotion are women, according to one analysis she cites. Women make up 18 percent of the active-duty force and meet entry standards at higher rates than men. She warns that a Pentagon review of women in ground combat, ordered in December 2025, could become a pretext to bar them from infantry roles, even though senior enlisted leaders and service vice chiefs testified this year that women in combat units have not hurt readiness.

Her forecast is political. What is likely to make Hegseth's position untenable, she writes, is losing support for defense spending and authorization bills once a Democratic Congress is seated in January. Her vehicle for repair is the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, in the lame-duck session or in January. She wants officers removed from promotion lists to get written notice of cause and a right of appeal, as in Senator Richard Blumenthal's Military Officer Promotion Integrity Act, with Senator Tammy Duckworth pushing to cover every removal since January 2025. She also backs the WARRIOR Act to bar gender-based exclusion from combat units, the return of the Defense Advisory Committee on Women in the Services, and tougher oversight, which Adam Smith, the likely next House Armed Services chair, has pledged through a dedicated subcommittee.

Robinson adds a request for whoever follows Hegseth: recall some of the dismissed talent, naming Admiral Lisa Franchetti, an Asia expert, among others.

Rivals measure American readiness in people as well as hardware. Factories can refill interceptor stocks in a few years once Congress pays for them. A thinned bench of senior commanders takes decades to rebuild, which is why Robinson wants the fix written into the defense bill while the incoming Congress holds the leverage.

text:
UGANDA’S SUCCESSION BATTLE HEATS UP AS SENIOR NRM OFFICIALS RESIST PLANS TO HAND POWER TO MUHOOZI KAINERUGABA.

Uganda’s long-running political succession debate has entered a sharper phase. Senior figures in the ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) have reportedly pushed back against President Yoweri Museveni’s efforts to position his son, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, as the party’s preferred successor for the 2031 presidential election. The resistance surfaced in closed-door meetings of the NRM’s Central Executive Committee (CEC), exposing divisions inside a party that has dominated Ugandan politics for nearly four decades.

The most recent flashpoint came on 10 November 2026 at State House Entebbe. According to multiple accounts from participants who spoke to outlets including Agence France-Presse and local Ugandan media, the committee began considering Muhoozi’s suitability as a future candidate. A vote was started but abandoned after only seven of the roughly 28 members had cast ballots—four in favour and three against—once open opposition drew applause. Some members cited Muhoozi’s combative social-media style, including threats directed at political opponents, as a source of unease. Others argued that a serving senior military officer should first move into a civilian role to build broader public connections before seeking the presidency. NRM vice-chairman for Eastern Uganda David Calvin Echodu was among those who urged Museveni to contest again in 2031, saying his son was not yet ready. Museveni indicated that further meetings would be held.

This followed an earlier CEC session on 27 October 2026 in which Museveni presented a succession discussion paper. The document acknowledged informal endorsements of Muhoozi among some NRM members and supporters for the 2031–2036 term. Museveni highlighted his son’s military record, patriotism, pan-African outlook, and role in strengthening the Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF). He wrote that, as Muhoozi’s father and a former resistance fighter who encouraged him to join the army, he knew him to meet many of the qualities required. Supporters at that meeting included State Minister Haruna Kasolo and others, while objections came from figures such as Hadijah Namyalo. Claims that Museveni had formally “endorsed” Muhoozi circulated quickly on social media, particularly from allies linked to the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU), but party officials disputed whether any binding resolution had been reached. Muhoozi himself later instructed PLU members to stop publicly discussing the paper and leave the matter to him and his father while focusing on grassroots endorsements.

These developments sit against a longer history. Museveni, born in 1944, seized power in January 1986 at the head of the National Resistance Army after years of guerrilla war. In his early speeches he criticised African leaders who overstayed in office. Over time the constitution was amended: presidential term limits were removed in 2005, and the upper age limit of 75 was scrapped in 2017 after parliamentary and court battles. He has now won multiple elections, most recently securing a seventh term in the January 2026 polls with roughly 72 per cent of the vote according to the Electoral Commission, against opposition figure Bobi Wine. At around 82, questions about physical capacity and the absence of a clear institutional succession process have grown louder, even as the NRM retains firm control of state institutions.

Muhoozi Kainerugaba, born in April 1974 in Dar es Salaam during his parents’ exile, joined the UPDF in 1999 and graduated from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst. He rose rapidly: commander of the Special Forces Command (then Special Forces Group) for several years, later Commander of Land Forces, and since 2024 Chief of Defence Forces. He has also held advisory roles close to the presidency. Supporters point to operations against the Lord’s Resistance Army and other groups, professionalisation of elite units, and contributions to regional security deployments. Critics note the speed of promotion, close family ties, and a series of inflammatory posts on X (formerly Twitter), including remarks about neighbouring countries and political opponents. In early November 2026 Muhoozi publicly stated that his time as CDF was ending, that he had completed the tasks assigned to him, and that he would hand over to another officer in the coming months before dedicating himself to other work, including religious commitment. Some interpreted this as preparation for a more overt political role; others saw it as managing the military-politics boundary.

The current resistance inside the NRM is notable because the party has long been tightly managed from the top. Senior “historical” figures from the 1980s bush war, regional representatives, and some long-serving officials have expressed caution about dynastic succession. Concerns include the perception of military influence over civilian politics, potential international reaction (Western partners have previously been wary of open succession by the army chief), and the need for wider party structures to have a say rather than a predetermined handover. At the same time, a significant bloc continues to back Muhoozi on the basis of continuity, security credentials, and the mobilisation already underway through the PLU. Museveni has so far kept the process internal, scheduling further CEC discussions rather than forcing a decision.

Uganda’s politics has repeatedly shown that formal rules can be adjusted and that elite consensus inside the NRM matters more than public campaigning alone. The present episode does not yet amount to a rupture, but it demonstrates that even after four decades the question of who comes next is not settled by presidential preference alone. Muhoozi’s supporters have been building organisational capacity and collecting endorsements; opponents inside the party are using the CEC platform to slow or reshape that process. Further meetings are expected. Whether the outcome is an eventual Muhoozi candidacy, a longer Museveni run, a broader internal competition, or some hybrid arrangement will shape the country’s direction well beyond 2031.

For ordinary Ugandans, the debate sits against persistent issues of service delivery, youth unemployment, and governance. The NRM’s ability to manage this transition without open fracture will influence both domestic stability and the country’s external partnerships. The November 2026 meetings have made the contest more visible; they have not yet resolved it.

Visa Cash App Racing Bulls Formula One™ Team is pleased to confirm that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue as its driver line-up for the 2027 FIA Formula One World Championship season.

Alan Permane, Team Principal and Co-CEO Sporting, said: “We’re delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027. Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing. I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Liam Lawson said: “I’m very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls next year. We’ve had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I’ve loved driving. It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the Constructors' Championship. It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory. I’m looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027; we’re building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

Arvid Lindblad said: "I'm very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls in 2027. Looking back on my first season in Formula One, it's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test. I'd like to thank everyone at VCARB and Red Bull for their trust and support. I'm incredibly grateful to everyone in the team for their hard work, commitment and collaboration throughout the season, and for the strong relationships we've built along the way. I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season. It's set to be an exciting year, and I look forward to continue driving alongside Liam." #VCARB #F1
