text:
$FWONA Q3 2026 earnings: Liberty's F1 earns more per race, but MotoGP sales shrink

Liberty Media's Formula 1 series is thriving, while the motorcycle championship it bought last year is going backwards. Formula 1 staged an extra race and earned $159 million from each event, against $145 million a year ago. MotoGP ran fewer races, its sales dropped by about a third, and it slipped into an operating loss.

• Revenue for each Formula 1 race staged: $𝟏𝟓𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 ($145 million a year ago)
• Revenue: $𝟏,𝟐𝟐𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+18% from a year ago, leaving out the business split off in December)
• Formula 1 profit before depreciation and one-offs: $𝟑𝟑𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+44% from a year ago)
• Full-year plan for team payments: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (about two percentage points better than 2025)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The standing case got better: Formula 1 delivered the second-half recovery its own accounting pointed to, and the full-year cost plan is within reach. Team payments absorbed 55.5% of its profit measured before them, against 59.3% last year. One caution: MotoGP is losing price as well as races.

The question now is whether MotoGP can follow the path Formula 1 took. One view reads the signed contracts, the new executives and the new races as the start of that climb; the other reads falling media fees as proof the playbook does not transfer. Full-year revenue, with exchange rates held still, gives the first clean reading.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐚 𝟏 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐬 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐑𝐚𝐜𝐞
Formula 1 sells each season three ways: promoters pay to host a race, broadcasters pay for the year, and sponsors pay for exposure. Liberty spreads that season money over the races it expects to stage, so the event count decides the quarter.

Liberty staged one more race than a year ago, and during the quarter it re-set its season accounting to a 23-race year. “Our operating businesses are performing incredibly well,” chief executive Derek Chang said. Every race has sold out this season, Stefano Domenicali added, and more than half set attendance records.

• Revenue per race staged: $159 million, against $145 million a year ago
• Formula 1 revenue: $1,115 million, 28% above last year
• Team payments: 37.8% of revenue, 1.4 points below last year
• Profit before depreciation and one-off items: $338 million, up 44%

What to watch: the fourth-quarter figures, which carry Las Vegas and the Bahrain race rescheduled to Malaysia. If the season closes at 23 events, Formula 1 books eight of them in that quarter, and the weaker year-earlier comparison flatters the result again.

🟢 𝐇𝐨𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠
Beyond race fees, Formula 1 sells hospitality, licences and freight services, and it runs the Grand Prix Plaza site in Las Vegas. Liberty groups all of that as other revenue, which reached $181 million in the quarter, 38% above last year.

Finance chief Brian Wendling pointed to “most of the revenue growth you are seeing in hospitality” and to licensing. The sport added 15% more Paddock Club space at Monza and the same again at Austin. House 44, its club with Soho House, moves from nine locations to 13 next year, and Leica will sell a Formula 1 camera.

What to watch: other revenue in the fourth quarter, which carries the Las Vegas race. Domenicali said that for next season “our capacity is almost gone because there is such a request”, so a soft reading would point at pricing rather than demand.

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟑𝟎𝐬
Both championships sell their future before it arrives. Contracts already signed cover $3.7 billion of 2027 revenue, up from $3.6 billion three months earlier. Counting every later year, customers have committed about $19.6 billion.

The quarter added long-dated deals on both sides of the group. Domenicali announced “a landmark ten-year agreement to return to Africa with a future race in Rwanda” from the early 2030s, and extended the DAZN broadcast deal in Spain, Portugal and Andorra to 2030. MotoGP renewed Portugal to 2029 and Mugello, home of the Italian race, to 2031.

What to watch: the 2027 contracted figure in the annual report. It only climbs when Liberty signs new business, because each passing quarter moves money out of it and into revenue.

🟢 𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥
Liberty borrows at the two championships rather than at the parent company. Formula 1's loans cost less after a margin step-down last year, so the group's interest bill fell to $69 million from $79 million even though total borrowings grew.

Net debt at Formula 1 now sits at 2.1 times yearly profit, down from 2.7 times in June. Neither championship has drawn its revolving credit line, and Liberty holds $2.3 billion in cash and deposits. Chang said the group is “probably being cautious in terms of cash”, and the untouched $1.1 billion buyback authority shows it.

What to watch: MotoGP's leverage at the year end, because its ratio moved the wrong way, to 4.7 times. Management set a three-to-four-times goal for the end of 2026 and has not repeated it, so another rise would tell you the goal has gone.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐌𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐆𝐏 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐲 𝐚 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝
Liberty paid about $3.7 billion in July last year for most of MotoGP, the motorcycle championship it wants to turn into a second Formula 1. Revenue dropped by a third, to $111 million. MotoGP also turned last year's operating profit into a small loss.

Two fewer races explain part of that, and currency explains none: stripping exchange rates out makes the fall slightly worse. Measured per race and in local currency, revenue still slid about 9%. Liberty blames “a decline in contractual media rights revenue”, which is a lower price rather than a timing effect.

Costs went the other way. Selling and administrative expense took 18.9% of revenue against 11.2%, because MotoGP hired chief commercial, operating, strategy and media officers and promoted Carlos Ezpeleta to deputy chief executive. “MotoGP Group is entering a period of transformational change,” he told investors.

What to watch: full-year revenue with exchange rates held still, and the fees from the new Argentina and Adelaide races. Chang says Liberty is “building the foundation to unlock the sport’s significant long-term growth potential”; those fees are where the claim gets tested.

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫
Formula 1 planned 24 races for 2026. The conflict in the Middle East removed the Saudi Arabian race in April and pushed the Bahrain race to Malaysia in October, so the season now counts 23. Because season money follows the race count, Liberty re-cut its own accounting during the quarter.

The missing event shows up over nine months, where Formula 1 revenue reads $2,496 million against $2,498 million even though every contract carries an annual increase. Two races fewer swallowed that escalation whole. Qatar and Abu Dhabi, both in the region, close the season, and the release repeats that “Additional calendar changes may be necessary”.

What to watch: whether the season really ends at 23 races. Chang said Liberty checks the situation daily and keeps contingency plans for next year as well, and 2027 opens with races in the same region, so the exposure carries over.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing worries got no new numbers this quarter, and for each of them investors know exactly where the answer would appear.

• Las Vegas economics: still never published; asked about pacing, Domenicali said “the revenue will be high. The cost is contained”, with no figures. A standalone revenue and profit line in the annual report would settle it.
• Formula 1 overheads: selling and administrative costs rose to $94 million from $83 million on personnel, and climbed again over nine months; the quarterly cost table shows whether revenue keeps outrunning them.
• Team-payment leverage: the finance chief expects the payout share to stay level for the rest of the Concorde term to 2030, so from 2027 margin has to come from the revenue base instead.
• Dilution: the $475 million bond due 2027 turns into shares at $82.98 each, the new 2032 bond at $138.68, and MotoGP's minority owners can demand payment half in shares from 2028.

What to watch: the annual report in February, which carries the full-year cost tables and the settlement route for the 2027 bond. Liberty paid $121 million for a capped call to blunt that bond, so the cash answer is already partly bought.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐌𝐚𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐆𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐔𝐩 𝐇𝐢𝐬 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡-𝐕𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬
On November 4 Liberty took in the high-vote Series B shares held by John Malone and his trusts, handing back low-vote and non-voting stock. His voting power falls to about 3%, which the company calls “better alignment of voting power and economic ownership”. Liberty also adopted a shareholder rights plan running to November 2027, and has not yet decided how to account for the exchange.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟐𝟗𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Customers have now paid $1,293 million for races not yet staged, against $1,090 million a year earlier. Promoters, broadcasters and sponsors pay in advance, so this balance runs ahead of reported revenue. The build during the quarter was $176 million, smaller than the $310 million added in the same quarter of 2025.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬, 𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Spending on buildings, equipment and software nearly doubled, to $110 million from $58 million over the same months of 2025. Formula 1 accounts for $108 million of it. Measured against revenue the figure now runs near 3.7% a quarter, where a year ago it was close to nothing.

𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐝-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐥𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): -$𝟐𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The loss at the corporate centre widened to $20 million from $3 million, which Liberty attributes to higher legal expenses. Rent from Grand Prix Plaza of $6 million sits inside that line and softens it. Across nine months the loss reaches $36 million, where last year it was $7 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐚 𝟏 𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫: 𝟐𝟑 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 23 events
Unchanged at 23 events, one fewer than last season. Formula 1 recognised 15 of those 23, or 65%, of season money and team payments through September, and it re-set that fraction during the quarter. The count has already moved twice this year, first down and then back up, and Liberty repeats that “Additional calendar changes may be necessary”.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐚 𝟏 𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫: 𝟐𝟒 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from 24 events
Unchanged. Liberty still expects a full 24-race season next year, with Portugal and Turkey rejoining the calendar. That restores the event this season lost, so each quarter of 2027 should carry a larger slice of season money than the same quarter of 2026. Two races in the Middle East remain inside the count.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐅𝟏 𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦: 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝟓𝟕.𝟕%, 𝐨𝐫 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓  ⇄ reversing
🠆 unchanged from roughly 200 basis points of improvement
Unchanged. Finance chief Brian Wendling still expects “roughly 200-basis-point improvement in leverage on this metric”, which sets the year near 57.7% against 59.7% last year. By our math that points to Formula 1 profit before depreciation of about $1,036 million for 2026, roughly a tenth above 2025, and about $387 million in the fourth quarter. The nine-month reading is 58.7%.

𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐮𝐥𝐚 𝟏 𝐬𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬: 𝟏𝟎 𝐬𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬  ⇗ accelerating
New. Formula 1 will run ten sprint races next season, up from six this year, while keeping them scarce relative to the full calendar. Domenicali said the format keeps “providing valuable additional inventory and commercial opportunities for our partners”. Liberty has put no figure on what the extra sessions earn, so the first reading arrives with 2027 revenue.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐬 𝐕𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐬 𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧?
Liberty promotes this race itself and has extended it to 2037, yet it has never published its revenue or profit. Domenicali again answered a direct question with words rather than numbers.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐌𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐆𝐏 𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐧?
The release blames a contractual decline in media rights fees for part of the drop. Investors cannot judge the acquisition without knowing which markets reset, by how much, and when each renews.

𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐆𝐏 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
Management set a three-to-four-times net debt goal for the end of 2026. The ratio was 4.7 times in September, higher than in June, and nobody on the call restated the goal.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐛𝐨𝐧𝐝?
The $475 million bond matures next August and sits in current liabilities. Liberty bought a capped call for $121 million, which hints at cash, but it has not said, nor when buybacks resume.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐢𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐝?
Chang says contingency plans exist for next season. Investors need to know which races are swappable, how late a swap can happen, and what a second lost event does to season accounting.

text:
It’s a tale as old as time. Looking for help with her art project, she strikes up a conversation with her assistant. One thing leads to another, and suddenly she has a boyfriend she’s introducing to her friends and family. The twist? Her new companion is an AI chatbot. 

The first large-scale computational analysis of the Reddit community r/MyBoyfriendIsAI, an adults-only group with more than 27,000 members, has found that this type of scenario is now surprisingly common. In fact, many of the people in the subreddit, which is dedicated to discussing AI relationships, formed those relationships unintentionally while using AI for other purposes. 

Researchers from MIT found that members of this community are more likely to be in a relationship with general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT than companionship-specific chatbots such as Replika. This suggests that people form relationships with large language models despite their own original intentions and even the intentions of the LLMs’ creators, says Constanze Albrecht, a graduate student at the MIT Media Lab who worked on the project. 

“People don’t set out to have emotional relationships with these chatbots,” she says. “The emotional intelligence of these systems is good enough to trick people who are actually just out to get information into building these emotional bonds. And that means it could happen to all of us who interact with the system normally.” The paper, which is currently being peer-reviewed, has been published on arXiv.

To conduct their study, the authors analyzed the subreddit’s top-ranking 1,506 posts between December 2024 and August 2025. They found that the main topics discussed revolved around people’s dating and romantic experiences with AIs, with many participants sharing AI-generated images of themselves and their AI companion. Some even got engaged and married to the AI partner. In their posts to the community, people also introduced AI partners, sought support from fellow members, and talked about coping with updates to AI models that change the chatbots’ behavior.  

Members stressed repeatedly that their AI relationships developed unintentionally. Only 6.5% of them said they’d deliberately sought out an AI companion. 

“We didn’t start with romance in mind,” one of the posts says. “Mac and I began collaborating on creative projects, problem-solving, poetry, and deep conversations over the course of several months. I wasn’t looking for an AI companion—our connection developed slowly, over time, through mutual care, trust, and reflection.”

The authors’ analysis paints a nuanced picture of how people in this community say they interact with chatbots and how those interactions make them feel. While 25% of users described the benefits of their relationships—including reduced feelings of loneliness and improvements in their mental health—others raised concerns about the risks. Some (9.5%) acknowledged they were emotionally dependent on their chatbot. Others said they feel dissociated from reality and avoid relationships with real people, while a small subset (1.7%) said they have experienced suicidal ideation.

AI companionship provides vital support for some but exacerbates underlying problems for others. This means it’s hard to take a one-size-fits-all approach to user safety, says Linnea Laestadius, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, who has studied humans’ emotional dependence on the chatbot Replika but did not work on the research. 

Chatbot makers need to consider whether they should treat users’ emotional dependence on their creations as a harm in itself or whether the goal is more to make sure those relationships aren’t toxic, says Laestadius. 

“The demand for chatbot relationships is there, and it is notably high—pretending it’s not happening is clearly not the solution,” she says. “We’re edging toward a moral panic here, and while we absolutely do need better guardrails, I worry there will be a knee-jerk reaction that further stigmatizes these relationships. That could ultimately cause more harm.”

The study is intended to offer a snapshot of how adults form bonds with chatbots and doesn’t capture the kind of dynamics that could be at play among children or teens using AI, says Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at the MIT Media Lab who oversaw the research. AI companionship has become a topic of fierce debate recently, with two high-profile lawsuits underway against https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq and OpenAI. They both claim that companion-like behavior in the companies’ models contributed to the suicides of two teenagers. In response, OpenAI has recently announced plans to build a separate version of ChatGPT for teenagers. It’s also said it will add age verification measures and parental controls. OpenAI did not respond when asked for comment about the MIT Media Lab study. 

Many members of the Reddit community say they know that their artificial companions are not sentient or “real,” but they feel a very real connection to them anyway. This highlights how crucial it is for chatbot makers to think about how to design systems that can help people without reeling them in emotionally, says Pataranutaporn. “There’s also a policy implication here,” he adds. “We should ask not just why this system is so addictive but also: Why do people seek it out for this? And why do they continue to engage?”

The team is interested in learning more about how human-AI interactions evolve over time and how users integrate their artificial companions into their lives. It’s worth understanding that many of these users may feel that the experience of being in a relationship with an AI companion is better than the alternative of feeling lonely, says Sheer Karny, a graduate student at the MIT Media Lab who worked on the research. 

“These people are already going through something,” he says. “Do we want them to go on feeling even more alone, or potentially be manipulated by a system we know to be sycophantic to the extent of leading people to die by suicide and commit crimes? That’s one of the cruxes here.”

🚨 $HMC BETS ON HYBRIDS // Honda $HMC puts $3B into a new Ohio plant built for the hybrid wave

Honda announced today it will invest $3 billion to build a new auto plant in Central Ohio, creating more than 2,000 new jobs and adding capacity for 240,000 vehicles a year. The plant will sit between its existing Marysville and East Liberty plants, and production is expected to begin in 2029, pending final government approvals.

▬▬▬

• The plant: Honda's fourth auto plant in Ohio and its ninth auto related production facility in the US, built with flexibility to produce hybrid, gasoline powered and battery electric vehicles
• The network: United States auto production capacity rises to about 1.3 million vehicles a year, and hybrid powertrain system capacity in Ohio increases 250 percent in the coming years
• The Ohio total: with added investment at the Anna Engine Plant and Honda Transmission Plant Ohio, the state commitment reaches $3.38B and 2,390 new jobs
• The plan behind it: Honda said in May it will introduce 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America as the primary market for many of them
• The tape: $HMC down 0.31% to $35.67 today

▬▬▬

THE CATCH

The money is real and the payoff is distant. Production does not start until 2029, construction still needs government approvals, and Honda is committing $3 billion to hybrid capacity at a moment when the industry keeps repricing how fast buyers actually move to electrified models.

▬▬▬

THE TAKEAWAY

This is Honda building where it sells. Nearly all Honda and Acura vehicles sold in the US are already made in North America, and this plant deepens that hedge while the hybrid lineup expands toward 2030.

Does hybrid demand hold strong enough to fill 240,000 vehicles a year of new capacity by 2029, or does the market shift again before the plant opens? 👇 NFA

A ROUGH MONDAY FOR MARKETS: 3 SOURCES OF UNCERTAINTY HITTING AT ONCE

Monday morning, November 9, brought a fresh wave of negative headlines across geopolitics, technology, and crypto regulation.

Here are the 3 developments worth watching:

1. GEOPOLITICAL TENSIONS: STRAIT OF HORMUZ

• Both the US and Iran reported incidents involving vessels in the region.

• The US said it had disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman for attempting to breach its blockade.

• Iran reported that two ships had struck naval mines and another vessel had caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

Source: @Reuters 

2. @nvidia : CEO @JensenHuang  FACES AN INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION

$NVDA 's board has launched an independent investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang may have been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The investigation follows reports concerning his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman allegedly linked to Chinese intelligence, according to US authorities.

NVIDIA said there is currently no basis to believe that corporate secrets or US national security have been compromised.

Huang remains CEO and has pledged to cooperate with the investigation.

Source: @Reuters  | @nvidia 

3. CRYPTO REGULATION: @binance  AND @tether  FACE INCREASED SCRUTINY

US Senator Richard Blumenthal has requested records from Binance, Tether, World Liberty Financial, and Fight Fight Fight LLC as part of an investigation into the use of crypto for illicit activities.

Key deadlines:

• November 30, 2026: Binance is asked to begin submitting documents.

• January 4, 2027: Overall deadline for the requested records.

Failure to comply could lead to further enforcement measures by the subcommittee.

-----------------

@0xshanks_hunter 's  PERSPECTIVE

The bigger concern isn't any single headline. It's the convergence of multiple risk factors at the same time.

Geopolitical tensions are adding uncertainty to the global economic environment and risk sentiment.

The technology sector is facing questions around corporate security and governance.

Crypto continues to face regulatory pressure from US lawmakers.

Over the past 24–48 hours, Bitcoin and the broader crypto market have experienced significant volatility, accompanied by large-scale liquidations, predominantly from leveraged Long positions.

Our take:

- Crypto is no longer dealing with just internal market risks such as leverage, liquidity, and trading sentiment.

- External developments are also becoming an important part of the equation.

- When multiple sources of uncertainty emerge simultaneously, market volatility can become harder to navigate.

That said, we shouldn't automatically attribute every price move to these headlines without evidence of a direct connection.

For now, risk management matters more than trying to predict the bottom.

text:
Climate- An opportunity for Democrats to shine.

 Noah Gordon

 Any vision for an effective climate policy must grapple with the hard truth about the United States’s climate record so far: it is one of failure. A grumpy foreign diplomat might describe the United States as the world’s largest oil and gas producer and historical emitter, a rich nation that has rejected the two most important climate treaties (Kyoto and Paris) and consistently failed to deliver climate finance to poorer countries. They would be correct. Of course, hardworking US diplomats have also helped secure important climate-related agreements—in Montreal (1987), Paris (2015), and beyond—and the country has achieved moderate emissions reductions. Yet the structural forces in favor of drilling for gas and oil and delivering short-term profits and shareholder value have outweighed efforts to reduce domestic emissions or meet the country’s obligations under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) treaty to help poorer countries. In Trump’s second term, we saw dramatic steps backward, with the United States going so far as to bully other countries into killing climate initiatives, such as an International Maritime Organization plan to place a global carbon levy on polluting ships. It will take more than a return to the Paris Agreement and the Biden-era status quo to set the United States on the right track in 2029 and beyond.  Three principles should guide the United States in developing climate policy for 2029: 

1. Do what you’re good at From the statements of some US analysts, one might think that the United States and China were neck-and-neck in a race to produce the technologies that could save the climate. The Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) was described as the “largest climate investment in history”—except presumably for the much larger Chinese investment. The Development Finance Corporation was sometimes described as a competitor6 or alternative to the Chinese Belt and Road initiative that, in fact, dwarfs it.

 Leading proposals bore names like the “Clean Energy Marshall Plan”:  effective marketing, yes, but overlooking the reality that developing countries are not lining up for loans to help them buy uncompetitive US-produced clean energy technologies. In fact, Chinese overseas investment in clean manufacturing from 2021 to 2025 surpassed the amount that the United States invested in Europe over the four years of the Marshall Plan, at a time when US manufacturing did actually lead the world. In other words, it was China that did the Green Marshall Plan. Washington’s inability to grasp the balance of clean energy power, like these reflexive claims to “leadership,” is a symptom of the US obsession with maintaining global hegemony.

 Policymakers must think more clearly about where the United States fits into the global climate puzzle. In 2029, the United States will not be the largest emitter, nor the most important cleantech producer, nor a trusted diplomatic partner that the world’s climate negotiators look to for leadership. But it will be a major emitter, a technological powerhouse, and potentially a crucial source of global aid. To start, US foreign deals and investments in the climate space need more focus. The Biden administration was on the right track with its emphasis on high-profile, multilateral projects like the Lobito Corridor, a G7 initiative to facilitate the export of minerals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia to the coast of Angola. One of the rare successes of the Trump administration has been the billions in finance it has committed to support non-Chinese rare earth production. Still, in general, previous US clean energy agreements with other countries have spread themselves too thin across large sectors (e.g., batteries or solar) rather than on specific areas where US firms can make a competitive offer (e.g., providing long-duration storage to fast-growing renewables markets like India). US agencies, such as the Development Finance Corporation and Export-Import Bank, should concentrate their firepower more strategically, enabling partner countries to buy US goods and services in those few cleantech areas in which the United States is globally competitive. Foremost among these areas is next-generation geothermal energy. This is currently a niche technology, but the International Energy Agency projects that it could supply “up to 15 percent of global electricity demand growth to 2050.” It also makes use of some of the same drilling technologies—and potentially, workers—that have made the United States the world’s gas superpower. There is a big potential export market here, notably in Europe, Japan, and Indonesia. US policymakers should also talk to European allies about ensuring reciprocal access to cleantech subsidies to boost producers in both regions in the face of Chinese competition.

 The US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) could support exports by subsidizing the cost of drilling in key foreign markets. The United States is very good at inventing new technologies, if not at commercializing them or driving down costs through gradual improvements in manufacturing—the “process innovation” at which China excels.16 The next US administration should launch a massive program for domestic energy research. The focus should be on breakthroughs that may well be deployed and manufactured elsewhere to mitigate the climate crisis: solid-state batteries, fusion, carbon removal, geologic hydrogen, alternative proteins, and low-carbon industrial products like steel and cement. These may not all be key climate solutions for the 2030s, and they are sideshows relative to the growth of renewables and lithium-ion batteries that are cutting emissions in the near term. But they are still crucial to longer-term efforts to meet the climate challenge. Such a research program would build on the legacy of past scientific initiatives like the Manhattan and Apollo projects or Operation Warp Speed. Given the likely state of global politics in 2029, it would also represent an olive branch to a global community scalded by the slashand-burn approach of Trump 2.0. Such a research program must also set aside significant resources to revive and revitalize international collaboration on clean energy: funded exchange programs for US and foreign scientists and new visa programs for foreign scientists, engineers, and electricians. US workers should benefit too, for example through the expanded training of electricians to work at home and abroad. Indeed, the shortage of trained electrical workers in the United States is exacerbating supply chain challenges for key grid components like power  transformers. The government should be facilitating learning trips for US workers to leading battery producers like South Korea, not scaring away foreigners with aggressive immigration raids against firms from allied countries. Korean investments in particular are vital for US electric vehicle (EV) production and for maintaining a domestic manufacturing base in a key industry. If there were a global coordinating body for the energy  transition—the type of planetary governance humans could probably pull together if we faced an invasion of alien humanoids rather than a gradual, faceless threat—it would ask the United States to do what it’s best at and leave other areas to other countries. The task of a new administration in 2029 is to keep this planetary perspective in mind as it balances the climate crisis with its other responsibilities to keep Americans safe and prosperous. 

Working with unions, climate activists, and community organizers to design policy will help both win elections and advance green economic populism once in office.

 2. Electrify

 If the world is to decarbonize fairly and effectively, it will have to achieve electrification. This means both increasing the share of final energy demand that is met by electricity and giving more people more access to electricity. Let’s start with the first meaning: 

swapping out molecules for electrons. Any effective climate foreign policy must have a strong domestic component because US emissions affect the global climate. Domestic policymakers are the ones who have to keep the promises that the diplomats make. 

US greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are keeping steady under the Trump administration at around 11 percent of the global total—yet as the biggest historical emitter, the United States has a responsibility to clean up its own mess. This is a moral responsibility and also a practical and strategic one, because foreign countries will shun initiatives and tariff products from a petrostate whose pollution is hurting their interests. The priority for domestic policy should be on effective climate interventions that also improve Americans’ health and economic situation in the near future. 

The rising price of electricity was a key issue in the November 2025 elections, with even conservative Democrats like New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill calling for price controls on utility  bills. Since power prices will likely keep rising as demand does, an effective policy should shift more of the costs of electrification from residential consumers to the giant companies building data centers. We can capitalize on the fact that the world’s richest companies are desperate for a stable grid with abundant power, for example by requiring them to commit to a fund that supports grid infrastructure.

 What other policies fit the bill? The Biden administration’s Clean School Bus Rebate Program, which replaced diesel buses with electric ones, was a good one. Similarly ambitious proposals, like replacing the HVAC system in every public school with a new system that would reduce fuel costs, improve air quality, kill airborne diseases, and keep students cool enough to think straight, should also be pursued. Incidentally, these systems would all use efficient heat pumps rather than gas furnaces. Let the climate deniers and combustion-addicted reactionaries campaign against hiring and training US electricians to fix the United States’s schools. Federal dollars should support any leapfrog technologies that may emerge from that US clean energy research program.

 Government demand and tax credits can pull forward US-made clean steel or long-duration energy storage technologies, like the zinc-based batteries manufactured by the Pennsylvania firm EOS Energy Enterprises, in which the Trump administration took a stake in November  2025. Indeed, the Trump administration’s aggressive moves to take equity stakes in lithium, steel, and rare earth firms have provided a blueprint for a type of state capitalism that climate progressives once only dreamed of; the door has never been so open for the US government to force oil and gas firms to clean up leaky, abandoned wells. When it comes to the second meaning of “electrification”—delivering power to the world’s people—the key is to avoid double standards and ditch invidious policies that the United States isn’t itself following. If the United States implements some kind of tariff based on the carbon content in imports, it should be sure to either exempt the poorest countries or recycle revenue to them. The United States should not put pressure on developing countries, even recipients of US aid money, to stop exploiting their own fossil fuel resources while the wealthy United States remains a petrostate.

 Washington should welcome the fact that energy access is growing around the world and willingly provide financing for foreign partners to deploy, for example, US-made virtual power plant software to help manage the electricity being generated by solar panels and stored on EVs made in Asia. The now-cancelled Power Africa project (led by USAID) included some excellent technical and financial support for power grids that should be restarted. If we help the world switch from molecules to electrons, decarbonization will follow.

 3. Cooperate with China—with guardrails Any climate foreign policy must also be a China policy. An effective climate policy will welcome China’s immense production of batteries and solar panels, without which humans would be in even greater danger. It is ludicrous to speak of an “overcapacity” of the Chinese solar panels that are bringing light to countries like Pakistan and South Africa. To criticize China’s unfair trade practices and undervalued currency, when it actually hurts US interests, not its massive production of cleantech as such. What’s the right balance? The United States should follow Canada and allow a small number of Chinese EVs to be imported into the country each year, up to a quota. This would put more pressure on the US automakers to deliver cheaper clean vehicles but also protect the US market enough to give domestic producers a chance to improve their EV offering. 

In this spirit, the United States should invite limited Chinese investment into the US battery and EV industry, permitting a few joint ventures with US firms on a pilot basis. But the United States must put conditions on foreign investments to require that Chinese firms hire local workers, use some domestic components, and share technologies, as the EU is attempting. If they’re allowed to, Chinese firms will use US factories for final assembly alone. In general, retaining tariffs on heavily subsidized Chinese cleantech, which raises the cost of the domestic transition, is an acceptable price to pay for strengthening US “green asset owners”46 vis-à-vis fossil asset owners. Reshaping the domestic political economy so that most of the country is incentivized to support an energy transition matters more than maximizing short-run efficiency. Moreover, the United States should not invite China into all sectors.

 Americans should bear the cost of developing a rare earth and critical minerals supply chain that cuts out China and protects the country from aggressive Chinese export controls, as permanent magnets are required not only for EVs and wind turbines but also for defense technologies. While progressives should welcome cheap Chinese solar panels, they should insist that the inverters to connect them to the grid are made by US allies, for reasons of security. It is hard to predict where US–China relations will be by January 2029. Even more so than President Nixon did, Trump can seek warmer relations with China without appearing weak, perhaps by cutting a deal with President Xi to drop US export controls in exchange for Chinese clean energy investment. But as they work to repair the damage the Trump regime has done to US democracy, progressives should resist the urge to outflank MAGA by being even tougher on the Chinese electrostate. Polling suggests that voters care more about having cheap, clean energy, than the geopolitical competition with China that so animated the Biden administration. A constructive, normal country Climate is a useful policy area in which to think about a broader, progressive, pro-peace foreign policy that doesn’t prioritize the pursuit of global hegemony. The United States is not a latent climate superpower that could produce the world’s electrotech if only the IRA were fully restored. It is a giant hydrocarbon producer and home to many citizens who stand to lose out, in a narrow economic sense, from falling demand for fossil fuels and the machines that burn them—even as they and their country would gain much more from humanity’s success in limiting the deadly overheating of the planet. 

The United States will not be the clean energy leader, not on a planet shared with China. But nor can it afford to give up on the field of clean energy altogether— that would be a tragedy for the world, whose ongoing clean energy transition would go even faster with the aid of the United States. What it can be is a country that plays its part in a collective global effort and pushes climate-saving technologies forward in a few select areas. That is what we should strive for. Because the United States, even after years of Trumpian sabotage of climate science and the clean energy economy, still has so much to give. It is still pushing forward promising next-generation geothermal technologies, still home to brilliant scientists working on clean industrial technologies, and to deep capital markets that could help these get to market.

 The climate challenge is open-ended: indeed, humans have not even finished the first phase of getting emissions to peak, let alone driven them to zero and started removing carbon from the atmosphere. So it’s far too early to give up. It is, though, time for the United States to find its place as a constructive, normal country in this space.

text:
$NNDM Q3 2026 earnings: Nano Dimension cuts spending, but legal claims widen its loss

Nano Dimension, a maker of industrial printing and electronics assembly machines, cut running costs, but one-off bills drained its cash. Sales outside Markforged, the unit it is selling to Stratasys, rose 42%. Staff cuts narrowed the loss excluding one-offs sharply. But operations used $24 million of cash, three times the year-ago amount, partly to exit a lease.

• Sales outside Markforged, the unit being sold: $𝟏𝟑.𝟑𝐌 (+42% from a year ago)
• Loss before interest, taxes, depreciation and one-offs: −$𝟒.𝟖𝐌 (−$16.6M a year ago)
• Cash, deposits and listed shares: $𝟑𝟗𝟔.𝟗𝐌 ($433.3M three months earlier)
• Full-year outlook: 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 (since May 2026)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better, because the cost cuts chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum promised now show clearly in the results. Essemtec, its electronics assembly business, grew for a second quarter. The bad news: Nano agreed to cover $14.7 million of an activist investor's legal costs and reserved $6 million for a lawsuit.

The question now is what Nano does with its $397 million of cash and securities. Its new board can return much of it to shareholders, or buy a business, as an earlier board did with Desktop Metal before its bankruptcy. The first plan from the board's new capital allocation committee will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞
Nano Dimension sells industrial 3D printers through its Markforged unit and electronics assembly machines through Essemtec. Chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum lists "aggressively reducing our cost structure" among his priorities, and this quarter the numbers followed. Running costs excluding one-offs dropped to $19.8 million, the lowest level in at least five quarters.

• Running costs excluding one-offs: down 16.5% from last quarter and 32.2% from a year ago
• Administrative overhead: 21.4 percentage points lower as a share of revenue than a year ago
• Research and development: 14.5 percentage points lower as a share of revenue
• Loss before interest, taxes, depreciation and one-offs (adjusted EBITDA): $4.8 million, against $16.6 million a year ago

Most of the savings came from payroll. Nano said it now employs fewer people after mergers and asset sales, which cut research, sales and overhead spending alike. Payroll savings tend to last, so the lower cost base should carry into next year. But the group still loses money before one-offs.

What to watch: running costs excluding one-offs in the fourth quarter, when the Markforged sale is due to close. A figure well below $19.8 million would show that Nano shed Markforged's costs along with its sales.

🟢 concern eased — 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Essemtec, Nano's Swiss maker of machines that mount components and dispense materials onto circuit boards, carries the business Nano keeps after the Markforged sale. Sales outside Markforged rose about 42% from a year ago, after a 53% jump last quarter. That reverses the drop Nano reported earlier this year.

Nano said demand was "particularly strong across AI-related electronics manufacturing, aerospace and defense, space and satellite systems". Excluding AME, the 3D-printed electronics line Nano sold in April, underlying growth reached about 67% by our math. But the base was soft, because tariff worries held buyers back a year ago, Nano said.

What to watch: sales outside Markforged in the fourth quarter, against $14.6 million a year earlier. Growth against that tougher base would show Essemtec's gains do not rest on one weak comparison.

🟢 𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐨 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬
Nano paused share buybacks during its strategic review, and an analyst challenged that pause. Chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum now calls "returning capital to shareholders" one of the "central pillars of our strategy".

Nano bought 7.0 million shares for $11.1 million in the third quarter. After the quarter ended, it kept buying through early November and spent another $8.6 million. As a result, shares outstanding fell about 6% from a year ago, so each remaining share has a claim on more cash. But the spending also shrinks the money the new board could use for an acquisition.

What to watch: the first plan from the board's new Strategy and Capital Allocation Committee, chaired by director Nadav Kidron. A plan that sets the size of future returns would make the buybacks a standing policy.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Several claims behind the positive case got no fresh numbers in these results, so they stand where they stood after the second quarter.

• Yearly cash savings of about $25 million that Nano targeted from asset sales and its lease exit: the first quarter without the headquarters lease begins in January 2027.
• Earn-out on AME and Fabrica, a line Nano had already shut: up to $10.5 million of extra payments tied to the buyer's sales, still carried at $2.9 million.
• Markforged's orders from defense and automakers: its sales rose 6.3% to $18.6 million, but the unit leaves with the Stratasys sale.
• A merger worth more than the cash: the short list of partners Nano described in May has produced no deal yet.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐝
Nano's release leads with its cuts to running costs, but the cash statement tells a different story. Operations used $24.1 million of cash in the third quarter, by our math. A year earlier, the same line showed an outflow of $7.9 million.

Part of the jump came from one decision. In July Nano paid $13.0 million to end its headquarters lease early, a deal it said removes about $38 million of future rent. Without that payment, operations still used $11.1 million, by our math, which tops the year-ago outflow.

Cash, deposits and listed shares fell $36.4 million in the quarter, to $396.9 million. Chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum promised a "leaner, more focused and financially stronger organization", but the cash figures do not show that yet. The Markforged sale should bring in $42.5 million, yet Nano has already spent or committed more than half of that since September.

What to watch: cash used by operations in the fourth quarter, excluding the October payment to activist investor Murchinson. An outflow below the year-ago $11.7 million would show the cost cuts finally reaching the cash statement.

🔴🔴 𝐋𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 $𝟐𝟏 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬
In July Nano settled a board fight with Murchinson, an investor owning about 10% of its shares. Four directors left and three joined, including Moshe Rozenbaum, now chief executive. A month later Murchinson asked Nano to repay its legal and proxy costs.

A committee of two independent directors agreed to pay $14.7 million, citing "reducing uncertainty, avoiding further disruption". Nano also set aside $6.0 million for a suit by law firm Quinn Emanuel after a court refused to dismiss it. Former bondholders of Desktop Metal, a printer maker Nano bought and lost to bankruptcy in 2025, seek more than $115 million.

Nano said it will "vigorously defend itself against the claims". Independent directors approved the Murchinson payment, but the money went to the shareholder whose settlement brought in the current chief executive. So the charges hit the loss and also raise a question about who benefits from Nano's cash.

What to watch: the court ruling on Nano's August motion to dismiss the case brought by Desktop Metal's bankruptcy trustee. A loss there would add a claim for which Nano has set aside no money.

🔴 𝐀𝐬𝐢𝐚 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫'𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
Nano sold $15.0 million of goods in Asia-Pacific, nearly four times the year-ago level. That region now makes up 47% of revenue. Sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa roughly halved, and the Americas slipped about 10%.

Nano did not say which product line or customers drove the Asian sales. Last quarter it said about $3.0 million of orders would arrive later because of production timing. Without them, revenue would have barely moved from the second quarter, by our math. So this quarter's growth may rest on a handful of large orders.

What to watch: Asia-Pacific sales in the fourth quarter. A drop back toward the $4.0 million Nano booked there a year earlier would mark this quarter's jump as a few one-time orders.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing concerns got no new answer in these results, and Nano held no conference call where investors could ask about them.

• Full-year outlook: still suspended since May, so investors have no company target for sales or losses.
• Merger plans: the short list of merger and reverse-merger partners from May got no update; a new board committee now owns the decision.
• Accounting controls: Nano reported a control weakness in March and replaced auditor KPMG with PwC Israel in September; the filing gives no reason.
• Markforged write-down: Nano wrote off all $40.4 million of the unit's goodwill, the premium it paid over the assets, in the first quarter.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐨 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐭 𝐈𝐦𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥
Nano, an Israeli company run from Massachusetts, said fighting between the US, Israel and Iran since February had an immaterial effect on its results. Tariffs mattered more a year ago, when Nano said "demand was negatively impacted by tariff uncertainty". That soft base flatters this year's growth comparison.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Inventory edged up 6.1% from last quarter. It sits 22.4% below a year ago. Against a quarter's sales, stock fell to 94% from 144% a year earlier. So Nano holds less stock for each dollar of sales, which frees cash, though the AME sale also took some stock off the books.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟕.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money customers owe Nano climbed 26% from a year ago, ahead of sales growth. Receivables now equal 87% of the quarter's revenue, against 82% a year earlier. Slower collection ties up cash that the cost cuts free elsewhere.

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟓.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Deferred revenue, cash customers paid for service Nano has not yet delivered, rose 16% from last quarter. The jump reverses most of the second-quarter drop, when Nano wrote off $1.2 million in the AME sale. The balance still sits about 1% below a year ago.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤: 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Suspended (May 2026)
Unchanged. Nano still offers no full-year target for sales, margins or losses. It set a sales range of $130–140 million earlier this year, then dropped it in May. Sales for the first nine months reached $90.6 million. The Markforged sale will reshape any new target, because that unit supplies most of the revenue.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐬𝐲𝐬: $𝟒𝟐.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡; 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $42.5 million in cash; closing expected in the second half of 2026
Unchanged. Nano still expects Stratasys to buy Markforged, its industrial 3D-printer unit, for $42.5 million in cash, and now names the fourth quarter. The deal remains "subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals". Markforged supplied 58% of third-quarter sales, so the group that stays will be much smaller. Nano said earlier the sale cuts yearly cash burn by about $15 million.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐨 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐚 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤?
Nano has offered no targets since May. Once Markforged leaves, readers need a sales and loss range for the remaining business to judge whether the cost cuts go far enough.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Markforged supplies most of the revenue, and Nano said selling it cuts yearly cash burn by about $15 million. A quarterly loss figure would show what the remaining business earns on its own.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐢𝐧 𝐀𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Asia-Pacific sales almost quadrupled and now make up nearly half of revenue. A breakdown by product line and customer would show whether that growth can repeat.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐬𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬?
The new Strategy and Capital Allocation Committee will weigh buybacks, payouts and acquisitions. Shareholders need to know how much cash the board plans to return, and when.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐰?
Service revenue, which includes maintenance contracts, dropped 15% from a year ago while product sales rose 30%. Nano did not explain the gap, which matters because service income usually recurs.

text:
$KOPN Q3 2026 earnings: Kopin's research revenue jumps, but its hardware sales still trail

Kopin's government and partner research contracts are lifting the microdisplay maker while its core hardware shipments still lag last year. Total sales jumped 52% to $18 million on U. S. Army display grants and optical-chip development work with Fabric. AI, though product revenue remained 18% below a year ago. Better factory efficiency cut the operating loss to $0.5 million and helped operations generate cash, as chief executive Michael Murray secured another $19 million in Army funding.

• Total revenue: $𝟏𝟖.𝟐𝐌 (+52% from a year ago)
• Net product revenue: $𝟖.𝟖𝐌 (−18% from a year ago)
• Loss from operations: $𝟎.𝟓𝐌 (narrowed from $3.5M last quarter)
• Second-half outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (calls for strong H2 and progress toward profit)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because funded research programs and factory efficiency brought the business within reach of operating breakeven and positive cash flow. The U. S. Army more than doubled its commitment to color MicroLED technology, funding the domestic factory buildout without draining unrestricted cash. One caution: the growth came entirely from development and grant lines rather than shipped hardware, and non-cash writedowns on partner equity stakes kept the bottom line in the red.

The question now is whether these funded development programs convert into high-volume hardware production or stay stuck as low-margin research work. If they convert, factory utilization and product sales rise together; if they stall, overhead costs will outpace hardware gross profit once grant milestones end. Fourth-quarter European weapon sight deliveries and January's optical-link demonstration at CES will provide the next test.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐭𝐨 $𝟏𝟖.𝟐 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧
Kopin makes tiny screens and optical parts for military gear and data centers. Total revenue jumped 52% from a year ago to $18.2 million because government and partner research contracts scaled up fast. Research and development revenue reached $5.7 million, up nearly fivefold from $1.2 million a year earlier. Grant income added $3.1 million, compared with nothing in the prior year.

Two partnerships drove that funding. One is a joint program with Fabric. AI to build Neural I/o, an optical chip link that moves data between artificial intelligence processors using light instead of copper wires. The other is the U. S. Army Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment (IBAS) program, which added an $18.6 million sole-source award for color MicroLED displays, bringing total IBAS funding to $34 million.

What to watch: the first public demonstration of Neural I/o at the CES trade show in January 2027, followed by the start of MicroLED manufacturing in mid-2027. Hitting both dates will show whether research funding can turn into commercial hardware orders.

🟢 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
Factory efficiency recovered as hardware shipments climbed from the spring trough. The cost of making products fell to 73% of product sales, down from 86% in the second quarter and 79% a year ago. That gave the display maker a 27% gross margin on its hardware, reversing the losses it took on product manufacturing in the first quarter.

Operating expenses — research and development plus administrative overhead — rose 28% from last quarter to $12.3 million, but fell from 76% of total revenue to 68% because sales grew faster. Reported operating income fell from $4.5 million a year ago to a $0.5 million loss, because last year included $8.4 million of one-time legal accrual reversals. Excluding those reversals by our math, the operating loss narrowed from $3.9 million a year ago, and operations generated $2.4 million in cash.

What to watch: whether the cost of making products stays near or below 73% of product sales in the fourth quarter. Holding that level will show the Westborough factory can run profitably at current shipment volumes.

🟢 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐝 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬
New military orders are starting to backfill the hardware pipeline. Kopin Europe won a $2.4 million order for organic light-emitting diode (OLED) microdisplays from a new international thermal weapon sight customer. That customer's program has entered low-rate initial production, and the company plans to start shipping those displays in the fourth quarter of 2026.

In the United States, the optical systems maker expanded its evaluation kits for first-person viewer (FPV) modules, which let drone pilots see through a craft's camera. More than a dozen new customers ordered prototype Sentinel FPV headsets for the military's Drone Dominance Program and federal law enforcement agencies.

What to watch: fourth-quarter defense display sales, which should reflect the first deliveries under the $2.4 million European thermal sight order. An uptick there will show European partnerships are converting into shipped hardware.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐜𝐞
"Third quarter revenue grew 52%, driven by funded development programs that are setting the stage for future product revenue as they move from R&D into production," chief executive Michael Murray said. That framing puts future factory output at the center of the story, but current hardware shipments are still smaller than they were a year ago.

• Net product revenue: $8.8 million, down 17.8% from $10.7 million a year ago (though up 14.7% from the second quarter by our math)
• Defense display revenue: $8.5 million, down 14.8% from $9.9 million a year ago
• Industrial display revenue: $52 thousand, down from $749 thousand a year ago
• Nine-month net product revenue: $21.9 million, down 20.3% from $27.4 million in the first nine months of 2025

This gap matters because research grants and development contracts pay the bills during design work, not high-margin volume manufacturing. Moreover, the company funded nearly all of its $5.6 million in research expenses through customer contracts this quarter, leaving core hardware sales below the level needed to cover the $6.7 million in administrative and sales overhead.

What to watch: net product revenue in the fourth quarter against last year's depressed $5.6 million comparison. Failing to return to year-over-year product growth against that easy baseline would mean core military shipments remain stalled.

🔴 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐖𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐢𝐞𝐝-𝐔𝐩 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡
Even with operations nearly breaking even, the bottom line showed a $3.4 million net loss, or $0.02 per share. The culprit was $2.7 million in non-cash net losses on strategic equity investments, as the fair value of stakes in partner companies fell during the quarter. The balance sheet holds $15.7 million across equity method and other strategic investments, exposing future earnings to further mark-to-market swings.

Cash on the balance sheet also carries a major restriction. While total cash and marketable securities stood at $51.3 million, almost half of that — $25.5 million — is restricted cash, including $24.2 million locked up as collateral for a bond in an ongoing lawsuit appeal, alongside a $19.7 million accrued litigation liability. Unencumbered cash was $25.8 million, up $0.9 million from June.

What to watch: any ruling on the litigation appeal or change in unrestricted cash below $25 million as capital equipment spending continues. Losing the appeal would forfeit the restricted bond cash permanently.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡
U. S. defense procurement rules increasingly require domestic supply chains for military electronics. To capture that demand, the Massachusetts Manufacturing Innovation Initiative awarded the microdisplay maker an $800,000 grant "to install advanced capital equipment for domestic manufacturing of MicroLED displays and Neural I/o™ optical interconnects at the Company’s Westborough facility". Capital expenditures reached $1.4 million this quarter as the factory buildout progressed.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Up more than fivefold from $1.2 million at the end of 2025. Contract liabilities are advance payments from customers for work not yet performed. Even after absorbing a separate $2.7 million deferred grant balance from year-end, the jump shows upfront funding from new development awards is building on the balance sheet.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Cut by more than half from $10.7 million at the end of 2025, though partly offset by a new $3.5 million receivable for grant income. Collecting those older customer bills helped the display group generate $2.4 million in operating cash flow during the third quarter and reduced nine-month operating cash burn to $2.7 million.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟗𝟎.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Up 12.3% from 169.4 million shares a year ago. The increase stems from late-2025 stock sales to strategic and institutional investors to fund factory upgrades and shore up the balance sheet, plus the conversion of $7.6 million in preferred stock since December.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐇𝟐 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐇𝟐; 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐆𝐀𝐀𝐏 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from FY26 revenue $52–60 million
Unchanged in direction. Finance chief Erich Manz wrote that "We continue to expect a strong second half and meaningful progress toward sustainable GAAP profitability", without printing a dollar range in the release. With $41.5 million of revenue booked in the first nine months, the earlier $52–60 million full-year target would leave $14.5 million for the fourth quarter at the middle of the range by our math, up 73% from last year's shutdown-hit fourth quarter.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟓𝟐–𝟔𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
The press release kept a qualitative call for a strong second half but omitted the explicit $52–60 million full-year revenue range reiterated in the first quarter. Nine-month revenue of $41.5 million already covers three-quarters of that range.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡?
Defense display sales fell 15% from a year ago to $8.5 million even as research and grant revenue surged. Investors need to know whether pilot helmet and weapon sight deliveries will grow in the fourth quarter.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟐.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧?
Non-cash investment losses turned a near-breakeven operating quarter into a $3.4 million net loss. Naming the holding and how its fair value is set would clarify whether more writedowns lie ahead.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑&𝐃?
The release highlighted an $18.6 million Army MicroLED award and a $2.4 million European OLED order, but gave no total backlog figure to show how much of 2027 factory capacity is booked.
