text:
Lorenzo Maria Pacini

The U.S. Election as a Manifestation of a Systemic Crisis

The result of November 3 lends itself to an easy interpretation: that of a defeat. The Democrats took the House and, against a Senate map that everyone had deemed favorable to the Republicans on the eve of the election, the Senate as well. The next day, Speaker Mike Johnson announced he would not run for minority leader, Trump acknowledged the outcome, and Wall Street closed higher. Counting seats, however, is of little use. What matters more is understanding what the election says about the United States’ ability to continue doing what it has done over the past eight months.

It’s worth starting with an observation that stands in stark contrast to the tone of the immediate reactions. The administration’s difficulties are real, but they remain under control. The system absorbed the blow without any institutional upheaval: no challenges to the outcome, markets relieved by the end of uncertainty, and a smooth transition of power in Congress. The presidency retains all the levers of foreign policy intact – from command of the armed forces to sanctions, from the veto to executive orders – and Congress lacks the two-thirds majority needed to override it. The precedent from 2006 is instructive. Back then, too, a midterm election punished an unpopular war and handed both chambers to the opposition, yet just a few months later, Washington reinvigorated its military commitment in Iraq. A drastic crisis – one that would force a major power to withdraw – is therefore still, by design, a distant prospect. This is due to the mechanics of the constitutional framework, not because the underlying causes have been eliminated.

The causes, in fact, are all still on the table. The war against Iran, which began on February 28 with joint U.S.-Israeli airstrikes, had been presented by the White House as a four- to six-week operation. Eight months have passed. In the meantime, a ceasefire was signed and then abandoned; a memorandum of understanding signed in June was declared “over” by Trump himself on July 8; and on the eve of the election, Brent crude was trading above $100 per barrel. Tehran is keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and making its reopening contingent on the end of the naval blockade of its ports, the suspension of oil sanctions, and the unfreezing of frozen funds. For the American voter, all of this has boiled down to a simple number. As early as May, gasoline cost an average of $4.48 per gallon, compared to less than three dollars before the war.

Exit polls measure this weariness with a certain bluntness. For 74% of voters, the war was a crucial or important factor in their choice, and within this group, Democrats prevailed with 62% to 35%; about six in ten voters consider the military intervention a mistake, and the president’s approval rating stands at 38%. Trump himself, speaking on Fox Business, admitted that part of the result can be explained by Iran. What weighs most heavily is the absence of a recognizable strategic outcome. The stated objectives have shifted from the nuclear issue and the regime to the reopening of the Strait – that is, to repairing the damage that the war itself has caused. A campaign whose purpose becomes merely to remedy its own effects struggles to be presented as a victory, and the electorate has sensed this without needing analysts.

However, reducing the issue to a president’s popularity would mean missing the core of the matter. The vote calls into question the sustainability of a foreign policy based on permanent military and economic pressure, and here the data matters more than the polls. As of October 16, the Pentagon had reported to Congress expenditures totaling $47.1 billion, with over 60% going toward ammunition; $29 billion was spent replacing depleted bombs and missiles, with global stocks of Patriot interceptors depleted and supplies drawn from commands in Asia and Europe. The Congressional Budget Office estimates an additional cost of two to three billion for each month of war and warns that replenishing arsenals could take five years or more; the Department of Defense’s inspector general speaks openly of strategic inventory shortages. A war against a medium-sized regional power has depleted reserves intended for a conflict between equal powers. This is the fact that should concern Washington far more than any lost seat in Pennsylvania.

And it is precisely on this point that the American information war is being fought. In May, testifying before Congress, Secretary Hegseth dismissed the claim that ammunition was running out as false, while Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Caine assured lawmakers that stockpiles were sufficient for the assigned missions. In September, the commander of operations, Admiral Brad Cooper, claimed to be unconcerned on this point at the very moment the CBO and the Inspector General were certifying the opposite. The discrepancy between the public narrative and the financial reports submitted to Congress is no mere communication glitch. It serves a specific purpose: to shift the discourse from the material level to that of political will. As long as the issue remains “the president is unpopular,” the nation’s power appears intact, and the problem seems solvable by changing the majority or the candidate. If, on the other hand, the issue becomes “the military-industrial complex cannot keep up with the pace imposed by the strategy,” the limitation is structural, and no election can remove it. It is striking that the midterm campaign itself remained almost entirely focused on the cost of living: even the opposition attacked the price of gasoline, leaving the more uncomfortable question of the country’s military resilience in the shadows.

The vote thus brings to the surface a contradiction that cuts across the entire ruling class, regardless of party affiliation. Washington intends to maintain its capacity for international projection, but must contend with a growing domestic reluctance to pay the price. As early as March, 56% of Americans said they opposed new emergency appropriations for the war. Now the administration’s request – which amounts to as much as 70 billion – will have to pass through committees controlled by the opposition. The “lame duck” window remains open: according to rumors reported by the U.S. press, the Pentagon has reportedly planned a multi-day campaign to begin after the election, and the new Congress will not be sworn in until January 3. If that plan were carried out, the administration would choose to act during the brief interval when the electoral defeat has not yet imposed institutional constraints. This would be the clearest confirmation that the problem is not the election result itself, but the attempt to circumvent its effects.

The American people remain, and they are the factor that will carry the most weight in the medium term. Three out of four voters say they are dissatisfied or angry with the direction of the country, and three in ten cite the fate of democracy as their top concern. In August, a University of Massachusetts poll recorded a 14-point drop in approval ratings among Republicans compared to March, and one in six Trump voters stated they would not vote for him again. The divide no longer runs solely between the two parties. It runs deep within the coalition that in 2024 had rewarded the promise to end endless wars – and that, even in the first weeks of the conflict, had called for a swift withdrawal and rejected the idea of an invasion. That pact has been broken, and the disappointment of those who had endorsed it is politically more corrosive than the hostility of opponents, which was to be expected.

American power thus encounters its limits at home before it does on the battlefield. The United States still has the means to strike, impose sanctions, and block, but each of these tools requires a society willing to bear the cost for years – in fuel, debt, and depleted arsenals. On November 3, that willingness visibly cracked. For European allies, accustomed to viewing American protection as a constant, this is the most important message emerging from the polls: Washington’s influence now depends on a domestic consensus that no one – not even the White House – is any longer able to guarantee.

Congress as a Source of Friction

So much for consensus. But the vote also has an institutional effect – less visible and more lasting – because as of January 3, 2027, the balance of power between Congress and the White House will shift. During the first eight months of the war, the Republican majority served as a shield. Every attempt to invoke the War Powers Resolution was rejected, and always by a very narrow margin: on May 13, the Senate rejected the resolution 49 to 50; the next day, the House blocked it with a 212-212 tie, by which time the 60-day deadline set by law had already expired two weeks earlier. That shield rested on a razor-thin margin, and on November 3, that margin shifted to the opposition. The next day, Chuck Schumer publicly promised to end the war.

The tools available to the new majority are well known and must be listed precisely, because their effectiveness varies greatly. The first is the investigation. The Armed Services, Foreign Affairs, and Oversight committees gain subpoena powers, and the Democrats have already announced a long series of investigations into the administration. Regarding the Iran dossier, they can demand accountability for the decision to go to war, for the erroneous predictions about its duration, and above all for the discrepancy – discussed in the first part – between public statements on stockpiles and actual accounting records. The second tool is the budget. The president cannot spend money that Congress has not appropriated, and any request for emergency funds – up to 70 billion – will have to pass through committees led by opponents; the expiration of the continuing resolution on December 11 is already sparking an initial clash during the lame-duck session. The third tool is legislative initiative: new resolutions on war powers, amendments to the annual defense bill, and reporting requirements. The fourth – perhaps the most effective – is oversight of the use of military resources. Congress can tie the replenishment of arsenals to different strategic priorities – for example, by preventing interceptors intended for the Indo-Pacific theater from ending up in the Gulf. On this front, the pacifist opposition could find unexpected allies among the hawks who view China, rather than Iran, as the true adversary.

Each of these tools, however, has a clear limitation. The Democrats do not have a majority in either chamber capable of overcoming a presidential veto, which requires sixty-seven votes in the Senate. Trump has already demonstrated how to use the veto in this area: in 2019 regarding Yemen, in 2020 regarding Iran itself, and in both cases, Congress failed to override it. The legislative route, therefore, almost always leads to a refusal to sign. That leaves the budget, which is the real weapon; but cutting funding for soldiers deployed in the field carries a very high political cost, and no opposition force likes to be accused of abandoning the troops. American history speaks for itself. The Case-Church Amendment – the most frequently cited example of a war ended by Congress – came about after the withdrawal from Vietnam had already been negotiated. Congress tends to formalize the end of wars that are already winding down; it rarely succeeds in ending those still underway.

There is also a more subtle effect, one that concerns the president’s political autonomy. Trump will not be able to run for re-election in 2028, and from this point on, every Republican lawmaker will begin to think more about the horizon of the next presidency than about the current term. The war has already become the dividing line in that succession. On one side is J.D. Vance, who has remained cautious and aligned with the grassroots’ skepticism toward prolonged military interventions; on the other is Marco Rubio, Secretary of State and National Security Advisor, who is unreservedly committed to a hardline stance and capable of capitalizing on a swift and favorable conclusion to the conflict. A war that shows no signs of ending and a party fresh off an electoral defeat are shifting the balance of power toward those who can present themselves as an alternative without openly breaking with the president. The result is a gradual loss of control over the party. The threat of the primaries – which for years ensured Trump’s control over congressional caucuses – holds less and less sway as his political horizon narrows, and a congressman looking ahead to 2028 has good reason to distance himself from a war that his constituents view as a mistake.

At this point, it is worth distinguishing between two concepts that are often conflated in public debate: the president’s formal authority to conduct military operations and his political ability to sustain them over time. The former remains virtually intact. As commander-in-chief, Trump can order airstrikes, maintain the naval blockade of Iranian ports, and even launch the multi-day campaign that has been discussed. In half a century, the War Powers Resolution has never halted an ongoing operation, and in the case of Iran, the sixty-day deadline passed without consequences. The second capacity, however, depends on factors beyond the president’s sole control: funding, the time it takes for the defense industry to replenish arsenals, the steadfastness of allies that host bases and provide logistics, and the support of an electorate that pays for gasoline. Congress acts only on this second level, but it is the decisive level for the kind of war the United States is fighting. A naval blockade and prolonged economic pressure are not won with a single blow; they are won by endurance – and endurance is precisely what a hostile majority can make more costly with every budget cycle.

This is where the most significant limitation lies. Congress can raise the political cost of presidential decisions, but it lacks the tools to impose a new diplomatic strategy. The conduct of negotiations is the responsibility of the executive branch, and no committee can sit at the table with Tehran or with the Qatari mediators. Indeed, there is an asymmetry that makes the situation more complex than it appears. The conditions set by Iran for reopening the Strait of Hormuz – namely, the suspension of oil sanctions and the unfreezing of frozen funds – partly concern sanctions enacted by Congress, and since 2015, any nuclear agreement with Tehran that provides for sanctions relief must undergo congressional review. Congress therefore has the power to block war through the budget and the power to block peace through the review of agreements, but it has no power of initiative regarding either. A stalemate between the institutions constructed in this way produces neither escalation nor an agreement. It is more likely to produce a protracted, low-intensity war, with the blockade still in place and the Strait still closed.

Furthermore, this slowdown may have the opposite effect in the short term. An administration that knows its days are numbered before facing a hostile Congress has an incentive to concentrate its force during the time it has left, prioritizing intensity over duration. Tehran, for its part, interprets the vote as a political victory: the speaker of the Iranian Parliament commented that the Americans have said no to war. If the Iranian leadership becomes convinced that time is on its side, it will have fewer reasons to make concessions and more reasons to wait for American weariness to run its course. In this way, the internal division in Washington, rather than opening a diplomatic window, risks prolonging the conflict.

The argument can therefore be stated plainly. After November 3, the American political system may become a factor slowing down the strategy against Iran, but it will not, for that reason, become a factor promoting peace. It functions as a brake, not as a rudder: it makes every step taken by the executive branch slower and more costly without pointing in a different direction. Those in Europe or the Gulf who expect a diplomatic breakthrough from the new Congress risk mistaking this friction for an alternative strategy.

Peace would require a decision from the White House, or a shift in the balance of power on the ground and in the energy markets – and neither of these depends on Capitol Hill.

Lindsay Clancy: Round Two? And What’s the Jury Situation Going to Be?

Three Rulings. Another Trial. And Another Jury.

Judge William Sullivan has issued three significant rulings in the Lindsay Clancy case:

1. Double jeopardy: Denied the defense's motion to dismiss the murder charges on double-jeopardy grounds.
2. Holdout juror: Denied the defense's request for an inquiry and records concerning the holdout juror, identified in reporting as Michael Péguy Desronvil, also referred to as "Juror Doe."
3. Gag order: Denied the prosecution's request for a gag order, without prejudice, leaving open the possibility of revisiting the issue.

What Happens Next?

The next status hearing is scheduled for November 16, 2026, in Plymouth Superior Court, when the parties are expected to discuss a retrial date. Sullivan has previously indicated he would like proceedings to begin as early as March 2027.

But there are still some unanswered questions.

What charges will Clancy face?

The Commonwealth has expressed an intention to retry Clancy, but prosecutors have not committed to whether they will pursue first-degree murder again or reduce the charges.

At the November 2 hearing, ADA Jennifer Sprague said the prosecution was not yet prepared to specify what the retrial would look like.

A reduction in charges could also open the door to a bench trial rather than another jury trial, depending on the charges and applicable procedures.

Could an appeal delay the retrial?

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has pushed for a spring trial, particularly given Sullivan's mandatory retirement in June 2027.

Co-counsel Martin Weinberg has reportedly indicated that the defense intends to appeal the double-jeopardy ruling. Depending on the appellate process, that could complicate the schedule.

Clancy remains in custody at Tewksbury Hospital. A negotiated resolution is still possible.

But What About the Jury?

This is what I'm particularly interested in.

The first trial attracted enormous public attention, extensive media coverage, and strong opinions about Clancy's mental state and criminal responsibility online.

Can they find 12 impartial jurors who haven't already formed an opinion? And even if they do, can those 12 reach a unanimous verdict?

Massachusetts has had several notable cases involving hung juries.

- Matthew Farwell: The former Stoughton police detective accused of murdering pregnant Sandra Birchmore. Jurors have reported being deadlocked, and deliberations are expected to resume Tuesday.
- Karen Read: Her first trial ended with a hung jury. On retrial, she was acquitted of the major charges and convicted of a misdemeanor.
- Caitlin Harding: The former teacher's case resulted in two separate hung juries.
- Terence Crosbie: His first trial ended with a deadlocked jury. A retrial produced a guilty verdict.

Is it just me, or are hung juries becoming a Massachusetts thing? Maybe it's something in the water. 🙃

So, what do you think? Will the Commonwealth retry Clancy? And if so, will a second jury see the evidence differently, or will we end up right back where we started?

🇺🇸 Judge clears path for Lindsay Clancy retrial after rejecting double-jeopardy bid

A Massachusetts court has refused to shield Lindsay Clancy from a second trial on three counts of first-degree murder for the 2023 strangulation deaths of her children, rejecting her claim that the September mistrial violated constitutional protections against double jeopardy.

Judge William Sullivan ruled Monday that the deadlock which ended the first trial created the required “manifest necessity” for a mistrial, so a retrial does not place Clancy in double jeopardy. He also denied the defense request to investigate or further question the single holdout juror and turned down a prosecution request for a gag order. The Plymouth County District Attorney’s office has not yet formally committed to retrying the case, though the court has indicated a possible March 2027 start date and scheduled a follow-up hearing for mid-November.

No party disputed the core facts of the January 24, 2023, killings in the family’s Duxbury home. Clancy, then a labor-and-delivery nurse, arranged for her husband Patrick to leave the house on an errand. While he was gone she used exercise bands to strangle five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson, and eight-month-old Callan in the basement. She then cut herself and jumped from a second-story window, an attempt that left her paralyzed from the waist down. Prosecutors argued the sequence was deliberate and premeditated; the defense maintained that severe postpartum psychosis rendered her not criminally responsible.

The first trial ran nearly seven weeks and ended in a hung jury after more than thirty-eight hours of deliberation. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on grounds of lack of criminal responsibility; one holdout prevented a unanimous verdict. Sullivan declined the defense’s bid to remove or more deeply interrogate that juror, citing the need to avoid coerced outcomes and protect the integrity of deliberations. His Monday opinion reaffirmed that the deadlock itself justified the mistrial.

Postpartum psychosis is a rare condition, occurring in roughly one to two per thousand births, and is associated in the medical literature with elevated risk of infanticide when untreated. Yet the legal threshold for a successful insanity defense requires proof that the defendant, at the moment of the acts, lacked substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of the conduct or to conform behavior to the law. Prosecutors contended that Clancy’s actions—clearing the house of the only adult witness, selecting a method that left no struggle, and targeting all three children—demonstrated capacity and intent. Expert testimony differed sharply on whether her documented depression, insomnia, and reported auditory commands met that high bar.

The children’s deaths remain the fixed center of the case. Cora, Dawson, and Callan were killed by the only parent present. Clancy’s subsequent paralysis and psychiatric history do not erase the sequence of steps that removed the children from the world. A second jury will again be asked to decide whether those steps were the product of a mental disease that fully negated criminal responsibility or the deliberate acts of a mother who chose to end three lives. Sullivan’s ruling keeps that question open for a new panel rather than closing it by judicial fiat.

text:
BOSTON HERALD, OPINION, 11/09/2026

https://t.co/2FUcb5czPk

Legislative Commission 

Massachusetts once abolished special religious privilege. In 1833 the state ended its system of tax support for Congregational churches, recognizing that government has no business elevating one faith above others. Nearly two centuries later, a bill pending on Beacon Hill would reverse that principle.
Senate Bill 2134 and its House companion, H.3351, would create a permanent “Commission on the Status of People Who Practice Islam.” The 11 members would be appointed by the governor, the attorney general, legislative leaders, and others. Each must have “demonstrated a commitment to the Muslim American community.” The commission would be permanent, staffed, and funded. Among its statutory duties is the explicit charge to “identify and recommend qualified American Muslims for appointive positions at all levels of government, including boards and commissions, as the commission considers necessary and appropriate.”
No other religious group in Massachusetts is granted a permanent state body with a pipeline into public appointments. Christians, Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, and nonbelievers receive no comparable official channel. Muslims make up roughly 2-3% of the state’s population. The legislation singles them out for special status in government hiring and appointments.
The bill’s supporters describe it as an effort to combat discrimination and promote inclusion. Those goals can be pursued through existing anti-discrimination laws, skills-based hiring practices, and general outreach. Creating a standing commission whose job includes recommending people for public positions because of their faith is something else entirely.
The First Amendment’s Establishment Clause, applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, forbids government from favoring one religion over others or conferring official benefits on the basis of religious affiliation. Recommending candidates for appointive office specifically because they are Muslim is religious preference. The Massachusetts Constitution reinforces the point. Article VIII prohibits the use of public money or property for founding, maintaining, or aiding any church, religious denomination, or society.
Proponents note that the state has created commissions for other groups. Those bodies track secular characteristics or address discrete, time-limited inquiries. Religion is different under the Establishment Clause. Courts have long rejected religious classifications in public employment and benefits.
Governor Maura Healey has not publicly endorsed the bill. It remains in the Senate Ways and Means Committee after earlier favorable action. It is live legislation with co-sponsors and a clear effective date of Dec. 1 if enacted. The current session runs into early January 2027. The window for preventing it is open, but it will not remain open indefinitely.
Equal treatment under the law is a constitutional requirement. Massachusetts abolished religious privilege long ago. Public appointments should go to the most qualified people based on skills, experience, and merit — not religion.

Ronald Beaty
West Barnstable

$SPCX KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM SPACEX’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

SpaceX’s results reinforce a significant divergence across the technology and communications investment landscape: scarce, operational AI infrastructure is generating attractive returns, while established connectivity providers face increasingly tangible competitive displacement. The most important market signals are the increase in Q4 capital expenditures to $35 billion to $40 billion, compute pricing above management’s previously discussed range, accelerating Starlink aircraft installations, and the development of a vertically integrated mobile network. The strongest positive implications concern NVIDIA, qualified AI-memory suppliers, power infrastructure, and existing revenue-producing compute capacity. The strongest negative implications concern incumbent aviation connectivity and competing satellite-to-mobile platforms. Importantly, these conclusions do not require acceptance of management’s $500 billion to $1 trillion year-end 2027 annualized revenue aspiration. Magnitudes below describe operating or competitive exposure, not predicted share-price moves; confirmed commercial relationships are distinguished from broader industry implications.

AI INFRASTRUCTURE AND CLOUD

EXISTING COMPUTE CAPACITY BENEFITS FROM SCARCITY PRICING DESPITE SPACEX’S EXPANSION (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: CoreWeave (CRWV: United States); Nebius Group (NBIS: Netherlands). Direction: Positive for near-term utilization and monetization, strongest for CoreWeave. Magnitude: High for available or repricing capacity, but materially smaller for revenue already committed under fixed-price contracts.

Supporting evidence: SpaceX reported SI revenue of $7.560 billion, up 195% sequentially, and SI adjusted EBITDA of $4.953 billion. Johnsen stated that pricing was “slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range” discussed last quarter. Musk said short-term contracts were renewing “at higher dollars per watt, not lower dollars per watt,” and described unsuccessful attempts to obtain additional capacity from other cloud providers.

The immediate read-through is not simply that SpaceX will take business from competing infrastructure providers. The more actionable conclusion is that commissioned compute remains scarce enough for multiple providers to earn attractive returns simultaneously. A competitor entering the market with substantial capacity would ordinarily threaten pricing. SpaceX’s ability to expand revenue while reporting strengthening renewal economics instead suggests that demand is currently absorbing supply additions.

CoreWeave provides independent corroboration. Its September 17 company release disclosed newly signed contracts lasting approximately 3 to 6 months at approximately $40 million of annualized revenue per MW. That explicitly defined annualized metric supports the broader scarcity argument, although it should not be directly compared with SpaceX’s per-watt commentary without reconciling hardware, utilization, and service scope. CoreWeave has identifiable exposure to the repricing mechanism; Nebius benefits through the value of available capacity and future contracting, but existing long-term agreements do not automatically reprice upward.

Near-term catalysts are upcoming earnings disclosures on realized rental rates, utilization, contract renewals, and conversion of installed capacity into revenue. The longer-duration distinction is between energized, billable infrastructure and announced power pipelines. SpaceX’s expansion raises the competitive hurdle for future projects, but it does not negate the current value of operating assets. The positive read-through should therefore favor demonstrated deployment and customer monetization rather than indiscriminate exposure to every announced AI data-center project.

SHORT-DURATION REVENUE MAKES FINANCING QUALITY MORE IMPORTANT, NOT LESS (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected companies: CoreWeave (CRWV: United States); Nebius Group (NBIS: Netherlands). Direction: Negative for the valuation of uncontracted, externally financed expansion; not evidence of an immediate deterioration in existing contracted cash flows. Magnitude: Potentially high for equity value because funding requirements and residual asset values can dominate reported EBITDA.

Supporting evidence: Musk described SpaceX’s approach as renting “at effectively the spot market rate, as opposed to sign these long-term deals.” SpaceX simultaneously raised Q4 capital expenditures to $35 billion to $40 billion. Despite generating $9.631 billion of quarterly operating cash flow, derived from its financial releases, it spent $19.593 billion on capital equipment and infrastructure.

The critical transmission mechanism is the mismatch between long-lived capital commitments and short-duration revenue. High spot prices improve current asset payback, but shorter customer commitments provide less protection against future pricing compression, underutilization, or refinancing constraints. A project can have excellent economics at prevailing rental rates while still requiring substantial equity or debt before those economics are realized.

SpaceX also has a profitable connectivity business and substantial liquidity supporting the buildout. That creates a more demanding competitive financing benchmark for specialized AI infrastructure providers. The read-through is not that their customers disappear; it is that investors should demand stronger evidence of funding coverage and durable project returns before assigning full value to prospective capacity.

CoreWeave and Nebius have important contracted businesses that mitigate this risk. Those contracts must be evaluated individually rather than treated as equivalent to SpaceX’s marginal spot-oriented strategy. The negative implication is concentrated in expansion dependent on future contracts, favorable debt markets, or continued peak pricing.

Near-term trading sensitivity is to financing announcements, capital-expenditure revisions, and the gap between contracted power and revenue-producing capacity. The longer-term fundamental risk emerges when refinancing or hardware replacement occurs under less favorable rental economics. This is a reason for greater differentiation within AI infrastructure equities, not a blanket sector short.

SEMICONDUCTORS AND AI SYSTEMS

NVIDIA RECEIVES A LARGE, NAMED DEMAND SIGNAL THAT DOES NOT DEPEND ON GROK WINNING (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected company: NVIDIA (NVDA: United States). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: High strategic and demand significance; the incremental revenue contribution cannot be quantified reliably from the call alone.

Supporting evidence: Management described bringing approximately 200,000 to 220,000 GB300-class units online monthly, predominantly using Vera Rubin for the 2027 expansion, and targeting a 440,000-unit Vera Rubin training cluster by the end of Q2 2027. SpaceX expects 2.5 GW to 3 GW of compute at year-end 2026 and approximately 13 GW by year-end 2027. The draft contains inconsistent hardware labels, so the unit references should not be treated as a precisely standardized shipment schedule.

The direct transmission mechanism is procurement of NVIDIA-based accelerated computing systems. The less obvious implication is that NVIDIA benefits whether SpaceX monetizes this infrastructure through Grok, Cursor, or external cloud customers. Management’s approximately 50% internal and 50% external allocation objective changes which application earns the downstream return, but not the immediate requirement for the underlying compute platform.

NVIDIA’s exposure also extends beyond accelerator chips. Its Rubin platform incorporates CPUs, interconnect, networking, and data-processing components. The architecture therefore offers broader system-content capture than a simple GPU-volume model implies. The call supports NVIDIA’s integrated platform strategy more directly than it supports an assumed order allocation to any particular independent networking vendor.

Near-term catalysts include confirmation of Blackwell deliveries and supplier commentary around SpaceX’s accelerated Q4 spending. The more important fundamental window is 2027 deployment and Rubin conversion. Commissioning dates should not be equated with NVIDIA revenue-recognition dates, and some procurement may already be reflected in existing expectations.

TerraFab does not undermine this near-term conclusion. Management discussed a functional test chip around May or June 2027 and possible volume production in the latter half of 2028. Neither establishes a competitive substitute for NVIDIA’s 2026 or 2027 systems. The high-conviction implication is stronger demand for the existing ecosystem, not an immediate threat from SpaceX-designed or SpaceX-fabricated replacement hardware.

QUALIFIED MEMORY SUPPLIERS BENEFIT FROM RUBIN DEPLOYMENT AND INTERNAL COMPUTE CONSUMPTION (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected companies: Micron Technology (MU: United States); SK hynix (000660: South Korea). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: High relevance for AI-memory demand and product mix; SpaceX-specific supplier shares remain undisclosed.

Supporting evidence: The call’s principal hardware commitments are the transition toward Vera Rubin during 2027 and the planned 440,000-unit training cluster. Management also indicated that approximately half of compute could be consumed internally, including substantial inference demand from Grok Bot.

The transmission mechanism is demand for qualified high-bandwidth memory and associated system memory embedded in these platforms. Micron’s March 2026 company announcement identified volume shipments of HBM4 designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin, alongside SOCAMM2 memory and data-center storage products. SK hynix’s September 2026 technical disclosure showed its HBM4 and SOCAMM2 incorporated into a Vera Rubin system. These establish relevant platform exposure without requiring an unsupported claim that either supplier has received a specific SpaceX allocation.

The important cross-portfolio point is that internal AI usage does not reduce upstream memory demand. Even if application monetization falls short of management’s aspirations, building and operating the announced systems still requires memory. Near-term supplier revenue can therefore remain strong while downstream software returns prove more variable.

The 2027 platform transition is the principal fundamental catalyst. Near-term trading catalysts are supplier disclosures on qualified capacity, customer commitments, pricing, and shipment conversion. Power and cooling delays could defer completed-system deployments, so announced GW should not be converted mechanically into memory revenue.

Geographically, this connects a predominantly US infrastructure expansion with both US and South Korean semiconductor earnings. It also creates overlapping exposure across NVIDIA, Micron, and SK hynix holdings. Owning all of these companies diversifies individual execution risk but does not diversify the underlying AI deployment cycle.

POWER, COOLING, AND ELECTRICAL INFRASTRUCTURE

POWER EQUIPMENT DEMAND CAN PRECEDE GPU INSTALLATION AND DOES NOT DEPEND ON THE WINNING AI MODEL (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected companies: Vertiv Holdings (VRT: United States); Eaton (ETN: Ireland); Schneider Electric (SU: France). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: High industry demand significance and medium-to-high relevance for their data-center businesses; no incremental SpaceX award to these companies was disclosed on the call.

Supporting evidence: Musk identified the principal constraints as “power and cooling and infrastructure” and discussed targeting approximately 20 GW of incremental power-and-cooling infrastructure during 2027, above the approximately 10 GW incremental compute target. Management also described factory-built modular inference clusters with integrated power and cooling.

The transmission mechanism is demand for electrical distribution, power conversion, backup systems, thermal management, controls, and integrated modular infrastructure. Crucially, management wants power and cooling installed ahead of GPUs. This can shift equipment procurement earlier than compute monetization and makes infrastructure readiness a separate spending priority rather than merely a proportional accessory to chip deliveries.

Vertiv and Eaton have publicly disclosed involvement in NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin infrastructure designs, including modular power-and-cooling systems. Schneider Electric has also disclosed Rubin-related reference designs. Those relationships establish relevant technical positioning, not guaranteed SpaceX market share. The strongest read-through is to the broader infrastructure category and competitive deployment response across the industry.

Near-term catalysts are order intake, lead-time commentary, and backlog conversion over the next several quarters. The longer-duration shift is toward denser, increasingly liquid-cooled and integrated installations, where system engineering and execution matter alongside individual component supply.

SpaceX’s vertical integration is an important limitation. Internal design and manufacturing could reduce its dependence on some external suppliers or pressure component economics. Nevertheless, the combination of large physical requirements and competitors’ need to accelerate their own deployments supports the direction of industry demand. The call does not justify assuming that every dollar of SpaceX infrastructure spending becomes revenue for a listed equipment supplier.

THE POWER BOTTLENECK FAVORS DISPATCHABLE GENERATION AND EXECUTION CAPABILITY OVER GENERIC ELECTRICITY EXPOSURE (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected companies: GE Vernova (GEV: United States); Siemens Energy (ENR: Germany); Solaris Energy Infrastructure (SEI: United States). Direction: Positive for gas-generation equipment and integrated power-delivery services. Magnitude: High sector relevance; company-specific upside depends on awards and commissioning rather than SpaceX’s headline GW target.

Supporting evidence: Musk said turbine blades and vanes were arriving 12 to 18 months behind other turbine components and described applying SpaceX’s casting capabilities to that bottleneck. He also emphasized using multiple power sources while pursuing rapid deployment of incremental compute.

The immediate implication is that access to dispatchable power remains a gating item with substantial economic value. Turbine equipment, balance-of-plant integration, energy management, commissioning, and ongoing maintenance can therefore capture spending even before the associated compute becomes fully productive.

GE Vernova and Siemens Energy provide exposure to generation equipment and service ecosystems. Solaris provides more concentrated exposure to integrated power infrastructure and execution. Its own recent disclosures describe expanded turnkey power-plant scope, batteries, energy-management systems, and additional infrastructure services. The call strengthens the demand rationale for those capabilities; it does not establish a new Solaris contract or permit attribution of SpaceX’s entire planned expansion to any provider.

The non-consensus distinction is between power-equipment demand and merchant electricity-price exposure. A data center served by dedicated generation does not necessarily create an equivalent increase in purchases from the public grid. The geography of Memphis and Southaven, together with management’s emphasis on rapid and modular deployment, supports site-specific generation and infrastructure solutions more clearly than a broad rally in all utilities or power producers.

Near-term catalysts are turbine awards, delivery schedules, emissions approvals, and commissioning milestones. The longer-duration benefit is the service revenue attached to a larger installed generation base. SpaceX manufacturing blades and vanes internally could accelerate deployment, but the call does not demonstrate that SpaceX can replace complete turbine systems or their lifetime service requirements.

SATELLITE AND AVIATION CONNECTIVITY

STARLINK’S CONTRACTED AIRCRAFT ARE BECOMING AN INSTALLATION-DRIVEN EARNINGS THREAT TO INCUMBENTS (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected companies: Viasat (VSAT: United States); SES (SESG: Luxembourg). Direction: Negative. Magnitude: High for competitive positioning in aviation connectivity; consolidated earnings impact depends on customer exposure, contract duration, and migration timing.

Supporting evidence: SpaceX reported approximately 12,000 contracted aircraft, agreements with 3 of the 4 major US carriers, and more than 3,800 equipped aircraft at quarter-end. Management said aviation production had quadrupled since the beginning of 2026 and was expected to double again before year-end. Lufthansa, Swiss, Copa Airlines, Korean Air, Austrian Airlines, and Asiana Airlines began operating Starlink-equipped aircraft during the quarter.

The transmission mechanism is increasingly concrete: signed agreements convert into active aircraft, reducing incumbent opportunities to retain fleets and increasing pricing pressure at renewals. Only approximately 32% of Starlink’s contracted aircraft were equipped at quarter-end. Roughly 8,200 additional aircraft therefore represent a substantial activation pipeline without requiring new contract wins.

This is more important than another announcement that an airline intends to adopt Starlink. Installation bottlenecks can delay competitive displacement for years. Management’s manufacturing ramp and reported activations suggest that deployment is becoming a more consequential source of earnings pressure during 2027.

Viasat faces direct competition in passenger connectivity. SES’s exposure includes Intelsat, whose acquisition it completed in 2025. The pressure can affect service revenue, terminal economics, renewal pricing, and returns on satellite capacity committed to mobility markets. High fixed costs mean that lost revenue or weaker pricing can have a disproportionate effect on segment profitability.

Not all 12,000 contracted aircraft represent existing customers being removed from these providers, and installations do not establish immediate contract termination. Aviation safety communications, government services, and other differentiated applications should also not be treated as interchangeable with passenger broadband.

Near-term catalysts are additional aircraft activations and competitor disclosures on fleet retention, backlog, and revenue per aircraft. The longer-duration threat is a structurally stronger low-Earth-orbit competitor with its own launch capability and an expanding capacity base. This is among the clearest negative fundamental read-throughs in the call.

DIRECT-TO-DEVICE SATELLITE SERVICES

STARLINK’S COMBINED SPECTRUM AND LAUNCH STRATEGY RAISES THE COMPETITIVE HURDLE FOR AST SPACEMOBILE (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected company: AST SpaceMobile (ASTS: United States). Direction: Negative for competitive scarcity value and future bargaining power. Magnitude: High strategic significance; limited evidence of an immediate change to contracted revenue.

Supporting evidence: Starlink Mobile exceeded 22 million monthly users, up 37% sequentially. Management discussed authorization for 15,000 mobile V2 satellites, a low-band spectrum acquisition, deployment of mobile V2 satellites beginning in 2027, and enhanced service in early 2028.

The transmission mechanism is not simply competition between satellite counts. SpaceX is combining owned launch infrastructure, satellite manufacturing, spectrum access, existing broadband distribution, and a proposed terrestrial network. If successfully deployed, that combination could support lower incremental capacity costs and broader commercial flexibility than a stand-alone wholesale satellite model.

For AST SpaceMobile, the likely pressure points are future operator-contract economics, geographic exclusivity, service differentiation, and the valuation premium assigned to scarce satellite-to-phone capability. Starlink’s expanding carrier relationships and user reach make it less reasonable to assume a lightly contested global market.

There are meaningful offsets. AST SpaceMobile’s operator-aligned model can be attractive to carriers that do not want to support a future retail competitor. Its definitive Verizon relationship illustrates that strategic role. Starlink’s 22 million monthly users are also not equivalent to 22 million paying broadband subscribers, and the call did not demonstrate superior per-user economics or service quality across all relevant use cases.

The highest-conviction conclusion is stronger competition, not technological defeat. Near-term trading catalysts include Starship launches, mobile satellite deployment, spectrum approvals, and new carrier agreements. Fundamental effects on pricing and market share are primarily a 2027 to 2028 issue. The shift from a previously discussed late-2027 service start to early 2028 also preserves an execution window for competing systems.

US WIRELESS TELECOMMUNICATIONS

STARLINK IS BECOMING A POTENTIAL RETAIL COMPETITOR, NOT MERELY A COVERAGE SUPPLIER (READ-THROUGH 9)

Affected companies: T-Mobile US (TMUS: United States); Verizon Communications (VZ: United States); AT&T (T: United States). Direction: Negative for longer-term competitive structure and coverage differentiation. Magnitude: Moderate strategic risk, with low immediate earnings impact from this call.

Supporting evidence: Management said spectrum integration would support becoming “a major mobile carrier in the United States.” The call described using existing Starlink locations for smaller terrestrial radios, while the financial release specified a proposed portfolio of up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band. Enhanced service is targeted for early 2028.

The transmission mechanism is a change in industry relationships. Satellite coverage supplied through existing carriers can improve their products and reduce churn. A standalone SpaceX retail offering could instead compete for the customer relationship, bundle broadband and mobile access, and force incumbent carriers to respond through pricing, retention spending, or satellite partnerships.

T-Mobile has the most direct partner-versus-competitor tension because its T-Satellite service uses Starlink. That existing relationship remains beneficial in the near term. The concern is whether SpaceX’s longer-term retail strategy reduces T-Mobile’s ability to treat satellite coverage as a differentiated feature under its own control.

Verizon and AT&T face a different exposure: potential pressure on coverage-based differentiation and a stronger incentive to develop independent satellite relationships. Their terrestrial networks, spectrum depth, distribution, billing systems, and enterprise relationships remain substantial defenses.

The low-band acquisition improves the credibility of a hybrid strategy, but it does not establish a nationwide network with equivalent urban capacity or indoor performance. Up to 14 MHz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band is not 800 MHz of bandwidth. Nor does a large satellite footprint remove the need for terrestrial densification and network integration.

Near-term trading catalysts are regulatory approvals, network architecture disclosures, retail plans, and changes to existing carrier partnerships. The fundamental threat is primarily beyond 2027. The call supports a higher long-term competitive-risk assessment, not immediate broad reductions to incumbent wireless earnings forecasts.

ENTERPRISE SOFTWARE AND AI APPLICATIONS

CURSOR AND GROK BOT INCREASE COMPETITION FOR PAID CODING AND AGENT BUDGETS, NOT NECESSARILY CORE SOFTWARE SEATS (READ-THROUGH 10)

Affected company: Microsoft (MSFT: United States). Direction: Negative for competitive economics in AI coding and enterprise-agent monetization. Magnitude: Moderate at the product level, low for near-term consolidated earnings.

Supporting evidence: Cursor contributed $608 million of revenue after its August 14 acquisition closing. Management reported 800,000 paid weekly Grok Bot users earlier in October, more than double the preceding month, and a 50% sequential increase in customers exceeding $1 million of run-rate revenue on a pro forma basis including Cursor. SpaceX also announced a combined Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor, and X Premium plan.

The transmission mechanism is increased competition for the incremental budget allocated to coding assistants and autonomous work tools. Cursor brings an established developer workflow and enterprise sales capability. Grok Bot extends the offering into persistent, task-oriented agents. Microsoft competes in the same spending categories through GitHub Copilot and its broader Copilot agent portfolio.

The important implication is pressure on premium

Both members of the NAPS Class of 2022 and key contributors to the Navy Football program, Purvis and Duhart chose to return to NAPS following graduation to coach for a season before reporting to their first units.

“Starting out my career at NAPS and then coming back here after graduation is a complete full circle moment for myself. NAPS is a challenging place, but getting through it, and coming back here being able to pass on wisdom to the next generation is a true blessing.”

2ndLt Andrew Duhart shares what the opportunity means to him:

“For myself it is an honor and a privilege to be able to come back to where my Navy football career started and have an impact on such an important group of young men for this program. Being able to be the first taste of Navy football and the Marine Corps for these NAPS football players is something that I will always remember. And as always, BEAT ARMY!”

From Midshipmen Candidates to Navy Football players to Marine Corps officers and now mentors, their journey embodies what NAPS is all about.

NAPS Athletics is incredibly grateful for their leadership, commitment, and willingness to invest in the next generation. Their impact extends far beyond the football field.

text:
$FNV Q3 2026 earnings: Franco-Nevada's oil royalties rise, but its gold mines miss targets

Oil royalties rescued Franco-Nevada's full-year plan while its gold, silver and platinum mines missed delivery targets. The gold royalty and streaming group grew revenue 13% from a year ago, but sales fell 5% from the second quarter after a Federal Reserve rate hike pushed gold prices down. Chief executive Paul Brink stepped back from his prior upper-half volume target to the middle of the 525,000–555,000 ounce range, cutting the outlook for every precious metal while raising the energy and iron ore forecast by $50 million.

• Gold equivalent ounces sold: 𝟏𝟑𝟎,𝟒𝟑𝟓 𝐆𝐄𝐎𝐬 (−6% from a year ago (−1% excluding Cobre Panamá))
• Revenue: $𝟓𝟒𝟗.𝟑𝐌 (+13% from a year ago, −5% from last quarter)
• Profit excluding one-offs: $𝟑𝟔𝟒.𝟓𝐌 ($𝟏.𝟖𝟗/𝐬𝐡) (+33% from a year ago (+21% before a $33M tax credit))
• Full-year volume outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐦𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 (precious metal targets lowered; energy raised $50M)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The standing case got worse because precious metal volumes are shrinking and a key partner is buying back half of a flagship gold royalty. Days after the quarter closed, IAMGOLD exercised its option to halve Franco-Nevada's royalty on the Côté Gold mine for at least $525 million, removing producing gold ounces starting in January while adding to a $4.8 billion capital pile the company is struggling to deploy. On the positive side, Cobre Panamá shipped its first stockpile concentrate since 2023 and a government panel recommended formal restart talks.

The question now is whether new mine expansions and a Cobre Panamá deal can replace the ounces lost to operator buy-backs and upcoming stream step-downs. Either management deploys its $5.3 billion war chest into large producing streams and gets a multi-year restart in Panama, or cash sits idle while gold volumes stagnate in 2027. The 2027 production outlook and five-year plan in March will settle it.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐄𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Franco-Nevada earns most of its money from gold and silver, but it also collects royalties on oil, natural gas and iron ore, which it groups as diversified assets. When mining deliveries fell short this quarter, higher oil prices and new wells in Texas and Canada filled the gap.

• Diversified revenue: $86.8 million, up 29% from a year ago
• Oil revenue: $48.9 million, up 61% from a year ago
• U. S. energy revenue: $50.8 million, up from $33.8 million a year ago
• Canadian energy revenue: $21.6 million, up from $15.6 million a year ago

Because diversified revenue reached $251.6 million in the first nine months, it had already passed the bottom of the company's initial $245–285 million full-year target with three months left. Management raised that full-year plan by $50 million at the middle of the range, to $300–330 million. Because Franco-Nevada converts non-gold revenue into gold equivalent ounces (GEOs, a single volume measure across all commodities) at fixed 2026 prices, those extra oil dollars kept the total volume target intact.

What to watch: fourth-quarter diversified revenue against the $63.4 million implied by the middle of the revised full-year outlook. Anything above $78.4 million would push the division past the top of the new range too.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐛𝐫𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐦á 𝐒𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐚𝐥𝐤𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞
Cobre Panamá, a large copper and gold mine in Panama operated by First Quantum Minerals where Franco-Nevada holds a precious-metals stream (a contract to buy a share of metal output), has been shut since November 2023. In April 2026, Panama's government allowed the operator to process ore that had been mined and stockpiled before the shutdown.

First Quantum brought all three processing lines back online and shipped the first copper concentrate in the third quarter. Franco-Nevada received and sold 3,716 GEOs from those shipments and reversed $10.3 million of its earlier write-down on the mine. On September 30, a government commission delivered its final report to Panama's president, "marking the Government of Panama’s (“GOP”) transition from technical assessment to the decision-making phase".

The commission recommended talks on a new contract that would settle arbitration and "establish conditions for a potential restart designed to achieve an orderly, self-financed closure". That wording shows why the mine remains a political risk as well as an upside option: any restart still requires cabinet approval, and the commission framed it around an eventual closure.

What to watch: fourth-quarter deliveries from Cobre Panamá against the roughly 4,500 GEOs needed to reach one-third of the 23,100 gold ounces and 265,000 silver ounces expected in the second half. A cabinet decision on formal negotiations would test whether a full mine restart is achievable.

🟢 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐓𝐨𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧
Franco-Nevada does not run mines itself, so its long-term volume growth depends on mining partners building new projects and expanding existing ones on land its royalties cover. Several partners cleared major funding and permitting hurdles during and just after the third quarter.

• Bullabulling (Australia): Franco-Nevada paid $121.0 million for an extra 1.45% gross royalty, lifting its stake to 3.90%, and bought $21.0 million of shares; three banks then committed A$410.0 million in debt, leaving the project fully funded
• Copper World (Arizona, 2.085% royalty): Hudbay and Mitsubishi approved construction in October for a late-2029 start, lifting planned first-decade copper output by 11% to 102,000 tonnes a year
• Antapaccay (Peru, gold and silver stream): Glencore finished land access deals in October for the Coroccohuayco expansion, which starts in late 2029 and extends mine life past 40 years
• Ring of Fire (Ontario, 1–3% royalties): Canada matched Ontario's C$1 billion road pledge in October

What to watch: the updated five-year production outlook through 2031, which management publishes with full-year results in March. It will show whether these project approvals add enough ounces to lift the 555,000–615,000 GEO target range set a year ago.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐫𝐮𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐄𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭
"Precious metal GEO deliveries were slightly below expectations in the period, although strong oil prices boosted our diversified revenue, and we are now tracking towards the mid-range of our annual guidance," chief executive Paul Brink said. Three months ago, management had told investors it was tracking toward the upper half of the 510,000–570,000 GEO plan.

• Precious metal GEOs sold: 110,904, down 7% from 119,109 a year ago
• Gold ounces sold: 90,083, down 11% from a year ago; full-year outlook cut by 10,000 ounces at the middle of the range
• Silver actual ounces sold: 1.06 million, down 23% from a year ago; full-year outlook cut by 250,000 ounces at the middle
• Platinum group metals sold: 7,924 ounces; full-year outlook cut by 2,500 ounces at the middle

Weather and labour caused the shortfall. Candelaria in Chile and Guadalupe-Palmarejo in Mexico both delivered less metal after an "impact to mining operations due to heavy rainfall from severe winter storms in Chile’s Atacama region" and rain delays in Mexico. At Stillwater in Montana, a five-week strike forced the operator to cut its 2026 production target because of the "impact of the strike and time required to rebuild operational performance in Q4 2026". Even stripping out Cobre Panamá from both years, total GEO volumes edged down 0.7% from a year ago by our math.

What to watch: fourth-quarter gold sales against the 97,535 ounces implied by the middle of the lowered full-year outlook. Meeting that number requires an 8% rebound from the third quarter, relying on higher-grade ore at Côté Gold and Tocantinzinho.

🔴🔴 𝐈𝐀𝐌𝐆𝐎𝐋𝐃 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂ô𝐭é 𝐆𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲
Many newer royalty contracts give the mine operator an option to buy back part of the royalty for a set return once the mine is running well. That option caps Franco-Nevada's upside on its best deals while leaving it holding the full stake in projects that struggle.

On November 5, 2026, IAMGOLD exercised its right to buy back half of Franco-Nevada's gross margin royalty (a royalty calculated after mine operating costs) on the Côté Gold mine in Ontario. The royalty rate drops from 7.5% to 3.75% on January 1, 2027, in exchange for at least $525.0 million in cash in December. This is the second major clawback in nine months, after SolGold and Jiangxi Copper bought back half of the Cascabel stream and royalty in March for $138.2 million in cash and gold.

Brink highlighted $4.8 billion in available capital — cash, tradable shares and credit lines — as "ample firepower to take advantage of a strong pipeline of deal opportunities". Yet the Côté payment will push available capital above $5.3 billion by year-end while deal spending is slowing: the group spent $133.9 million on royalties this quarter, and capital payments for Cascabel, Copper World and i-80 Gold all slipped from 2026 into 2027. Instead of putting cash into new mines, the portfolio is returning cash and losing producing gold ounces for 2027.

What to watch: the 2027 GEO production outlook issued in March 2027. It will show whether new royalties from i-80 Gold and Casa Berardi can replace the lost half of Côté Gold.

🔴 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐃𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐏𝐞𝐚𝐤
Because Franco-Nevada has almost no fixed operating costs, its revenue and cash flow move directly with metal prices. That worked in its favour early in 2026 when gold hit record highs, so third-quarter revenue of $549.3 million was still up 13% from a year ago.

Quarter to quarter, the trend has turned down. Revenue fell 5.4% from $580.9 million in the second quarter and is down 15.6% from the first-quarter peak of $650.7 million by our math. The company noted in its report that "during Q3 2026, gold continued to decline driven by the sharp increase in real-yields, the September Federal Reserve rate hike, and the strength of the US dollar". Lower metal prices also pulled operating cash flow down to $429.2 million, missing the $450–500 million quarterly run-rate management had pointed to at mid-year.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue per GEO sold against this quarter's $4,211 by our math (down from $4,387 in the second quarter). A further drop below $4,000 would pull quarterly revenue below $520 million even if mine deliveries recover.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐚𝐫𝐛𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐬 𝐓𝐚𝐱 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Third-quarter net income rose 38% to $395.5 million, and profit excluding one-offs rose 33% to $364.5 million ($1.89 per share), outpacing the 13% revenue gain. Nearly a third of that profit growth came from a one-time tax adjustment in Barbados: after filing its 2024 return under new Global Minimum Tax rules, Franco-Nevada qualified for a transitional exemption and reversed a $32.8 million tax charge. Without that credit, the tax rate was 20.2% instead of 13.0%, and profit excluding one-offs grew 21% by our math.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟕𝟕.𝟓%  ⇗ accelerating
Operating margin rose 7.6 percentage points from a year ago to 77.5% by our math, reversing the unit-cost rise seen in the first half. Depletion — the accounting charge for mined-out reserves — fell 3.5 percentage points of revenue to 14.3%, and cash cost of sales fell 1.8 points to 7.8% ($330 per GEO sold, down from $340 a year ago).

𝐆𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐢𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟏𝟐.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Holdings of physical gold and silver bullion and stream inventory stood at $112.7 million, unchanged from $112.6 million in June and nearly triple the $40.1 million held at the end of 2025. The gold streamer received $52.6 million of metal in kind this quarter and sold $43.3 million, keeping extra bullion on the balance sheet.

𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒,𝟖𝟏𝟗.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Available liquidity climbed 12% from last quarter and is up nearly $2.0 billion since December 2025. The total combines $1,232.2 million of cash (up $218.0 million in the quarter), $1,337.1 million of tradable mining shares, and $2.25 billion of untouched credit lines, with zero debt.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐆𝐄𝐎𝐬 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝: 𝟓𝟐𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎–𝟓𝟓𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐆𝐄𝐎𝐬  ⇄ reversing
🠇 cut from 510,000–570,000 GEOs (tracking towards upper half)
Cut from the prior upper-half view. The Toronto-based group narrowed the formal band around the same 540,000-ounce middle (4.0% growth for the year), but stepped back from last quarter's statement that it was tracking toward 540,000–570,000. By our math, the middle of the range leaves 140,807 GEOs for the fourth quarter — up 8.0% from the third quarter and down 0.6% from a year ago.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝: 𝟑𝟓𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎–𝟑𝟖𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐨𝐳  ⇄ reversing
🠇 cut from 360,000–400,000 oz
Cut. The middle of the range came down by 10,000 ounces, to 370,000 ounces (1.0% growth for the full year), after storm disruptions at Candelaria and Guadalupe-Palmarejo. By our math, that leaves 97,535 gold ounces for the fourth quarter, which is 8.3% above the third quarter and 3.6% below last year's record fourth quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐒𝐢𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝: 𝟒,𝟕𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎–𝟓,𝟎𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐨𝐳  ⇄ reversing
🠇 cut from 4,700,000–5,500,000 oz
Cut. Management trimmed the top of the range by 500,000 ounces, lowering the middle by 250,000 ounces to 4.85 million. With 3.65 million ounces sold in the first nine months, the middle of the plan leaves 1.20 million ounces for the fourth quarter by our math, a 13.3% step-up from the third quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐏𝐆𝐌𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝: 𝟑𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎–𝟑𝟒,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐨𝐳  ⇄ reversing
🠇 cut from 32,000–37,000 oz
Cut. The royalty group lowered the middle of the range by 2,500 ounces to 32,000 after the five-week strike at Stillwater. With 23,623 ounces sold through September, the middle of the new range leaves 8,377 ounces for the fourth quarter by our math, up 5.7% from the third quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐃𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟑𝟎𝟎–𝟑𝟑𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $245–285 million
Raised. The middle of the outlook moved up $50 million, to $315 million (21.2% growth for the year), catching up with strong oil prices and Permian well activity. By our math, that leaves $63.4 million for the fourth quarter — up 14.6% from a year ago, though 27.0% below the third quarter's $86.8 million pace.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟑𝟐𝟎.𝟎–𝟑𝟒𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from $310.0–340.0 million
Raised at the low end. Franco-Nevada lifted the bottom of the non-cash depletion range by $10 million, moving the middle up $5 million to $330 million as Cobre Panamá deliveries resumed. By our math, that implies $89.5 million of depletion in the fourth quarter, up from $78.6 million this quarter.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐄𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞: 𝟐𝟎–𝟐𝟑%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 20–23%
Unchanged. The full-year tax rate plan stays at 20–23%. Through nine months, the reported effective tax rate is 19.3% ($290.4 million on $1,508.5 million of pre-tax profit) because of the $32.8 million Barbados credit; excluding that credit, the nine-month rate is 21.4% by our math, right in the middle of the plan.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂ô𝐭é 𝐛𝐮𝐲-𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞?
IAMGOLD is buying back half of the 7.5% Côté Gold royalty on January 1, 2027, following the 50% Cascabel buy-back in March. Management has not stated how many GEOs those two clawbacks remove from its 2027 and 2030 targets.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐛𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐛 $𝟓.𝟑 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥?
With the $525 million Côté payment arriving in December, available liquidity will top $5.3 billion while third-quarter royalty purchases were $133.9 million. Investors need to know what deal sizes and return hurdles management is targeting to put that cash to work.

𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐛𝐫𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐦á 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐩 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠-𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐞?
Panama's Interministerial Commission recommended negotiating a restart "designed to achieve an orderly, self-financed closure". Management did not explain whether a closure-focused restart limits Cobre Panamá to processing existing pits rather than a multi-decade operation.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐝𝐚'𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐞𝐫-𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐭𝐚𝐱𝐞𝐬?
While Barbados qualified for a 2024 Global Minimum Tax safe harbour, Canada enacted new transfer-pricing rules effective for 2026 onward. The MD&A says the company is still evaluating the impact after three quarters under the law.
