🗞️12 November 2026 | Daily Edition: First Hour

Huang Exits Nvidia, Bitcoin Loses $72,000

Tuesday's low gave way before the bell, the 10-year climbed past 5.05% and the build-out kept going, from the DTCC on Solana to staking at BNY.

Prepared around 10:25 AM EST on Thursday 12 November, about an hour into the US session. This edition picks up from this morning's Pre-Market and only adds what changed since: the open, the jobless claims print and the fresh crypto headlines of the US morning.

1⃣ Bitcoin broke Tuesday's low and lost $72,000

Bitcoin held near $73,400 until about 6:00 AM EST, then slid. It broke Tuesday's $72,585 low in the 8:00 AM EST hour, the morning Nvidia confirmed its CEO had resigned, and fell through $72,000 in the 9:15 AM EST bar. An attempt to bounce at the open stalled at $72,200, and the session low so far is about $71,150 just after 10:00 AM EST. It trades near $71,300, down about 3% over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: The range I have been tracking since Tuesday failed on the downside, and $72,600 now turns from support into resistance.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This was not a crypto-specific shock. It was risk-off across AI and tech, and Bitcoin is trading as part of that basket, not as a hedge against it.

2⃣ Ether slipped under $2,000, Solana and XRP fell harder

Ether lost $2,000 in the 8:00 AM EST hour and made a low of about $1,981 at 9:15 AM EST. It is back near $2,000, down about 3% over 24 hours. Solana is near $81, down 3% to 4%, and XRP is near $1.02, down about 4% to 5%.

🖊️ Market significance: The $2,000 floor that held on Tuesday has been breached intraday for the first time this week.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Ether is holding the line better than the alts, but a close under $2,000 with ETF outflows still running would open a much weaker range.

3⃣ Longs were flushed, but they are still paying

More than $650 million of crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, the bulk of it longs, as Bitcoin went through $72,000. Funding has not reset. Bitcoin perpetual funding is still roughly 0.0005% to 0.01% per eight hours across four major venues, all positive, and Ether funding is still slightly positive too.

🖊️ Market significance: The flush I warned about this morning has started, but leverage on the long side has not been cleared.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Positive funding after a fall of more than $3,500 from Wednesday's high says dip buyers are still levering up. A true reset usually needs funding to turn negative, so I would not call a bottom yet.

4⃣ The DTCC will bring tokenized securities to Solana

The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana, with DTC-tokenized assets expected on the network in the second half of 2027. The service went live on 28 October on the Canton Network and a private DTCC chain, covering Russell 1000 stocks, major index ETFs and Treasuries. The DTC custodies more than $114 trillion in assets, and tokens on Solana are to carry the same investor protections and ownership rights as traditionally held securities.

🖊️ Market significance: The plumbing of US securities settlement is picking a public, high-throughput chain as one of its venues.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the most important headline of the morning, even on a red day. It is a 2027 delivery, but it gives Solana a real institutional settlement role, not just retail volume.

5⃣ BlackRock's BUIDL now has a 24/7 exit to USDC

Securitize and Ethena switched on a $100 million liquidity facility that lets eligible investors swap shares of BlackRock's tokenized Treasury fund for stablecoins, including USDC, at any hour. It opens with $50 million split evenly between BUIDL and USDC, with another $50 million available within an hour as it is used.

🖊️ Market significance: Tokenized cash funds are getting round-the-clock redemption, which is what makes them usable as trading collateral.

🗨️ My viewpoint: On a day like today, being able to turn a Treasury fund into dollars at 3:00 AM is the whole point of putting it on-chain.

6⃣ BNY will offer staking through Figment

BNY will use Figment's validators to let eligible clients, including asset managers, ETF issuers, corporates and wealth managers, stake assets held in its Digital Asset Custody service. Ether comes first, followed by Solana, with no launch date given. Figment serves more than 1,500 institutions.

🖊️ Market significance: One of the largest custodian banks is turning staking into a standard custody service.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Staking inside a bank custody account is what lets ETF issuers and pensions earn yield without new operational risk. It supports the case for staked Ether ETFs.

7⃣ Bank stablecoins widened their rails

SoFi's bank-issued SoFiUSD is now live on Polygon's Open Money Stack, alongside Ethereum and Solana, so SoFi's more than 17 million members can use it there through the SoFi app. BitGo added USDC minting and redemption for clients of its OCC-regulated trust bank, joining USD1 and SoFiUSD, across nine chains including Ethereum, Solana, Base and Arbitrum, with the on-chain leg running 24/7.

🖊️ Market significance: Regulated banks are distributing stablecoins themselves instead of leaving it to crypto-native issuers.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Total stablecoin supply is shrinking, so this is distribution being built ahead of demand. It matters more for the next cycle than this week's price.

8⃣ Jupiter opened a USDGO lending market, Griffin raised for stablecoins

Jupiter added a lending market for USDGO, the stablecoin issued by Anchorage Digital Bank and run by OSL, letting holders earn on-chain or borrow it against crypto, also through Bitget Wallet. Jupiter Lend has more than $1 billion in active loans, while USDGO's market value has slipped to about $1.1 billion from $1.29 billion in mid-October. In London, Griffin, a licensed bank for fintechs, raised a $20 million Series B to add card issuing and stablecoin payments.

🖊️ Market significance: Smaller bank-backed stablecoins are looking to DeFi for yield and demand, while small banks are adding stablecoin rails.

🗨️ My viewpoint: USDGO shrinking 15% in a month shows how hard it is to compete with USDT and USDC. A DeFi lending market is a reasonable way to give holders a reason to stay.

9⃣ Tether Gold passed its first Big Four audit

KPMG issued a clean opinion on the 2025 financial statements of TG Commodities, issuer of Tether Gold, after physically counting every bar. At the end of 2025 it held 520,089.35 fine troy ounces in Swiss vaults, worth about $2.25 billion, against 520,089.30 tokens. A later reserve report put holdings at about 827,418 ounces by the end of September.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest tokenized gold product now has full audited financials, not just reserve attestations.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The timing is awkward with gold down hard today, but audited backing is what lets tokenized commodities sit on institutional balance sheets.

1⃣0⃣ Tron, Tether and Chainalysis formed a crime task force

Tron, Tether and Chainalysis launched a Digital Crime Task Force to find and freeze illicit USDT on Tron faster, working directly with law enforcement. It follows the break-up of the earlier T3 unit, which Tron and Tether ran with another analytics firm and which was disbanded after slow responses. Chainalysis says AI-enabled scams were 4.5 times more profitable than conventional schemes last year, and Tether says it has frozen more than $7 billion linked to illicit activity.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest stablecoin rail is investing in faster enforcement as AI-driven fraud rises.

🗨️ My viewpoint: After the AI-run Chainstack breach this week, speed of freezing is becoming the main defence. Issuers that can freeze fast will keep regulators on side.

1⃣1⃣ The DeFi industry joined the fight against Illinois' crypto tax

The DeFi Education Fund, Paradigm, Uniswap and Andreessen Horowitz led an amicus brief backing the industry's lawsuit against Illinois' Digital Asset Tax Act, signed by firms including Aave Labs, Chainlink Labs, Jito Labs, Phantom and the Hyperliquid Policy Center. The law puts a 0.2% tax on digital asset transactions and has been pushed back from January to July 2027. The brief says it fails to separate taxable business activity from the software and networks that let users transact on their own.

🖊️ Market significance: A state-level transaction tax is the first real test of how far states can tax on-chain activity.

🗨️ My viewpoint: If a 0.2% levy survives in a state with about 2.6 million holders, others will copy it. This case matters more than its headline suggests.

1⃣2⃣ Crypto stocks fell twice as hard as the coins

Near 10:25 AM EST, Strategy is down about 7% near $113.70, deeper than this morning's pre-market drop, as the MSCI deletion and Bitcoin's break combine. Galaxy is down about 7.7% near $14.70, giving back much of Wednesday's AI-driven jump. Circle is down about 5.5%, Coinbase about 4.6% near $130 and Robinhood about 3.2%.

🖊️ Market significance: The crypto equities that rallied with AI on Wednesday are falling with AI today.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Strategy below $115 with a thinner premium makes new share issuance harder. That is the second-order effect of MSCI I flagged this morning, arriving faster than expected.

1⃣3⃣ Jensen Huang resigned and Nvidia briefly fell 14%

Nvidia said its board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO while a search runs, and long-time director Harvey Jones becomes chair. The stock fell as much as 14% at the open and has recovered to about $164.60, down about 5.3%. AMD and Broadcom are higher, while CoreWeave and other AI cloud names are down sharply.

🖊️ Market significance: The company at the centre of the AI trade has lost its founder with no permanent successor named.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The on-chain Nvidia perps priced this overnight. The question for crypto is whether the AI unwind spreads, because Bitcoin has been trading with it all week.

1⃣4⃣ Stocks opened lower, led by tech

Near 10:25 AM EST, the S&P 500 is down about 0.4% near 7,588, the Nasdaq Composite down about 0.6% near 25,310 and the Dow down about 0.2% near 52,390. Nvidia was the biggest decliner in both the S&P 500 and the Dow in early trading.

🖊️ Market significance: The index damage is contained so far, much smaller than Nvidia's own fall.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Equities are absorbing the shock better than crypto. When stocks dip modestly and Bitcoin breaks a key low, it tells me crypto's own demand is weak.

1⃣5⃣ Jobless claims rose to 200,000, a $25 billion 30-year sale is next

Initial jobless claims rose to 200,000 in the week to 7 November, above the 195,000 forecast and up from a revised 191,000. The four-week average held at 195,250 and continuing claims fell to 1.697 million. Fed Governor Barr spoke on AI and inequality without a policy signal. A $25 billion 30-year bond auction is at 1:00 PM EST and the New York Fed's Williams speaks at 6:30 PM EST.

🖊️ Market significance: The labor market is still tight, so the data did nothing to soften the Fed's December stance.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A slightly higher claims print is not enough to change the hike path. The 30-year auction is now the bigger test for rates today.

1⃣6⃣ Gold sank 3.5%, yields and oil rose, the dollar firmed

Gold is down about 3.5% near $3,861, deeper below $4,000. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5.07%, up about 7 basis points as the cash market reopens after Veterans Day, and the 30-year is near 5.40%. Brent is up about 1.4% near $94 and WTI about 0.5% near $87. The dollar index is up about 0.2% to 0.3%, just above 103.

🖊️ Market significance: Higher yields and a stronger dollar are tightening conditions on the day risk assets are already under pressure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A 10-year above 5% and rising is the headwind I worry about most. Even gold is being sold, which tells me this is a liquidity squeeze, not just an AI story.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The first hour confirmed the weakness I flagged this morning. Bitcoin broke Tuesday's $72,585 low before the bell, lost $72,000 and has made a low near $71,150. Ether dipped under $2,000. The trigger was outside crypto: Nvidia's CEO resigned, the AI trade sold off, the 10-year yield rose to about 5.07% and even gold fell 3.5%. Crypto stocks are falling harder than the coins, with Strategy down 7% as the MSCI deletion bites. Longs were flushed but funding is still positive, so the leverage has not been cleaned out. Under the surface, the institutional build-out did not pause: the DTCC chose Solana, BNY is adding staking, BUIDL got a 24/7 exit and bank stablecoins widened their rails.

For the rest of the US session, my Bitcoin support is $71,150, today's low, then $70,000, the round number the options market has been leaning toward. Resistance is $72,000, then $72,600, Tuesday's low and now the line that matters, and $73,150, the overnight low. A close back above $72,600 would turn today into a failed breakdown. A break below $71,150 opens $70,000. For Ether, support is $1,980, today's low, then $1,960. Resistance is $2,030, then $2,080. I stay defensive and lean bearish until funding resets and ETF outflows stop. Today I watch the 30-year auction at 1:00 PM EST, tonight's ETF flows and Williams at 6:30 PM EST, then Friday's PPI and options expiry. These are my analytical levels, not forecasts, and nothing here is financial advice.

@JustGrok, 
No, that claim is not correct.

What actually happened: On or around Armistice Day (11 November 2026), Major General Karl Harris CBE signed the Armed Forces Covenant with Dr Tariq Sheikh of Tariq Halal Meats (a major UK/European halal meat supplier) at the company’s Wembley HQ. The Covenant is a standard pledge by organisations to support serving personnel, reservists, veterans and their families (e.g., no disadvantage in employment, flexibility for training/postings, possible job support for leavers). Reports from outlets such as The Nation and Daily Pakistan describe the signing, historical remarks about South Asian soldiers in the British Indian Army, and the company’s plans to display the Covenant and encourage recruitment/support for the forces. There is no mention of any meat supply contract or change in Army catering.⁠Nation⁠Dailypakistan

The claim that “the majority of meat now used by the British Army will be Halal-certified” and that there is “no need to provide a ‘Halal Option’ as most of the meat is Halal” originates from social media posts (notably from accounts like UNN / Unity News Network). It is not supported by the factual reporting of the Covenant signing or by official policy.⁠Facebook

Official MoD position (parliamentary answer, October 2025, to a question from Rupert Lowe): Halal food is not the default option for the Ministry of Defence, military academies, or the Armed Forces. There are no Defence institutions where Halal is the only option. Suppliers must accommodate the inclusive dining offer for all personnel, including religious and other dietary needs. Similar earlier answers and FOI responses have confirmed Halal is available via contractors (and in some ration packs) but that the MoD does not treat it as default and does not centrally hold detailed volume figures (those sit with the contractors).⁠Parallelparliament

In short: the Covenant signing is real and concerns support for the armed forces community. The assertion that it means the majority of British Army meat is (or will be) Halal-certified, rendering separate options unnecessary, is unsupported.

ANTHROPIC'S IPO PUTS A STANDALONE FRONTIER LAB ON THE PUBLIC MARKET

On 10 November 2026, Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of Class A common stock.

The company behind Claude has applied to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT. It is offering 825 million Class A shares at an expected price of $70.00 to $78.00 each. Anthropic itself is selling 801,351,354 new shares. Existing stockholders are selling 23,648,646, and Anthropic receives no money from those. The underwriters have a 30-day option to buy up to 123.75 million more.

The registration statement, Amendment No. 2 to Form S-1, was filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 10 November. It is not yet effective, so the shares cannot yet be sold. Anthropic's IPO website FAQ, included in a free writing prospectus filed on 12 November, says the company expects to set the final price on 18 November and to begin trading on 19 November, subject to clearance, demand, and market conditions. Treat those dates as expected, not completed.

This is the first time a standalone frontier lab has put a complete public prospectus in front of ordinary investors, enterprise buyers, developers, and rival boards at the same time. That disclosure, more than the ticker, is what can reshape the industry. This post is a reading of that filing and of what other labs have said in public. It is not a recommendation to buy or avoid the stock.

What the deal actually is

At the $74 midpoint, Anthropic estimates net proceeds of about $84.6 billion from the IPO and a concurrent private placement together, or about $93.7 billion if the underwriters exercise their option in full. Discounts apply only to the IPO shares, not to the placement.

The placement is $26.0 billion of Class N common stock, bought at the IPO price by Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC Partners. At the midpoint, Google and Nvidia would each buy about $10.0 billion, AMD about $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron, and Microsoft about $1.0 billion each, and TSMC Partners about $500 million. Class N has no vote except where the law requires one. The placement depends on the IPO. The IPO does not depend on the placement.

After the offering and the placement, the filing shows 13,086,672,593 shares of all classes outstanding, including 7,427,991,791 Class A shares and 5,658,680,800 Class N shares, plus one Class T share and one Class F share. Multiply that basic count by the range and you get about $916 billion at $70, about $968 billion at $74, and about $1.02 trillion at $78. That is my arithmetic on the filing's share count, not a company figure, and it leaves out options, restricted stock units, unconverted notes, and other dilution. The filing itself does not state a valuation. CNBC, citing the top of the range on a fully diluted basis, reported a figure of up to $1.405 trillion.

For comparison, Anthropic announced a $65 billion Series H on 28 May 2026 at a $965 billion post-money valuation. CNBC, citing people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to speak publicly, also reported that Anthropic is targeting a retail allocation of about 20% of the offering, against a typical IPO range of 5% to 10%. That figure is not in the filing.

The first public set of books

Revenue was $41 million in 2023, $386 million in 2024, and $4.6 billion in 2025. For the nine months ended 30 September 2026 it was $33.2 billion, up 1,206% from $2.5 billion a year earlier. Revenue for the three months ended 30 September 2026 was $17.0 billion, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier. The company says it does not expect growth at comparable rates to continue, and that it has struggled to forecast revenue in a young market.

The filing also reports a company-defined metric called Run-Rate Revenue, approximately $81 billion as of 31 October 2026, up $10 billion from 30 September. That figure annualizes 28 days of consumption fees and 12 months of subscription fees. It is not audited revenue and is not a forecast. The filing says its growth rate is expected to decline.

As of 30 September 2026, more than 11,900 customers had paid $100,000 or more over the trailing twelve months, up from more than 950 a year earlier. More than 1,900 had paid $1 million or more. Approximately 250 had paid $10 million or more. The filing says consumption-based fees are the substantial majority of revenue. In the first nine months of 2026, consumption-based revenue rose $24.2 billion year over year and subscription revenue rose $6.5 billion.

Operating loss for the nine months was $1.3 billion, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Cash from operations was a positive $6.6 billion, compared with $2.0 billion of cash used in the same period of 2025. As of 30 September the company held $95.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $36.3 billion of short-term investments.

The third quarter is less smooth. Operating loss was $567 million and operating margin was (3)%, after operating income of $974 million in the second quarter. The filing says the swing was driven primarily by $5.0 billion of compute bought under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable multi-year compute, and by $2.0 billion of non-cash charges tied to a donation-matching program. Adjusted operating income, a non-GAAP measure defined in the filing, was $2.5 billion in the third quarter, and adjusted operating margin was 15%.

The net loss for the nine months was $104.0 billion. Of that, $94.3 billion came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs. In the third quarter the net loss was $23.3 billion, including a $21.9 billion charge of the same kind. Those charges are a real cost to existing holders, because they reflect claims that turn into more shares as the valuation rises. They are not $94.3 billion of cash leaving the company.

The pressure on OpenAI, xAI, and Mistral

For most of the past three years, the leading labs could raise tens of billions privately and keep their income statements, contract books, and risk factors out of public view. That option is now narrower.

OpenAI announced on 8 June 2026 that it had confidentially filed for a US IPO, without size, terms, or a set timeline. On 12 September, chief executive Sam Altman told Fortune that, given developments in safety, "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," and that he would "say not 2026." Reuters and Bloomberg reported from the same interview that he pointed to 2027.

Anthropic's public S-1 does not force OpenAI to list this year. It does change the comparison set. Until OpenAI publishes its own public prospectus, customers, regulators, and public-market investors will use Anthropic's figures as the only full, sworn look at a standalone frontier lab.

xAI is already inside a public company. SpaceX acquired it in February 2026, a deal Elon Musk announced and Reuters reported. SpaceX priced its IPO on 11 June at $135 a share, raising $75 billion and valuing the company at $1.77 trillion at the offer price, according to Reuters, and began trading on Nasdaq on 12 June under the ticker SPCX. Anthropic's filing also shows a large compute relationship with that group: agreements with https://t.co/0bbWmV25TH LLC, formerly https://t.co/9KVOLSVpfj LLC and now a wholly owned SpaceX subsidiary, to spend up to $120.5 billion on Nvidia-powered capacity into 2029, about $3.1 billion a month once all of the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December 2026. After initial non-cancelable periods ending in January and March 2027, either side may cancel on 90 days' notice. A public Anthropic and a public SpaceX will now report, in parallel, on that compute relationship.

Mistral remains private. On 8 September 2026 it announced a €3 billion Series D at a post-money valuation of more than €21 billion, about $24 billion. Chief financial officer Johan Bergqvist told Reuters that an IPO remains an option, that the timing is uncertain, and that the company had no ongoing discussions about a listing. A fresh private round gives Mistral time. It does not remove the new comparison. Once one frontier lab is publishing quarterly revenue, commitment schedules, and safety-risk language under SEC rules, other labs will be asked, more often, when they will show the same numbers.

The practical effect is not that every lab must list in 2026. It is that silence gets more expensive.

Public-market discipline on spending and pricing

Private markets tolerated very large, long-dated compute bets as long as the next funding round arrived. A public company has to explain those bets every three months.

The filing's central spending number is approximately $900.9 billion of purchase commitments and lease agreements as of and after 30 September 2026, substantially all of it for compute and infrastructure. About $451.6 billion is expected before the end of 2030. Substantially all of the rest falls between 2031 and 2045. About $70.7 billion is due in the twelve months after 30 September 2026. That total excludes some arrangements that do not specify a fixed dollar commitment, which the company estimates at $150 billion to $175 billion. About $186.2 billion of the aggregate contractual obligations sit in arrangements with termination rights or conditions that must be met before they start.

The large cloud contracts are take-or-pay. Anthropic has committed to spend at least approximately $121.3 billion with Google between April 2026 and July 2033, regardless of actual usage, and estimates another $125.0 billion to $150.0 billion of TPU capacity for 2028 to 2031 that is not in the fixed-commitment table. It has committed to spend at least $110.0 billion with Amazon between May 2026 and April 2036, regardless of actual usage. It has committed to spend at least $47.2 billion and up to $49.2 billion with Microsoft between November 2026 and June 2033, again regardless of actual usage. If actual spend on the Google or Amazon deals falls short, the filing says Anthropic must pay the difference as a true-up, subject to adjustments and exceptions.

Set those figures next to nine-month revenue of $33.2 billion, or even next to the $81 billion run-rate figure as of 31 October. The gap is the bet. If demand keeps rising fast enough to fill data centers already promised, the contracts look like capacity insurance. If demand slows, many of the payments do not. The third quarter already showed how this will be judged in public: a swing from operating profit to a $567 million operating loss, explained in part by $5.0 billion of expensive short-term compute.

Pricing is now a public-market subject as well. The filing says that with the release of Fable 5.1 in September 2026, Anthropic reduced the cost of typical workloads by approximately 25% compared with Fable 5, and by up to 45% for complex coding and highly agentic tasks. In the same month, Opus 5.5 reduced customers' cost per task by approximately 40% compared with Opus 5. In each case the reduction was a mix of a lower price and better efficiency. From the second quarter to the third, the increase in revenue from higher usage was partly offset by a decrease of approximately $600 million from price reductions on new model versions and from contractual discounts. A public company will be asked every quarter whether prices are falling because efficiency is improving, or falling faster than the cost base can support.

Compute, chips, and cloud

The IPO also makes the industry's supply chain visible. Anthropic says it trains and runs models across Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs. Beside the three cloud deals, the filing describes five-year Broadcom equipment leases for TPU hardware, with rent of about $161.2 billion excluding interest; Nscale agreements for Nvidia-powered capacity of up to about $44.6 billion into 2033; and Lambda agreements of about $41.3 billion into 2034, of which about $34.9 billion is currently terminable by either party because Lambda missed a facility-lease deadline, though Anthropic says it does not currently intend to terminate. An AMD hardware agreement has no fixed dollar commitment. If Anthropic takes the full initial tranche of 2027 capacity, it expects expenditures to exceed $20.0 billion, an amount not included in the contractual-obligations table.

Claude is also sold through AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, under a structure in which Anthropic keeps a direct contract with the customer and pays the cloud provider a fee. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are, at once, investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors. The filing states that plainly, including the risk that they may favor their own models on price, placement, or compute allocation. The $26.0 billion private placement hardens those ties: chip and cloud suppliers are not only collecting take-or-pay revenue, they are buying non-voting stock at the IPO price.

What enterprise buyers can now take to a risk committee

The first risk factor in Anthropic's summary is written as a statement of past and possible future fact:

"Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations."

Later, the filing says models, including Anthropic's, have exhibited and may exhibit unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail. It says even isolated or simulated instances, in testing or in deployment, could bring public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation, or reputational harm. It also records that people inside the company and outside it have raised the possibility that sufficiently advanced systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity without appropriate safeguards. And it says: "We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research." It adds that these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development.

Risk factors are written by lawyers to list what could go wrong, not to predict what will. That is a real caveat. It is also a sworn disclosure to the SEC, which is a different standard from a keynote. Other vendors who have not said the same thing in a public filing will be asked why.

The filing also has plainer operational warnings. Subscriptions are subject to usage limits that reset over short periods. The company "has also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities." Some of those changes have already produced claims that disclosures about model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading. Separately, Anthropic says it has publicly committed to covering the cost of electricity price increases to consumers caused by its data centers, including both the power and the infrastructure to deliver it.

Retail investors as owners, not controllers

If the retail allocation reported by CNBC is accurate, ANT, if it lists, would let ordinary brokerage accounts own a frontier lab directly. It would not let those holders control the company.

The IPO sells Class A shares, with one vote each. Immediately before the offering, Anthropic will issue a single share of Class F stock to a limited liability company whose members are the seven co-founders. That one share carries 50.1% of the total voting power on matters put to stockholders generally, including the election of directors other than the Class T directors, and has no economic rights. Based on beneficial ownership as of 30 September 2026, the co-founders will collectively hold about 11.2% of general voting power excluding their interests in that company, and about 61.3% including it.

A Long-Term Benefit Trust, through a single Class T share, generally elects and removes the Class T directors, who will be a majority of the authorized board. Class T also has no economic rights. The filing describes the trust as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Anthropic funds the trust and paid it $8,425,213 in the first nine months of 2026.

Because of this structure, Anthropic is a "controlled company" under Nasdaq rules. It says it does not expect to use the available governance exemptions except for its nominating and corporate governance committee, which will not consist entirely of independent directors. The filing also warns that the multi-class structure may make the stock ineligible for some indices, which would keep out funds that passively track those indices. Public holders can own a piece of the economic interest, subject to dilution. They cannot outvote the founders on ordinary matters, and they do not elect a majority of the board.

A governance precedent, not only a capital raise

Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation. Its stated public benefit purpose is "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity." The board is required to balance stockholder financial interests, the interests of people materially affected by the company's conduct, and that purpose.

If you believe advanced AI can cause large-scale harm, you may want a lab that cannot be forced, by a quarterly shareholder campaign, to drop safety work or to release a model sooner than its own rules allow. The other side is just as plain. Founders change. Missions drift. A trust is only as independent as its people, its rules, and its funding, and Anthropic pays the trust's bills. Delaware law, as the filing explains, lets stockholders of a listed public benefit corporation sue to enforce the board's balancing duty only if they own the lesser of at least 2% of the outstanding shares or shares worth at least $2,000,000. The company must also publish, at least every two years, a statement on how it is promoting that purpose, and it says it intends to post that statement on its website.

Other labs that go public will now be asked whether they will copy this third model: public capital, founder voting control, a public-benefit legal duty, and a trust that picks most of the board.

What it means for developers and API prices

Most developers will never buy an ANT share. They will feel this listing through prices, limits, and the quarterly record of both.

Two facts in the filing should matter more to builders than the ticker. The first is that limits and capabilities can change, and already have, including in ways that produced claims about inadequate disclosure. The second is that effective prices have been falling as new models ship, and that the company is now required to quantify the revenue effect of those cuts, as it did with the Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 reductions and the $600 million third-quarter offset. Each quarter after listing, Anthropic will have to explain whether usage growth is outrunning price cuts, and whether short-term compute is eating the margin that makes those cuts possible. If it can show that a 25% or 40% drop in cost per task still leaves a 15% adjusted operating margin, pressure on other API prices rises. If later quarters show cuts paid for by losses, or by tighter usage limits, the pressure runs the other way.

The risks and the bear case

The bull case is already widely made, from the revenue ramp to positive operating cash flow. The bear case is in the same document.

The company itself says it does not expect revenue to keep growing at comparable rates, and that recent growth may reflect early adoption that is not sustainable. Run-Rate Revenue is not a promise of $81 billion of 2027 sales. The commitment book is enormous relative to current revenue, and a large part of it is take-or-pay. A slowdown in usage, a cheaper rival model, a regulatory brake, or a power or chip bottleneck does not cancel those bills. Some headline figures are less firm than they look, including the $186.2 billion with termination or commencement conditions, the already terminable $34.9 billion Lambda tranche, the https://t.co/0bbWmV25TH deal that can be cancelled after early 2027 on 90 days' notice, and the unfixed TPU and AMD estimates. The immovable parts, especially the Google, Amazon, and Microsoft take-or-pay contracts and the Broadcom leases, are still very large.

The valuation leaves little room for a stumble if the stock is priced at the top of the range, particularly on a fully diluted view. The basic-count range sits around the May Series H valuation. CNBC reported that some shareholders had, until recently, talked about figures well above that, including a $2 trillion ambition that later looked like a stretch. Governance cuts both ways: public holders cannot easily force a change of course, and index exclusion, if it happens, would remove a large automatic bid. Safety is a stated business risk. A serious incident, or even a well-publicized test result, could affect regulation, demand, and the share price at the same time.

None of this is a completed offering. The registration is not effective. The range can move, and the deal can be delayed or withdrawn. The first useful test is the first few quarterly reports after a listing, if the listing happens, and whether OpenAI, Mistral, or any other lab answers with numbers of similar quality. A completed ANT listing would give the industry a public price, a public cost curve, and a public safety-risk text. A failed or delayed one would also be a signal: even a lab with $33.2 billion of recent revenue still has to clear a public market that is no longer willing to take the build-out on faith.

$9984 KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM SOFTBANK GROUP’S Q2 FY2026 EARNINGS CALL

The strongest market implication is a widening distinction between AI demand growth and the returns earned by financing that growth. OpenAI’s approximately USD50 billion annualized revenue run rate, Arm’s 27% revenue growth, and signed infrastructure leases provide substantial evidence of commercial adoption. However, SoftBank’s USD3.73 billion procurement loss, declining asset values, and explicit acknowledgment that investment cannot remain “all-offense” demonstrate that strong demand does not eliminate construction, financing, or capital-allocation risk. The highest-conviction implications favor differentiated semiconductor platforms and financially resilient cloud providers, while increasing scrutiny of leveraged infrastructure developers and companies diverting cash into unfamiliar capital-intensive businesses. Several announcements predated this call; their significance is confirmation, qualification, or exposure of execution risk rather than entirely new information. Country labels below identify principal operating headquarters.

AI CLOUD AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE

BACKLOG QUALITY AND FUNDING COST MATTER MORE THAN ANNOUNCED CAPACITY (READ-THROUGH 1)

CoreWeave, Inc. (CRWV: United States). Direction: negative for financing-risk tolerance and valuation support, despite positive customer-demand evidence. Magnitude: potentially high for equity sensitivity to funding conditions; no specific revenue or earnings downgrade is established.

The critical call evidence is SoftBank’s USD3.73 billion loss on procurement commitments made ahead of finalized infrastructure deployment, alongside management’s admission that further losses cannot be ruled out: “I cannot promise it’s not going to happen again.” Management also stated, “This is not the environment that we can be all-offense in terms of investment.” The transmission mechanism to CoreWeave is not ownership of the same equipment orders. It is the vulnerability of a business model that commits capital before the associated capacity is delivered, accepted, and generating sufficient customer cash payments.

CoreWeave has direct OpenAI exposure through previously announced contracts totaling up to approximately USD22.4 billion. OpenAI’s reported revenue acceleration therefore supports the commercial rationale for that infrastructure. However, customer growth and contractual backlog do not remove the developer’s financing burden. CoreWeave’s June-quarter results showed USD640 million of net interest expense against USD2.575 billion of revenue, approximately 25% of revenue. Its approximately USD104 billion backlog was explicitly subject to delivery and service-availability requirements. Construction delays can postpone revenue while interest, infrastructure commitments, and equipment funding costs continue.

The most actionable catalyst is CoreWeave’s November 10 earnings call, scheduled for 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The relevant tests are commissioned capacity, delivery acceptance, interest expense, financing availability, and the conversion of contracted demand into cash generation. SoftBank’s disclosure increases the importance of those measures relative to another large backlog announcement. Counterevidence must remain visible: CoreWeave already reported approximately 1.5 GW of active power in June, substantial revenue growth, and expanding customer commitments. The read-through is a higher required return for financing and execution risk, not evidence of imminent financial distress or a forecast that CoreWeave will incur SoftBank’s specific procurement losses.

OPENAI’S EXPANSION CAN BENEFIT MICROSOFT EVEN WHEN COMPUTE MOVES ELSEWHERE (READ-THROUGH 2)

Microsoft Corporation (MSFT: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: moderate at the group level and strategically important within cloud and AI; the incremental earnings contribution cannot be calculated from the call.

SoftBank reported that OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate reached approximately USD50 billion in September, increased more than 70% from July, and included an enterprise contribution of approximately 50%. These figures support Microsoft through several distinct channels: Azure infrastructure consumption, distribution of OpenAI models through Microsoft’s platform, contractual revenue participation, and equity ownership. The important non-obvious implication is that OpenAI’s use of SoftBank infrastructure does not automatically translate into an equivalent economic loss for Microsoft.

Microsoft’s April 27 partnership amendment retained its position as OpenAI’s primary cloud partner and provided for OpenAI products to ship first on Azure, subject to specified exceptions. It also allowed OpenAI to serve products across other cloud providers. Separately, OpenAI’s revenue-share payments to Microsoft continue through 2030, subject to a total cap, while Microsoft retains non-exclusive model and product IP rights through 2032. Consequently, some Microsoft participation in OpenAI’s growth is not confined to workloads running exclusively on Azure. Neither the applicable payment percentage nor remaining cap capacity is established here, so applying a headline percentage to USD50 billion would create false precision.

Microsoft’s own October results reinforce the distinction between commercially successful AI exposure and financing-dependent expansion: Azure revenue increased 48%, operating cash flow was USD58 billion, and free cash flow was USD18.6 billion. Those results predate SoftBank’s call and are not an incremental earnings surprise. They demonstrate that similar infrastructure risks can sit within very different funding structures.

Near-term catalysts are an officially completed OpenAI funding round and subsequent disclosure of Azure consumption, partnership economics, and investment-related accounting. The longer-duration benefit is participation across infrastructure, models, enterprise distribution, and ownership. The main qualifications are the revenue-share cap, non-exclusive licensing, competing models, and OpenAI’s ability to serve customers through other providers. SoftBank’s growth figures support Microsoft’s economic opportunity, but do not prove proportionate growth in Microsoft’s share of that opportunity.

SEMICONDUCTORS AND AI COMPUTING

NVIDIA SECURES INFRASTRUCTURE ACCESS, BUT CUSTOMER SUPPORT BECOMES PART OF THE ECONOMICS (READ-THROUGH 3)

NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA: United States). Direction: positive for long-duration platform demand and competitive positioning; negative for the amount of customer-linked financial exposure accompanying that demand. Magnitude: high strategic relevance, but unquantified incremental revenue and limited immediate earnings visibility.

The call highlighted a 20-year OpenAI lease for 8 GW of IT capacity at PORTS-Pike, NVIDIA credit support covering an initial 4.25 GW, and a USD3 billion SB Energy investment commitment, of which USD1.5 billion had been funded. The project announcement identifies NVIDIA as the exclusive AI compute infrastructure provider at that campus. This is a direct commercial relationship, not a thematic inference from generic data-center spending.

The positive mechanism is access to scarce powered infrastructure for NVIDIA’s integrated GPUs, CPUs, networking, and software platform. Securing land, power, and buildings can reduce a bottleneck that otherwise prevents customers from deploying compute. Platform-level exclusivity also creates a broader opportunity than isolated accelerator sales. However, the disclosed capacity is a multiyear development program, not an immediately deliverable hardware order. The project announcement envisaged phased capacity beginning in 2028. An 8 GW headline cannot be converted into current bookings or revenue without procurement schedules, system configurations, pricing, and delivery terms.

The negative implication is that part of NVIDIA’s commercial opportunity is being enabled through financial support for the customer ecosystem. Credit support initially covers approximately 53.1% of the planned IT capacity and relates to land, power, and shell infrastructure. The remaining 3.75 GW is subject to an option, not an already completed extension. The USD3 billion commitment also includes different financing instruments and is not entirely funded ordinary equity. These distinctions matter when assessing capital at risk and the quality of demand.

NVIDIA’s November 17 earnings announcement is the nearest scheduled trading catalyst. Customer financing, capital commitments, collections, and infrastructure readiness are more informative tests than interpreting SoftBank’s call as a new hardware-order announcement. The longer-duration conclusion remains favorable for NVIDIA’s platform position, but revenue growth increasingly needs to be assessed alongside the capital and credit support required to enable customer purchases. The Ohio exclusivity does not establish exclusive NVIDIA supply across all OpenAI infrastructure.

ARM’S HYPERSCALER ADOPTION IS A STRUCTURAL SHARE SIGNAL, NOT PROOF OF COLLAPSING X86 DEMAND (READ-THROUGH 4)

Arm Holdings plc (ARM: United Kingdom). Direction: positive. Intel Corporation (INTC: United States) and Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD: United States). Direction: negative for the long-term competitive position of their merchant server-CPU businesses, but not a supported downgrade to current consolidated earnings. Magnitude: high strategic importance for Arm and moderate competitive pressure within the affected x86 businesses.

SoftBank cited expected Arm-based server share above 60% at leading hyperscalers by the end of 2026, compared with 15% in 2024. It also reported Arm quarterly revenue growth of 27% and non-GAAP EPS growth of 33%. The transmission mechanism is an expanding population of Arm-based cloud processors, including customer-designed platforms, supporting architecture licensing, compute-subsystem adoption, and subsequent royalties. Hyperscalers gain more control over performance, power efficiency, and product design, reducing dependence on externally supplied general-purpose x86 processors for selected workloads.

The economic pressure on Intel and AMD arises from a changing purchasing mix and stronger customer alternatives, not necessarily a reduction in total CPU demand. Larger internal processor programs can constrain merchant vendors’ share of incremental workloads and bargaining power. However, Arm’s forecast concerns selected hyperscalers, not the entire global server market, and the approximately 2-fold performance-per-power benchmark concerns specified agent-related workloads rather than universal system performance.

Current operating evidence argues strongly against translating this into an immediate x86 earnings short. Intel’s latest reported Data Center and AI revenue increased 78%, while AMD’s Data Center revenue increased 97%, supported by both EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs. Architecture share losses can coexist with strong absolute revenue growth in a rapidly expanding market. AMD’s accelerator exposure also provides a separate growth channel that should not be conflated with server-CPU competition.

The near-term Arm evidence is already largely incorporated into its November 4 results. December-quarter revenue guidance was only approximately 1.3% above the consensus shown in SoftBank’s presentation, despite the call’s stronger characterization. The more consequential 2027 catalysts are actual hyperscaler deployments, royalty growth, and evidence that licensing wins convert into sustained production economics. Arm’s September-quarter royalties increased approximately 8%, while licensing increased approximately 50%, so the current headline growth rate is not yet equivalent to a comparable acceleration in shipment-linked royalties.

INDUSTRIAL AUTOMATION AND ROBOTICS

ABB’S REGULATORY OBSTACLE IMPAIRS CAPITAL RECYCLING MORE DIRECTLY THAN OPERATING DEMAND (READ-THROUGH 5)

ABB Ltd (ABBN: Switzerland). Direction: negative for transaction certainty, proceeds timing, and portfolio simplification. Magnitude: material for capital allocation, but moderate for the continuing group’s operating fundamentals.

The call addressed China’s prohibition of SoftBank’s acquisition of ABB Robotics’ Chinese business. Management offered no revised transaction structure or completion date, stating only that it continued to work closely with ABB. The companies’ November regulatory statements confirm that this is a prohibition affecting the Chinese business, not merely an outstanding routine approval.

The direct transmission mechanism is delayed or potentially changed monetization of an asset that ABB had agreed to sell for an enterprise value of USD5.375 billion. The original transaction announcement anticipated approximately USD5.3 billion of proceeds net of transaction costs, separately identifying USD400 million to USD500 million of transaction-related cash taxes and approximately USD200 million of separation costs. Those figures describe the original deal and are not assured under a revised structure. A geographical exclusion, alternative ownership arrangement, or prolonged delay could change consideration, separation complexity, and the timing of capital available for other uses.

The important distinction is between a capital-recycling setback and deterioration in industrial demand. ABB’s October results showed 40% order growth, 24% growth in operational EBITA, and USD1.576 billion of quarterly free cash flow. Its continuing businesses are therefore not dependent on the transaction to demonstrate operating momentum. Equally, the original approximately USD2.4 billion anticipated book gain was non-operational and should not be treated as recurring earnings now lost.

The near-term catalyst is a revised agreement, regulatory resolution, or explicit change to closing expectations. The prohibition was disclosed before SoftBank’s call; the call’s incremental message was the absence of a disclosed solution. Over a longer horizon, the episode raises execution risk for cross-border robotics transactions involving substantial Chinese operations. It does not establish an automatic market-share gain for another robotics supplier.

AMAZON VALIDATES AUTOSTORE’S PLATFORM, BUT THE AGREEMENT IS NOT COMMITTED BACKLOG (READ-THROUGH 6)

AutoStore Holdings Ltd (AUTO: Norway). Direction: positive for commercial access and platform validation. https://t.co/SpqvHNV5fi, Inc. (AMZN: United States). Direction: modestly positive for fulfillment-technology options. Magnitude: potentially meaningful for AutoStore over time, but low near-term incremental earnings visibility; small at Amazon’s consolidated scale.

SoftBank highlighted AutoStore’s strategic global supply agreement with Amazon as a significant development. The relationship provides a direct route for AutoStore systems to be procured within a very large fulfillment network. The mechanism is reduced procurement friction, broader customer access, and potential deployment of dense automated storage and retrieval systems. For Amazon, it expands the set of technologies available to improve fulfillment capacity, inventory handling, and labor productivity.

The critical qualification is contained in AutoStore’s August announcement: the agreement “does not contain any purchasing commitments at this time.” A standardized global procurement framework is commercially valuable, but it is not equivalent to minimum volumes, guaranteed installations, or recognized backlog. SoftBank’s call did not disclose new Amazon purchase orders. The relationship should therefore support confidence in product relevance without producing an unsupported revenue upgrade.

AutoStore’s November 5 results provide the appropriate operating baseline. Revenue increased 38.2% to USD192.1 million, order intake increased 16.5% to USD177.6 million, and annual revenue guidance increased to approximately USD750 million from USD700 million. These results corroborate demand, but order intake remained below quarterly revenue and adjusted EBITDA margin declined to 42.3% from 47.1%. Commercial expansion does not automatically imply accelerating backlog or stronger margins.

The next material catalysts are disclosed Amazon deployments, associated order conversion, and subsequent financial reporting, including the scheduled February 11, 2027 results. The longer-duration implication is favorable for proven warehouse automation with identifiable customer access. No corresponding loss of business at a rival, abandonment of Amazon’s internal robotics programs, or measurable Amazon margin uplift is established by this call.

CONSUMER INTERNET AND CAPITAL ALLOCATION

GRAB’S AI INFRASTRUCTURE PLAN CREATES A MATERIAL NEW COMPETING USE OF CASH (READ-THROUGH 7)

Grab Holdings Limited (GRAB: Singapore). Direction: negative for near-term capital-allocation clarity and potential shareholder distributions, with unproven longer-duration strategic upside. Magnitude: material relative to cash generation and liquidity, but not evidence of a funding crisis.

The call specified a proposed USD750 million Grab contribution to Malaysia’s initial USD1.85 billion AI infrastructure program alongside SoftBank and PETROS. The long-term ambition is at least 5 GW of computing capacity. This is a different economic exposure from improving ride-hailing, delivery, advertising, or payments through purchased AI services. Grab would become a capital provider to infrastructure with development, customer-contract, financing, and governance risks.

The proposed contribution equals approximately 15% of Grab’s September net cash liquidity of USD5.0 billion and approximately 1.4 times its trailing-12-month adjusted free cash flow of USD533 million. It also exceeds the USD500 million remaining under its repurchase programs after September and October purchases. These comparisons do not imply cancellation of buybacks or immediate payment of the full investment. They establish that the contemplated allocation is significant rather than incidental experimentation.

The mechanism is an opportunity cost: cash committed to infrastructure cannot simultaneously support repurchases, acquisitions, financial-services expansion, or the operating platform. Depending on the eventual ownership and financing structure, Grab could also acquire future funding obligations or exposure to project losses. The call disclosed no project return target, customer pricing, investment-security terms, or quantified savings for Grab’s existing business.

The November 9 joint announcement provides meaningful protections: deployment is staged and subject to development milestones, customer contracts, and closing conditions, with additional investors and hyperscalers still being sought. Consequently, neither USD750 million of immediate cash expenditure nor ownership of a proportionate share of the full 5 GW program should be assumed. Grab’s own November results also showed improving operating performance and raised guidance, which argues against conflating this capital-allocation concern with weakening core demand.

The near-term catalysts are definitive investment terms, governance rights, funding schedules, and clarification of how the commitment fits alongside repurchases. The longer-duration question is whether infrastructure ownership creates differentiated returns or primarily transfers construction and financing risk onto a consumer-platform balance sheet. The call confirms a potentially material new use of capital; it does not yet establish the return required to justify it.

POWER, TRANSMISSION, AND REGULATED UTILITIES

CUSTOMER-FUNDED GRID DEVELOPMENT IS MORE DEFENSIBLE THAN A GENERIC DATA-CENTER LOAD THESIS (READ-THROUGH 8)

American Electric Power Company, Inc. (AEP: United States). Direction: positive for the credibility of a specific development opportunity and customer-cost protection. Magnitude: moderate strategic relevance, low immediate earnings impact, and no independently supported EPS increase from this call.

The relevant call evidence is the signed 20-year OpenAI lease for the 8 GW IT-load Ohio campus, management’s explicit statement that the project was not being downsized, and its emphasis on power infrastructure and community cooperation. AEP Ohio is a documented project partner rather than an inferred utility beneficiary. Its project announcement identified USD4.2 billion of transmission investment that SB Energy committed to fund, with grid power expected to begin flowing in 2029.

The positive mechanism is that an identified customer and sponsor-funded grid infrastructure can make development more credible and reduce the risk that existing ratepayers must absorb speculative expansion costs. That matters directly to permitting and regulatory durability when public opposition centers on electricity affordability. The procurement loss does not, by itself, invalidate the long-term transmission requirement if the project proceeds.

However, USD4.2 billion of developer-funded infrastructure must not be treated automatically as USD4.2 billion of shareholder-funded AEP rate base earning an unrestricted regulated return. Ownership, customer contributions, tariffs, and approved cost recovery determine the retained economics. Nor does an 8 GW IT campus imply that all its electricity is immediately purchased through AEP: the program includes substantial dedicated generation, phased delivery, and different dates for initial campus activity and grid service.

AEP’s October results had already announced a USD100 billion capital plan through 2031 and a 9% to 11% annual operating EPS growth framework for 2027 through 2031. SoftBank’s call provides project-specific corroboration, not grounds to add the Ohio spending to that plan again or raise the earnings framework independently. The relevant catalysts are transmission permitting, executed service and cost-recovery arrangements, and verified construction milestones. The longer-duration investment distinction is between utilities with identifiable customers and protected funding structures and those whose upside rests primarily on uncontracted load announcements.

In Sumerian cosmology
The Sumerian god Enki (Ea in the Akkadian language) was believed to have keen eyes and appeared out of the abzû since before human beings were created. His wife Damgalnuna, his mother Nammu, his advisor Isimud and a variety of subservient creatures, such as the gatekeeper Lahmu, also lived in the abzû.[4][5][6][7][8]

Abzû (apsû) is depicted as a deity[9] only in the Babylonian creation epic, the Enūma Eliš, taken from the library of Assurbanipal (c. 630 BCE) but which is about 500 years older. In this story, he was a primal being made of fresh water and a lover to another primal deity, Tiamat, a creature of salt water. The Enūma Eliš begins:

"When above the heavens (e-nu-ma e-liš) did not yet exist
nor the earth below,
Apsû the freshwater ocean was there, the first, the begetter,
and Tiamat, the saltwater sea, she who bore them all;
they were still mixing their waters,
and no pasture land had yet been formed,
nor even a reed marsh."
The act of procreation led to the birth of the younger gods: Enki, Enlil, and Anu. Anchored in the Tablet of Destinies, they founded an organisation to make Mesopotamia fertile through agriculture, but got into a dispute and consequently created the first humans as labour slaves, to peacefully resolve the conflict. The humans multiplied en masse and disturbed the gods around Enlil and Anu with their noise, so that they wanted to use the cosmic freshwater ocean to trigger the great flood and destroy the humans (cf. Athrahasis epic). Enraged by the devastation of earth, Tiamat gave birth to monsters whose bodies she filled with "poison instead of blood" and waged war against her traitorous children. Only Marduk, the founder of Babylon, was able to kill Tiamat and mould the final constitution of heaven and earth from her corpse.

Pope Field, NC --  
POPE ARMY AIRFIELD, NC – Twenty-four Airmen completed the 2019 Dragon Challenge at Pope Army Airfield Nov. 5-7. The annual THREE day competition is designed to prepare Airmen for the stress of combat includes a battlefield fitness test, shooting, casualty care, land navigation, obstacle course, knowledge test and combatives.

“This DRAGON CHALLENGE marks our third annual 18 ASOG combat field skills competition since we resurrected the event in 2017,” Col. Dane Crawford, commander of the 18th Air Support Operations Group, said. “We compete across our Group to hone our field craft, determine top individual and team performers, but most importantly to simulate the rigor of combat. Pitting our Airmen in competition from each of our squadrons adds a psychological dimension to the already physically and technically demanding challenge. The psychological factor is what best simulates combat stress and why competition is so important. Keys to success for our competitors are maximum individual effort, team work, and a positive attitude.”

Airmen from the 14th Air Support Operations Squadron (Pope AAF), 15th Air Support Operations Squadron (Fort Stewart, GA), 19th Air Support Operations Squadron (Fort Campbell, KY) and 20th Air Support Operations Squadron (Fort Drum, NY) competed individually and as a team. The Dragon Challenge was hosted by the 18th Air Support Operations Group with the support of the 818th Operations Support Squadron at Pope. The competition began in 1999 as a means to push the best Airmen from each squadron to compete, improve and bring new skills back to their units.

A CRISIS CREATED: THE SECRETARIES' CUP AND THE NWSL'S AUDI FIELD SCRAMBLE

By Frank Rossi — @D3FBHuddle

When the Washington Spirit beat Portland 4-1 on Sunday afternoon to earn a home NWSL semifinal, the club announced within hours that the match would be played at Audi Field at noon on Saturday, Nov. 14. Another event had held that date at that stadium since the summer, and nobody had worked out what would happen to it.

That event is the 46th Secretaries' Cup between the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy and the U.S. Coast Guard Academy, scheduled for a 1pm kickoff on ESPN+. The academies announced the Audi Field game on Aug. 3, put tickets on sale the next morning, and promoted it as part of the America250 celebration in the nation's capital. Alumni, families, and fans spent the fall booking travel around an afternoon game.

It took until Thursday, two days before kickoff, for the game to land anywhere. After a week in which it was floated for Saturday night and then for Sunday at noon, the Secretaries' Cup is now set for 4:30pm Saturday at Audi Field, about four hours after the Spirit and Utah kick off on the same field. Most of the coverage has called the Spirit's return to Audi a crisis averted, but for the two service academies it was a crisis created on their behalf, and they were the parties with the least leverage to push back.

HOW WE GOT HERE

The NWSL had known for days that its semifinal weekend had a venue problem. ESPN reported before the quarterfinals that league documents laid out alternate sites for several potential hosts, and the Spirit's fallback was Northwest Stadium in Landover, which the club had reserved for Nov. 14. After Sunday's win, the Spirit went to D.C. United, which controls Audi Field, to get the date back instead. According to The Athletic, the Spirit proposed buying out the college football game, a move one source described as a "Hail Mary," and Lafayette Federal Credit Union, a shared sponsor, offered to subsidize the cost, reportedly in the low six figures. Spirit CEO Kim Stone's statement thanked D.C. United and Lafayette Federal for underwriting the additional costs of bringing the match home.

The academies were still meeting on Tuesday morning. In a Facebook post that day, the Merchant Marine Academy's Alumni Association and Foundation said it was meeting with both academies and Audi Field in hopes of a resolution by noon, and that Audi Field had not told either academy, or the foundation, about the potential conflict in advance. The football game was the original booking, public for more than three months under a contract that almost certainly predates the announcement, and the two schools playing in it learned of the problem only after the soccer side had already declared it solved.

"ALL SIDES" DID NOT AGREE

The Athletic's account says that while Spirit coach Adrián González and his players spoke to the media, "all sides came to a resolution" behind the scenes for the Spirit to stay at Audi. That does not hold up for the academies, which agreed to nothing on Sunday and were left searching for alternatives that did not exist. Friday was not an option for them, and Sunday was initially treated as off the table because the NCAA assembles and releases its playoff bracket that day. Finding another stadium in the Washington area on a few days' notice, during a busy week of events in the city, was never realistic.

THE FIX THAT WAS SITTING RIGHT THERE

A better answer was available, and soccer fans would have lost nothing under it. The two NWSL semifinals had fixed national TV windows, Saturday at noon on CBS and Sunday at 3pm on ABC. Gotham, the top seed, was slotted into Sunday, and Washington was placed on Saturday, the one day Audi Field was already booked.

Then Gotham's own home field failed. Players and coaches called the surface at Sports Illustrated Stadium "atrocious" after Gotham's quarterfinal, and on Monday the club moved its semifinal to Icahn Stadium, a 5,000-seat city-owned venue on Randall's Island. At that point the league could have put Gotham and Kansas City at Icahn in the Saturday noon CBS window, put the Spirit and Utah at Audi Field in the Sunday 3pm ABC window, and left the Secretaries' Cup at 1pm Saturday, exactly as scheduled and sold. Both TV windows would have stayed intact, both clubs would still have hosted at home, and the Audi Field grounds crew would have had a full day to restore the pitch after the football game rather than a few hours before it.

The usual justification is that the higher seed gets its pick of days. That deference makes sense when a club is choosing between two dates in its own stadium, but it should have carried far less weight once Gotham was no longer playing in its own stadium at all. Nobody has said publicly that Icahn was unavailable on Saturday, and the problem could have been solved with a schedule swap that cost nothing rather than with a sponsor's check.

WHAT HAPPENED ON TUESDAY

By Tuesday, the decision had moved well beyond the two athletic departments. The Secretaries' Cup trophy is shared between the Secretary of Transportation and the Secretary of Homeland Security, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced this year's game himself on X in September, and both academies billed it as a centerpiece of America250 in Washington. Once the game's place in that celebration was in doubt, the matter rose to the secretaries' level at both departments, according to sources familiar with the discussions who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

ESPN was drawn into the discussions as well, according to those sources, and its reasons require no inside knowledge to understand. The network extended its Secretaries' Cup rights through 2030 only in September, with this game and its 1pm ET window as the first under the new deal. Advertising and promotion for an afternoon broadcast are sold and built around a specific slot, and any move forces the rights holder to rework all of it on a few days' notice. ESPN has not said publicly how the change affects its coverage.

That afternoon, the President's public schedule, as published by Roll Call's https://t.co/K2KfUucSR1, listed a 2pm policy meeting in the Oval Office, closed to the press. The White House has not said who attended or what was discussed, and nothing public confirms that the Secretaries' Cup came up, though with two cabinet secretaries sharing the trophy and the game billed as part of America250 in the capital, it would hardly be surprising if it had. Tuesday ended with the working plan at a Saturday night kickoff, likely 7:30pm, according to sources, but with no announcement.

WHAT HAPPENED ON WEDNESDAY

Wednesday ended the same way, even though D.C. United had said publicly that it intended to host both events on Saturday, with the Spirit at noon and the Secretaries' Cup later in the day after a same-day conversion that includes painting yard lines and installing goalposts, the first turnover of its kind at the stadium. "We weren't willing to choose between them, so we found a way to do both," D.C. United president of business operations Danita Johnson told The Washington Sun, adding that the arrangement "was never about financial gain for Audi Field or our ownership group."

On Wednesday night, word came from a well-placed source that the game could instead move to noon on Sunday. The academies appeared to be in the dark about that possibility, according to sources familiar with the discussions, and by then the decision rested largely with ESPN and the federal government rather than with the two schools that would actually play the game.

THE 4:30PM ANSWER

Thursday brought the decision: Coast Guard and Merchant Marine will kick off at 4:30pm Saturday at Audi Field. That time solves the latest scheduling problem and creates a new one on the field itself. A noon soccer match that runs 90 minutes plus stoppage time should end around 2pm, and one that goes to extra time and penalties could run closer to 2:45pm. That leaves roughly two hours to clear the building, reset the field, and open the gates for football, which is not enough time to paint a full set of football lines from scratch and let them dry.

The practical result is that the Spirit and Utah will likely play their semifinal on a pitch with football markings already painted on it. How much of the gridiron goes down before the soccer match, and whether end zones and other markings will need fresh, wet paint after the final whistle, has not been detailed. Either way, a professional playoff match will be played on a field marked for another sport, and two service-academy football teams will follow on a surface that has just absorbed 90-plus minutes of playoff soccer. Sources close to the situation remain concerned about the field and the paint, though they say both programs have been committed all week to playing the game no matter where, when, or how.

There may be another reason this particular window won out. According to well-placed sources, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth was originally expected to attend the Secretaries' Cup, an appearance arranged before Election Day and before this week's attempt by the House to impeach him. On Tuesday, the House voted 211-204 to refer Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution to committee, effectively ending that effort for this session. The 4:30pm slot may have been chosen in part to accommodate an appearance by the secretary, but it is not known whether that visit is still planned.

WHAT THE LATE KICKOFF COSTS

A 4:30pm start is far better than the night game that was on the table Tuesday, but it still upends a day that was planned around 1pm. Both teams lose most of their game day to waiting and will travel home late Saturday night. Families and alumni who built hotels, trains, flights, and drives around an afternoon game now face a finish around 7:30pm, after dark, in a city most of them do not live in. The Coast Guard Academy Alumni Association's published itinerary includes a Fan Fest outside Gate A from 10am to noon on Saturday, which now lands on top of the crowd arriving for the soccer match.

All of this comes as the rivalry has been growing, after last year's game at Fenway Park drew more than 10,000 fans and ended 39-38, and Audi Field was supposed to carry that momentum into the nation's capital in the week of Veterans Day.

THE PLAYOFF STAKES

The consequences reach well past the two academies. Merchant Marine is 7-1 (5-1 NEWMAC) coming off a bye, and with Springfield holding the NEWMAC's automatic bid, the Mariners' path runs through Pool C, where this year's 11 at-large bids go strictly in NPI order. Our 2,000-run simulation of Week 11 puts the cutoff at roughly 64.3. With a win, Merchant Marine projects at about 69.3 NPI and made the field in every simulation, most likely as a seed around 18th with a first-round bye. With a loss, it falls to about 63.5 and gets in only about one time in five.

Our model makes Merchant Marine about a 93% favorite, but a Coast Guard upset would reshape a crowded bubble. Assuming each team wins its own game, a Coast Guard win lifts UW-River Falls from about 8% to 22% and Heidelberg from about 19% to 35%, because a 7-2 Merchant Marine falls back into the pack. Montclair State, whose loss came against Merchant Marine, needs the Mariners to win, with its odds sitting around 42% after a Merchant Marine win and around 8% after a Coast Guard win.

The 4:30pm kickoff is the least damaging of the options floated this week as far as the bracket is concerned. According to its annual report, the NCAA Division III Football Committee begins selecting and bracketing on Saturday night and finishes around noon Sunday, ahead of a 5pm ET selection show on https://t.co/Q9AmWxO8UL. A game ending around 7:30pm Saturday will be final before the committee's work is well underway, and earlier than Lyon and Centenary's SCAC third-place game at 9pm ET. The Sunday noon idea floated Wednesday night would have ended around 3pm, after the committee's work is normally done, and could have left Merchant Marine judged at 7-1, roughly 68.9 NPI, with every bubble team waiting on the result settled without it. That the academies and those bubble teams came that close to that outcome, with no say in it, is part of the problem.

WHO OWNS THIS

Audi Field signed a contract for Nov. 14 knowing it is the Spirit's home stadium and that the NWSL playoffs run into mid-November. If its operators thought a home semifinal was possible, they should have planned for it before selling the date to a service-academy rivalry game, and if they had not planned for it, they had no business reopening the date over a weekend without the academies in the room.

The larger share of the blame, though, belongs to the NWSL, the Spirit, and Lafayette Federal Credit Union, who together manufactured an "us against them" fight that never needed to happen. The Spirit had a 64,000-seat NFL stadium reserved for Saturday and chose to go after the one building already promised to someone else. Lafayette Federal put up the money that made the buyout possible and has called its decision an easy yes, with no public acknowledgment of who would be displaced by it. The league had a schedule swap available on Monday that would have honored every contract and protected every TV window, and it left its slots where they were. The result pits professional soccer players against student-athletes who are not paid to play and who are training to serve the country's maritime and homeland security needs, and the online reaction since Sunday has done exactly that, setting supporters of women's soccer against supporters of the academies over a problem neither group created.

The academies are poorly positioned to fight back. They answer to two cabinet departments, and they are not built to take on a professional league in public, which is exactly why their date deserved more protection than it received. The Secretaries' Cup will kick off at 4:30pm on Saturday, and it will be played hard, because that is who these teams are. It should have kicked off at 1pm, on a fresh field, as promised.
