I hate to break it to you, but yes, we do have countless collaboration/cooperation agreements codified into law in the defense and foreign policy space. Similarly, our military collaboration with Israel began in earnest, ~60 years ago. You do know they were the first foreign country we sold our F-35s w/ stealth technology too, right? Israel has been designated as a statutorily defined "major Non-NATO ally" for ~40 years. 

And by law, the US will ensure that whatever weapons we sell to Middle Eastern countries, that Israel must retain the advantage in the region because of its small size and hostile neighbors. When the Soviet Union flooded Arab countries in the Middle East with advanced weapons after the 1967 War, the US adopted the position above, and we began supplying them superior weapons to what the Soviets were supplying Egypt and Syria with, in particular. It's just how the Cold War went (and still goes).

Ro wants you to believe the current legislation, Section 219 as it is called, is some kind of shocking new development. It's really a nothingburger he's using for political points. Don't fall for it. 

👇🏼 Grok is your friend when you want to learn instead of advance a narrative no matter the facts.  https://t.co/c4gQRFos2J

𝟭. 𝗧𝗲𝗻 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗨𝗦 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗮𝘄 (𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀, 𝗼𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗡𝗗𝗔𝗔 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀)

These are established legal frameworks for cooperation with allies and partners. Many involve technology sharing, joint development, intelligence, arms transfers, or mutual defense commitments. The claim of “thousands” is hyperbolic, but dozens of substantial ones exist.

1. 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝘁𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘆 (𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗢, 𝟭𝟵𝟰𝟵): Senate-ratified treaty establishing collective defense (Article 5). Framework for ongoing military integration, interoperability standards, and joint capabilities among members.

2. 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗝𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗻 (𝟭𝟵𝟲𝟬): Mutual defense treaty underpinning US basing, joint exercises, and security cooperation.

3. 𝗠𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗼𝗳 𝗞𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗮 (𝟭𝟵𝟱𝟯): Bilateral mutual defense commitment supporting US troop presence and joint operations.

4. 𝗔𝗡𝗭𝗨𝗦 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘆 (𝟭𝟵𝟱𝟭) with Australia and New Zealand: Mutual defense framework (still operative with Australia).

5. 𝗔𝗨𝗞𝗨𝗦 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 (Australia-UK-US): Codified in US law (22 U.S.C. Chapter 111). Includes NDAA authorizations for nuclear submarine technology transfer, advanced capability collaboration (AI, cyber, hypersonics, undersea), streamlined export controls, and oversight mechanisms. Nuclear propulsion agreement entered into force in 2025.

6. 𝗨𝗦-𝗨𝗞 𝗠𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 (𝟭𝟵𝟱𝟴, 𝗮𝘀 𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟰): Treaty under the Atomic Energy Act framework for deep nuclear weapons, materials, components, and submarine propulsion technology sharing and co-development. Unique in scope among US nuclear partners.

7. 𝗧𝗮𝗶𝘄𝗮𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗔𝗰𝘁 (𝟭𝟵𝟳𝟵, 𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗟𝗮𝘄 𝟵𝟲-𝟴): US statute committing to provide Taiwan with defensive arms and treating threats to its security as of grave concern to the United States. Basis for ongoing arms sales and security cooperation.

8. 𝗔𝗿𝗺𝘀 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝘁 (𝗔𝗘𝗖𝗔) 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗔𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝘁: Core statutes authorizing and regulating Foreign Military Sales (FMS), Direct Commercial Sales, and Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programs with dozens of countries. These enable large-scale technology and equipment transfers under congressional oversight and notification rules.

9. 𝗠𝗮𝗷𝗼𝗿 𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗢 𝗔𝗹𝗹𝘆 (𝗠𝗡𝗡𝗔) 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (e.g., 22 U.S.C. § 2321k): Statutory status granting preferential access to defense articles, excess equipment, cooperative research, and other benefits. Held by countries including Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, and others.

10. 𝟭𝟬 𝗨.𝗦.𝗖. § 𝟮𝟯𝟱𝟬𝗮: Authorizes the Secretary of Defense to enter into cooperative research and development agreements with NATO organizations, NATO members, and other allied/friendly foreign countries on defense equipment and munitions.

Additional examples include recurring NDAA programs such as the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, Pacific Deterrence Initiative, Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative, and various bilateral foundational agreements with India (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA) supported by statute and executive agreements.

𝟮. 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗨𝗦-𝗜𝘀𝗿𝗮𝗲𝗹 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆/𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀

These are longstanding and heavily codified or formalized. They go well beyond ordinary aid.

- 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗘𝗱𝗴𝗲 (𝗤𝗠𝗘): Explicitly defined and required by statute (Naval Vessel Transfer Act of 2008, Pub. L. 110-429, amending the AECA at 22 U.S.C. § 2776(h)). The President must assess Israel’s ability to counter conventional threats from states or non-state actors with superior means and minimal damage, and certify that arms sales to other Middle Eastern countries will not adversely affect it. This has shaped US regional arms policy for decades and was further reinforced in later laws (e.g., 2012 US-Israel Enhanced Security Cooperation Act).

- 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗠𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗙𝗠𝗙) 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮 𝗼𝗳 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗠𝗢𝗨𝘀): Current 2019–2028 MOU provides approximately $3.3 billion annually in FMF (mostly for purchase of US-origin systems) plus $500 million for missile defense cooperation (totaling roughly $38 billion over 10 years). Israel is the largest cumulative recipient of US military assistance. These are implemented through annual appropriations and authorizations. Earlier multi-year MOUs date back to the 1990s/2000s.

- 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗼-𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼-𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Arrow system (joint US-Israel development since the 1980s), David’s Sling/Stunner (with Raytheon), and Iron Dome (US funding support starting around 2011; co-production of Tamir interceptors in the United States via Raytheon-Rafael joint ventures). Repeatedly authorized and funded in successive NDAAs. US has invested billions in these programs.

- 𝗙-𝟯𝟱 𝗟𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜𝗜 (𝗙-𝟯𝟱𝗜 𝗔𝗱𝗶𝗿): Israel is a Security Cooperation Participant with high-level access (first foreign operator). It operates customized aircraft with unique Israeli avionics, electronic warfare, and systems integration allowed by the US. Significant modifications have been approved for operational needs. Israel shares combat and operational data with the United States, which has informed upgrades to the platform. This is among the closest levels of fifth-generation fighter technology access granted to any partner.

- 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀: Deep intelligence-sharing relationship; regular joint exercises; US prepositioned munitions and equipment stockpiles in Israel (War Reserve Stockpile Allies-Israel); Major Non-NATO Ally status since 1987; and existing cooperative R&D authorities under statutes such as 22 U.S.C. § 2767 and 10 U.S.C. § 2350a that already enable technology collaboration.

𝗗𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: The United States recognized Israel in 1948. Major arms sales began in the early 1960s (e.g., Hawk missiles under Kennedy). Cooperation intensified after the 1967 and especially 1973 wars (Operation Nickel Grass airlift). Formal strategic cooperation was institutionalized with the 1981 Memorandum of Understanding under the Reagan administration, followed by the creation of joint political-military groups, designation as a Major Non-NATO Ally in 1987, and a comprehensive 1988 MOU. Joint exercises, co-development (e.g., Arrow), prepositioning, and intelligence ties have been continuous and deepening since the 1980s. Close collaboration on Middle East security threats has therefore spanned more than 50 years in substance, with formal strategic partnership frameworks in place for over 40 years.

These arrangements show that Section 219 builds on an already extensive, legally grounded partnership rather than creating an unprecedented structure. Similar (though not identical) statutory and treaty-based mechanisms exist with multiple other close allies.

text:
Most of Nvidia's $165B partner exposure is contingent and years away
​
Aletheia cut Nvidia $NVDA  to Hold on Monday over $165B of financial commitments tied to its AI cloud partners. So I pulled up the July 10-Q to see what's actually in that number. It matches four items in the commitments and guarantees notes. All four live in the notes, none is on the balance sheet at face value, and almost none of it comes due before fiscal 2028.
​
If partner risk shows up in the Nov 17 numbers, it'll come through somewhere else: about $94B of equity stakes that do sit on the balance sheet.
​
Where the $165B comes from
​
Here's what the 10-Q for the quarter ended July 26 shows:
​
- AI cloud agreements: $36B
- Data center leases Nvidia signed and expects to hand off to third parties: $20B
- Land, power and shell guarantees for AI cloud partners: $3.5B
- Guarantees on SB Energy's Ohio campus, leased to an OpenAI affiliate and signed in August: capped at $105B
​
Add those up and you get $164.5B. Aletheia hasn't published its breakdown, so that's my reconstruction, not theirs.
​
Two bigger numbers aren't in there at all. Supply and capacity commitments, mostly memory and manufacturing, come to $279B, and the cloud service agreements Nvidia uses for its own research are another $29B. Those are bets on Nvidia's own demand. They don't tie Nvidia to anyone else's balance sheet.
​
Contingent, capped and late
​
The AI cloud agreements are basically a backstop. Nvidia commits to buy cloud capacity, and the filing says "Our commitments decrease as capacity is used by third-party customers." In plain English, Nvidia pays for whatever the partner can't sell. None of the $36B is scheduled for the rest of fiscal 2027. The first $6B lands in fiscal 2028.
​
The third-party leases are further out still. $17B of the $20B falls in fiscal 2032 or later.
​
Ohio is the biggest piece and the most conditional one. The guarantee "generally becomes effective upon commencement of the applicable lease," and the first phase isn't expected until fiscal 2029. It only pays out on tenant defaults, and it ends early if OpenAI gets a satisfactory credit rating. So read $105B as a ceiling on gross exposure, not money out the door.
​
The one guarantee already live is the $3.5B. Partners have put $712M in escrow against it, and Nvidia says the fair value of these guarantees isn't significant.
​
The exposure already on the books
​
The investments are where partner risk hits the income statement first. Non-marketable equity securities were $51.2B at the end of July, up from $22.3B in January. Marketable equity securities went from $12.9B to $42.8B. The 10-Q doesn't say what the holdings are.
​
Those stakes get marked through GAAP earnings. Nvidia booked $7.77B of equity gains in fiscal Q2, and GAAP EPS of $2.46 landed $0.24 above non-GAAP EPS of $2.22. When AI valuations climb, GAAP runs ahead of the operating business. When they drop, the same line works against it. And the quarter that ended Oct. 25 wasn't a calm one for neoclouds: CoreWeave's 2031 and 2032 bonds were yielding over 15% by late October, per CNBC.
​
How fast it got here
​
The speed is what gives me pause. In the April 10-Q, the only partner item was the $3.5B guarantee. Three months later the partner items totaled $59.5B, and that's before the $105B Ohio deal signed after quarter end. Over the same quarter revenue grew 18%, from $81.6B to $96.2B, while supply commitments more than doubled from $119B to $279B.
​
Two caveats. That's only two data points. And the filings don't say whether the AI cloud line is new business or a new label on older deals. According to CNBC, Nvidia's February annual report didn't mention AI cloud agreements at all.
​
Contingent doesn't mean zero, either. If the neoclouds can't fund their buildouts, unsold capacity is exactly what the AI cloud agreements cover. Aletheia estimates CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN need $124B over the next 12 to 15 months. It's an estimate, but it describes the scenario where the backstop starts costing real cash. The Ohio ceiling doesn't go away until OpenAI earns that rating.
​
When the 10-Q that follows the Nov 17 results comes out, I'll put three numbers next to their July levels. The AI cloud agreements total ($36B), and whether any of it slides into fiscal 2027. The equity securities line, and whether $7.77B of gains turns into losses that pull GAAP EPS below non-GAAP. And the $108.5B guarantee total, to see whether anything was added after Ohio.
​

$MARA Q3 2026 earnings: MARA pays off its Bitcoin loans, but lease targets slip

MARA, a Bitcoin miner expanding into artificial intelligence data centers, saw mining revenue drop while paper gains lifted net profit. Revenue fell 35% to $164 million as lower Bitcoin prices outweighed a 5% rise in coins mined. Reported profit reached $632 million only because of an $885 million accounting gain on its coin stash. After the quarter ended, the finance chief sold 13,597 Bitcoin to pay off $750 million of debt.

• Revenue: $𝟏𝟔𝟒.𝟐𝐌 (-35% from a year ago)
• Operating loss, excluding crypto paper swings: -$𝟐𝟐𝟔𝐌 (-$182M a year ago, by our math)
• Bitcoin holdings after October sales: 𝟐𝟎,𝟒𝟏𝟓 𝐁𝐓𝐂 (35,577 BTC at the end of Q2, by our math)
• Data center lease outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 (2 leases targeted for 2026 could slip into 2027)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because solving the debt risk came with another delay in signing data center tenants. Paying off the $750 million loan freed 17,477 pledged coins and removed the threat of collateral calls. The bad news: the chief executive warned that its goal of signing two data center leases this year could slip into 2027, leaving only a $79 million cloud deal as proof of the new business.

The question now is whether MARA's power sites can attract large data center tenants on financeable terms. Either waiting secures better lease economics as power gets scarcer, or rival operators lock up the best customers first. Signed lease announcements over the next two quarters will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝 $𝟕𝟓𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐏𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭
MARA, a Bitcoin miner expanding into data centers, borrowed $750 million against its digital coins in August to help buy the Long Ridge power plant. That loan locked up more than half of its Bitcoin stash as collateral and raised the risk of forced top-ups if coin prices fell. After the third quarter ended, the finance chief sold 13,597 Bitcoin at about $81,039 each, raising $1.1 billion in cash.

The company used $750 million of those proceeds to pay off the Bitcoin-backed loans in full. That payment freed 17,477 pledged coins, "leaving less than 5% of our BTC holdings loaned or pledged" according to the chief executive. Selling coins after prices rose from $64,000 created an estimated $170 million net benefit, the finance chief said, though MARA also sold 3.8 million shares in July.

What to watch: how much cash MARA sets aside for its 2027 convertible bond obligations. Bondholders can force the company to buy back those notes next year, so keeping cash on hand avoids new borrowing.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐨 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐇𝐮𝐫𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐭 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞
MARA wants to turn its 1.9 gigawatts of power capacity into a 4.8-gigawatt platform for artificial intelligence data centers. After the quarter ended, federal energy regulators approved its purchase of Long Ridge, an Ohio natural gas plant with 485 megawatts of power capacity. The finance chief expects the deal to close by year-end and bring immediate cash flow, "with roughly 70% of its output under long-term contracts".

Separately, Exaion, MARA's majority-owned cloud computing unit in Europe, signed a four-year, $79 million contract with its first US customer. The buyer agreed to pay for the graphics-chip capacity whether it uses the machines or not, which the chief executive called "an early proof point" for the business. However, Exaion's broader $3 billion pipeline consists of "indications of demand and are not yet contracted or committed".

What to watch: the closing statement for Long Ridge in the fourth-quarter report. It will show how much plant debt joins the balance sheet and how much power profit the plant generates.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐒𝐥𝐢𝐩 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕
For three quarters, MARA has promised to sign large data center tenants to long-term leases alongside its partner Starwood. In the first quarter it targeted at least one lease by the end of 2026, and in the second quarter it raised that goal to two. Management frames the delay as discipline, with the chief executive writing that "waiting has improved the terms available to us".

Yet the quarter ended with zero signed data center leases, and management softened its timeline. "While we are targeting signing two leases before year-end, market conditions are fluid and that timing could slip into next year," the chief executive wrote. Meanwhile, MARA posted a $100 million letter of credit after quarter-end for grid studies at its 2-gigawatt Texas site, committing capital before any tenant signs.

What to watch: any signed lease announcement with a named data center tenant before the fourth-quarter report. Another quarter without a contract would leave MARA relying entirely on Bitcoin and gas power sales.

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐌𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬
MARA reported $632.1 million in net income and $857.7 million in Adjusted EBITDA, a profit measure that excludes interest, taxes, depreciation, and stock pay. Both numbers look high only because accounting rules include an $885.3 million paper gain from higher Bitcoin prices during the quarter. Revenue fell 35% to $164.2 million because the average price of Bitcoin mined dropped 37% from a year ago.

• Operating loss excluding crypto and derivative paper swings: $226.4 million by our math, wider than $182.2 million a year ago
• Power and hosting costs: 72.8% of revenue, up 25.8 percentage points from a year ago by our math
• Depreciation and overhead (G&A): 91.9% and 46.2% of revenue, up 25.6 and 12.4 percentage points by our math
• Purchased energy cost per Bitcoin at owned sites: $39,674, up 1.1% from a year ago

By our math, stripping out the $885.3 million crypto paper gain leaves Adjusted EBITDA at negative $27.7 million. Unit energy costs crept up, "primarily driven by higher power costs and global network difficulty outpacing our hashrate growth" according to the finance chief, and third-party hosting contracts worth $71.5 million a quarter do not begin expiring until late 2027.

What to watch: purchased energy cost per Bitcoin in the fourth quarter. If network competition keeps rising faster than MARA's computing capacity, mining margins will stay compressed unless coin prices climb.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing financial, cost, and legal risks received no detailed update in the shareholder letter.

• Overhead cost trend: G&A excluding stock pay and deal costs was $45.4 million by our math, up from $42.4 million last quarter, and the full 10-Q filing will show whether Exaion drove the increase.
• 2027 convertible bond puts: management noted it is monitoring bondholder repayment rights next year, but the 10-Q debt footnotes will show the exact cash liability remaining.
• Legal appeals and international revenue goal: the release did not mention the pending legal appeals or the older goal of getting half of revenue outside the US by 2028.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐚 $𝟓𝟎𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤
After the quarter ended, MARA's board approved a programme to buy back up to $500 million of its common stock. Management said the authorization gives it another way to allocate capital alongside debt reduction and data center spending, though it does not obligate the company to buy any specific amount. The digital infrastructure group has not repurchased any shares yet and still has $1.5 billion left on its share-sale programme.

𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐀𝐈 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬
The chief executive noted that investors and lenders have grown more cautious toward artificial intelligence infrastructure because of local community opposition, higher borrowing costs, and complex tenant credit structures. While compute demand remains strong, lenders and customers now demand permitted power and guaranteed delivery schedules before committing capital. MARA said this stricter financing environment slows down industry deal-making but favors operators that already control energized land.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟑𝟒,𝟎𝟏𝟐 𝐁𝐓𝐂  ⇘ decelerating
Total Bitcoin held fell by 1,565 coins from last quarter and by 18,838 coins from a year ago. MARA mined 2,247 coins during the quarter but sold 3,891 coins at an average price of $75,300. After quarter-end, the company sold another 13,597 coins to pay off debt, leaving about 20,415 coins by our math.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟗𝟒𝟔.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Unrestricted cash more than doubled from $421.3 million last quarter and rose 73% from $547.1 million at the end of 2025. The increase came from borrowing against Bitcoin, selling mined coins, and issuing 3.8 million shares in July. Combined cash and Bitcoin totaled $3.8 billion at quarter-end, up from $2.5 billion in the second quarter.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟒𝟗𝟔.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The diluted share count rose 5.6% from 470.1 million a year ago, while basic shares grew 3.7% to 385.7 million. Because MARA posted a GAAP profit this quarter, potential shares from convertible bonds were counted in the diluted total. The company also resumed selling stock in July, issuing 3.8 million shares after two quarters of zero sales.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 (𝐘𝐄 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔): 𝟐 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐝 (𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐬𝐥𝐢𝐩 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from At least 1 to 2 leases before year-end
Cut. The chief executive still targets signing two tenant leases before year-end, but warned that fluid market conditions could push the signings into 2027. In the first quarter management targeted one or more leases this year, and in the second quarter it aimed for at least two without any caveat. Zero data center leases have been signed across the past three quarters.

𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐍𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 (𝟏𝐇 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕): 𝟓𝟎𝟓 𝐌𝐖  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from 505 MW in 2H 2026
Cut. The Ohio natural gas plant is authorized to sell 485 megawatts today and is now expected to reach its full 505-megawatt capacity in the first half of 2027. In the first quarter, management had expected that 20-megawatt expansion to happen in the second half of 2026. The acquisition itself received federal approval and remains on track to close by year-end 2026.

𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐇𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 (𝐐𝟑 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕–𝐐𝟏 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖): 𝟐𝟗% 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Expiring Q3 2027 to Q1 2028
Unchanged. Management reiterated that its largest third-party hosting contracts, which make up about 29% of total energy capacity, will begin expiring in the third quarter of 2027 and end completely in the first quarter of 2028. Exiting those sites will eliminate third-party hosting expenses, which cost $71.5 million this quarter and $210.7 million over the first nine months of 2026.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐢𝐝𝐠𝐞 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬?
MARA raised $1.1 billion from October Bitcoin sales and spent $750 million to pay off crypto-backed loans. Because those loans were originally taken to fund the Long Ridge purchase, investors need to know how much cash the closing itself will consume before year-end.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐌𝐀𝐑𝐀 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐉𝐮𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬?
The company sold 3.8 million shares under its at-the-market stock programme in July after two quarters without dilution, then authorized a $500 million buyback after quarter-end. Management did not give the July sale price or explain what changed its view on issuing equity.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐓𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐬 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭?
After quarter-end, MARA posted a $100 million letter of credit for grid interconnection studies at its 2-gigawatt Matagorda County site. Management has not disclosed when the state grid operator will finish the study or when purchase payments to the seller begin.

𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐢𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐚𝐢𝐨𝐧'𝐬 $𝟕𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐔𝐒 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫?
Exaion signed a four-year, $79 million graphics-chip contract with its first US buyer on take-or-pay terms. Management did not disclose the customer's credit profile, how much capital MARA must spend to buy the chips, or when the revenue starts.

Morning Call: Europe set for a strong open, but Wall Street still has to prove the recovery

Wednesday, November 11, 2026 | Morning briefing
© 2026 https://t.co/qNaD2GrTsz - All rights reserved.

■ European equity markets are expected to open sharply higher on Wednesday. DAX futures are trading around 26,667 and approximately 1.23% higher. S&P 500 futures are up around 0.61% and Nasdaq 100 futures approximately 1.37%. Taiwan and South Korea are also advancing strongly. Technology is attracting renewed buying following Tuesday's weakness. CoreWeave's strong results are providing additional support because demand for computing capacity remains far above available supply.

■ Stronger futures deserve attention, but they do not yet prove that Wall Street has established a durable bottom. US inflation was higher than expected on Tuesday and the ten-year Treasury yield moved to almost 5%. That is a significant headwind for technology, real estate and companies relying heavily on debt financing. The US bond market is closed today for Veterans Day. The main test will therefore be whether strong Nasdaq futures survive the Wall Street open and whether NVIDIA can stabilise following its sharp decline.
Asia

■ Taiwan leads the important Asian markets with a gain of approximately 2.70%. South Korea's KOSPI is up 2.21% and the Nikkei gains 1.25%. Taiwan and South Korea are particularly relevant for Europe because semiconductor companies carry substantial index weights. The move provides a supportive signal for ASML, ASMI and BESI at the open.

■ The advance is not broad across all of Asia. Hong Kong's Hang Seng is down approximately 0.83% and Shanghai loses around 0.24%. Shenzhen is almost unchanged. Investors are therefore primarily buying technology and semiconductor shares, while the signal from Chinese equities remains much weaker. That distinction matters for European companies with greater exposure to Chinese consumers.

■ Japan is approximately 1.25% higher, but the Japanese bond market provides a less favourable signal. The ten-year yield is moving toward 2.76%. Long-term Australian yields have also risen. Hotter US inflation is therefore feeding directly into the cost of capital in other parts of the world.

■ SoftBank is under pressure in Japan after reporting a quarterly loss of around ¥1.1 trillion. High spending on data-centre investments was one factor. The figures again illustrate how strong demand for additional capacity can coexist with increasing financial risk from the size and cost of the required investment.

Wall Street and US futures

■ Wall Street failed to confirm Monday's strong rally on Tuesday. The S&P 500 declined 0.38% to 7,520.93, the Nasdaq fell 0.74% and the Dow Jones lost 0.30%. The Russell 2000 declined around 0.7%. Hotter inflation and sharply higher Treasury yields ultimately outweighed the benefit from lower oil prices.

■ Semiconductor shares held up relatively well. The SOX declined only around 0.35% after gaining almost 7% on Monday. Only a small part of the previous advance was therefore surrendered. The sector remains one of the most important indicators of whether the recovery attempt can continue.

■ NVIDIA was again the clear exception. The shares lost more than 5% on Tuesday and now stand well below their October high. In addition to higher yields, uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang is becoming increasingly important. NVIDIA's performance will therefore be a major test for the Nasdaq and the wider semiconductor sector today.

■ The VIX closed Tuesday at 19.46 and remained below 20. That is notable following hotter inflation, a sharp move in yields and renewed technology weakness. Uncertainty remains high, but markets are not showing the same level of stress seen during last week's sell-off when the VIX moved above 28.

■ US futures are substantially higher this morning. S&P 500 futures are gaining around 0.61% and Nasdaq 100 futures approximately 1.37%. The Nasdaq move is particularly important. Investors are buying technology again, but regular trading from 15:30 CET must show whether that demand remains at higher prices.

■ The main explanation is the combination of bargain hunting and CoreWeave's results. Operational demand for artificial-intelligence computing capacity remains exceptionally strong. That reduces fears that the investment cycle has suddenly stopped, although it does not remove concerns surrounding debt, interest expense and investment returns.

Macroeconomics and interest rates

■ US consumer prices increased 0.4% in October from September, compared with expectations of 0.3%. Core inflation was 0.3%, also one tenth above consensus. The data were strong enough to shift interest-rate expectations materially higher.

■ The US two-year Treasury yield is around 4.75%. The ten-year yield ended Tuesday close to 5.00% after trading below 4.90% before the inflation report. The ten-year yield deserves particular attention. Around 5%, government bonds become an increasingly competitive alternative to highly valued equities.

■ Markets now almost fully price a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve increase in December. There is also roughly a 10% probability of a 50-basis-point move. Investors additionally expect several more increases toward the middle of 2027.

■ This changes the valuation equation for technology. Companies whose profits lie far in the future become less valuable as discount rates rise. The same applies to businesses funding large data-centre investments with debt. Banks can benefit from higher margins as long as credit losses remain manageable.

■ Germany's ten-year government-bond yield is around 3.31%. European long-term rates also moved higher following the US inflation data. The ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.50% in late October, but Christine Lagarde has made clear that a December increase remains possible if inflation requires further action.

■ Final German October inflation is released at 08:00 CET. The preliminary estimate was 2.8% year on year, down from 3.3% in September. Preliminary core inflation stood at 2.1%. Confirmation of that decline would provide some counterweight to the upward pressure coming from US yields.

■ Today is Veterans Day in the United States. NYSE and Nasdaq trade normally, but SIFMA recommends a full closure of the Treasury and wider US dollar fixed-income markets. A major live signal from the cash bond market will therefore be missing during US equity trading. Rate futures continue to trade.

■ ECB President Christine Lagarde participates in a panel at the Paris Peace Forum at 10:45 CET. There is no prepared speech. Any comments on inflation or rates could therefore emerge directly from the discussion and create unexpected market moves.

■ Germany also auctions €1.5 billion of a 30-year Bund with a 2.90% coupon and €1.0 billion of a bond maturing in 2047. Following the rise in long-term yields, investor demand at the auction will provide a useful signal on appetite for European sovereign debt.

Geopolitics and international trade

■ Russia and Ukraine continue US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi today, their first such negotiations since February. The US side described the first day as productive, although substantial differences remain. Territory and the future security structure for Europe remain major obstacles.

■ Tangible progress could have immediate implications for European defence stocks. A credible path toward reduced fighting could trigger profit-taking after strong multi-year gains. The structural case for higher European defence spending will not disappear quickly, however, particularly without a durable agreement.

■ Security in the Strait of Hormuz remains another risk. Recent data show 37 attacks on vessels in and around the strait during October and further incidents during November. Even if political tensions with Iran ease, mines, insurance costs and reluctance among shipping companies could delay a rapid normalisation of traffic.

■ Political pressure on the US semiconductor industry is also increasing. Republican and Democratic senators are using the controversy surrounding NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang to push for tighter control of advanced-chip exports to China. The NVIDIA governance issue is therefore increasingly connected to the wider US-China trade and technology relationship.

Oil and energy

■ WTI is trading around $87.15 per barrel and is approximately 0.2% higher. Brent is near $92. Crude is recovering slightly from roughly two-month lows, while remaining far below late-October levels.

■ The modest rebound reflects continued shipping risks around Hormuz. At the same time, the United States is not currently pursuing another major escalation against Iran. Markets are therefore balancing hopes for de-escalation against the risk of renewed disruption.

■ US crude inventories increased by approximately 9 million barrels last week, according to the American Petroleum Institute. That is a substantial build and provides a clear restraint on another major oil-price rally.

■ Dutch TTF natural gas is trading around €84 to €86 per MWh. This is well below the peak above €100 earlier this month, although still high by historical standards. The gas market remains sensitive to LNG supply, winter temperatures and disruption to international shipping routes.

■ Current energy prices are more supportive for European equities than several weeks ago. Airlines, transport, chemicals and other heavy energy users benefit. Shell and TotalEnergies receive less support if oil remains around $90 to $95.

■ OPEC releases its monthly report today. New estimates for global demand, production and spare capacity may influence crude prices. Investors will focus on whether the organisation sees reason to revise demand growth following the recent sharp fall in oil.

Currencies, gold and commodities

■ EUR/USD is trading around 1.1164. The dollar index is near 102.2. The US currency is benefiting from higher rate expectations following the inflation data. A somewhat weaker euro can help European exporters, although broad dollar strength also signals tighter global financial conditions.

■ USD/JPY is around 158.9. The yen remains extremely weak even as Japanese long-term yields rise. That combination increases the possibility of renewed verbal or actual intervention from Tokyo.

■ Gold is trading around $4,040 to $4,050 per troy ounce and is attempting to recover a small part of Tuesday's sharp decline. A strong dollar and higher yields remain clear headwinds. With the ten-year yield close to 5%, a strong gold rebound is less straightforward.

■ Silver is trading around $52.3 per troy ounce and is outperforming gold. In addition to its precious-metal characteristics, silver benefits from industrial demand including power networks, solar panels and electronics. This can provide greater support when technology and industrial metals recover.

■ Copper is near $6.29 per pound and is up approximately 1%. Structural demand from electricity grids, data centres and new power generation remains supportive. Weak Chinese equities and higher global interest rates provide the main counterweights.

Bitcoin and crypto

■ Bitcoin is trading around $73,700 and remains close to its lowest level since August. Ether is near $2,050. Crypto continues to lag the strong Nasdaq futures.

■ The divergence is important. Technology shares are attracting renewed demand, while the same willingness to take additional risk is barely visible in cryptocurrencies. Higher US yields and a stronger dollar remain clear negatives for Bitcoin.

■ The sector also continues to deal with the aftermath of the major Binance theft and expectations that the new US Congress could pursue tighter regulation. Until Bitcoin participates more clearly in the recovery, crypto remains a warning signal alongside stronger equity futures.

AI, semiconductors and corporate news

■ CoreWeave is the main positive catalyst for technology this morning. Third-quarter revenue increased almost 170% to $3.66 billion and beat market expectations. Backlog rose from $104 billion at the end of June to $132.5 billion at the end of September. The shares gained roughly 5% after hours.

■ Operational demand is exceptionally strong. CoreWeave says demand for next year is approximately ten times available capacity. Quarterly capital expenditure increased from $9.4 billion to $14.5 billion. The figures illustrate how much capital is required to convert that demand into usable computing capacity.

■ Financing remains the weak point. CoreWeave had approximately $46.9 billion of debt at the end of September. The company does not want to issue new unsecured debt at current yields and expects approximately $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits during the next three months. This reduces its immediate dependence on expensive new capital.

■ CoreWeave targets adjusted profitability during the first half of 2028. Its results therefore send two signals simultaneously. Demand for computing capacity remains extremely strong, while the investment and financing required to meet it remain exceptionally large. With the US ten-year yield near 5%, that distinction is becoming increasingly important.

■ NVIDIA is in focus today. The stock lost more than 5% on Tuesday. Republican Senator Kevin Cramer, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, has now called for Jensen Huang to step down. Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is also pressing for tighter rules governing exports of advanced chips to China. Political and governance pressure has therefore intensified.

■ NVIDIA says there is no evidence that company secrets or US national-security interests were compromised and its board is investigating the matter. For markets, today's key question is whether the shares stabilise. Nasdaq 100 futures are more than 1% higher despite NVIDIA's difficulties, giving the rest of the semiconductor sector room to recover for now.

■ ASML receives a clear positive read-through from Taiwan, South Korea and strong US futures. Gains in Asian chip shares and the exceptional demand reported by CoreWeave support the view that end demand for computing capacity has not collapsed. Higher rates remain a valuation headwind.

■ ASMI benefits from the same backdrop. Demand for advanced semiconductor equipment remains dependent on the capital-expenditure plans of major chipmakers. CoreWeave is not a direct order indicator, but it does reinforce the view that demand for additional computing power remains large.

■ BESI may also benefit from the rebound in advanced semiconductors and stronger Nasdaq futures. The US session later today will matter more than the initial European move. Another positive SOX session would make the recovery considerably more convincing.

■ ABN AMRO reports third-quarter results at 07:00 CET. It is the first quarter in which NIBC is consolidated from August. Investors will focus on net interest income, fees, costs, credit losses and the CET1 ratio. At the half-year stage ABN AMRO raised its 2026 commercial net-interest-income outlook to €6.8 billion including NIBC and lowered its cost guidance to €5.5 billion.

■ The NIBC acquisition is particularly relevant for ABN AMRO. The bank previously expected the transaction to reduce its CET1 ratio by approximately 70 to 75 basis points. Today's results will show the actual impact and whether the remaining capital position continues to provide room for shareholder distributions.

■ Avantium is due to publish the outcome of its rights offering before 09:00 CET. The company aims to raise €55.45 million through a fully committed and underwritten offering at €1.65 per share. Subscription levels and the rump placement may create significant volatility today.

■ CSG releases its nine-month trading update today, with an investor and analyst presentation at 10:00 CET. Revenue growth, margins, order intake and the outlook will be important. The timing also coincides with the second day of Ukraine peace talks, making the defence stock particularly sensitive to geopolitical headlines.

■ Siemens Energy reports fourth-quarter and full-year results at 07:00 CET. Grid Technologies remains a major focus because global demand for electricity networks continues to rise with data centres, electrification and new power generation. Gas Services, Siemens Gamesa, free cash flow and the new annual outlook will also be important.

■ Siemens Energy also announced on Tuesday that it plans to expand its share-buyback programme by as much as €9 billion through 2030. That is a strong statement about expected cash generation and capital capacity. Today's results will show whether the operating performance supports that step.

■ RWE reports its first nine months around 07:00 CET. Renewable generation, flexible power plants, trading, investment and full-year guidance will be the main areas of focus. Its conference call follows at 13:00 CET. Recent declines in gas and power prices also make the outlook important.

■ E.ON also reports before the market opens. Electricity networks are the key business to watch. Rapid growth in power demand from industry, heat pumps, electric vehicles and data centres requires substantial grid investment. Investors will focus on regulated earnings, capital expenditure and confirmation of full-year guidance.

■ Vestas releases third-quarter results today, followed by its conference call at 10:00 CET. Order intake, turbine margins, Service and free cash flow will be important. Investors particularly want to see whether profitability continues to improve while the order backlog remains strong.

Economic calendar and earnings

■ 07:00 CET: ABN AMRO, Siemens Energy and RWE publish results. Several other European companies also report around this time.

■ 07:30 CET: Vestas reports third-quarter results. The reaction could also influence other European wind-energy stocks.

■ 08:00 CET: Germany publishes final October inflation. The preliminary estimate was 2.8% year on year and minus 0.2% month on month.

■ Before 09:00 CET: Avantium publishes the result of its rights offering. European equity markets open at 09:00. DAX futures are currently around 26,667 and approximately 1.23% higher.

■ 10:00 CET: CSG presents its nine-month trading update. The Vestas conference call also begins around this time and Italy publishes industrial-production data.

■ 10:45 CET: ECB President Christine Lagarde participates in a panel at the Paris Peace Forum. There is no prepared text, meaning comments on inflation or interest rates could come unexpectedly.

■ Around 11:30 CET: Germany auctions €1.5 billion of a 30-year Bund and €1.0 billion of a bond maturing in 2047. Demand is relevant following the recent increase in long-term yields.

■ Today: OPEC publishes its monthly report with new estimates for oil demand, production and supply.

■ 13:00 CET: RWE holds its investor and analyst conference call.

■ 15:30 CET: Wall Street opens. NYSE and Nasdaq trade normally despite Veterans Day. The US bond market is closed, giving the reaction in NVIDIA, the SOX and the Nasdaq additional importance in assessing the recovery.

European opening outlook and the remainder of the session

■ A strong European opening is the most likely outcome. DAX futures are approximately 1.23% higher, S&P 500 futures around 0.61% stronger and Nasdaq 100 futures approximately 1.37% higher. Taiwan and South Korea are also posting substantial gains. Technology and semiconductor shares could therefore lead the opening move.

■ Stronger futures are not simply a reaction to Tuesday's decline. CoreWeave confirms that underlying demand for computing power remains exceptionally strong. Its backlog, revenue growth and the ratio between demand and available capacity provide fundamental support to the investment cycle.

■ CoreWeave's financial numbers also explain why doubts remain. Debt is high, investment is enormous and the company does not want to issue new unsecured debt at current yields. Markets are increasingly distinguishing between strong operational demand and whether every investment remains financially attractive.

■ Interest rates therefore remain the largest counterweight. A US ten-year yield around 5% can continue to pressure expensive valuations. With the US cash bond market closed today, equities receive less guidance from a live Treasury signal.

■ NVIDIA is the second major test. Political pressure surrounding Jensen Huang is increasing just as the shares have already fallen sharply. If NVIDIA stabilises and the SOX rises again, the technology recovery becomes more convincing. Renewed heavy selling in NVIDIA could quickly make strong Nasdaq futures look less impressive.

■ Europe also receives significant new information before and shortly after the open. ABN AMRO, Siemens Energy, RWE, E.ON, Vestas, Avantium and CSG can all produce substantial individual moves. A higher index opening therefore does not imply that every sector will move in the same direction.

■ The direction for the morning is clearly positive. Attention then shifts to whether the DAX and AEX retain their opening gains and whether European technology remains strong beyond the first trading phase. The decisive confirmation arrives after 15:30 CET. Wall Street must show that the buying visible in futures also survives regular trading.

🇷🇺🇦🇫|A Russian Government Aircraft Landed at Kabul Airport. On Board: A Deputy Prime Minister and Seventy Businesspeople. The Cargo Was Not a Demand. It Was an Offer.

The aircraft carried Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk, more than 70 business representatives from Russian companies in transport, logistics, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals, and Zamir Kabulov, Russia’s Special Envoy for Afghanistan. They met Mullah Abdul Ghani Baradar, the Taliban’s deputy prime minister for economic affairs, at the presidential palace.

The Western headline was written before the plane landed: Russia legitimises the Taliban. The actual manifest was a trade mission, and the numbers are the indictment of the Western model.

The Transaction: What Russia Brought and What It Asked For

Overchuk stated trade between Russia and Afghanistan reached approximately $350 million in the first eight months of 2026 more than double the same period last year. Russian imports of Afghan fruit and vegetables have begun.

The Taliban’s offer was specific. Baradar invited Russian companies to extract copper, zinc, and chromite in partnership with Afghan firms, and to invest in factories, industrial parks, special economic zones, dry ports, and specialised hospitals.

The Taliban’s shopping list: Russian cars, grain, fertilisers, medicines, and equipment.

Read the structure. Russia is buying Afghan produce and offering to build industrial capacity in partnership with Afghan firms. The Taliban is buying Russian goods and inviting Russian investment. It is a two-way transaction goods for goods, capital for minerals, expertise for infrastructure. The growth is shared because the deal requires the Afghan side to be a partner, not a supplicant.

The Looting Model: What Washington Left Behind

The United States spent $2.3 trillion in Afghanistan over twenty years, lost 2,400 service members, and withdrew in August 2021. It then did three things.

It froze the money. Roughly $7 billion in Afghan central bank reserves were frozen after the Taliban took power. US and international economists have publicly urged Washington to return the funds, stating the refusal is worsening the economic collapse.

It cut the aid. US assistance inside Afghanistan ceased altogether in 2025. The aid that had sustained the economy was switched off.

It kept the sanctions. The unilateral sanctions cut Afghanistan off from the international banking system, choking the foreign exchange the country needs to import food and medicine.

That is the looting model. It does not send a delegation. It sends a freeze order. It does not build a factory. It blocks the bank account that would pay for one. The result is a country with $1 trillion in untapped minerals; lithium, copper, iron ore, rare earths and a population that cannot access its own money.

What Washington Wants Now: The Bagram-for-Lithium Offer

The record shows Washington’s actual model, and it is not reconstruction. Reporting in August 2026 documented the Taliban offering the Trump administration access to Afghanistan’s estimated $1 trillion in minerals: lithium, gold, copper, rare earths in exchange for sanctions relief and the return of frozen assets.

The framing of the offer was reported as Bagram for lithium and gold. The United States is not being asked to build a factory. It is being asked to return the money it froze and lift the sanctions it imposed in exchange for access to the resources.

That is the extractive model stated as a transaction: give us the minerals, and we will give you back your own money. The Taliban is offering it because the blockade has left no other path.

The Comparison, Stated as Arithmetic

Washington’s balance sheet in Afghanistan: $2.3 trillion spent, $7 billion frozen, aid cut to zero, sanctions maintained, no ambassador in Kabul, and a proposed deal that trades mineral access for the release of the frozen reserves.

Russia’s balance sheet: $350 million in trade in eight months, doubled year-on-year, 70+ companies on the ground, a delegation led by a deputy prime minister, an embassy that never closed, and a partnership offer on mining, factories, industrial parks, and hospitals.

One side froze the assets and cut the aid. The other side flew in seventy businesspeople and doubled the trade. One side’s model requires the country to stay poor so its resources can be accessed on favourable terms. The other side’s model requires the country to trade so the resources can be developed with a local partner.

The Bill

The aircraft: a Russian government aircraft at Kabul Airport. Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk. 70+ business representatives in transport, logistics, agriculture, and pharmaceuticals. Zamir Kabulov.

The trade: $350 million in eight months, double the previous year. Afghan fruit and vegetables entering Russia. Russian grain, fertilisers, and medicines entering Afghanistan.

The investment offer: copper, zinc, chromite in partnership with Afghan firms. Factories, industrial parks, special economic zones, dry ports, hospitals.

The Western model: $7 billion frozen. Aid ceased in 2025. Sanctions maintained. No ambassador. A $1 trillion mineral offer framed as a trade for the release of Afghanistan’s own reserves.

The Western headline: Russia legitimises the Taliban. The Western model is the one that froze the money, cut the aid, and left the country to negotiate access to its own resources while it starves. The Russian model is the one that landed a plane full of businesspeople and doubled the trade. The bill is being paid in frozen reserves and blocked bank accounts, and the receipt is a trade mission the Western press will report as a threat while the Afghan central bank’s $7 billion sits in a US account.

🧭 BOUGAINVILLE ISLAND | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Fly from Port Moresby to Buka Airport, located on neighbouring Buka Island. Cross the Buka Passage by local boat to reach Bougainville Island. Arrange onward road transport with a trusted local operator and confirm flight schedules before departure.

🗺️ What to Explore

Northern Bougainville offers coastal villages, tropical landscapes and opportunities for locally arranged boat excursions. The island's volcanic terrain is another distinctive feature, but Mount Bagana is active and should be appreciated only from safe locations.

⏱️ Time Needed & Where to Stay

Allow at least 4–5 days for a focused visit, with extra flexibility for transport disruptions. Buka is a practical arrival base, while accommodation on Bougainville Island includes locally operated guesthouses and lodges. Confirm availability directly.

🌤️ Planning & Access

Expect hot, humid weather and substantial rainfall throughout the year. Tourism infrastructure is limited, so arrange transfers and accommodation in advance.

⚠️ Important: Check current government travel advisories. Central Bougainville, particularly the Panguna mine area, carries serious security risks and should be avoided. Confirm entry requirements and local conditions before committing to a trip.

Standalone Myteries Versus Series
 A mystery reader’s bookshelf can hold two very different kinds of comfort. In the question of **standalone mysteries versus book series**, one book offers the pleasure of a complete case wrapped up by bedtime, while the other invites readers back to familiar streets, familiar suspects, and perhaps one very determined dog with a nose for trouble.

Neither choice is better for every reader or every moment. Sometimes you want a fresh town, a new puzzle, and a satisfying farewell. Other times, you want to check in on the people and animals who already feel like neighbors. The real joy is knowing what each type of mystery does especially well.

## What Makes a Standalone Mystery Special?

A standalone mystery tells its full story in one volume. The crime, the clues, and the main character’s emotional journey generally reach a meaningful resolution by the final page. There is no need to remember what happened three books ago, and no pressure to keep reading if one adventure is all you have time for.

That makes standalones wonderfully inviting for readers in between commitments. A vacation, a rainy weekend, a book club selection, or a busy month can all be perfect occasions for one complete whodunit. You meet the sleuth, learn the lay of the land, gather clues, and get the answer without needing a map of past events.

Standalones also give authors room to take a big creative swing. A new setting can have its own personality: an old inn with a locked library, a coastal town preparing for a festival, or a quiet neighborhood where everyone seems to know everyone else’s business. The author can build a mystery around a particular event or historical detail, then leave that world behind once the case is closed.

There is a lovely finality to that approach. A good standalone can feel like a warm visit with a fascinating stranger. You may not see them again, but you remember the conversation.

### The Trade-Off of One Complete Case

The same quality that makes a standalone easy to pick up can make it harder to leave. Readers only have so many pages to get to know the detective, their friends, their home, and their heart. A talented author can make those pages count, but there is less time for gradual changes and long-running friendships.

For readers who enjoy watching a character grow through several seasons of life, one book may feel a little brief. The ending can be satisfying and still leave you wishing there were another porch conversation, another town gathering, or another chance for a favorite animal sidekick to investigate something suspicious.

## Why Book Series Keep Readers Coming Back

A mystery series offers a different promise: the next case may be new, but the heart of the story remains familiar. Returning to a favorite fictional town can be as cozy as visiting a beloved local café. You know who makes the best pie, which neighbor is likely to gossip, and which trusted sleuth will notice the clue everyone else missed.

Series mysteries are especially satisfying in the cozy tradition because community matters. Each installment can introduce a new crime, while continuing the relationships that make readers care about the outcome. A sheriff may become more trusting. A shy neighbor may find courage. A rescue pet may settle into a permanent home. These changes do not need to rush. They can unfold naturally, book by book.

For animal lovers, a series has another special reward. Dogs and cats are not simply decorations in the background. They can become companions whose habits, quirks, and loyalty deepen over time. A clever canine might recognize a scent that does not belong, react to a nervous visitor, or lead a human sleuth toward a detail nobody thought to question. That is not magic. It is observation, instinct, and sometimes a warm snout in exactly the right place.

The Doc and Daisy Mysteries use that lasting connection to bring readers back to small-town Florida, where canine forensics, local history, and Daisy’s lively point of view keep each new puzzle feeling fresh.

### The Trade-Off of Returning to the Same World

A series can ask a bit more from its readers. While many cozy mysteries are designed so each book works on its own, a new reader may wonder whether they have missed an earlier relationship, an old feud, or an important personal milestone. Starting with book one often gives the richest experience.

Authors also face a cheerful but real challenge: keeping the setting recognizable without making it repetitive. Readers want the comfort of a favorite town, yet they also want an unpredictable mystery. The best series balances both. The diner can still serve its famous peach cobbler, but the next crime should not feel like the last one wearing a different hat.

A long series may also leave readers waiting for favorite storylines to develop. That patience can be part of the fun, like tending a garden and watching what comes up in the next season. Still, readers who prefer quick resolution may be happier with a standalone when they want every major thread neatly tied.

## Standalone Mysteries Versus Book Series: Choose by Mood

The easiest way to choose is not to ask which format is objectively best. Ask what kind of reading companion you need right now.

Choose a standalone when you are craving a clean start and finish. Perhaps you want a single satisfying puzzle for a flight, a book club, or a weekend curled up with a cat at your feet. You may be trying a new author or a new mystery style and want a low-commitment introduction. A standalone lets you sample freely.

Choose a series when you want to settle in. Maybe life has been busy, and you would rather return to characters who already know their way around the town square. Maybe you enjoy noticing small changes in friendships and romances alongside the central investigation. Or maybe you simply want more time with a dog narrator who has earned your trust, even if their opinion of the mail carrier remains a work in progress.

There is also a practical difference. Readers who borrow books, travel often, or have unpredictable reading schedules may appreciate that a standalone never leaves them halfway through a larger story. Readers who like to keep a dependable pile of books ready for the next cozy evening may find a series especially comforting. Once you discover a world you love, you already know where to go next.

## What Readers Get From Both

Despite their differences, strong standalones and strong series share the same essentials. Both need fair clues, memorable characters, a setting that feels alive, and an ending that rewards attention. In a cozy mystery, they also need a sense of safety and heart. The crime may shake up a community, but the story should leave room for kindness, humor, and the belief that careful observation can bring truth to light.

Both formats also benefit from a sleuth with a reason to care. The most engaging investigators are not merely solving a puzzle for sport. They are protecting a friend, seeking justice for a neighbor, preserving the peace of a town they love, or following a clue that will not stop scratching at the back of their mind.

That emotional connection is what makes readers remember a mystery long after they have guessed the culprit. A clever reveal is delightful. A clever reveal that matters to people we have come to care about is even better.

## A Reading Life Has Room for Both

There is no rule saying a reader must pledge loyalty to one kind of mystery. A standalone can refresh the palate between installments of a beloved series. A series can provide a welcome homecoming after several one-book adventures. Many readers happily switch between the two without giving it a second thought.

Think of the choice as matching a book to a moment. Some days call for a complete little journey, with one map, one mystery, and one tidy destination. Other days call for an open invitation to return, sniff around familiar corners, and see what trouble has found the neighborhood this time.

The best next mystery is the one that makes you want to pour something warm, settle into your favorite chair, and turn just one more page.

$NBIS Q3 2026 comprehensive summary outside the headline numbers. 

$NBIS Unit economics & commercial terms:

ARR $6.4B at end-September (+113% QoQ from $3.0B).

AI Cloud adjusted EBITDA margin 53.2%.

Q3 contracts: ACV >$25M per MW, GPU-hour prices +20% QoQ.
Payback improved to 1 year 7 months.

Prepayments on Q3 deals covered >100% of related capex (up from 50-60% in Q2).
$12B new TCV signed since start of Q3. 
Token Factory approaching multi-hundred-million run rate (contract value +17x QoQ).
New data centers & capacity

Biggest QoQ capacity increase to date; four new sites began generating revenue in Q3 (US + Europe), plus additional New Jersey tranches.

New owned sites expected to deploy capacity in 2027: Missouri (Independence, now 1.1 GW site after 300 MW expansion), Lappeenranta (Finland), second Mäntsälä (Finland), and Alabama (Birmingham/BHM01, ~300 MW).

At full scale these four owned sites represent >3 GW, to be delivered over the next 3–3.5 years.

Additional: 100 MW multi-campus rights secured in Alberta (2027, scalable to several hundred MW), 50 MW new colocation in South Carolina (2027), first APAC sites in India targeted for 2027.

Contracted power already >4 GW, targeting 5 GW by year-end 2026. Plan for >1 GW of new capacity online each year from 2027. Majority of future capacity from owned sites.
2027 CapEx and funding coverage

2027 capex guidance: $40–45 billion (sized for >1 GW of new capacity).

Company expects 75–85% of that to be covered by customer prepayments + available investment-grade asset-backed financing (against existing IG contracts such as Microsoft/Meta and others), along with the balance sheet.

Expected customer prepayments: $17–20B in 2027 (up from ~$10B committed in 2026).
Amount left to raise (external / other sources)

On $40B capex: 75% covered = $30B → $10B left; 85% covered = $34B → $6B left.

On $45B capex: 75% covered = $33.75B → $11.25B left; 85% covered = $38.25B → $6.75B left.

Rough residual external funding need of roughly $6-11.25B depending on final capex and exact coverage percentage. Management notes they remain opportunistic on additional capital (further prepayments, more ABF, balance sheet, corporate debt or equity) and are not dependent on any single source.
Other notes

1/ 2026 revenue guided to low end of $3.0–3.4B; capex ~$27B; ARR >$7B shifted to February.
2/ Some third-party/Microsoft New Jersey capacity pushed into 1H 2027.
3/ ~$325M of Q3 revenue was non-recurring asset-light.
4/ Cash ~$7.4B; Q3 capex ~$7.3B; operating cash flow negative ~$273M.
