text:
The Islamic Slave trade.    Jefferson and the Barbary Pirates
The Barbary states (the North African Ottoman regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, plus independent Morocco) ran a long-standing system of state-sponsored corsairing. They seized merchant ships, enslaved crews, and demanded tribute payments from European powers (and later the United States) for “protection” from further attacks. After independence, American ships lost the protection of the Royal Navy and became targets. In the mid-1780s, Algerian corsairs seized American vessels and crews, creating a crisis for the new republic.
As U.S. minister to France, Jefferson worked with John Adams (minister to Britain) on the problem. In March 1786 in London they met the Tripolitan ambassador Abd al-Rahman (Abdrahaman). When they asked by what right Tripoli attacked nations that had done it no injury, the ambassador replied that it was founded on the laws of their Prophet, written in the Koran: nations that had not acknowledged their authority were sinners; it was their right and duty to make war on them wherever found, enslave prisoners, and that any Muslim slain in such battle was assured of Paradise. He described the incentives for corsairs (extra slaves for the first boarder) and their aggressive tactics.
Jefferson consistently rejected the European practice of paying tribute. He viewed it as dishonorable, ineffective (it only invited higher demands), and more expensive over time than building a navy and using force. He advocated naval action and tried to organize a coalition of affected powers. In a July 1786 letter to Adams he wrote that he had early thought it best “to effect a peace thro’ the medium of war.” As Secretary of State under Washington he continued to argue the same line, though Congress and the weak early federal government limited options. The U.S. paid substantial tribute and ransom in the 1790s under the Washington and Adams administrations.
As President, Jefferson put his long-held preference into practice. In 1801 the pasha of Tripoli demanded more money and, when refused, declared war in the traditional manner by chopping down the flagpole at the U.S. consulate. Jefferson dispatched a naval squadron. The First Barbary War (1801–1805) followed: naval blockades, the famous raid in which Stephen Decatur burned the captured USS Philadelphia in Tripoli harbor, and a land expedition that included U.S. Marines (the origin of “to the shores of Tripoli” in the Marines’ Hymn). A 1805 treaty ended hostilities with Tripoli; it involved a ransom for American prisoners but stopped the ongoing tribute relationship with that state on the prior terms. Fighting and tribute issues with other Barbary states continued until the Second Barbary War under Madison (1815).
Jefferson’s earlier ownership of Sale’s Quran and his later encounters with the religious justification offered by the Barbary ambassador are related but distinct. He bought the book for study as a law student; the piracy crisis and the ambassador’s explicit appeal to the Quran came later. He treated the Barbary threat primarily as a practical and commercial problem of predation that required a naval response rather than continued payments, while remaining committed to religious liberty at home (including for Muslims).

text:
Joey Bart: Pirates A-to-Z

Oh boy, the day I’d been waiting patiently for is finally here! 

When I came up with the idea of writing an in-depth retrospective on every player who donned a Pirates jersey in 2026, I knew I would early on have to spend my 3am hour contemplating the late, great Joey Bart. What a lucky guy I am.

So it’s obviously opposite day at the Early Shift. If you’ve hung out here last offseason into the first half, you know that I was Bart’s biggest critic who couldn’t wait for him to be traded and leave town. So it’s only fitting that I should be made to spill ink on him as some sort of penance for my advocacy.

Revisiting the Origin Story

There was a time when Joey Bart was a great big deal.

Selected in the 27th round of the 2015 draft out of high school, he elected to go to college at Georgia Tech where he was declared by scouts the best catcher to ever come through that program. It was high praise given that catchers Jason Varitek and Matt Wieters were also products of the same school.

Bart was selected 2nd overall by the Giants in 2018 and was expected to become the next Buster Posey. He was billed as the total package -- a HR-hitting, high-OBP guy who had well above-average defensive skills. He did a quick run through the minors where he continued to hit before debuting in the COVID-shortened 2020 season. 

It didn’t go well. More time at AAA would follow where he would continually hit well -- he has an .840 OPS across ~1,200 PA in the minors -- but just couldn’t seem to get it going with the Giants. He had a .623 OPS in 162 games for San Fran across three major league seasons. Worst, his defense that was once declared the best in Georgia Tech history had all but evaporated. 

A -6 DRS in 700 innings for the Giants in 2022 with a .660 OPS, his most substantial year there, suggested the guy was just a failed prospect. Days ahead of the 2024 season, he was unceremoniously traded to the Pirates for Austin Strickland, a pitcher who hasn't gotten past A+ in multiple attempts.

Bart joined the Pirates at a time when the team’s own highly-regarded 1st round catching prospect was underperforming. Henry Davis premiered the previous season and had flopped both offensively and defensively, stuck in RF in a particular low point of the Cherington era. Bart was brought on alongside Yasmani Grandal to stabilize the catcher position, and he ended up having a breakout season.

Bart achieved a 2.2 WAR in 80 games for the Pirates in 2024, with a .265/.337/.462 line that included 13 HR. Even though his defense was still subpar, there was every expectation in 2025 that Bart was a signficiant solution at backstop. And then he put up a .699 OPS with 4 HR and a -6 DRS in 332 PA.

“Newman!”

Looking Back at 2026

I know this about myself, but I tend to be harsher on players who get my hopes up and then dash them. I was pretty high on Bart before the 2025 season, so when he underperformed, I felt tricked. Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice… you can’t get fooled again, amiright?

My smear campaign to oust Bart focused on his $2.53M contract for 2026 in his second year of arbitration. In a year where the Pirates had dramatically increased payroll and brought in a bunch of bats, Cherington had passed on free agent left-handed starters and was messing around with Jose Urquidy. Surely Bart’s salary could be better spent elsewhere.

The return from injury of Endy Rodriguez and the acquisition of Rafael Flores Jr. suggested a potential logjam at catcher. But I’d been overly optimistic about their timetables. They would spend the beginning of the year in AAA, and that meant more innings for Bart.

Unfortunately, there was little improvement for him in 2026. In 62 PA across 21 games for the Pirates, he had a .670 OPS with similar lackluster defense. With Endy up and hitting well in mid-May, the writing was on the wall. Bart was flipped in mid-June to the Braves for a familiar face, Hunter Stratton. 

Bart appeared in 20 games for Atlanta and was flipped again at the deadline to the White Sox where he went hitless in three starts before getting beaned and suffering a fifth metacarpal fracture in his left hand

It was an unceremonious end to his 2026 season. Born in Buford, GA, it had to feel good to be sent to Atlanta only to be shipped off to Chicago two months later where he promptly breaks his hand. Wah waaah.

On the Horizon -- 2027 & Beyond

Bart is a member of the Chicago White Sox, and in a typical season, he would likely miss the first month as he continues coming back from the broken hand. But more likely, he’ll be fully healed by the time the season commences sometime later in 2027.

He is entering his final year of arbitration eligibility before becoming a free agent in 2028, so it is a bit of a put-up-or-shut-up season for him. The White Sox were acquiring him as they awaited starting catcher Kyle Teel’s return from the IL. Bart will have a shot at being Teel’s backup for Chicago assuming they don’t acquire anyone else this offseason.

Bart’s .799 OPS for the Pirates in 2024 likely gets him multiple attempts to catch on (a pun!) for other teams. Catcher is a position without much depth across the sport, so a backup with HR potential who isn’t a complete brick wall behind the plate is going to continue getting opportunities.

A Final Word

The catcher position has been a big mess for the Pirates since Francisco Cervelli left town in 2019. The emergence of Flores last year was a silver lining and I have a lot of hope for Easton Carmichael and Axiel Plaz coming up from the minors. It seems 2024 was just a big ol' mirage for Bart who got the hopes up of Pirates fans desperate for offense.

Looking at Bart’s Statcast data, there’s nothing all that unique about his 2024 data. He’s always had above-average bat speed. When it’s going well, his barrel % and chase % are roughly average and that bat speed gets the job done. But there is also a healthy amount of luck and sequencing in that 2024 data, with him having improved across the board in 2025 and yet dropped 100 points of OPS.

It just goes to show what a difficult game baseball is. In the end, I have no hard feelings for Bart despite my constant, at time annoying calls to send him packing. The rollercoaster from #2 overall pick to trade deadline fodder is soul-sucking and nothing to celebrate.

There. Look at me. A Joey Bart remembrance with no profanity or schadenfreude. I’m proud of myself.

text:
Thursday morning headlines from #Georgia, 12 November

● Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze is attending the ninth European Political Community summit in Dublin. On 12 November, he is scheduled to attend the summit’s opening plenary session and a roundtable on security and defence in democratic Europe. His delegation includes Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili and Head of the Government Administration Levan Zhorzholiani.

● Speaking at the Institute of International and European Affairs in Dublin, Irakli Kobakhidze said the Georgian government was concerned about developments in Europe related to migration and ethnic or religious identity. He described what he called “negative trends” in Europe and said it was important for the continent to preserve traditional values. Kobakhidze linked Georgia’s European identity to its Christian traditions and culture, saying the country remained committed to these values.

● Metropolitan Iove (Akiashvili) of Mroveli-Urbnisi described the government as “unfaithful and unchurched” during a sermon at Urbnisi Cathedral, saying it had exhausted its capacity to govern. “We must sound the alarm. Things cannot go on like this,” he said. Earlier, Metropolitan Ilarion of Mestia and Upper Svaneti called on the government in a written statement to “stop illegal surveillance of citizens and clergy”. Ruling party MP Levan Machavariani and parliamentary Culture Committee Chairman Giorgi Gabunia dismissed the metropolitan’s remarks as unfounded, while opposition representatives welcomed his criticism. Read more here https://t.co/fZCCtPkZNA

● Parliament has approved amendments to the Election Code in the first reading, with 79 votes in favour and 10 against. Under the draft law, the Central Election Commission (CEC), rather than district commissions, would determine election results, and the deadline for doing so would be reduced from 26 to 15 days. Recounts to correct random errors would be abolished if they affected no more than five polling stations. CEC protocols could be challenged in court only under conditions specified by law. Decisions on registering election observers would be made by the CEC chairperson rather than the commission itself.

● Finance Minister Lasha Khutsishvili has presented the main parameters of the 2027 state budget to parliament. The government forecasts real economic growth of 5% in 2027, nominal GDP of 126.4 billion lari and a budget deficit of 2.5% of GDP. Pension spending will increase: people aged 70 and over will receive 555 lari (approximately $215) a month, while those under 70 will receive 415 lari (approximately $160).

● Davit Sturua, Davit Zhgenti, Konstantin Kokaia and Kakhaber Mzhavanadze, convicted in the 4 October case involving an alleged attempt to storm the presidential administration, have signed plea agreements. A first-instance court had sentenced each of them to five years in prison. Under the agreements, their sentences have been reduced to one year and two months in prison and two years of probation. They are expected to be released in December.

● A man has been arrested in Tbilisi on suspicion of murdering a married couple in a residential building. According to the Interior Ministry, he shot them with an automatic rifle as they were waiting for the lift, then fled the scene. Both died at the scene. Investigators say the murder was preceded by a property dispute, including the suspect’s failure to meet financial obligations. The offence carries a sentence of up to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment.

● Former journalist Lalo Beria, wife of Nodar Chachua, also a former journalist who was arrested on drug-related charges, has reached a plea agreement with the prosecution. She was sentenced to six months in prison, three years of probation and a fine of 3,000 lari (approximately $1,150). According to the Interior Ministry, cocaine, methadone, MDMA, alpha-PVP and ketamine were found at her home. Chachua claims his wife was arrested to put pressure on him and force him to testify against others. The ministry denies this and says it has audio and video evidence of Chachua allegedly selling drugs. Beria worked for the pro-government outlet POSTV, while Chachua worked for Georgia’s Public Broadcaster.

Illinois Election Law, Government Resources & Homeless Voter Rights at Center of Challenge

CHICAGO — November 12, 2026

Chicago Flips Red (CFR) is questioning whether Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias’s nomination papers for Chicago’s 2027 mayoral election comply with state election law.

On November 2, Zoe Marsh-Leigh filed an objection, Case No. 27-EB-MUN-014, citing 10 ILCS 5/10-7, which addresses simultaneous candidacies for incompatible public offices.

EXPERIENCED HEARING OFFICER ASSIGNED

Terence E. Flynn, an experienced Chicago electoral hearing officer, is assigned to the dispute, according to Marsh-Leigh.

Official election records document Flynn’s involvement in nomination-paper and ballot-eligibility disputes dating back to 2007, including a 2023 aldermanic eligibility case.

GOVERNMENT RESOURCES UNDER QUESTION

CFR INVESTIGATES: HOMELESSNESS SHOULD NOT INVALIDATE A REGISTERED VOTER’S PETITION SIGNATURE

CHICAGO — November 12, 2026

Chicago Flips Red (CFR) is questioning petition signature challenges involving registered voters experiencing homelessness, housing instability, or recent address changes during Chicago’s 2027 mayoral election.

As Danielle Carter-Walters faces challenges to thousands of signatures, CFR asks: Should a registered voter’s signature be invalidated because their housing circumstances changed during the 90-day petition circulation period?

ILLINOIS LAW PROTECTS HOMELESS VOTERS

Under 10 ILCS 5/3-2, Illinois recognizes voting residency rights for homeless individuals. Under 10 ILCS 5/3-1.2, a petition signer may satisfy the registration-address requirement if registered at the petition address when signing or when the petition is reviewed.

A voter could sign in August, lose housing in September, and relocate by October. A different address in November does not automatically invalidate the original signature.

CHICAGO’S HOMELESSNESS CRISIS

CPS has reported approximately 22,438 students experiencing homelessness, many with families struggling to secure stable housing.

CFR has also sought housing assistance for unhoused Chicagoan Ken Turner, who periodically sleeps in his vehicle. We have asked Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration and Housing Committee Chairman Byron Sigcho-Lopez to help locate housing for him.

CFR CALLS FOR FAIR PETITION REVIEW

Election officials should examine registration history and signing dates before rejecting signatures over address discrepancies.

Homelessness is not election fraud. Moving is not election fraud. Housing instability should not erase a legally valid signature.

North Korea’s Drone Modernisation: The Kursk Battlefield Experience and the Emerging Military Balance on the Korean Peninsula 
North Korea is acquiring the ingredients of a more capable unmanned-warfare system, but its ability to manufacture and employ that system at operational scale remains unproven.

The 29 October 2026 exhibition established Pyongyang’s political commitment to reconnaissance, one-way attack drones, armed unmanned aircraft and military artificial intelligence. It did not independently establish production rates, electronic-warfare resilience, combat reliability or the effectiveness of a newly revealed flying-wing aircraft.

The more consequential development is North Korea’s military involvement in Russia. A multinational official investigation documented the deployment of more than 11,000 North Korean troops in late 2024, including Russian instruction in unmanned aerial vehicle operations. Ukraine subsequently attributed reconnaissance and artillery-fire adjustment to North Korean drone operators in the Kursk area. msmt.info+1

A separate multinational assessment reported North Korean labour participation in military-drone manufacturing in Russia. This creates a credible route for industrial learning, although the return of specific technologies, personnel or production methods to North Korea has not been independently established. https://t.co/7I81g8UxVs

The principal risk to South Korea and United States Forces Korea is cumulative: better reconnaissance, cheaper precision attacks, improved artillery correction, greater tactical dispersion and defensive saturation—not an immediate reversal of allied air superiority.

The decisive intelligence question is whether combat experience and industrial exposure are being converted into standardised doctrine, trained personnel, sustained production and fielded formations within the Korean People’s Army.

North Korea’s Drone Revolution: How Russia Is Reshaping the Military Balance on the Korean Peninsula
North Korea’s most consequential military advance may not be the drones it displays, but its ability to turn Russian battlefield experience and industrial knowledge into a sustainable force before South Korea and the United States adapt their defences. The “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development–2026” exhibition of 29 October presented more than 30 estimated drone configurations, a new flying-wing aircraft and weapons demonstrations for which Pyongyang claimed 100% target accuracy. Yet production volumes, electronic-warfare resilience and operational availability remain unverified. Meanwhile, North Korean personnel have received Russian UAV training, supported military operations in Kursk and entered Russia’s drone-manufacturing industry. The contradiction is immediate: Pyongyang is acquiring knowledge through a functioning wartime military-industrial system, while Seoul and Washington must decide how much to invest in defending against capabilities whose actual scale remains uncertain.

The exhibition demonstrated technological ambition, not operational superiority
The 29 October 2026 exhibition marked a significant expansion in North Korea’s public presentation of unmanned aviation. Strategic reconnaissance aircraft, armed multipurpose UAVs, loitering munitions, FPV platforms and expendable attack drones appeared alongside a previously undisclosed tailless flying-wing aircraft. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un described the pursuit of “absolute superiority” in unmanned technology as a national defence priority, explicitly associating military artificial intelligence with the modernisation of conventional forces.

The accompanying demonstration included tactical attack drones, air-launched weapons, cruise missiles and the upgraded 600 mm “Sniper” multiple rocket launcher. KCNA claimed that selected weapons achieved 100% accuracy against an island target. Released imagery also showed attacks against mock military installations and equipment resembling South Korean and American systems. Yet the official account did not disclose the total number of attempted launches, aborted missions, independently measured impact errors or representative electronic-warfare conditions. The percentage therefore describes an attributed demonstration result, not a validated measure of combat reliability. Exhibition “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026” — KCNA, October 2026.

The distinction is particularly important for the new flying-wing aircraft, whose estimated wingspan of 17–20 metres and upper-surface intake suggest an interest in low-observable aviation. Its flight capability, radar signature, sensors and propulsion remain independently unverified. The established Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9, by contrast, were publicly demonstrated in July 2023, before North Korean troops entered the Russian campaign. Their existence confirms an indigenous development trajectory that Russian cooperation may accelerate but cannot retrospectively explain. Current Status of North Korea’s Drone Program — 38 North, September 2025; Soft Reveal of New North Korean Stealth Strategic UAV — 38 North, November 2026.

The numbers measure exposure and industrial ambition, not deployable combat power
The scale of Russia–North Korea cooperation is substantial, but its figures describe different populations and capabilities. The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) documented the deployment of more than 11,000 North Korean troops in late 2024, followed by an estimated 3,000 additional personnel between January and March 2025. South Korean intelligence subsequently estimated approximately 9,000 North Korean combat personnel near Kursk in September 2026. These are deployment and presence estimates for different periods, not figures that can be added to produce an operational force total. Unlawful Military Cooperation including Arms Transfers between North Korea and Russia — MSMT, May 2025; South Korean NIS Assessment — KBS World, September 2026.

The industrial figures require similar discipline. The MSMT estimated 15,000–30,000 North Korean workers across Russia at the end of 2025, employed through approximately 70–80 North Korean companies in multiple sectors. Ukrainian intelligence separately reported a plan to recruit 12,000 workers for Alabuga, while other reporting cited figures as high as 25,000. The September 2026 multinational investigation confirmed North Korean participation in Russian military-drone manufacturing but stated that actual numbers were below several public estimates. Planned recruitment cannot be treated as completed employment, and the countrywide workforce cannot be equated with drone-factory personnel. The DPRK’s Use of Overseas Labour to Violate and Evade UN Sanctions — MSMT, September 2026.

Russia’s Alabuga complex illustrates the scale of the industrial environment to which North Korean personnel have gained access. CSIS satellite analysis identified 17 facilities, up to 116 buildings and approximately 2.82 million square metres of associated infrastructure. It also reported an output estimate exceeding 5,500 drones per month. These figures concern Russian industrial capacity, not North Korean production. The critical intelligence question is how much technical knowledge employees acquire and subsequently reproduce within North Korea’s own manufacturing system. A Closer Look at the Yelabuga UAV Factory — CSIS, March 2026.

Kursk offers something more valuable than copied airframes: practical military knowledge
The qualitative significance of the Kursk deployment lies in the opportunity for North Korean personnel to operate within a battlefield where reconnaissance drones, artillery, electronic warfare and counter-drone measures interact continuously. The MSMT documented Russian instruction in UAV, artillery and infantry operations. On 5 March 2025, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service identified signs that North Korean troops were learning Russian drone tactics. On 16 October 2025, the Ukrainian General Staff reported that North Korean UAV operators were identifying Ukrainian positions around Sumy and helping adjust Russian multiple-launch rocket fire from the Kursk region. The underlying intercepted communications were not independently released, but the report described a specific operational function rather than general technical familiarisation. Seoul’s Spy Agency Detects Signs of Drone Training — Yonhap, March 2025; North Korean UAV Operators Adjust Russian Fire — Ukrainian General Staff, October 2025.

A separate account from a captured North Korean soldier offered a narrower illustration of practical adaptation. Reported in March 2025, the testimony described six Russian-supplied counter-drone jamming devices within his company and seven Russian soldiers providing liaison and operational support. The jammers reportedly became less effective as Ukrainian drone communications changed. Although the figures cannot be extrapolated beyond the unit described, the episode illustrates a problem that controlled demonstrations rarely reproduce: military technology faces an adversary capable of continuously altering its methods. North Korean POW Describes Counter-Drone Operations — Yonhap, March 2025.

The potential result is not necessarily an immediate breakthrough in aircraft technology. It is greater familiarity with the organisational requirements of drone-supported warfare: reliable observation, useful communication with conventional units, recognition of equipment limitations and recurring adaptation. Russian unmanned-systems specialist Samuel Bendett has examined how the Russia–Ukraine conflict has driven continuous changes in drone employment and development. Exposure to that environment may shorten North Korea’s learning process, but neither battlefield participation nor foreign instruction proves that those lessons have been institutionalised throughout the Korean People’s Army. UAV/Drone Dimension of the War in Ukraine — Samuel Bendett, Oxford University Press, 2026.

Alabuga creates an industrial transmission channel, but not a turnkey North Korean drone industry
North Korean participation in Russia’s drone factories adds a manufacturing dimension to the military relationship. Alabuga produces Iranian-derived Shahed/Geran-family attack drones within a Russian industrial system involving foreign components, domestic adaptation and substantial production infrastructure. Participation in that environment could expose North Korean workers to assembly procedures, quality-control practices and the demands of serial manufacturing. Yet the technical benefit depends on actual job assignments and access to engineering knowledge. A worker performing repetitive assembly does not automatically acquire the ability to reproduce propulsion, guidance software or complete production lines. Human Rights Abuses in Drone Production at Yelabuga — CSIS and George W. Bush Institute, October 2026.

The strongest evidence of technical feedback between Moscow and Pyongyang concerns ballistic missiles, not UAVs. The May 2025 MSMT investigation reported Russian feedback that contributed to improvements in North Korean missile guidance. It also documented transfers of electronic-warfare and air-defence equipment, including at least one Pantsir-class vehicle. These findings demonstrate that military-technical cooperation extends beyond arms purchases and troop deployment. They do not establish that Russia has transferred complete Lancet or Geran designs, advanced autonomous targeting software or fibre-optic drone-control technology to North Korea. Unlawful Military Cooperation including Arms Transfers between North Korea and Russia — MSMT, May 2025.

The industrial consequence is conditional. North Korea already operates domestic UAV development facilities, including the expanded infrastructure around Panghyon Airbase. Russian manufacturing experience could improve production organisation and consistency if technically qualified personnel return to relevant institutions and the necessary equipment and components are available. But expanded facilities and access to foreign expertise cannot by themselves establish sustainable output. The manufacturing challenge is converting designs into repeatable, maintainable products without assuming that North Korea can reproduce the industrial conditions available inside Russia. North Korean Strategic UAV Activity at Panghyon Airbase — CSIS, April 2025.

Sanctions restrict the relationship without eliminating the channels of cooperation
The Russian–North Korean relationship also operates within a legal framework that complicates industrial and military cooperation. The MSMT assessed relevant arms transfers, military training and technical assistance against UN Security Council Resolutions 1718 (2006), 1874 (2009) and 2270 (2016), while its September 2026 labour investigation examined overseas employment arrangements under Resolutions 2375 (2017) and 2397 (2017). The latter investigation identified visa practices, recruitment intermediaries and employment structures that could conceal the nature of North Korean labour in Russia. MSMT Military Cooperation Report — May 2025; MSMT Overseas Labour Report — September 2026.

The consequence is a persistent verification problem. Formal restrictions do not prevent every prohibited transaction, while opaque employment arrangements make it harder to determine where personnel work and which technologies they encounter. Enforcement authorities must distinguish financial and labour violations already documented from alleged technology transfers that remain unverified. For defence planners, the same distinction prevents a misleading inference: sanctions evasion establishes prohibited cooperation, but not the operational maturity of every weapon that cooperation might eventually support.

Seoul has reorganised command, but procurement and readiness remain separate tests
South Korea has begun a substantial institutional response. In June 2026, its Ministry of National Defense announced plans to acquire more than 20,000 expendable drones and train approximately 500,000 operators. On 1 November 2026, the government established the Defence Drone Headquarters, redistributing operational drone units to the military services while concentrating development, certification, standardisation and procurement coordination in the new organisation. The Ministry of National Defense stated that the proportion of field-grade officers in the headquarters would rise from less than 20% to more than 50%. These are consequential organisational decisions, but announced acquisitions and training targets are not completed capabilities. Military to Make Drones Standard Equipment — Republic of Korea Government, June 2026; Establishment of the Defence Drone Headquarters — Ministry of National Defense, November 2026.

The United States and South Korea are also testing defensive integration. During Freedom Shield 26 in March, US Air Force security personnel and Army air-defence units rehearsed combined counter-UAV procedures at Osan. In August 2026, Exercise Dragon Flight used a Group 3 unmanned aircraft to examine detection, reporting and defensive coordination involving US and South Korean personnel. The exercises demonstrate institutional adaptation, not comprehensive protection against the entire North Korean drone portfolio. They also expose the procurement dilemma: defending major installations requires suitable detection, identification, communications, interception and continuity arrangements, rather than simply purchasing more interceptors. USAF and Army Integrate Air Defence During Freedom Shield 26 — 51st Fighter Wing, March 2026; Dragon Flight Marks Osan’s First Group 3 UAS Defence Exercise — 51st Fighter Wing, August 2026.

The wider alliance has an additional coordination requirement. Freedom Edge 26, concluded on 11 September 2026, brought Japan, South Korea and the United States together for exercises involving air defence and information sharing. But a regional framework capable of addressing ballistic missiles and advanced aircraft does not automatically provide adequate local protection against small drones. South Korea faces the immediate defence of densely populated areas and forward installations; United States Forces Korea must preserve operational continuity at deployed bases; Japan has distinct territorial and regional security responsibilities. Cooperation reduces fragmentation only when national systems and procedures can function together. Freedom Edge 26 Concludes — US Indo-Pacific Command, September 2026.

The next 12–24 months will determine who absorbs the cost of adaptation
Between November 2026 and November 2028, the decisive development will be whether North Korea moves beyond exhibitions into recurring production, permanent unit assignments, standardised operator training and sustained drone employment. The most credible near-term change is not a fleet of operational stealth aircraft, but the wider integration of smaller unmanned systems with existing conventional forces. That development could impose additional requirements on South Korean and American installation protection, surveillance and logistics without overturning allied advantages in advanced aviation.

The immediate costs of preparing for that possibility will fall on South Korea’s defence procurement and training system, United States Forces Korea and the military organisations responsible for protecting critical installations. More expansive counter-drone coverage requires equipment, qualified personnel, maintenance and recurring exercises. A defensive response based on the apparent sophistication of North Korea’s exhibition platforms risks misallocating resources; one that ignores the potential scale of simpler systems risks leaving installations inadequately prepared. Both errors impose costs on military budgets, while failures of protection could disrupt civilian aviation and essential infrastructure, as the five-drone incursion of 26 December 2022 demonstrated. Five North Korean Drones Cross the Inter-Korean Border — Yonhap, December 2022.

The political cost will fall on the governments responsible for reconciling military readiness with procurement discipline and alliance coordination. Pyongyang has already demonstrated political commitment, access to Russian training and participation in a major military-drone manufacturing environment. It has not demonstrated that these advantages amount to a fully institutionalised operational capability. The military balance will be affected not by how many drones North Korea can exhibit, but by how reliably it can manufacture, deploy and employ them—and how efficiently Seoul and Washington can protect their forces without allowing defensive costs to expand faster than the threat itself.

🎵 Music ⋆ 📺 Television ⋆ 🎬 Film & Animation ⋆ 📚 Publishing & Literature ⋆ 🎭 Theatre ⋆ 📻 Radio ⋆ 🎮 Games & Other Cultural Firsts

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Every author, as far as he is great and at the same time original, has had the task of creating the taste by which he is to be enjoyed.” — William Wordsworth, Essay, Supplementary to the Preface, 1815.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎭 THE CURTAIN RISES. THE CLOCK TURNS BACK. THE MAGIC BEGINS!

“The beauty of art is that you can see a great painting… and it’s about whatever the hell you think it’s about.” — Tom Petty, interview with The Petty Archives (1995)

November 12 brings together artists, storytellers, performers, and inventors who found ways to make familiar forms feel new.

A pop superstar releases the album that turns her into a household name, while a rock original and a composer-scientist celebrate birthdays. On television, a sharp-tongued British comedy makes its first appearance, and a new streaming platform changes how audiences find entertainment.

Cinema offers two very different journeys: a screwball heroine challenges small-town respectability, while a Disney production premieres in Atlanta and leaves behind a complicated cultural legacy. Agatha Christie sends Miss Marple into another deadly mystery, Broadway checks into a grand Berlin hotel, and an arcade full of hostile robots begins talking back to its players.

Different decades. Different creative instincts. One date that reminds us culture never stands still.

THE PAST IS CALLING. THE MEMORIES ARE ALIVE. LET US RELIVE THE MAGIC! ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎵 MUSIC

1984 — Madonna Releases Like a Virgin 💿

On November 12, 1984, Madonna released Like a Virgin, her second studio album and the record that transformed her from a rising pop performer into one of the defining stars of the decade.

Produced by Nile Rodgers of Chic, the album blended dance-pop, post-disco, and polished pop hooks into a sound built for radio, clubs, and the emerging MTV generation. Its nine tracks included “Material Girl,” “Angel,” “Dress You Up,” and the title song, which became Madonna’s first U.S. No. 1 single.

The album spent three weeks at the top of the Billboard 200 and produced four U.S. Top Five singles. Its commercial success was matched by a bold visual identity: Madonna’s fashion, videos, and performances became inseparable from the music itself.

Like a Virgin did more than deliver a run of hit singles. It helped establish the idea of the pop star as a complete cultural force—artist, performer, image-maker, and provocateur.

🧩 TRIVIA: The title track spent six weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, while the album itself topped the Billboard 200 for three weeks.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A breakthrough album can make a star—but a distinctive creative identity can make that star unforgettable.

───────────────

1976 — Queen Releases “Somebody to Love” in the United Kingdom 🎤

On November 12, 1976, Queen released “Somebody to Love” as a single in the United Kingdom, introducing one of Freddie Mercury’s most ambitious vocal performances to a wider audience.

Written by Mercury for A Day at the Races, the song used a gospel-inspired arrangement. Mercury, Brian May, and Roger Taylor layered their voices to create the impression of a much larger choir, while the piano-led composition moved from intimate pleading to a soaring chorus.

It reached No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart. Its emotional power came from the contrast between gospel language and the personal loneliness at the heart of the lyrics.

🧩 TRIVIA: Freddie Mercury’s model for the song was Aretha Franklin. He admired her gospel recordings and wanted to capture something of that approach in Queen’s music.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes the biggest sound comes from a small group willing to build something extraordinary together.

───────────────

1945 — Neil Young Is Born in Toronto 🎸

On November 12, 1945, Neil Young was born in Toronto, Ontario. He would become one of the most distinctive singer-songwriters and guitarists in modern popular music, moving between folk, country, hard rock, and experimental sounds with a restless independence.

Young first gained major attention with Buffalo Springfield, whose songs included “For What It’s Worth.” He later joined David Crosby, Stephen Stills, and Graham Nash in Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, while building a major solo career with albums such as After the Gold Rush, Harvest, and Rust Never Sleeps.

His music moves freely between acoustic folk, country, hard rock, and experimental sounds, often alongside Crazy Horse.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before heading to California and joining Buffalo Springfield, Young briefly played in the Mynah Birds, a Toronto group that also included a young Rick James.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: An artist’s most recognizable sound can come from refusing to settle on just one.

───────────────

1833 — Alexander Borodin Is Born in St. Petersburg 🎼

On November 12, 1833, Alexander Borodin was born in St. Petersburg, Russia. He would become a major figure in Russian Romantic music, known for his richly melodic compositions and for helping shape a distinctly Russian national style.

Borodin was also a physician and research chemist, earning a doctorate and teaching at the Imperial Medical-Surgical Academy. He joined The Five, a group of composers seeking a musical style rooted in Russian history and traditions.

His best-known works include the opera Prince Igor, his symphonies, and In the Steppes of Central Asia. The “Polovtsian Dances” from Prince Igor later found a new life in the Broadway musical Kismet.

🌀 OBSCURE: Borodin never completed Prince Igor. After his death, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Glazunov assembled and orchestrated the surviving material so the opera could reach the stage.

🐶 SPOT: His work for women’s education extended beyond music: Borodin helped establish medical courses for women in St. Petersburg.

🧩 TRIVIA: Borodin first became fascinated by music at eight, after hearing an army band performance. He was able to reproduce what he had heard on the piano.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Creativity does not always follow one profession, one schedule, or one set of expectations.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📺 TELEVISION

1992 — Absolutely Fabulous Makes Its BBC Debut 🍸

On November 12, 1992, BBC Two broadcast “Fashion,” the first episode of Absolutely Fabulous, the comedy created by and starring Jennifer Saunders.

Saunders played Edina Monsoon, a flamboyant public-relations executive determined to remain fashionable, youthful, and socially relevant. Her closest companion was Patsy Stone, played by Joanna Lumley, a fashion-magazine editor whose appetite for excess matched Edina’s own. Edina’s teenage daughter Saffron, played by Julia Sawalha, was left to provide the exhausted voice of reason.

The series turned fashion, celebrity culture, consumerism, and self-absorption into a comic playground, becoming one of Britain’s most recognizable television comedies.

🌀 OBSCURE: The characters began life in a sketch on Jennifer Saunders and Dawn French’s comedy series French and Saunders. Saunders developed the idea into a full sitcom, giving Edina and Patsy a world of their own.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first episode, “Fashion,” revolves around Edina’s attempt to stage a successful fashion show while battling a hangover and trying to secure an impressive guest list.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The best satire does not need to invent ridiculous people. It simply turns up the volume on the ones already around us.

───────────────

2019 — Disney+ Launches a New Streaming Era 🌌

On November 12, 2019, The Walt Disney Company launched Disney+ in the United States, Canada, and the Netherlands, bringing a vast collection of film and television entertainment together on a subscription streaming platform.

The service launched with nearly 500 films and 7,500 television episodes from Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, and National Geographic, alongside original programming including The Mandalorian, the first live-action Star Wars series.

Created by Jon Favreau, the series follows a lone bounty hunter operating beyond the reach of the central galactic authorities. Its day-one premiere helped make it one of Disney+’s signature early attractions.

The launch marked a major industry shift: studios were building direct relationships with viewers through their own streaming platforms.

🧩 TRIVIA: At launch, Disney+ allowed subscribers to stream on up to four devices simultaneously.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A new way of delivering stories can change not only where audiences watch, but how the entertainment business itself works.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎬 FILM & ANIMATION

1936 — Theodora Goes Wild Arrives in Theatres 🎬

On November 12, 1936, Columbia Pictures released Theodora Goes Wild, a screwball comedy starring Irene Dunne and Melvyn Douglas.

Dunne plays Theodora Lynn, a seemingly respectable young woman in a small Connecticut town who is secretly the author of a scandalous bestseller published under a pseudonym. When her identity becomes entangled with the town’s moral guardians and a sophisticated New York publisher, Theodora begins to challenge the narrow expectations that have governed her life.

Directed by Richard Boleslawski and written by Sidney Buchman, the film turns small-town propriety and personal freedom into a comedy of secrets, romance, and social embarrassment.

Dunne earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress. The film is regarded as an early example of the screwball comedy style that flourished in 1930s Hollywood.

🌀 OBSCURE: The Production Code Administration initially rejected the screenplay. Its objections included the film’s portrayal of respectable churchgoing citizens as ridiculous and its suggestion that the heroine’s supposedly scandalous behavior could be attractive. A revised script eventually received approval.

🐶 SPOT: Dunne was reportedly reluctant to make a comedy, but Columbia insisted this film fulfill the first picture in her new contract.

🧩 TRIVIA: The film received two Academy Award nominations: Best Actress for Irene Dunne and Best Film Editing for Otto Meyer.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Comedy can be a remarkably effective weapon against the rules that society insists nobody should question.

───────────────

1946 — Song of the South Premieres in Atlanta 🐇

On November 12, 1946, Walt Disney’s Song of the South premiered in Atlanta, Georgia.

The film combined live-action performances with animated sequences inspired by Joel Chandler Harris’s Uncle Remus stories. It followed a young boy who encounters Uncle Remus, whose tales of Br’er Rabbit, Br’er Fox, and Br’er Bear become a central part of the film’s storytelling.

Directed by Harve Foster, with animation sequences directed by Wilfred Jackson, the production combined live actors and animated characters.

Its song “Zip-A-Dee-Doo-Dah” won the Academy Award for Best Original Song. Yet the film’s romanticized depiction of the post-Civil War South and its treatment of race and African-American life have been widely criticized, leaving it a deeply contested part of Disney history.

🧬 HUMAN ANGLE: Baskett, who gave the film its central live-action performance, was not allowed to attend its Atlanta premiere. Segregation laws barred him and the film’s other Black cast members from the festivities—a bitter contradiction for a production celebrating his work.

🐶 SPOT: Song of the South has never received an official U.S. home-video release. Its absence from the American home-video market is part of the film’s unusual and contested place in Disney history.

🧩 TRIVIA: James Baskett, who portrayed Uncle Remus, received an honorary Academy Award in 1948 for his performance. It was the first Academy Award received by an African-American actor.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Cultural history is not always comfortable. Preserving it honestly means recognizing both artistic achievement and the harm embedded in the stories a society once accepted.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

📚 PUBLISHING & LITERATURE

1815 — Elizabeth Cady Stanton Is Born in New York ✍️

On November 12, 1815, Elizabeth Cady Stanton was born in Johnstown, New York. She would become one of the central intellectual leaders of the nineteenth-century woman’s rights movement, helping to define the arguments that shaped the struggle for women’s equality and suffrage.

Stanton helped organize the 1848 Woman’s Rights Convention at Seneca Falls and co-authored its Declaration of Sentiments, a document modeled on the Declaration of Independence that demanded equal rights for women, including the right to vote.

Her partnership with Susan B. Anthony became one of the most influential collaborations in American reform history.

A forceful writer and speaker, Stanton challenged legal restrictions, social expectations, and religious arguments used to justify women’s subordination. Her work helped establish the language and political framework that later generations of activists would carry forward.

🧬 HUMAN ANGLE: Stanton later recalled her father’s grief after her brother died. He turned to her and said, “Oh, my daughter, I wish you were a boy!”—a painful reminder of the unequal expectations placed on girls.

🧩 TRIVIA: In 1869, Stanton helped found the National Woman Suffrage Association and became its first president.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Lasting movements are often built first by people willing to put an uncomfortable truth into words.

───────────────

1962 — Agatha Christie Publishes The Mirror Crack'd from Side to Side 🔍

On November 12, 1962, Agatha Christie’s novel The Mirror Crack'd from Side to Side was published in the United Kingdom by Collins Crime Club.

The story brings Miss Marple into a mystery involving a glamorous American film star, Marina Gregg, who has moved into the English village of St. Mary Mead. At a village gathering, Heather Badcock suddenly suffers a fatal seizure after meeting the actress. The apparent victim may not have been the intended target, and Miss Marple begins examining the motives and hidden histories behind the tragedy.

The novel uses Hollywood glamour entering a traditional English village to explore celebrity, envy, memory, and hidden emotional wounds. It was adapted for film in 1980, with Angela Lansbury as Miss Marple and Elizabeth Taylor as Marina Gregg.

🐶 SPOT: Christie admired Rutherford’s acting but believed her screen portrayal was not particularly close to the Miss Marple she had created.

🧩 TRIVIA: Christie dedicated the novel to actress Margaret Rutherford, who had portrayed Miss Marple in four films beginning with Murder, She Said in 1961.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A great mystery is not only about discovering who committed the crime. It is about understanding the human secrets that made it possible.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎭 THEATRE

1989 — Grand Hotel Opens on Broadway 🛎️

On November 12, 1989, the musical Grand Hotel opened at the Martin Beck Theatre in New York.

Set in Berlin in 1928, the production follows an interconnected collection of guests and employees whose lives briefly cross inside a luxurious hotel. Among them are a terminally ill bookkeeper seeking one last taste of life, a fading ballerina, a desperate businessman, a young typist, and a charming but financially troubled baron.

With a book by Luther Davis and music and lyrics by Robert Wright and George Forrest, the musical adapted Vicki Baum’s novel and drew on the atmosphere of the 1932 film.

Directed and choreographed by Tommy Tune, it used a large ensemble and fluid staging to make the hotel feel like a living world. Grand Hotel ran for more than two years.

🌀 OBSCURE: The show did not remain in one Broadway home for its entire run. It began at the Martin Beck Theatre and transferred to the Gershwin Theatre in February 1992.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Broadway production played 1,017 performances before closing on April 25, 1992.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes the most compelling stories happen when strangers briefly share the same space—and then return to lives that will never be quite the same.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🎮 GAMES & OTHER CULTURAL FIRSTS

1980 — Berzerk Brings Talking Robots to the Arcade 🤖

On November 12, 1980, Stern Electronics released Berzerk in North American arcades, introducing players to a maze filled with armed robots, electrified walls, and an increasingly relentless enemy.

Designed by Alan McNeil, the game placed players in maze-like rooms where they had to survive robotic attacks and find an exit. The greatest threat was Evil Otto, an indestructible bouncing smiley face that could pass through walls.

Berzerk stood out for its synthesized speech: the robots taunted players, turning the arcade cabinet into a talkative opponent. Its action, maze navigation, and electronic voices made it a memorable early arcade game.

🌀 OBSCURE: Berzerk’s speech was generated through a dedicated speech-synthesis system using encoded language data—not simply by playing back ordinary recorded voice clips. At a time when electronic speech was expensive and technically demanding, the talking robots became one of the game’s defining features.

🧩 TRIVIA: The robots could shout “Chicken! Fight like a robot!” when a player escaped a room without destroying every enemy.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A small technological leap can give an entertainment experience a personality audiences remember for decades.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

AND WHAT A SHOW IT HAS BEEN! 🎭

November 12 has taken us from the dance floors of the 1980s to nineteenth-century Russia, from sharp British television comedy to the talking robots of an arcade machine.

Madonna released the album that helped establish her as a defining pop-culture figure, while Queen brought gospel-inspired grandeur to “Somebody to Love.” Neil Young and Alexander Borodin remind us that musical identity can take many forms—and sometimes share space with other pursuits.

Television welcomed Edina and Patsy, while Disney+ opened a new chapter in how audiences access entertainment. Cinema gave us Irene Dunne’s rebellious heroine and a Disney premiere whose history cannot be separated from the racial controversy surrounding its storytelling.

Agatha Christie delivered another mystery, Broadway checked into Grand Hotel, and Berzerk gave arcade players something unexpected: robots with voices and very poor attitudes.

Some creations entertain. Others challenge conventions. A few change the business around them. The most interesting milestones often do all three.

DIFFERENT VOICES. DIFFERENT WORLDS. ONE ENDLESS STORY: CULTURE NEVER STOPS EVOLVING. ✨

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🍬 CANDY

November 13, 2015.

A hugely successful musical partnership entered unfamiliar territory. The voices were still there, the spotlight was still bright, but something had changed—and the next chapter would prove to be more consequential than anyone might have expected.

What happened when a global phenomenon had to find its footing in a new configuration? And what made this release such an important turning point?

Ankara prosecutors investigate alleged Turkey links in Epstein case: report
By SCF -February 3, 2026
 Share

The Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office has opened a new investigation into claims of Turkey links in the Jeffrey Epstein case after a Turkish opposition lawmaker said US records included allegations that girls from Turkey were taken to Epstein’s island, Turkish Minute reported, citing Deutsche Welle’s Turkish service.

The prosecutors launched the probe on December 23, following an X post a day earlier by Turhan Çömez, deputy parliamentary group chair of the nationalist opposition İYİ (Good) Party, who claimed documents released by the US Department of Justice said girls from Turkey were taken to the island and faced difficulties because they did not speak English.

Sources cited by DW said the prosecutor’s office is reviewing Turkey-related sections in millions of documents released by the Justice Department and is looking for evidence of suspects and possible Turkey-based links.

The new inquiry follows an earlier complaint filed on January 16, 2024, by a Turkish nonprofit that focuses on children and women. The group asked prosecutors to examine claims that Epstein’s network had connections in Turkey and that children from Turkey may have been drawn into exploitation.

Over that complaint, prosecutors issued a decision of non-prosecution on June 16, 2025, saying the file contained no evidence that the alleged crimes were committed in Turkey.

As part of that earlier inquiry, the prosecutor’s office heard testimony from one person, a woman identified as Banu K., who lives in the US and was named in the complaint. She said she had no connection to the Epstein case and that she was not the Banu K. referenced in the Epstein documents, adding that she lived in California, not Florida, and submitted a court decision from the US District Court for the Southern District of New York to corroborate her claims.

The nonprofit’s lawyer, Hediye Gökçe Baykal, told DW that new evidence has emerged through the Justice Department’s latest releases and that the group will appeal the June 2025 non-prosecution decision and seek a broader investigation.

Baykal said the earlier probe appeared to be limited to the single name mentioned in the complaint and did not include steps prosecutors could take on their own to identify other potential suspects. She said effective investigations into human trafficking and child sexual exploitation often require broader steps because perpetrators may operate through organized structures and links can surface only through deeper inquiries. Baykal also cited Turkey’s obligations under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, saying authorities should act even when there is serious suspicion, not only after evidence is finalized.

The renewed focus in Turkey comes after the Justice Department released new Epstein records on January 30 under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, publishing more than 3 million pages of investigative records, 180,000 images and more than 2,000 videos compiled by federal and state law enforcement agencies. The department said the files are heavily redacted to protect victims’ privacy and do not include new indictments or criminal charges and warned that some documents may not be electronically searchable because they are embedded in non-indexed PDF files.

Main opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP) lawmaker Sevda Erdan Kılıç submitted a parliamentary motion in January 2024 to inquire into Turkey-related revelations in the Epstein case. Kılıç said the disclosures underscored the need for Turkey to examine potential domestic connections.

Parliament has yet to debate the proposal.

“The Epstein file is not only America’s file, it is the file of an international darkness,” Kılıç said in a statement on social media. “And yes, this darkness has links extending to Turkey.”

The latest release revived debate over whether Epstein’s network trafficked minors from Turkey, particularly children who went missing after earthquakes in 1999 in northwestern Turkey that killed more than 17,000 people.

On Tuesday, Turkey’s Center for Combating Disinformation (DMM) said claims circulating on social media that “more than 10,000” children go missing each year in Turkey and that nearly 100,000 have gone missing over eight years are false and based on official data taken out of context. The center said the statistics cited refer to children for whom an official missing-person report was filed and who were later found and that no official data are published under a category of “missing and not found” children.

CEO of pro-government holding in the files
Ahmet Mücahit Ören, chief executive officer of the pro-government İhlas Holding, appeared in a 2004 email exchange with Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s longtime associate.

“I need to learn more from you to be more ‘naughty,’” Ören wrote in an email to Maxwell as part of an exchange seeking business networking assistance involving British entrepreneur Richard Branson.

Ören denied wrongdoing in a statement on X, saying he read the claims “with laughter and astonishment,” adding, “Anyone who has knowledge of the English language understands what that email was written for.”

Robert College email shows 2014 fundraising request
The disclosures also include a November 7, 2014, email sent by Landon C. Thomas Jr., then a New York Times journalist and a member of Robert College’s American Board of Trustees, seeking advice from Epstein on fundraising for the İstanbul-based school, according to media reports.

In his emails to Epstein, Thomas described the school’s mission and Turkey’s political climate at the time, with Epstein responding briefly and suggesting a future meeting.

In a statement on Sunday Robert College said it learned of the email with the latest release and said Thomas “was not, and has never been, an administrator or employee” of the institution, while acknowledging his board membership at the time of the correspondence.

“The personal views expressed in the letter do not reflect the views of Robert College or its Board of Trustees,” the statement said. The school added that it did not accept donations from Epstein or from anyone connected to him.

Thomas left The New York Times in 2019 following ethics concerns related to his social connections with Epstein and also departed from the Robert College board that year.

Rixos responds to spa training emails
According to the released emails, Lesley Groff, who served as Epstein’s assistant, and managers at Rixos Antalya’s The Land of Legends spa facility discussed arranging a short-term training program for a woman described as working at “Jeffrey Epstein’s private spa as a personal masseuse.”

One email sent to Rixos Antalya’s owner Fettah Tamince by Dubai-based businessman Sultan Bin Sulayem said, “Dear Fettah, attached is a copy of her passport. She works at our friend Jeffrey Epstein’s private spa as a personal masseuse. It would be appreciated if you could arrange for her internship at Rixos Antalya Spa to gain better experience.”

Replies from a Rixos staff member outlined a 10-day training program at The Land of Legends Spa and requested passport copies and travel details.

Rixos Hotels said in a statement on Monday that the matter involved “a limited information-sharing support provided within the scope of professional training, upon the request of an international group.”

The company said the process complied with ethical and legal standards and that social media posts circulating on the issue were taken out of context. It described such professional training arrangements as routine in the international tourism sector.

Convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died in a New York jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges, ending the criminal case against him but not the investigations and civil litigation that followed. His former associate Ghislaine Maxwell was later convicted in US federal court for helping recruit and abuse underage girls and is serving a prison sentence.

The renewed global attention in recent days, triggered by the new dump, also produced immediate political and institutional aftershocks in Europe.

In Slovakia, foreign policy adviser Miroslav Lajčák resigned after he was linked in the newly released materials to discussions about a 2018 trip involving Epstein. In Norway, Crown Princess Mette-Marit issued a public apology over her past interactions with Epstein as Norwegian media reported new details from the release. In Britain, the Metropolitan Police Service said it is reviewing multiple reports of alleged misconduct in public office after the latest US release prompted new scrutiny over contacts between Epstein and former minister and diplomat Peter Mandelson.

In Sweden, Joanna Rubinstein stepped down as chair of Sweden for UNHCR after reports based on the new materials said she and her family visited Epstein in 2012 and later emailed him thanking him for his hospitality.

The new documents increase scrutiny of how Epstein built access to political and business circles, with many claims suggesting that the financier was an intelligence operative running a “honeytrap” operation to blackmail individuals in the higher echelons.
